mlmaths:01.01.q: A spam filter has a label (spam or not), a word count, a predicted spam probability from a sigmoid, and 5,000 weights. Name the set each one lives in.
mlmaths:01.01.s: Step 1, the label has two possible values, so it lives in {0,1}. Step 2, a word count is a whole number that cannot be negative, so it lives in ℕ. Step 3, a probability lies between 0 and 1. A sigmoid never outputs exactly 0 or 1 in exact maths, so the output lives in the open interval (0,1), which sits inside [0,1]. Step 4, each weight is a real number and there are 5,000 of them, so the weight vector lives in ℝ5000.
mlmaths:01.01.t: Special Sets and the Number-System Ladder

mlmaths:01.02.q: A tokenizer maps 50,000 strings to ids. Is the vocabulary equal to {0,…,49999}, equivalent to it, or neither? Why does the answer matter for a model?
mlmaths:01.02.s: Step 1, equal would mean the same elements. The vocabulary contains strings like "cat" and the other set contains numbers, so they are not equal. Step 2, equivalent means a one-to-one pairing with nothing left over. The tokenizer's lookup table gives each string exactly one id and each id exactly one string, so it is a bijection, and the sets are equivalent. Step 3, why it matters: the model can work entirely with ids (numbers that index rows of an embedding table) and the bijection lets you translate back to text without losing anything.

mlmaths:01.03.q: The labels in a batch are (2,0,2,1,0,2). Write the set of labels that appear, its size, and say whether {0,1}⊆ it.
mlmaths:01.03.s: Step 1, collect the distinct values: 2, 0 and 1. As a set, {0,1,2}; order and repeats are dropped. Step 2, its size is ∣{0,1,2}∣=3. Step 3, every element of {0,1} (that is, 0 and 1) is in {0,1,2}, so yes, {0,1}⊆{0,1,2}. In code: set(labels) gives the set and len(...) its size.

mlmaths:01.04.q: Ages are (15,22,37,64,70). Describe the working-age set (18 or over, under 65) by a membership condition, list it, and write the NumPy line.
mlmaths:01.04.s: Step 1, the condition has two parts joined by "and": a≥18 and a<65. Step 2, test each age: 15 fails the first part, 22, 37 and 64 pass both, 70 fails the second. Step 3, the set is {22,37,64}. Step 4, in NumPy: ages[(ages >= 18) & (ages < 65)], with brackets around each comparison because & binds tighter than >=.

mlmaths:01.05.q: Write in set-builder notation, then in Python: (a) the hard negatives, items j other than the positive p=0 with score sj>0.5, for s=(0.9,0.3,0.7,0.6,0.1); (b) all pairs of indices i<j from {0,1,2,3}. Give each result.
mlmaths:01.05.s: (a) Step 1, where to look: indices {0,…,4}. Step 2, the test: j≠p and sj>0.5. So the set is {j∈{0,…,4}:j≠0, sj>0.5}. Step 3, check: index 0 is the positive, 2 and 3 have scores 0.7 and 0.6, so the result is {2,3}. Python: [j for j in range(5) if j != 0 and s[j] > 0.5]. (b) The set is {(i,j):0≤i<j≤3}. Listing: (0,1), (0,2), (0,3), (1,2), (1,3), (2,3), six pairs, which is (42)=6. Python: [(i, j) for i in range(4) for j in range(4) if i < j].

mlmaths:01.06.q: Which of the points (0,0.5), (1,1), (−0.6,0.6) and (0,−1) are in {(x,y):x2+y2≤1}, and which are in {(x,y):y≥2x+1}?
mlmaths:01.06.s: Step 1, the disc test is x2+y2≤1. (0,0.5): 0.25, in. (1,1): 2, out. (−0.6,0.6): 0.72, in. (0,−1): 1, in (on the edge, and the ≤ includes it). Step 2, the half-plane test is y≥2x+1. (0,0.5): 0.5≥1? No. (1,1): 1≥3? No. (−0.6,0.6): 0.6≥−0.2? Yes. (0,−1): −1≥1? No. So only (−0.6,0.6) is in the half-plane.

mlmaths:01.07.q: Predictions y^=(1,0,2,2,1) and labels y=(1,2,2,0,1). Write accuracy with indicators and compute it. Then write the number of class-2 examples predicted correctly as a sum of products of indicators.
mlmaths:01.07.s: Step 1, the indicators 𝟏[y^i=yi] are (1,0,1,0,1). Step 2, accuracy is their average: 15(1+0+1+0+1)=0.6. Step 3, "label is 2 and prediction is right" is an "and" of two conditions, so multiply indicators: ∑i𝟏[yi=2]⋅𝟏[y^i=yi]. Step 4, 𝟏[yi=2] is (0,1,1,0,0); the products are (0,0,1,0,0), so the answer is 1.

mlmaths:01.08.q: A batch has sentences of lengths 3 and 5, padded to length 5. Per-token losses are 1 everywhere. Write the mask, the correct mean loss, and the mean you would get by dividing by all 10 positions if padded positions had loss 0.
mlmaths:01.08.s: Step 1, the mask is mit=𝟏[t<leni]: (1,1,1,0,0) and (1,1,1,1,1). Step 2, the number of real tokens is ∑mit=8. Step 3, the correct mean is ∑mitℓit/∑mit=8/8=1. Step 4, dividing by 10 with zeros at the padding gives 8/10=0.8: too low, because padding is being treated as perfectly predicted text.

mlmaths:01.09.q: Training ids are {10,11,12,13,14} and test ids are {13,14,15}. Compute the union and intersection, say what the intersection means, and give the cleaned test set.
mlmaths:01.09.s: Step 1, union: everything in either, {10,11,12,13,14,15}. Step 2, intersection: what is in both, {13,14}. Step 3, a non-empty intersection means examples 13 and 14 were seen in training, so the test score would be too optimistic (leakage). Step 4, remove them: the cleaned test set is {15}, which is the test set minus the training set.

mlmaths:01.10.q: With U={1,…,8}, A={1,2,3,4}, B={3,4,5,6}, compute A∖B, B∖A, Ac, and check (A∪B)c=Ac∩Bc.
mlmaths:01.10.s: Step 1, A∖B keeps elements of A not in B: {1,2}. Step 2, B∖A={5,6}, so difference depends on order. Step 3, Ac=U∖A={5,6,7,8}. Step 4, A∪B={1,…,6}, so (A∪B)c={7,8}. Step 5, Bc={1,2,7,8}, so Ac∩Bc={7,8}. The two sides match.
mlmaths:01.10.t: Difference, Complement and De Morgan's Laws

mlmaths:01.11.q: You grid-search learning rate in {10−4,3⋅10−4,10−3}, batch size in {32,64,128,256} and weight decay in {0,0.01}. Write the search space, its size, and say how random search over the same ranges differs.
mlmaths:01.11.s: Step 1, every combination of one value from each list is a Cartesian product: {10−4,3⋅10−4,10−3}×{32,64,128,256}×{0,0.01}. Step 2, sizes multiply: 3×4×2=24 runs. Step 3, random search draws 24 random points from ranges (learning rate on a log scale in [10−5,10−2], and so on). It then tries 24 different learning rates instead of 3. Since the learning rate usually matters most, random search usually finds a better one for the same cost.

mlmaths:01.12.q: How many grid points does a 10-per-axis grid on [0,1]d need for d=3 and d=10? In d=10, roughly what fraction of uniform random points in [−1,1]10 fall inside the unit ball, and what does this mean for nearest-neighbour methods?
mlmaths:01.12.s: Step 1, sizes multiply, so the grid has 10d points: 103=1000 for d=3 and 1010 for d=10. Step 2, the ball's share of the cube is about 0.0025 in 10 dimensions, so only about 1 point in 400 lands inside the ball. Step 3, most points sit in the corners, far from the centre and far from each other. Distances between random points become similar, so "nearest" neighbours are not much nearer than the rest, and you need enormous amounts of data to cover the space.

mlmaths:01.13.q: 1,000 users clicked an ad, 300 bought something and 200 did both. How many did at least one? How many clicked but did not buy? If there are 5,000 users, how many did neither?
mlmaths:01.13.s: Step 1, at least one is the union: 1000+300−200=1100. Step 2, clicked but not bought is ∣C∖B∣=∣C∣−∣C∩B∣=1000−200=800. Step 3, neither is the complement of the union: 5000−1100=3900.

mlmaths:01.14.q: Which of these sets of pairs are functions from {0,1,2} to ℝ: (a) {(0,5),(1,5),(2,7)}, (b) {(0,5),(0,7),(1,1),(2,2)}, (c) {(0,1),(2,3)}? Explain each.
mlmaths:01.14.s: Step 1, (a) is a function: each of 0, 1, 2 appears exactly once. Two inputs sharing the output 5 is allowed. Step 2, (b) is not: input 0 appears twice with different outputs (5 and 7). Step 3, (c) is not a function on {0,1,2}: input 1 has no output. It is a function on the smaller set {0,2}.

mlmaths:01.15.q: Give three upper bounds and one lower bound for A={0.2,0.5,0.9}. Is (0,∞) bounded above? Bounded below? Is the set of possible sigmoid outputs bounded?
mlmaths:01.15.s: Step 1, any number ≥0.9 is an upper bound: for example 0.9, 1 and 100. Step 2, any number ≤0.2 is a lower bound, for example 0. Step 3, (0,∞) has no upper bound (for any u, the number u+1 is in the set and bigger), but 0 is a lower bound. So it is bounded below, not above. Step 4, sigmoid outputs lie in (0,1), so 1 is an upper bound and 0 a lower bound: the set is bounded.

mlmaths:01.16.q: Write in interval notation: (a) probabilities, (b) sigmoid outputs, (c) learning rates (positive), (d) a dropout rate that may be 0 but not 1. Which of these contain their endpoints?
mlmaths:01.16.s: Step 1, (a) probabilities can be 0 or 1: [0,1], both ends included. Step 2, (b) a sigmoid gets arbitrarily close to 0 and 1 but never reaches them in exact maths: (0,1), no ends. Step 3, (c) any positive real: (0,∞), with a round bracket at 0 and at infinity. Step 4, (d) [0,1): 0 included, 1 excluded (dropping every unit would delete the layer).

mlmaths:01.17.q: Which of the points (0.3,0), (0.5,0.5), (1,0) are in the ball B0.8((0,0))? On the real line, write B0.1(2) as an interval.
mlmaths:01.17.s: Step 1, compute distances to the origin. (0.3,0): 0.3. (0.5,0.5): 0.25+0.25≈0.707. (1,0): 1. Step 2, the ball keeps distances strictly less than 0.8: the first two are in, (1,0) is out. Step 3, on the line, B0.1(2)=(1.9,2.1).

mlmaths:01.18.q: For A=[0,1), classify each of 0, 0.5, 0.999, 1 and 1.5 as interior, boundary or exterior, and say which belong to A.
mlmaths:01.18.s: Step 1, 0.5: the ball (0.4,0.6) fits inside, so interior, and in A. Step 2, 0.999: the ball of radius 0.0005 fits, so interior, in A. Step 3, 0: every ball around 0 contains negative numbers (outside) and small positive ones (inside), so boundary, and 0∈A. Step 4, 1: every ball contains numbers just below 1 (inside) and above 1 (outside), so boundary, but 1∉A. Step 5, 1.5: the ball (1.4,1.6) misses A completely, so exterior.

mlmaths:01.19.q: Classify as open, closed, both or neither: (0,1), [0,1], [0,1), {x∈ℝ2:∥x∥≤1}, {x:w⊤x+b>0}, ℝ.
mlmaths:01.19.s: Step 1, (0,1): every point has room, so open. Step 2, [0,1]: contains both boundary points 0 and 1, so closed. Step 3, [0,1): 0 is a boundary point in the set, so not open; 1 is a boundary point not in the set, so not closed. Neither. Step 4, the disc with ≤ contains its circle edge, so closed. Step 5, the strict half-space w⊤x+b>0 leaves out its boundary line, so open. Step 6, ℝ has no boundary points at all, so it is both open and closed.

mlmaths:01.20.q: Find the maximum and minimum, if they exist, of {3,7,7,1}, [0,1], (0,1] and {1−1/n:n=1,2,3,… }.
mlmaths:01.20.s: Step 1, {3,7,7,1}={1,3,7}: max 7, min 1. Step 2, [0,1]: max 1, min 0, both in the set. Step 3, (0,1]: max 1; no min, because 0 is not in the set and any a>0 in it has a/2 smaller and still in it. Step 4, {0,0.5,0.667,0.75,… }: min 0 (at n=1); no max, because the values climb toward 1 without reaching it.
mlmaths:01.20.t: Maximum and Minimum of a Set

mlmaths:01.21.q: Which are compact: [0,1], (0,1), [0,∞), the closed unit disc, {w∈ℝd:∥w∥≤10}, ℝd? For each non-compact one, say which property fails.
mlmaths:01.21.s: Step 1, [0,1]: closed and bounded, compact. Step 2, (0,1): bounded but not closed (edges missing), not compact. Step 3, [0,∞): closed but not bounded, not compact. Step 4, the closed unit disc: compact. Step 5, the ball ∥w∥≤10: closed (non-strict inequality) and bounded (radius 10), compact. Step 6, ℝd: closed but not bounded, not compact.

mlmaths:01.22.q: For each, say whether a minimum is guaranteed and why: (a) f(x)=x2 on [−1,2], (b) f(x)=x on (0,1], (c) f(x)=e−x on [0,∞), (d) a continuous loss on {w:∥w∥≤5}.
mlmaths:01.22.s: Step 1, (a) continuous on a closed, bounded interval: guaranteed. The min is 0 at x=0. Step 2, (b) the set is not closed (0 missing), and indeed there is no min: values approach 0 but never reach it. Step 3, (c) the set is not bounded, and there is no min: e−x approaches 0 as x grows. Step 4, (d) a closed ball is closed and bounded and the loss is continuous, so the theorem guarantees a minimum.

mlmaths:01.23.q: Logistic regression on linearly separable data, no regularisation. What are inf⁡wL(w) and arg⁡min⁡wL(w)? What do you see in training, and what fixes it?
mlmaths:01.23.s: Step 1, separable means some w puts every point on the right side. Scaling that w by 2, 10, 100 keeps every point right but pushes the predicted probabilities toward 0 and 1, so the loss keeps falling toward 0. So inf⁡wL(w)=0. Step 2, no finite w reaches loss 0, because a sigmoid never outputs exactly 0 or 1. So arg⁡min⁡wL(w)=∅. Step 3, in training: ∥w∥ grows without limit, the loss creeps down forever, and probabilities pile up at 0 and 1. Step 4, fix: add λ2∥w∥2 (L2), which makes big weights costly and gives a unique finite minimiser; early stopping also works in practice.

mlmaths:01.24.q: For each, give the max (or sup) and the argmax: (a) f(x)=−(x−2)2 on ℝ, (b) f(x)=−(x2−1)2 on ℝ, (c) f(x)=−e−x on ℝ.
mlmaths:01.24.s: Step 1, (a) −(x−2)2≤0, with equality only at x=2: max 0, argmax {2}. Step 2, (b) −(x2−1)2≤0, with equality when x2=1: max 0, argmax {−1,1}, a tie between two points. Step 3, (c) −e−x is always negative and approaches 0 as x grows: sup 0, never reached, so the argmax is ∅.

mlmaths:01.25.q: Validation accuracy per epoch is (0.81,0.86,0.88,0.88,0.87). Give the max, the full argmax (epochs counted from 1), what np.argmax returns, and the index to use for "keep the latest best checkpoint".
mlmaths:01.25.s: Step 1, the max is 0.88. Step 2, it occurs at epochs 3 and 4, so arg⁡max⁡={3,4}, a tie. Step 3, np.argmax returns only the first index, counted from 0: 2 (epoch 3). Step 4, for the latest best, reverse the array: len(acc) - 1 - np.argmax(acc[::-1]) gives 3, which is epoch 4.
mlmaths:01.25.t: Reading Argmax and Argmin from Data

mlmaths:02.01.q: Which of these are statements, which are predicates, and which are neither? (a) "The validation loss at epoch 10 was 0.31." (b) "The loss at epoch t is below 0.3." (c) "Lower the learning rate." For each predicate, fill the blank once to make a true or false statement.
mlmaths:02.01.s: Step 1, (a) refers to one fixed epoch and one number, so it is either true or false: a statement. Step 2, (b) has a blank, the epoch t. On its own it has no truth value, so it is a predicate P(t). Filling it in, P(10) is "the loss at epoch 10 is below 0.3", which is false if the loss was 0.31. Step 3, (c) is an instruction. It is neither true nor false, so it is neither.

mlmaths:02.02.q: Early-stopping rule: stop when p∨q, with p = "no improvement for 5 epochs" and q = "epoch is 100". At epoch 40 there has been no improvement for 6 epochs. Do you stop? What if the rule were p∧q?
mlmaths:02.02.s: Step 1, at epoch 40, p is true (6 epochs without improvement is at least 5) and q is false (40 is not 100). Step 2, p∨q needs at least one true part. p is true, so p∨q is true: stop. Step 3, p∧q needs both. q is false, so p∧q is false: keep training. Step 4, with ∧ the run only stops at epoch 100, and only if it has also stalled. A one-symbol change gives a very different rule.

mlmaths:02.03.q: Build the truth table of ¬(p∧q) and of ¬p∨¬q. Are they equivalent?
mlmaths:02.03.s: Step 1, list the four rows (p,q): TT, TF, FT, FF. Step 2, p∧q is T, F, F, F, so ¬(p∧q) is F, T, T, T. Step 3, ¬p is F, F, T, T and ¬q is F, T, F, T. Their OR is F, T, T, T. Step 4, the two columns match on every row, so ¬(p∧q)≡¬p∨¬q. This is one of De Morgan's laws.

mlmaths:02.04.q: Two annotators label an image as "cat" (true) or "not cat". You want to flag images where they disagree. Which connective do you use, and what does it give for the label pairs (T, T), (T, F), (F, F)?
mlmaths:02.04.s: Step 1, "disagree" means exactly one said cat. That is XOR. Step 2, (T, T): both agree, T⊕T=F, not flagged. Step 3, (T, F): they disagree, T⊕F=T, flagged. Step 4, (F, F): both agree, F⊕F=F, not flagged. Step 5, inclusive OR would wrongly flag (T, T), because T∨T=T.

mlmaths:02.05.q: Batch losses are (0.3,0.0,1.2,0.4). Decide each claim: (a) ∀i, ℓi≥0; (b) ∃i, ℓi=0; (c) ∀i, ℓi<1.
mlmaths:02.05.s: Step 1, (a) check every loss: 0.3, 0.0, 1.2, 0.4 are all at least 0. True. Step 2, (b) we need one zero: ℓ2=0.0. True. Step 3, (c) every loss must be below 1, but ℓ3=1.2 is not. One failure is enough, so (c) is false.

mlmaths:02.06.q: Negate: "for every learning rate η<2/L, gradient descent converges on every L-smooth convex function". What would a counterexample look like?
mlmaths:02.06.s: Step 1, write the structure: "for all η<2/L, for all L-smooth convex f, GD converges on f". Step 2, flip each "for all" into "there exists" and negate the inside: "there exist a learning rate η<2/L and an L-smooth convex f such that GD does not converge on f". Step 3, so a counterexample is one concrete pair (η,f), with a starting point, where the iterates fail to converge. One is enough. Step 4, note: the original is in fact true (for the function values), so no counterexample exists. The exercise is about the form of the negation.

mlmaths:02.07.s: Step 1, (a): given any integer x, choose y=x+1. Then y>x. The choice of y depends on x, which is allowed. True. Step 2, (b): we need one fixed integer y bigger than every integer. Take x=y: then y>x fails. So no such y exists. False. Step 3, the only change was the order, and it changed the answer.

mlmaths:02.08.q: For an=1/n and L=0, find a cut-off N that works for ε=0.01. Then explain why swapping to ∃N ∀ε would fail.
mlmaths:02.08.s: Step 1, we need 1/n<0.01 for all n≥N, which means n>100. So N=101 works. Step 2, smaller ε needs larger N: ε=0.001 needs N=1001. Step 3, ∃N ∀ε would require one fixed N that works for every tolerance, including ε=1/(2N). But aN=1/N>1/(2N), so that N fails. No fixed N works.

mlmaths:02.09.q: A paper says "our method beats the baseline". List the hidden quantifiers you would ask about.
mlmaths:02.09.s: Step 1, over which datasets: for all of the tested ones, or some? Step 2, over which seeds: is it the mean over seeds, or for every seed? Step 3, over which budgets and sizes: for every compute budget, or only the one reported? Step 4, over which metrics. Each answer turns the vague claim into a precise statement that could be checked or broken.

mlmaths:02.10.q: Rule: "if the gradient check passes, the backward pass is correct". On which of the four rows of (passes, correct) is the rule broken?
mlmaths:02.10.s: Step 1, p = "the gradient check passes", q = "the backward pass is correct". Step 2, the rule p⇒q is false only when p is true and q is false. Step 3, so it is broken only on the row where the check passes but the backward pass is wrong. Every other row is consistent with the rule.

mlmaths:02.11.q: Is "every negative eigenvalue of this covariance matrix is larger than 5" true, given that covariance matrices have no negative eigenvalues?
mlmaths:02.11.s: Step 1, rewrite it: "for every eigenvalue λ, if λ<0 then λ>5". Step 2, a covariance matrix has no negative eigenvalues, so the premise λ<0 is false for every λ. Step 3, an implication with a false premise is true, so the claim is true for every eigenvalue. It is vacuously true, and it tells you nothing useful.

mlmaths:02.12.q: "If a model is overfitting, its validation loss rises while training loss falls." Your validation loss is falling. What can you conclude? Write the contrapositive and the converse, and say which is valid.
mlmaths:02.12.s: Step 1, p = "the model is overfitting", q = "validation loss rises while training loss falls". The rule is p⇒q. Step 2, contrapositive: ¬q⇒¬p, "if validation loss is not rising while training loss falls, the model is not overfitting". Valid whenever the rule is. Step 3, converse: q⇒p, "if validation loss rises while training loss falls, the model is overfitting". Not valid: a distribution shift or a learning-rate spike can give the same pattern. Step 4, your validation loss is falling, so q is false. The contrapositive gives ¬p: no overfitting of this kind yet. Step 5, that is only as good as the rule, which is a rule of thumb.

mlmaths:02.13.q: "If my fix works, the loss drops. The loss dropped, so my fix works." Name the error and describe the experiment that would actually test the fix.
mlmaths:02.13.s: Step 1, the rule is p⇒q with p = "the fix works" and q = "the loss drops". Step 2, the argument goes from q to p: that is affirming the consequent. Other causes (a new learning-rate schedule, a different seed, a data change) can also make the loss drop. Step 3, to test the fix, run an ablation: the same setup and seeds with and without the fix, changing nothing else. If the loss drops only with the fix, across several seeds, you have real evidence.

mlmaths:02.14.q: Is "f′′(x0)>0 at a stationary point x0" necessary, sufficient, both or neither for x0 to be a strict local minimum?
mlmaths:02.14.s: Step 1, sufficient: if f′(x0)=0 and f′′(x0)>0, the curve bends upward at x0, so it is a strict local minimum. Yes. Step 2, necessary: is every strict local minimum one with f′′>0? No. f(x)=x4 has a strict minimum at 0, but f′′(0)=0. Step 3, so it is sufficient but not necessary.

mlmaths:02.15.q: Prove: for a real number x, x2=0  ⟺  x=0.
mlmaths:02.15.s: Step 1, direction x=0⇒x2=0: 02=0. Step 2, direction x2=0⇒x=0: if x≠0, then x2>0, so x2≠0. That is the contrapositive, so the direction holds. Step 3, both directions hold, so the "iff" holds.

mlmaths:02.16.q: Prove by contrapositive: if n2 is even then n is even.
mlmaths:02.16.s: Step 1, the contrapositive is "if n is odd, then n2 is odd". Step 2, write an odd n as n=2k+1. Step 3, n2=4k2+4k+1=2(2k2+2k)+1, which is odd. Step 4, the contrapositive is proved, so the original claim holds.
mlmaths:02.16.t: Direct Proof and Proof by Contrapositive

mlmaths:02.17.s: Step 1, a "for all" claim needs one counterexample. Step 2, try a=3, b=4: 9+16=5 but a+b=7. Step 3, 5≠7, so the claim is false.

mlmaths:02.18.q: You want to drop examples that are "too short and low quality" and keep the rest. Write the keep condition with De Morgan, and name the common bug.
mlmaths:02.18.s: Step 1, drop = short∧lowq, so keep = ¬(short∧lowq). Step 2, by De Morgan, keep = ¬short∨¬lowq: keep anything long enough or good enough. Step 3, the common bug is ¬short∧¬lowq, which keeps only examples that are both long and good, and throws away far more data.

mlmaths:02.19.q: Per-token losses are (2.0,1.0,3.0,0.0,0.0) and the last two tokens are padding. Compute the correct masked mean, and the wrong one you get from (loss * mask).mean().
mlmaths:02.19.s: Step 1, the real tokens are the first three, so the correct mean is (2+1+3)/3=2.0. Step 2, (loss * mask).mean() divides the same sum by all 5 positions: 6/5=1.2. Step 3, the fix is to divide by the number of real tokens: (loss * mask).sum() / mask.sum(), which gives 2.0.

mlmaths:03.01.q: For w=(3,4) and x=(2,1), compute w⊤x, ∥w∥ and ∥x∥. Is (4,−3) perpendicular to w?
mlmaths:03.01.s: Step 1, w⊤x=3⋅2+4⋅1=10. Step 2, ∥w∥=9+16=5. Step 3, ∥x∥=4+1=5≈2.236. Step 4, (3,4)⊤(4,−3)=12−12=0, so yes, they are perpendicular.

mlmaths:03.02.q: Find two points on 3x1+4x2=12, and check whether (2,1.5) is on it.
mlmaths:03.02.s: Step 1, set x1=0: 4x2=12, so (0,3). Step 2, set x2=0: 3x1=12, so (4,0). Step 3, check (2,1.5): 6+6=12. Yes, it is on the line.

mlmaths:03.03.q: For the plane x1+2x2−x3=4 in ℝ3, give the normal vector and check that it is perpendicular to the direction between the points (4,0,0) and (0,2,0).
mlmaths:03.03.s: Step 1, the normal is the coefficient vector w=(1,2,−1). Step 2, both points are on the plane: 4=4 and 4=4. Step 3, the direction between them is (0,2,0)−(4,0,0)=(−4,2,0). Step 4, w⊤(−4,2,0)=−4+4+0=0, so they are perpendicular.

mlmaths:03.04.q: A classifier has w=(1,−1), b=0 and predicts class 1 when w⊤x+b>0. Classify (3,1), (1,3) and (2,2).
mlmaths:03.04.s: Step 1, (3,1): 3−1=2>0, class 1. Step 2, (1,3): 1−3=−2<0, class 0. Step 3, (2,2): 0, exactly on the boundary; the rule >0 gives class 0, but a tiny change would flip it.

mlmaths:03.05.q: A classifier has w=(3,4), b=−5 and predicts positive when w⊤x+b>0. Give the signed distance of x=(2,1), and say what happens to the score and the distance if you double w and b.
mlmaths:03.05.s: Step 1, score: w⊤x+b=6+4−5=5. Step 2, ∥w∥=5. Step 3, distance 5/5=1, on the positive side. Step 4, doubling gives w=(6,8), b=−10: score 12+8−10=10, twice as big. But ∥w∥=10, so the distance is still 1. The boundary line has not moved, so the raw score is not a fair confidence; the distance is.
mlmaths:03.05.t: Distance from a Point to a Hyperplane

mlmaths:03.06.q: Write the line through a=(1,2) and b=(3,1) in parametric form, and give the points at t=0.5 and t=2.
mlmaths:03.06.s: Step 1, direction v=b−a=(2,−1). Step 2, the line is (1,2)+t(2,−1). Step 3, t=0.5: (1+1,2−0.5)=(2,1.5), the midpoint. Step 4, t=2: (1+4,2−2)=(5,0), past b.

mlmaths:03.07.q: Find the equation of the plane through (0,0,0) spanned by u=(1,0,1) and v=(0,1,1).
mlmaths:03.07.s: Step 1, the normal is u×v=(0⋅1−1⋅1, 1⋅0−1⋅1, 1⋅1−0⋅0)=(−1,−1,1). Step 2, the plane passes through the origin, so b=0: −x1−x2+x3=0, or x3=x1+x2. Step 3, check: u gives −1−0+1=0 and v gives 0−1+1=0.

mlmaths:03.08.q: Write as Ax≤b: x1≥0, x2≥0, x1+x2≤1. Describe the region.
mlmaths:03.08.s: Step 1, rewrite each as "≤": −x1≤0, −x2≤0, x1+x2≤1. Step 2, rows of A: (−1,0), (0,−1), (1,1), and b=(0,0,1). Step 3, the region is the triangle with corners (0,0), (1,0), (0,1).

mlmaths:03.09.q: Classify each system: (a) x+y=3, x−y=1; (b) x+y=3, x+y=5; (c) x+y=3, 2x+2y=6.
mlmaths:03.09.s: Step 1, (a) the lines have different slopes, so they cross once. Adding gives 2x=4, so (2,1). Step 2, (b) same left side, different right sides: parallel lines, no solution. Step 3, (c) the second equation is twice the first: the same line, infinitely many solutions.

mlmaths:03.10.q: Where does A=(2101) send (1,0), (0,1) and (1,1)?
mlmaths:03.10.s: Step 1, A(1,0) is the first column, (2,0). Step 2, A(0,1) is the second column, (1,1). Step 3, A(1,1)=(2+1,0+1)=(3,1), the sum of the two columns. So the unit square becomes the parallelogram with corners (0,0), (2,0), (3,1), (1,1).
mlmaths:03.10.t: Matrices as Maps of the Plane

mlmaths:03.11.q: Compute det⁡A for (2003), (1101) and (3112). What area does a disk of area 2 have after the third map?
mlmaths:03.11.s: Step 1, 2⋅3−0=6. Step 2, 1−0=1: a shear keeps area. Step 3, 6−1=5. Step 4, every area is multiplied by 5, so the disk's image has area 10.

mlmaths:03.12.q: What is det⁡ of the rotation by angle θ, (cos⁡θ−sin⁡θsin⁡θcos⁡θ)? And of the reflection (100−1)?
mlmaths:03.12.s: Step 1, rotation: cos⁡2θ−(−sin⁡θ)(sin⁡θ)=cos⁡2θ+sin⁡2θ=1. Area and orientation are kept. Step 2, reflection: 1⋅(−1)−0=−1. Area is kept, orientation flipped.
mlmaths:03.12.t: Sign of the Determinant and Orientation

mlmaths:03.13.q: For A=(1224), find a non-zero x with Ax=0, and two different inputs with the same output.
mlmaths:03.13.s: Step 1, the second column is twice the first, so 2⋅col1−col2=0. That means x=(2,−1) gives Ax=0. Step 2, add it to any input: (1,1) and (1,1)+(2,−1)=(3,0). Step 3, A(1,1)=(3,6) and A(3,0)=(3,6): the same output.

mlmaths:03.14.q: A=(2103), B=(1041). Compute det⁡(AB) and det⁡(3A) without multiplying matrices.
mlmaths:03.14.s: Step 1, both are triangular: det⁡A=2⋅3=6, det⁡B=1⋅1=1. Step 2, det⁡(AB)=6⋅1=6. Step 3, det⁡(3A)=32⋅6=54, not 3⋅6=18, because each of the 2 dimensions is scaled by 3.

mlmaths:03.15.q: Σ=10−3I in 300 dimensions. What is det⁡Σ, what does float64 store, what is log⁡det⁡Σ, and is Σ close to singular?
mlmaths:03.15.s: Step 1, diagonal, so det⁡Σ=(10−3)300=10−900. Step 2, float64 can't go below about 10−308, so it stores 0.0. Step 3, log⁡det⁡Σ=300ln⁡(10−3)≈−2072.3, easy to store. Step 4, it is not nearly singular: every direction is shrunk by the same factor, so its condition number is 1, the best possible. Judge singularity with the condition number, not the determinant.

mlmaths:03.16.q: Write the augmented matrix of x+2y+z=4, 2x+4y+3z=9, x+y=1.
mlmaths:03.16.s: Step 1, list the coefficients of x,y,z in each equation, writing 0 for a missing variable. Step 2, rows: [1,2,1∣4], [2,4,3∣9], [1,1,0∣1]. Step 3, the third row has z coefficient 0 because z does not appear in x+y=1.
mlmaths:03.16.t: Systems of Equations as Augmented Matrices

mlmaths:03.17.q: Apply R2 ← R2 − 2·R1 to (124259). What does the new row 2 say?
mlmaths:03.17.s: Step 1, 2·R1 is (2,4,8). Step 2, R2 − 2·R1 = (2−2, 5−4, 9−8)=(0,1,1). Step 3, the new row 2 says 0x+1y=1, so y=1. Row 1 is unchanged: x+2y=4, so x=2.

mlmaths:03.18.q: Eliminate below the first pivot in (21144331087924). What are the multipliers?
mlmaths:03.18.s: Step 1, the pivot is 2. Step 2, row 2 multiplier 4/2=2: R2 − 2·R1 = (0,1,1,2). Step 3, row 3 multiplier 8/2=4: R3 − 4·R1 = (0,3,5,8). Step 4, the first column is now (2,0,0), and the next step uses the 1 in row 2 as the pivot.

mlmaths:03.19.q: Solve 2x+y+z=4, y+z=2, 2z=2 by back substitution.
mlmaths:03.19.s: Step 1, bottom row: 2z=2, so z=1. Step 2, middle row: y+1=2, so y=1. Step 3, top row: 2x+1+1=4, so x=1. The solution is (1,1,1).

mlmaths:03.20.q: Is (120300410000) in row echelon form? Where are the pivots?
mlmaths:03.20.s: Step 1, row 1's first non-zero entry is in column 1. Row 2's is in column 3, further right. Row 3 is all zeros and is at the bottom. Step 2, so yes, it is in row echelon form. Step 3, the pivots are the 1 in column 1 and the 4 in column 3. There are 2 pivots, so the rank is 2.

mlmaths:03.21.q: Reduce (124011) to RREF and read off the solution of the system it represents.
mlmaths:03.21.s: Step 1, the pivots are already 1. Step 2, clear above the second pivot: R1 − 2·R2 =(1,0,2). Step 3, RREF is (102011). Step 4, read off: x=2, y=1.

mlmaths:03.22.q: Solve x+y+z=3, x+2y+3z=6. Which variable is free? Give two solutions.
mlmaths:03.22.s: Step 1, R2 − R1 gives y+2z=3. Pivots are in the x and y columns, so z is free. Step 2, set z=t: y=3−2t, x=3−y−z=t. Step 3, solutions (t,3−2t,t). With t=0: (0,3,0). With t=1: (1,1,1).

mlmaths:03.23.q: Show that x+y=2, 2x+2y=5 has no solution.
mlmaths:03.23.s: Step 1, R2 − 2·R1 =[0,0∣1]. Step 2, that row says 0x+0y=1, i.e. 0=1, impossible. Step 3, so there is no solution. Geometrically the two lines are parallel (x+y=2 and x+y=2.5).

mlmaths:03.24.q: Write all solutions of x+2y=4 as a particular solution plus a homogeneous part.
mlmaths:03.24.s: Step 1, one particular solution: y=0 gives x=4, so xp=(4,0). Step 2, solve x+2y=0: y=t gives x=−2t, so xh=t(−2,1). Step 3, all solutions: (4,0)+t(−2,1).

mlmaths:03.25.q: Solve 10−20x+y=1, x+y=2 with and without pivoting, in floating point.
mlmaths:03.25.s: Step 1, without pivoting the multiplier is 1020. Row 2 becomes (1−1020)y=2−1020, which rounds to −1020y=−1020, so y=1. Then 10−20x=0, so x=0. Wrong. Step 2, with a swap the pivot is 1 and the multiplier 10−20. Row 2 becomes (1−10−20)y=1−2⋅10−20, so y≈1 and x=2−y≈1. Correct.

mlmaths:03.26.q: You must solve Ax=b for 1,000 different b with the same 10,000×10,000 matrix A. Compare the cost of 1,000 calls to solve with one LU factorisation followed by 1,000 triangular solves.
mlmaths:03.26.s: Step 1, each solve factors A again: about 23n3≈6.7×1011 operations, so 1,000 calls cost about 6.7×1014. Step 2, one LU costs 6.7×1011. Each pair of triangular solves costs about 2n2=2×108, so 1,000 of them cost 2×1011. Step 3, total about 8.7×1011, roughly 770 times cheaper.

mlmaths:03.27.q: Which call would you use for (a) a 3×3 invertible system, (b) 100 equations in 3 unknowns, (c) 2 equations in 5 unknowns?
mlmaths:03.27.s: Step 1, (a) np.linalg.solve, which uses LU with pivoting. Step 2, (b) np.linalg.lstsq: there is generally no exact solution, and it returns the least-squares fit. Step 3, (c) np.linalg.lstsq as well: there are infinitely many solutions, and it returns the one with the smallest norm.

mlmaths:03.28.q: Check that (1−1−12) is the inverse of (2111).
mlmaths:03.28.s: Step 1, multiply: top-left 2−1=1, top-right −2+2=0. Step 2, bottom-left 1−1=0, bottom-right −1+2=1. Step 3, the product is I, so yes.

mlmaths:03.29.q: Invert (3142) with the formula and check one entry of the product.
mlmaths:03.29.s: Step 1, det⁡=6−4=2. Step 2, swap and negate: (2−1−43). Step 3, divide by 2: (1−0.5−21.5). Step 4, check the top-left of AA−1: 3⋅1+1⋅(−2)=1.

mlmaths:03.30.q: Simplify (A⊤B)−1 in terms of A−1 and B−1.
mlmaths:03.30.s: Step 1, reverse order: (A⊤B)−1=B−1(A⊤)−1. Step 2, (A⊤)−1=(A−1)⊤. Step 3, so (A⊤B)−1=B−1(A−1)⊤.

mlmaths:03.31.q: X⊤X in a regression has eigenvalues from 104 down to 10−6. What is its condition number, roughly how many digits can you trust in float64, and what are two fixes?
mlmaths:03.31.s: Step 1, κ=104/10−6=1010. Step 2, float64 has about 16 digits, so about 16−10=6 are trustworthy. Step 3, fixes: solve with QR or SVD on X instead of forming X⊤X (that avoids squaring κ(X)); standardise the features; or add ridge regularisation λI, which lifts the smallest eigenvalue to at least λ.

mlmaths:03.32.q: A is a 10,000×10,000 diagonal matrix and U is 10,000×10. Roughly how expensive is inverting A+UU⊤ directly versus with Woodbury?
mlmaths:03.32.s: Step 1, directly: about n3=1012 operations. Step 2, with Woodbury: inverting the diagonal A costs n; the k×k matrix I+U⊤A−1U costs about nk2=106 to form and k3=1,000 to invert. Step 3, so about a million operations instead of a trillion.

mlmaths:03.33.q: For A=(2001) and b=(1,−1), compute f(0,0), f(2,2) and f(1,1). Is the midpoint kept?
mlmaths:03.33.s: Step 1, f(0,0)=(1,−1). Step 2, f(2,2)=(5,1). Step 3, f(1,1)=(3,0). Step 4, (1,1) is the midpoint of (0,0) and (2,2), and (3,0) is the midpoint of (1,−1) and (5,1). Yes.

mlmaths:03.34.q: Write the homogeneous matrix for A=(2001), b=(1,−1), and apply it to (2,2).
mlmaths:03.34.s: Step 1, M=(20101−1001). Step 2, M(2,2,1)=(4+1, 2−1, 1)=(5,1,1). Step 3, drop the final 1: (5,1), the same as Ax+b.

mlmaths:03.35.q: Two layers h=W1x+b1, y=W2h+b2 with no activation, W1∈ℝ512×784, W2∈ℝ10×512. Write the single equivalent layer and compare parameter counts.
mlmaths:03.35.s: Step 1, substitute: y=(W2W1)x+(W2b1+b2). Step 2, single layer: 10⋅784+10=7,850 parameters. Step 3, two layers: 512⋅784+512+10⋅512+10=407,050. Step 4, 52 times more parameters, and nothing new computed. A ReLU between them breaks the collapse.

mlmaths:04.01.q: With v1=(1,0) and v2=(1,2), compute 3v1+v2, and find c1,c2 with c1v1+c2v2=(0,4).
mlmaths:04.01.s: Step 1, 3v1+v2=(3,0)+(1,2)=(4,2). Step 2, for (0,4) we need c1+c2=0 (first entries) and 2c2=4 (second entries). Step 3, so c2=2 and c1=−2. Check: −2(1,0)+2(1,2)=(0,4).

mlmaths:04.02.q: Compute (1102)(31) in both the row view and the column view.
mlmaths:04.02.s: Step 1, row view: row 1 dotted with (3,1) is 3+1=4; row 2 is 0+2=2. Result (4,2). Step 2, column view: 3⋅(1,0)+1⋅(1,2)=(3,0)+(1,2)=(4,2). Step 3, same answer, two readings.

mlmaths:04.03.q: Is (2,3,5) in the span of (1,0,1) and (0,1,1)? Is (2,3,7)?
mlmaths:04.03.s: Step 1, a combination is c1(1,0,1)+c2(0,1,1)=(c1,c2,c1+c2). Step 2, for (2,3,5): c1=2, c2=3, and c1+c2=5. Yes. Step 3, for (2,3,7): the third entry would have to be 2+3=5, not 7. No.
mlmaths:04.03.t: The Span of a Set of Vectors

mlmaths:04.04.q: You one-hot encode a feature with 3 levels and also keep an intercept column of ones. Show the columns are dependent and say what that does to least squares. Give two fixes.
mlmaths:04.04.s: Step 1, each row has exactly one 1 among the one-hot columns eA,eB,eC, so eA+eB+eC=𝟏. Step 2, so eA+eB+eC−𝟏=0 with coefficients (1,1,1,−1), not all zero: dependent. This is the "dummy variable trap". Step 3, least squares has infinitely many equally good coefficient vectors: add t to each level and subtract t from the intercept and no prediction changes. Step 4, fixes: drop one level (reference coding), drop the intercept, or add ridge regularisation.

mlmaths:04.05.q: Columns (1,2,3) and (2,4.000001,6). Are they independent? Are they nearly dependent? What does matrix_rank say with the default and with tolerance 10−5?
mlmaths:04.05.s: Step 1, the second column is not exactly twice the first (the middle entry differs by 10−6), so technically they are independent. Step 2, but it is extremely close to twice the first, so they are nearly dependent; the ratio smin⁡/smax⁡ is below 10−6. Step 3, matrix_rank with the default tolerance gives 2; with tolerance 10−5 it gives 1, the honest answer.

mlmaths:04.06.q: Which are subspaces of ℝ2: (a) {(t,2t)}; (b) {(t,2t+1)}; (c) {(x,y):x≥0,y≥0}?
mlmaths:04.06.s: Step 1, (a) contains (0,0); sums and multiples of points (t,2t) stay of that form. Subspace. Step 2, (b) does not contain (0,0) (that would need 0=1). Not a subspace. Step 3, (c) contains (1,1) but not −1⋅(1,1). Not closed under scaling, so not a subspace.

mlmaths:04.07.q: A=(100111). Describe C(A) and decide whether Ax=(2,3,5) and Ax=(2,3,7) have solutions.
mlmaths:04.07.s: Step 1, outputs are x1(1,0,1)+x2(0,1,1)=(x1,x2,x1+x2): the third entry is the sum of the first two. Step 2, (2,3,5): 2+3=5, so it is in C(A), with x=(2,3). Step 3, (2,3,7): 2+3≠7, not in C(A), no solution.

mlmaths:04.08.q: A full-rank linear layer maps ℝ4096→ℝ1024. What is the dimension of its null space, and what does that mean for a later layer trying to recover the input?
mlmaths:04.08.s: Step 1, W is 1024×4096 with rank 1024. Step 2, rank-nullity: dim⁡N(W)=4096−1024=3072. Step 3, two inputs that differ by a null-space vector give the same output, Wx=W(x+n). No later layer can tell them apart, so information along those 3072 directions is lost.

mlmaths:04.09.q: For A=(123246), give the dimension of each of the four subspaces.
mlmaths:04.09.s: Step 1, m=2, n=3, rank r=1. Step 2, column space: dimension 1 (the line through (1,2)). Left null space: 2−1=1. Step 3, row space: dimension 1 (the line through (1,2,3)). Null space: 3−1=2.

mlmaths:04.10.q: Is {(1,1),(1,−1)} a basis of ℝ2? Is {(1,2),(2,4)}? Is {(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)}?
mlmaths:04.10.s: Step 1, (1,1) and (1,−1) are independent (lesson 04.04) and two independent vectors in ℝ2 span it. Basis. Step 2, (2,4)=2(1,2), dependent. Not a basis. Step 3, three vectors in ℝ2 are always dependent. They span ℝ2 but are not a basis.

mlmaths:04.11.q: Find the coordinates of x=(3,1) in the basis b1=(1,1), b2=(1,−1).
mlmaths:04.11.s: Step 1, solve c1(1,1)+c2(1,−1)=(3,1): c1+c2=3 and c1−c2=1. Step 2, adding: c1=2, then c2=1. Step 3, check: 2(1,1)+(1,−1)=(3,1). Coordinates (2,1).

mlmaths:04.12.q: For b1=12(1,1), b2=12(−1,1), find the coordinates of x=(3,1) and check the length is kept.
mlmaths:04.12.s: Step 1, c1=b1⊤x=(3+1)/2=4/2≈2.83. Step 2, c2=b2⊤x=(−3+1)/2≈−1.41. Step 3, c12+c22=8+2=10=32+12. Length kept.

mlmaths:04.13.q: A vector has coordinates (2,1) in basis b1=(1,1), b2=(1,−1). Find its coordinates in the basis d1=(1,0), d2=(1,1).
mlmaths:04.13.s: Step 1, convert to standard: x=2(1,1)+1(1,−1)=(3,1). Step 2, solve c1(1,0)+c2(1,1)=(3,1): c2=1, then c1=2. Step 3, coordinates (2,1) in the new basis too, by coincidence; check: 2(1,0)+(1,1)=(3,1).

mlmaths:04.14.q: A=(2112), basis b1=(1,1), b2=(1,−1). Find A in this basis and use it to compute A(3,1).
mlmaths:04.14.s: Step 1, Ab1=(3,3)=3b1 and Ab2=(1,−1)=1b2. Step 2, so in this basis A′=diag(3,1). Step 3, (3,1) has coordinates (2,1); applying A′ gives (6,1). Step 4, back to standard: 6(1,1)+1(1,−1)=(7,5). Direct check: A(3,1)=(7,5).

mlmaths:04.15.q: Check that A=(2112) and diag(3,1) have the same determinant, trace and rank.
mlmaths:04.15.s: Step 1, determinants: 4−1=3 and 3⋅1=3. Step 2, traces (sum of the diagonal): 2+2=4 and 3+1=4. Step 3, ranks: both 2 (non-zero determinant). All match, as they must for similar matrices.

mlmaths:04.16.q: A hidden layer h=Wx feeds y=Vh. Show that replacing W by BW and V by VB−1 (for invertible B) gives the same y. What does this say about interpreting single neurons?
mlmaths:04.16.s: Step 1, new hidden values h′=BWx=Bh. Step 2, new output y′=VB−1h′=VB−1Bh=Vh=y. Step 3, so the network computes exactly the same function with hidden coordinates Bh instead of h. Step 4, the training objective can't prefer one basis over another (unless something like a ReLU or regulariser breaks the symmetry), so an individual coordinate of h need not be meaningful.

mlmaths:04.17.q: What is the dimension of (a) the plane x1+x2+x3=0 in ℝ3; (b) the span of (1,2,3) and (2,4,6); (c) {0}?
mlmaths:04.17.s: Step 1, (a) one equation in 3 unknowns leaves 2 free variables, so dimension 2. Step 2, (b) the second vector is twice the first, so the span is a line: dimension 1. Step 3, (c) the zero subspace has the empty basis: dimension 0.

mlmaths:04.18.q: Find the rank of (101011112) and of the outer product uv⊤ with u=(1,2,3), v=(1,0,−1,2).
mlmaths:04.18.s: Step 1, column 3 = column 1 + column 2, and columns 1 and 2 are independent, so rank 2. Step 2, every column of uv⊤ is a multiple of u (column j is vju), so rank 1.

mlmaths:04.19.q: A 5×8 matrix has rank 4. What are the dimensions of its null space, column space and left null space?
mlmaths:04.19.s: Step 1, rank-nullity: dim⁡N(A)=8−4=4. Step 2, column space: dimension equals the rank, 4. Step 3, left null space: m−r=5−4=1.

mlmaths:04.20.q: LoRA adapts a 4096×4096 weight with ΔW=BA, B∈ℝ4096×16, A∈ℝ16×4096. What is the maximum rank of ΔW, and how many trainable parameters does it have versus a full update?
mlmaths:04.20.s: Step 1, rank⁡(BA)≤16 because B has 16 columns. Step 2, parameters: 4096⋅16+16⋅4096=131,072. Step 3, a full update has 40962=16,777,216, which is 128 times more. Step 4, LoRA can't represent any update of rank above 16.

mlmaths:04.21.q: A 100×100 matrix of exact rank 3 has small noise added. What does matrix_rank report, and how would you find the "real" rank?
mlmaths:04.21.s: Step 1, with noise, all 100 singular values are non-zero, so matrix_rank with its default tolerance reports 100. Step 2, plot or print the singular values: three are large, then they drop off a cliff to the noise level. Step 3, so the honest answer is "rank 3 plus noise". Choose the tolerance at the cliff.

mlmaths:05.01.q: For A=(2112), which of (1,1), (1,−1), (1,0) are eigenvectors, and with which eigenvalues?
mlmaths:05.01.s: Step 1, A(1,1)=(3,3)=3(1,1): eigenvector, λ=3. Step 2, A(1,−1)=(1,−1): eigenvector, λ=1. Step 3, A(1,0)=(2,1), which is not a multiple of (1,0): not an eigenvector.

mlmaths:05.02.q: Find the eigenvalues of (4123) and check them against the trace and determinant.
mlmaths:05.02.s: Step 1, trace 7, determinant 12−2=10. Step 2, λ2−7λ+10=0 factors as (λ−5)(λ−2)=0, so λ=5 and 2. Step 3, check: 5+2=7 and 5⋅2=10.

mlmaths:05.03.q: Find an eigenvector of A=(4123) for λ=2 and for λ=5.
mlmaths:05.03.s: Step 1, λ=2: A−2I=(2121). Both rows say 2v1+v2=0, so v=(1,−2). Check: A(1,−2)=(2,−4)=2(1,−2). Step 2, λ=5: A−5I=(−112−2), so v1=v2, giving v=(1,1). Check: A(1,1)=(5,5).

mlmaths:05.04.q: Find the eigenvalues of (0−220). What does the matrix do geometrically?
mlmaths:05.04.s: Step 1, trace 0, determinant 0+4=4, so λ2+4=0 and λ=±2i. Step 2, complex eigenvalues mean rotation; ∣±2i∣=2 means lengths double. Step 3, the matrix is a 90 degree rotation followed by scaling by 2.

mlmaths:05.05.q: A linear RNN updates ht=Wht−1 with eigenvalues 1.05 and 0.6. What happens to ht after 100 steps, and to gradients flowing back 100 steps?
mlmaths:05.05.s: Step 1, write h0=av1+bv2 in the eigenvector basis. Step 2, h100=a(1.05)100v1+b(0.6)100v2. Step 3, 1.05100≈132 and 0.6100≈6.5×10−23: the v1 part grows, the v2 part vanishes. Step 4, backpropagation multiplies by W⊤ (same eigenvalues) each step, so gradients explode along one direction and vanish along the other.

mlmaths:05.06.q: Power iteration on a matrix with λ1=10 and λ2=9. Roughly how many steps to shrink the error by a factor of 1,000? What if λ2=1?
mlmaths:05.06.s: Step 1, the error shrinks by 0.9 per step. Step 2, 0.9k=10−3 needs k=3/log⁡10(1/0.9)≈66 steps. Step 3, with λ2=1 the ratio is 0.1, so 3 steps.

mlmaths:05.07.q: Diagonalise A=(2112) and use it to compute A(3,1).
mlmaths:05.07.s: Step 1, eigenvectors (1,1) with λ=3 and (1,−1) with λ=1, so V=(111−1), Λ=diag(3,1). Step 2, coordinates of (3,1) in the eigenbasis: (2,1). Step 3, scale: (6,1). Step 4, back: 6(1,1)+(1,−1)=(7,5).

mlmaths:05.08.q: Use A=VΛV−1 to find A10 for A=(2112), entry (1,1).
mlmaths:05.08.s: Step 1, A=QΛQ⊤ with Q columns 12(1,1), 12(1,−1), Λ=diag(3,1). Step 2, A10=Q diag(310,1)Q⊤. Step 3, entry (1,1) is 12310+12⋅1=59049+12=29525.
mlmaths:05.08.t: Powers and Functions of a Matrix

mlmaths:05.09.q: Show that J=(3103) is not diagonalisable.
mlmaths:05.09.s: Step 1, J is triangular, so both eigenvalues are 3. Step 2, eigenvectors solve (J−3I)v=0, i.e. (0100)v=0, so v2=0. Step 3, only the direction (1,0): one eigenvector, not enough for a basis of ℝ2.

mlmaths:05.10.q: Show that eigenvectors of a symmetric A with different eigenvalues λ≠μ are perpendicular.
mlmaths:05.10.s: Step 1, let Au=λu, Av=μv. Step 2, λu⊤v=(Au)⊤v=u⊤A⊤v=u⊤Av=μu⊤v, using A⊤=A. Step 3, so (λ−μ)u⊤v=0, and since λ≠μ, u⊤v=0.

mlmaths:05.11.q: Rebuild A=(2112) from q1=12(1,1), λ1=3 and q2=12(1,−1), λ2=1.
mlmaths:05.11.s: Step 1, q1q1⊤=12(1111), q2q2⊤=12(1−1−11). Step 2, 3⋅12(1111)+12(1−1−11)=(2112).
mlmaths:05.11.t: Symmetric Matrices as Sums of Projections

mlmaths:05.12.q: Classify (1221) and (2112). Give an x with x⊤Ax<0 if one exists.
mlmaths:05.12.s: Step 1, first matrix: trace 2, determinant −3, eigenvalues 3 and −1. Indefinite. Step 2, x=(1,−1): x⊤Ax=1−2−2+1=−2<0. Step 3, second matrix: eigenvalues 3 and 1, positive definite.

mlmaths:05.13.q: The Hessian at a point has eigenvalues {50,2,0.01}. Is it a minimum? What step size is safe, and why is training slow along one direction?
mlmaths:05.13.s: Step 1, all eigenvalues positive, so (with zero gradient) a strict local minimum. Step 2, stability needs ∣1−ηλi∣<1 for all i, so η<2/50=0.04. Step 3, along λ=0.01 the factor is 1−0.04⋅0.01=0.9996: halving the error takes about ln⁡2/0.0004≈1,700 steps. Step 4, the condition number 5,000 is the cause; momentum, Adam or preconditioning help.

mlmaths:06.01.q: Compute (1,2,3)⊤(4,5,6), (3,4)⊤(4,−3) and (3,4)⊤(3,4). Which pair is perpendicular?
mlmaths:06.01.s: Step 1, (1,2,3)⊤(4,5,6)=4+10+18=32. Step 2, (3,4)⊤(4,−3)=12−12=0. Step 3, (3,4)⊤(3,4)=9+16=25. Step 4, the second pair has dot product 0, so (3,4) and (4,−3) are perpendicular.
mlmaths:06.01.t: The Dot Product in N-Dimensional Euclidean Space

mlmaths:06.02.q: Find ∥(3,4)∥, the distance between (3,4) and (4,−3), and check the expansion formula.
mlmaths:06.02.s: Step 1, ∥(3,4)∥=9+16=5, and ∥(4,−3)∥=5 too. Step 2, (3,4)−(4,−3)=(−1,7), with length 1+49=50≈7.07. Step 3, the formula: 25+25−2⋅0=50, and 50 matches.

mlmaths:06.03.q: Embeddings a=(3,4), b=(6,8), c=(4,−3). Give the cosine similarity and the Euclidean distance of b and of c from a.
mlmaths:06.03.s: Step 1, a⊤b=18+32=50, ∥a∥=5, ∥b∥=10, so cos⁡=50/50=1. Distance ∥(−3,−4)∥=5. Step 2, a⊤c=12−12=0, so cos⁡=0. Distance ∥(−1,7)∥=50≈7.07. Step 3, b points exactly the same way as a but is twice as long; cosine ignores that, distance does not.

mlmaths:06.04.q: Check Cauchy-Schwarz for x=(1,2) with y=(3,1) and with y=(2,4). When is it an equality?
mlmaths:06.04.s: Step 1, x⊤(3,1)=5, while ∥x∥∥y∥=510=50≈7.07. So 5≤7.07. Step 2, x⊤(2,4)=10, and ∥x∥∥y∥=520=10. Equal. Step 3, equality happened because (2,4)=2x is a multiple of x.

mlmaths:06.05.q: Queries and keys have i.i.d. entries with mean 0 and variance 1, in d=128. What are the mean and standard deviation of q⊤k? Why divide by d before the softmax?
mlmaths:06.05.s: Step 1, q⊤k is a sum of 128 terms qiki. Step 2, each term has mean 0 and variance E[qi2]E[ki2]=1. Step 3, the terms are independent, so the sum has mean 0 and variance 128, standard deviation 128≈11.3. Step 4, softmax of scores spread over about ±20 puts almost all weight on the largest; its gradients become tiny. Dividing by 128 brings the spread back to 1.

mlmaths:06.06.q: Data has mean 0 and covariance Σ=diag⁡(100,1). Compare the Euclidean and Mahalanobis distances of (5,0) and (0,5) from the mean.
mlmaths:06.06.s: Step 1, both points have Euclidean distance 5. Step 2, Σ−1=diag⁡(0.01,1). Step 3, (5,0): 25⋅0.01=0.5. Step 4, (0,5): 25⋅1=5. Step 5, the first is half a standard deviation out (normal); the second is five standard deviations out (very unusual).
mlmaths:06.06.t: Other Inner Products and Mahalanobis Distance

mlmaths:06.07.q: Check that q1=(0.6,0.8) and q2=(−0.8,0.6) are orthonormal, then write x=(5,0) in this basis.
mlmaths:06.07.s: Step 1, q1⊤q1=0.36+0.64=1 and q2⊤q2=1. Step 2, q1⊤q2=−0.48+0.48=0. Orthonormal. Step 3, coordinates: q1⊤x=3 and q2⊤x=−4. Step 4, check: 3q1−4q2=(1.8+3.2, 2.4−2.4)=(5,0).

mlmaths:06.08.q: Q=(0−110). Check Q⊤Q=I, compute Q(3,4), and undo it.
mlmaths:06.08.s: Step 1, the columns (0,1) and (−1,0) have length 1 and dot product 0, so Q⊤Q=I. Step 2, Q(3,4)=(−4,3), still length 5. Step 3, Q−1=Q⊤=(01−10), and Q⊤(−4,3)=(3,4).

mlmaths:06.09.q: Let u=(1,0). Write H=I−2uu⊤, apply it to (3,4), and give det⁡H.
mlmaths:06.09.s: Step 1, uu⊤=(1000), so H=(−1001). Step 2, H(3,4)=(−3,4): mirrored across the vertical axis. Step 3, det⁡H=−1, as for every reflection.

mlmaths:06.10.q: S is the line through (0,0,1) in ℝ3. Describe S⊥ and split (2,3,5) into its two parts.
mlmaths:06.10.s: Step 1, S⊥ is every x with x⊤(0,0,1)=0, i.e. x3=0: the horizontal plane. Step 2, (2,3,5)=(0,0,5)+(2,3,0), one part in each. Step 3, dimensions 1+2=3.

mlmaths:06.11.q: κ(A)=105 in float64 (about 16 digits). Roughly how many correct digits can you expect when solving least squares via QR, and via the normal equations A⊤Ax=A⊤y?
mlmaths:06.11.s: Step 1, digits lost is about log⁡10κ. Step 2, QR works with κ(A)=105: lose about 5, keep about 11. Step 3, the normal equations work with κ(A⊤A)=1010: lose about 10, keep about 6.
mlmaths:06.11.t: Why Numerical Code Uses Orthogonal Matrices

mlmaths:06.12.q: A 50-layer linear network uses random orthogonal 64×64 matrices. What is ∥Q50⋯Q1x∥ for a unit vector x? What changes with scaled Gaussian matrices?
mlmaths:06.12.s: Step 1, each Qi keeps length, so the product does: the output has length exactly 1, for every input. Step 2, Gaussian layers stretch some directions and squeeze others. Step 3, over 50 layers these effects multiply, so a few directions are amplified and many are crushed; the output length depends strongly on the input.

mlmaths:06.13.q: Project b=(1,2,3) onto the line through a=(1,1,1). Give the projection and residual, and check they are perpendicular.
mlmaths:06.13.s: Step 1, a⊤b=6 and a⊤a=3, so the coefficient is 2 and p=(2,2,2). Step 2, r=b−p=(−1,0,1). Step 3, a⊤r=−1+0+1=0. Step 4, the mean of b is 2: projecting onto (1,1,1) replaced each entry by the mean, and r is b centred.

mlmaths:06.14.q: Project b=(2,3,5) onto the plane spanned by (1,0,0) and (0,1,0).
mlmaths:06.14.s: Step 1, A⊤A=I and A⊤b=(2,3), so x^=(2,3). Step 2, p=Ax^=(2,3,0). Step 3, the residual (0,0,5) points straight up, perpendicular to the floor.

mlmaths:06.15.q: For u=(0.6,0.8), write P=uu⊤. Check P2=P, find its trace, and apply I−P to u.
mlmaths:06.15.s: Step 1, P=(0.360.480.480.64). Step 2, P2=u(u⊤u)u⊤=uu⊤=P since u⊤u=1. Step 3, tr⁡P=0.36+0.64=1, the dimension of the line. Step 4, (I−P)u=u−u=0: the complement kills u.

mlmaths:06.16.q: Apply Gram-Schmidt to a1=(1,1,0) and a2=(1,0,1).
mlmaths:06.16.s: Step 1, q1=(1,1,0)/2. Step 2, q1⊤a2=1/2, so the part of a2 along q1 is 12(1,1,0). Step 3, v2=(1,0,1)−(12,12,0)=(12,−12,1), with length 3/2. Step 4, q2=(1,−1,2)/6. Check q1⊤q2=0.

mlmaths:06.17.q: For a1=(2,0), a2=(1,2), write A=QR using the Gram-Schmidt result q1=(1,0), q2=(0,1).
mlmaths:06.17.s: Step 1, r11=∥a1∥=2. Step 2, r12=q1⊤a2=1. Step 3, r22=∥v2∥=2. Step 4, Q=I and R=(2102); indeed QR=A.

mlmaths:06.18.q: Classical Gram-Schmidt on a matrix with κ(A)=108 in float64 can give ∥Q⊤Q−I∥ near what size? And Householder QR?
mlmaths:06.18.s: Step 1, classical Gram-Schmidt's loss of orthogonality grows with roughly κ2ϵ where ϵ≈10−16, so with κ=108 it can reach order 1: orthogonality is lost completely. Step 2, Householder QR stays near ϵ≈10−16 whatever κ is.

mlmaths:07.01.q: Expand x⊤Ax for A=(2113) and evaluate it at x=(1,−1). Then write q(x)=x12−6x1x2+4x22 as x⊤Bx.
mlmaths:07.01.s: Step 1, x⊤Ax=2x12+x1x2+x2x1+3x22=2x12+2x1x2+3x22. Step 2, at (1,−1): 2−2+3=3. Step 3, for q: the diagonal is (1,4) and the cross coefficient −6 is split evenly, so B=(1−3−34).

mlmaths:07.02.q: Classify x⊤Ax for A=(1221) and give the directions where it curves up and down.
mlmaths:07.02.s: Step 1, trace 2, determinant 1−4=−3, so λ2−2λ−3=(λ−3)(λ+1)=0. Step 2, λ=3 with eigenvector (1,1) and λ=−1 with (1,−1). Step 3, mixed signs: a saddle, curving up along (1,1) and down along (1,−1).

mlmaths:07.03.q: For A=diag⁡(1,100), where does the level set x⊤Ax=1 cross each axis? How elongated is it?
mlmaths:07.03.s: Step 1, x⊤Ax=x12+100x22. Step 2, on the x1-axis, x12=1 gives ±1=±1/1. Step 3, on the x2-axis, 100x22=1 gives ±0.1=±1/100. Step 4, the ellipse is 10 times longer than it is tall; the ratio is 100/1=κ.

mlmaths:07.04.q: For f(x,y)=ex+y2 at (0,0), write the second-order approximation and evaluate it at d=(0.1,0.2). Compare with the true value.
mlmaths:07.04.s: Step 1, f(0,0)=1, ∇f=(ex,2y)=(1,0), H=diag⁡(ex,2)=diag⁡(1,2). Step 2, the approximation is 1+d1+12(d12+2d22). Step 3, at (0.1,0.2): 1+0.1+12(0.01+0.08)=1.145. Step 4, true: e0.1+0.04=1.14517. Very close.

mlmaths:07.05.q: Classify the critical point at the origin of f(x,y)=x2+4xy+y2.
mlmaths:07.05.s: Step 1, the gradient (2x+4y, 4x+2y) is zero at the origin. Step 2, H=(2442), trace 4, determinant −12. Step 3, λ2−4λ−12=(λ−6)(λ+2), so λ=6,−2. Step 4, mixed signs: a saddle. Along (t,t), f=6t2; along (t,−t), f=−2t2.

mlmaths:07.06.q: Gradient descent on f=12x⊤Ax with A=diag⁡(1,100). With η=0.019, what happens to each coordinate, and about how many steps shrink the first coordinate 1000 times? What happens with η=0.021?
mlmaths:07.06.s: Step 1, each step multiplies x1 by 1−η and x2 by 1−100η. Step 2, with η=0.019: factors 0.981 and −0.9; x2 flips sign and shrinks. Step 3, 0.981k=10−3 gives k=ln⁡(10−3)/ln⁡(0.981)≈360 steps. Step 4, with η=0.021 the factor for x2 is −1.1: it grows 10% per step and diverges. The cut-off is 2/λmax⁡=0.02.

mlmaths:07.07.q: For A=(3045), compute ∥Ae1∥, ∥Ae2∥ and ∥A(1,1)/2∥. Which is the largest stretch?
mlmaths:07.07.s: Step 1, Ae1=(3,4), length 5. Step 2, Ae2=(0,5), length 5. Step 3, A(1,1)/2=(3,9)/2, length 90/2=45≈6.71. Step 4, the third is largest; in fact 45=σ1, the maximum over all unit vectors.

mlmaths:07.08.q: Find the singular values of A=(3045) by hand via A⊤A, and check two identities.
mlmaths:07.08.s: Step 1, A⊤A=(25202025). Step 2, trace 50, determinant 225, so λ2−50λ+225=0 and λ=45,5. Step 3, σ1=45≈6.71, σ2=5≈2.24. Step 4, checks: σ1σ2=15=∣det⁡A∣ and σ12+σ22=50=9+16+25, the sum of squared entries.

mlmaths:07.09.q: A matrix has singular values 10,5,1,0.1. What is its rank, what share of ∥A∥F2 does the first piece carry, and the first two together?
mlmaths:07.09.s: Step 1, all four are non-zero, so rank 4. Step 2, ∑σi2=100+25+1+0.01=126.01. Step 3, first piece: 100/126.01≈79.4%. Step 4, first two: 125/126.01≈99.2%.
mlmaths:07.09.t: The SVD as a Sum of Rank-1 Pieces

mlmaths:07.10.q: A matrix has singular values 10,5,1,0.1. Give the spectral and Frobenius errors of its best rank-2 approximation.
mlmaths:07.10.s: Step 1, spectral error is the first dropped value, σ3=1. Step 2, Frobenius error is 12+0.12=1.01≈1.005. Step 3, relative to ∥A∥F=126.01≈11.2, that is about 9%.

mlmaths:07.11.q: A 1024×1024 layer is replaced by its rank-64 truncation, which keeps 90% of ∥W∥F2. What fraction of the parameters is stored, and what is the relative Frobenius error?
mlmaths:07.11.s: Step 1, the factors hold 64×1024×2=131,072 numbers against 1,048,576: 12.5%. Step 2, 10% of the squared norm is dropped, so the relative error is 0.1≈0.32. Step 3, that error is in the weights; whether the model still works depends on which input directions it hits, so check validation loss and usually fine-tune briefly.

mlmaths:07.12.q: A=(122436) and b=(1,2,3). All solutions of Ax=b satisfy x1+2x2=1. Which one does A+b return?
mlmaths:07.12.s: Step 1, A has rank 1, so there is a line of solutions. Step 2, the shortest point on the line x1+2x2=1 is its projection of the origin: along the normal (1,2), x=15(1,2)=(0.2,0.4). Step 3, that is what A+b gives.
mlmaths:07.12.t: The Pseudoinverse and Other SVD Tools

mlmaths:08.01.q: Fit y=β0+β1x to (0,1),(1,2),(2,2),(3,4). Give the coefficients, residuals, and check the residuals are perpendicular to both columns.
mlmaths:08.01.s: Step 1, xˉ=1.5, yˉ=2.25, Sxx=5, Sxy=4.5. Step 2, slope 4.5/5=0.9, intercept 2.25−0.9⋅1.5=0.9. Step 3, predictions 0.9,1.8,2.7,3.6; residuals 0.1,0.2,−0.7,0.4. Step 4, they sum to 0 (perpendicular to the ones column), and 0+0.2−1.4+1.2=0 (perpendicular to the x column).

mlmaths:08.02.q: Why prefer np.linalg.lstsq(X, y) over np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X) @ X.T @ y? What does each do if one column of X duplicates another?
mlmaths:08.02.s: Step 1, forming X⊤X squares κ: 106 becomes 1012, losing about 12 of 16 digits instead of 6. Step 2, with a duplicated column, X⊤X is singular: inv raises an error or, after rounding, returns huge meaningless numbers. Step 3, lstsq detects the reduced rank and returns the minimum-norm solution, splitting the weight equally between the two copies. Step 4, the fitted values Xβ^ are the same in every case; only the coefficients are ambiguous.

mlmaths:08.03.q: Houses of 50, 80 and 120 m² sold for 150, 210 and 320 thousand. Write X and y, and say which house has the most leverage.
mlmaths:08.03.s: Step 1, X=(1501801120), y=(150,210,320). Step 2, for a line, hii=1n+(xi−xˉ)2/Sxx, with xˉ≈83.3. Step 3, the 120 m² house is farthest from the mean, so it has the most leverage (about 0.878).

mlmaths:08.04.q: For the four points (0,1),(1,2),(2,2),(3,4) the line fit has SSE =0.70. Compute SST, R2 and σ^2.
mlmaths:08.04.s: Step 1, yˉ=2.25; SST =1.5625+0.0625+0.0625+3.0625=4.75. Step 2, R2=1−0.70/4.75≈0.853. Step 3, n=4, p=2, so σ^2=0.70/2=0.35.

mlmaths:08.05.q: A centred X has singular values 10 and 0.1, and λ=1. By what factor is each direction shrunk, and why is that usually good?
mlmaths:08.05.s: Step 1, direction 1: 100/101≈0.99, almost untouched. Step 2, direction 2: 0.01/1.01≈0.0099, almost removed. Step 3, the OLS variance along direction i is proportional to 1/σi2, so direction 2 is 104 times noisier. Ridge trades a little bias for a large drop in variance exactly where the data says little.

mlmaths:08.06.q: Data points (1,2),(2,4),(3,6). Centre them, compute S, and find the variance of the projection onto w=(1,0).
mlmaths:08.06.s: Step 1, means (2,4); centred points (−1,−2),(0,0),(1,2). Step 2, S11=(1+0+1)/2=1, S22=(4+0+4)/2=4, S12=(2+0+2)/2=2. Step 3, S=(1224), and w⊤Sw=S11=1.

mlmaths:08.07.q: S=(21.51.52). Find the principal components and the share of variance the first one explains.
mlmaths:08.07.s: Step 1, trace 4, determinant 4−2.25=1.75, so λ2−4λ+1.75=0 and λ=3.5,0.5. Step 2, eigenvectors (1,1)/2 for 3.5 and (1,−1)/2 for 0.5. Step 3, the first explains 3.5/4=87.5%.
mlmaths:08.07.t: Principal Components as Directions of Maximum Variance

mlmaths:08.08.q: Data has covariance eigenvalues 3.5 and 0.5. Keeping one component, what is the average squared reconstruction error per sample?
mlmaths:08.08.s: Step 1, the discarded eigenvalue is 0.5. Step 2, by the Pythagoras split of lesson 08.07, average squared error equals discarded variance: 0.5 (up to the n versus n−1 factor). Step 3, that is 0.5/4=12.5% of the total.

mlmaths:08.09.q: Covariance eigenvalues are 4.0, 2.5, 1.0, 0.3, 0.2. How many components explain at least 85%? Keeping 2, what is the mean squared reconstruction error?
mlmaths:08.09.s: Step 1, total 8.0. Step 2, cumulative: 50%, 81.25%, 93.75%. So 3 components. Step 3, keeping 2 discards 1.0+0.3+0.2=1.5, i.e. 18.75% of the total.

mlmaths:09.01.q: A model y^=w1x1+w2x2 has squared loss L=(y^−y)2 on one example x=(1,2), y=3. Write L as a function of (w1,w2) and evaluate it at (1,1) and (1,0).
mlmaths:09.01.s: Step 1, y^=w1+2w2, so L(w1,w2)=(w1+2w2−3)2. Step 2, at (1,1): (1+2−3)2=0. Step 3, at (1,0): (1−3)2=4.

mlmaths:09.02.q: For f(x,y)=x2+y2, write the slice at y=1 and the slice along the line through the origin in direction (1,1)/2.
mlmaths:09.02.s: Step 1, at y=1: f(x,1)=x2+1, a parabola one unit up. Step 2, along t(1,1)/2: f=t2/2+t2/2=t2, a parabola through 0.

mlmaths:09.03.q: Describe the level set x2+4y2=4 and check that (2,0) and (0,1) lie on it.
mlmaths:09.03.s: Step 1, divide by 4: x2/4+y2=1, an ellipse crossing the x-axis at ±2 and the y-axis at ±1. Step 2, (2,0): 4+0=4. Step 3, (0,1): 0+4=4. Both lie on it.

mlmaths:09.04.q: For f(x,y)=x2+100y2, how far must you walk along each axis from the origin to reach f=1?
mlmaths:09.04.s: Step 1, along x: x2=1, so 1 unit. Step 2, along y: 100y2=1, so 0.1 units. Step 3, the contours are 10 times tighter in y: the function is 10 times steeper that way.

mlmaths:09.05.q: For w=(3,4), b=−5, find the signed distance from x0=(3,2) to the boundary, and which side it is on.
mlmaths:09.05.s: Step 1, w⊤x0+b=9+8−5=12. Step 2, ∥w∥=5, so the distance is 12/5=2.4. Step 3, positive, so x0 is on the side w points to.

mlmaths:09.06.q: Classify the level sets of f(x,y)=x2−y2. What does the level set f=0 look like?
mlmaths:09.06.s: Step 1, A=diag⁡(1,−1) is indefinite, so f is a saddle. Step 2, f=c≠0 gives hyperbolas. Step 3, f=0 means x2=y2: the two lines y=x and y=−x crossing at the saddle point.

mlmaths:09.07.q: A model outputs probability p=0 for the true class. What is the cross-entropy −log⁡p, and how do frameworks avoid it?
mlmaths:09.07.s: Step 1, −log⁡0=+∞: the loss is infinite and its gradient is undefined. Step 2, one fix is clamping: −log⁡max⁡(p,ϵ). Step 3, the standard fix is to compute from logits with log_softmax, which never forms a probability that could round to zero.

mlmaths:09.08.q: Is (0.6,0.7) in the open unit ball around the origin? Is the set {(x,y):x>0} open?
mlmaths:09.08.s: Step 1, ∥(0.6,0.7)∥=0.36+0.49=0.85≈0.92<1: yes. Step 2, for a point with x=a>0, the ball of radius a around it stays in x>0. So the half-plane is open.

mlmaths:09.09.q: Find lim⁡(x,y)→(1,2)(x2y+3) and lim⁡(x,y)→(0,0)x2yx2+y2.
mlmaths:09.09.s: Step 1, the first is a polynomial, so plug in: 1⋅2+3=5. Step 2, for the second, ∣x2y∣/(x2+y2)≤∣y∣ because x2≤x2+y2. Step 3, ∣y∣→0, so the limit is 0 (squeeze).

mlmaths:09.10.q: Show that lim⁡(x,y)→(0,0)xyx2+y2 does not exist.
mlmaths:09.10.s: Step 1, along y=0: 0/x2=0. Step 2, along y=x: x2/(2x2)=1/2. Step 3, along y=mx: m/(1+m2), which depends on m. Different paths give different values, so there is no limit.

mlmaths:09.11.q: Is f(x,y)=xy/(x2+y2) with f(0,0)=0 continuous at the origin? Is ReLU⁡(w⊤x) continuous in w?
mlmaths:09.11.s: Step 1, the limit at the origin does not exist (lesson 09.10), so f is not continuous there. Step 2, w↦w⊤x is linear and ReLU is continuous, and a composition of continuous functions is continuous. So yes.

mlmaths:09.12.q: For f(x,y)=x2y+sin⁡y, find fx and fy, and evaluate both at (1,0).
mlmaths:09.12.s: Step 1, treat y as a constant: fx=2xy. Step 2, treat x as a constant: fy=x2+cos⁡y. Step 3, at (1,0): fx=0 and fy=1+1=2.

mlmaths:09.13.q: With x=2, y=5, w=1, b=0, compute L, ∂L/∂w and ∂L/∂b. Which way should each move?
mlmaths:09.13.s: Step 1, prediction 2, error −3, L=9. Step 2, ∂L/∂w=2(−3)(2)=−12. Step 3, ∂L/∂b=2(−3)=−6. Step 4, both negative, so increasing either lowers the loss; w matters twice as much because its input is 2.

mlmaths:09.14.q: For f(x,y)=x2y+sin⁡y, compute all four second partials.
mlmaths:09.14.s: Step 1, fx=2xy, fy=x2+cos⁡y. Step 2, fxx=2y, fyy=−sin⁡y. Step 3, fxy=∂y(2xy)=2x and fyx=∂x(x2+cos⁡y)=2x. Equal, as Schwarz's theorem says.

mlmaths:09.15.q: For f(x,y)=x2+3xy at (1,2), find the rate of change in the direction of (3,4).
mlmaths:09.15.s: Step 1, fx=2x+3y=8, fy=3x=3. Step 2, unit direction u=(0.6,0.8). Step 3, Duf=8⋅0.6+3⋅0.8=7.2.

mlmaths:09.16.q: f(x,y)=xy/(x2+y2) with f(0,0)=0. Do its partials exist at the origin? Is it differentiable there?
mlmaths:09.16.s: Step 1, on both axes f=0, so fx(0,0)=fy(0,0)=0. Step 2, but on the diagonal f=1/2, so f is not even continuous at the origin. Step 3, a function that is not continuous cannot be differentiable. Partials exist; differentiability fails.

mlmaths:09.17.q: f(x,y)=x2+y2 at (1,2) with step d=(0.1,−0.2). Predict the change in f linearly, then compare with the true change.
mlmaths:09.17.s: Step 1, ∇f=(2,4), so the predicted change is 0.2−0.8=−0.6. Step 2, the true value at (1.1,1.8) is 1.21+3.24=4.45, a change of −0.55. Step 3, the gap 0.05=12d⊤Hd=12⋅2⋅(0.01+0.04).

mlmaths:09.18.q: z=xy with x=t2, y=3t. Find dz/dt at t=1 by the chain rule and check directly.
mlmaths:09.18.s: Step 1, at t=1: x=1, y=3. Step 2, path through x: y⋅2t=6. Path through y: x⋅3=3. Step 3, total 9. Step 4, directly z=3t3, so dz/dt=9t2=9.

mlmaths:09.19.q: For L=(wx+b−y)2 with x=2, y=5, w=1, b=0, run the forward and backward passes through the nodes u=wx, v=u+b, e=v−y, L=e2.
mlmaths:09.19.s: Step 1, forward: u=2, v=2, e=−3, L=9. Step 2, backward: ∂L/∂e=2e=−6. Step 3, ∂L/∂v=−6, ∂L/∂b=−6, ∂L/∂u=−6. Step 4, ∂L/∂w=−6⋅x=−12.
mlmaths:09.19.t: The Chain Rule on Computation Graphs

mlmaths:09.20.q: A forward-difference check with h=10−5 in float64 shows relative errors around 10−5. Is backprop wrong?
mlmaths:09.20.s: Step 1, forward differences have leftover error h2f′′, about 10−5: exactly this size for a correct gradient. Step 2, switch to central differences: error about h2=10−10 plus rounding 10−16/10−5=10−11. Step 3, a correct gradient then shows errors near 10−7 or less; 10−2 would mean a real bug.

mlmaths:09.21.q: For f(x,y)=x2+3xy, write ∇f and evaluate it at (1,2).
mlmaths:09.21.s: Step 1, fx=2x+3y and fy=3x. Step 2, ∇f=(2x+3y, 3x). Step 3, at (1,2): (8,3).

mlmaths:09.22.q: For f(x,y)=x2+3xy at (1,2), what is the maximum rate of increase, and in which direction is the rate zero?
mlmaths:09.22.s: Step 1, ∇f=(8,3), so the maximum rate is 73≈8.54. Step 2, the rate is zero for directions perpendicular to (8,3), such as (3,−8)/73.

mlmaths:09.23.q: For f(x,y)=x2+4y2 at (2,0) on the level set f=4, find ∇f and the tangent direction of the curve.
mlmaths:09.23.s: Step 1, ∇f=(2x,8y)=(4,0). Step 2, at (2,0) the ellipse is at its rightmost point, so its tangent is vertical, (0,1). Step 3, (4,0)⋅(0,1)=0: perpendicular.
mlmaths:09.23.t: Gradients Are Perpendicular to Level Sets

mlmaths:09.24.q: For f(x,y)=x2+y2, what is −∇f at (1,0), (0,2) and (−1,−1)? Where do all arrows point?
mlmaths:09.24.s: Step 1, −∇f=(−2x,−2y). Step 2, (−2,0), (0,−4), (2,2). Step 3, every arrow points at the origin, the minimum, and longer arrows sit further away.

mlmaths:09.25.q: Write the layer h=ReLU⁡(Wx) with W=(1−120) as two component functions and evaluate at x=(1,3).
mlmaths:09.25.s: Step 1, h1=ReLU⁡(x1−x2), h2=ReLU⁡(2x1). Step 2, at (1,3): h1=ReLU⁡(−2)=0, h2=2.

mlmaths:09.26.q: For r(t)=(cos⁡t,sin⁡t), find the velocity at t=0 and the speed.
mlmaths:09.26.s: Step 1, r′(t)=(−sin⁡t,cos⁡t). Step 2, at t=0: (0,1). Step 3, speed ∥r′∥=sin⁡2t+cos⁡2t=1 for every t.

mlmaths:09.27.q: One example x=(1,2), label y=1, logistic weights w=(0,0). Compute the gradient and one step with η=0.1.
mlmaths:09.27.s: Step 1, z=0, σ(z)=0.5. Step 2, gradient (0.5−1)x=(−0.5,−1). Step 3, w←(0,0)−0.1(−0.5,−1)=(0.05,0.1). Step 4, now z=0.25 and σ≈0.562: closer to the label.

mlmaths:09.28.q: Compute the Jacobian of F(x,y)=(x2y, x+3y) at (1,2).
mlmaths:09.28.s: Step 1, row 1 from x2y: (2xy, x2)=(4,1). Step 2, row 2 from x+3y: (1,3). Step 3, J=(4113).

mlmaths:09.29.q: For F(x,y)=(x2y, x+3y) at (1,2), predict F(1.01,2) with the Jacobian and compare with the exact value.
mlmaths:09.29.s: Step 1, F(1,2)=(2,7), J=(4113). Step 2, Jd=J(0.01,0)=(0.04,0.01). Step 3, prediction (2.04,7.01); exact (2.0402,7.01).

mlmaths:09.30.q: F(x)=Wx with W=(1201) and G(y)=∥y∥2. Find ∇x(G∘F) at x=(1,1).
mlmaths:09.30.s: Step 1, y=Wx=(3,1). Step 2, JG=2y⊤=(6,2). Step 3, JF=W. Step 4, JGJF=(6,2)W=(6, 12+2)=(6,14).
mlmaths:09.30.t: The Chain Rule as Jacobian Products

mlmaths:09.31.q: A model maps 106 parameters to a scalar loss. How many passes does each mode need for the full gradient?
mlmaths:09.31.s: Step 1, forward mode gives one directional derivative per pass, so 106 passes. Step 2, reverse mode gives the whole gradient in one backward pass, at a few times the cost of the forward pass. Step 3, forward mode wins when inputs are few and outputs many.

mlmaths:09.32.q: For polar coordinates (x,y)=(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ), compute det⁡J.
mlmaths:09.32.s: Step 1, J=(cos⁡θ−rsin⁡θsin⁡θrcos⁡θ). Step 2, det⁡J=rcos⁡2θ+rsin⁡2θ=r. Step 3, small polar boxes far from the origin cover more area.

mlmaths:09.33.q: For f(x,y)=x2+3xy+5y2, compute ∇f, its Jacobian H, and one Newton step from (1,1).
mlmaths:09.33.s: Step 1, ∇f=(2x+3y, 3x+10y)=(5,13) at (1,1). Step 2, H=(23310). Step 3, d=−H−1(5,13); since ∇f=H(x,y) for this quadratic, d=−(1,1) and the step lands on the minimum (0,0).
mlmaths:09.33.t: The Hessian as the Jacobian of the Gradient

mlmaths:09.34.q: L is a scalar, W is 3×5, X is n×3 and G=∂L/∂(XW) is n×5. Which of XG, X⊤G, GX⊤ can be ∇WL?
mlmaths:09.34.s: Step 1, ∇WL must be 3×5. Step 2, XG needs 3=n: generally invalid. Step 3, X⊤G is (3×n)(n×5)=3×5: valid. Step 4, GX⊤ is n×n: wrong shape.

mlmaths:09.35.s: Step 1, f=∑i,jAijxixj. Step 2, terms with xk have i=k or j=k. Step 3, ∂f/∂xk=∑jAkjxj+∑iAikxi=(Ax)k+(A⊤x)k. Step 4, so ∇f=(A+A⊤)x.
mlmaths:09.35.t: Gradients of Linear and Quadratic Functions

mlmaths:09.36.q: Use differentials to find ∇Xtr⁡(AX).
mlmaths:09.36.s: Step 1, dL=tr⁡(A dX). Step 2, match with tr⁡(G⊤dX): G⊤=A. Step 3, ∇XL=A⊤.

mlmaths:09.37.q: Derive ∇WL for L=12∥XW−Y∥F2 and check its shape.
mlmaths:09.37.s: Step 1, R=XW−Y, L=12tr⁡(R⊤R). Step 2, dL=tr⁡(R⊤dR) and dR=X dW. Step 3, dL=tr⁡(R⊤X dW), so G=X⊤R. Step 4, shape: (d×n)(n×k)=d×k, same as W.

mlmaths:09.38.q: X=(1234), G=(1−1). Compute ∂L/∂W.
mlmaths:09.38.s: Step 1, X⊤G=(1324)(1−1). Step 2, =(−2−2). Step 3, shape 2×1, same as W.

mlmaths:09.39.q: Approximate the area under f(x)=x2 on [0,1] with 4 strips using right endpoints.
mlmaths:09.39.s: Step 1, Δx=0.25, points 0.25,0.5,0.75,1. Step 2, heights 0.0625,0.25,0.5625,1, sum 1.875. Step 3, area ≈0.25×1.875=0.46875. The exact value is 1/3; right endpoints overestimate an increasing function.
mlmaths:09.39.t: Area Under a Curve by Partitions

mlmaths:09.40.q: With n=4 on [0,1] for x2, compute the midpoint sum.
mlmaths:09.40.s: Step 1, midpoints 0.125,0.375,0.625,0.875. Step 2, squares 0.015625,0.140625,0.390625,0.765625, sum 1.3125. Step 3, times 0.25: 0.328125, already within 0.005 of 1/3.

mlmaths:09.41.q: Compute ∫−11x dx and ∫−11∣x∣ dx from the picture.
mlmaths:09.41.s: Step 1, x is negative on [−1,0] and positive on [0,1] with equal triangles of area 1/2: they cancel, so ∫x=0. Step 2, ∣x∣ gives two positive triangles: ∫∣x∣=1.

mlmaths:09.42.q: Compute ∫01x2 dx with an antiderivative. For the density 2e−2x on x≥0, find P(X≤0.5).
mlmaths:09.42.s: Step 1, x3/3 has derivative x2, so ∫01x2=1/3. Step 2, −e−2x has derivative 2e−2x, so P(X≤0.5)=−e−1+1≈0.632.

mlmaths:09.43.q: With n=2 strips on [0,1] for x2, compute the trapezoid and Simpson estimates.
mlmaths:09.43.s: Step 1, points 0,0.5,1 with values 0,0.25,1. Step 2, trapezoid: 0.5⋅(0/2+0.25+1/2)=0.375. Step 3, Simpson: 0.53(0+4⋅0.25+1)=0.53⋅2=1/3, exact, because Simpson is exact for cubics and below.

mlmaths:09.44.q: For the density p(x)=2x on [0,1], check normalisation and find 𝔼[X] and 𝔼[X2].
mlmaths:09.44.s: Step 1, ∫012x dx=1. Step 2, 𝔼[X]=∫012x2 dx=2/3. Step 3, 𝔼[X2]=∫012x3 dx=1/2.

mlmaths:09.45.q: With N=10,000 samples and σ=2, what is the standard error? How many samples for a tenth of it?
mlmaths:09.45.s: Step 1, 2/10,000=0.02. Step 2, a tenth needs N ten times larger, so N=106.

mlmaths:09.46.q: Estimate ∬(x+y) dA over [0,1]×[0,2] with a 2×2 grid of cells and midpoint heights.
mlmaths:09.46.s: Step 1, the cells are 0.5 wide and 1 tall, so each has area 0.5. Step 2, the midpoints are (0.25,0.5), (0.75,0.5), (0.25,1.5), (0.75,1.5), with heights 0.75,1.25,1.75,2.25. Step 3, the sum is 0.5×6=3, which is the exact answer here because f is linear.

mlmaths:09.47.q: Compute ∬xy2 dA over [0,2]×[0,3] both ways.
mlmaths:09.47.s: Step 1, inner in y: ∫03xy2 dy=9x, then ∫029x dx=18. Step 2, inner in x: ∫02xy2 dx=2y2, then ∫032y2 dy=18. Same answer.

mlmaths:09.48.q: Write ∬Tf dA for the triangle with corners (0,0), (1,0), (1,1) in both orders.
mlmaths:09.48.s: Step 1, outer x from 0 to 1, inner y from 0 to x: ∫01∫0xf dy dx. Step 2, outer y from 0 to 1, inner x from y to 1: ∫01∫y1f dx dy.

mlmaths:09.49.q: Compute ∬D(x2+y2) dA over the unit disc.
mlmaths:09.49.s: Step 1, in polar, x2+y2=r2 and dA=r dr dθ. Step 2, ∫02π∫01r3 dr dθ=2π⋅14=π2.

mlmaths:09.50.q: Under T(u,v)=(2u+v, −u+v), what is the area of the image of the unit square?
mlmaths:09.50.s: Step 1, JT=(21−11). Step 2, det⁡JT=2+1=3. Step 3, the image has area 3×1=3.
mlmaths:09.50.t: Change of Variables With the Jacobian

mlmaths:09.51.q: X and Y are independent standard normals. Compute P(X2+Y2≤1) exactly.
mlmaths:09.51.s: Step 1, the joint density is 12πe−(x2+y2)/2. Step 2, in polar: ∫02π∫0112πe−r2/2r dr dθ=[−e−r2/2]01. Step 3, that is 1−e−1/2≈0.393.
mlmaths:09.51.t: Joint Densities and the Gaussian Integral

mlmaths:09.52.q: Find the critical points of f(x,y)=x3−3x+y2.
mlmaths:09.52.s: Step 1, ∇f=(3x2−3, 2y). Step 2, set both to zero: x=±1, y=0. Step 3, the critical points are (1,0) and (−1,0).

mlmaths:09.53.q: Classify the critical points of f(x,y)=x3−3x+y2.
mlmaths:09.53.s: Step 1, the Hessian is (6x002). Step 2, at (1,0) the eigenvalues are 6,2: a minimum. Step 3, at (−1,0) they are −6,2: a saddle.

mlmaths:09.54.q: For f(x,y)=12(x2+25y2), what is the largest stable step size?
mlmaths:09.54.s: Step 1, the Hessian is diag(1,25), so L=25. Step 2, stability needs η<2/25=0.08.

mlmaths:09.55.q: With β=0.9 and a constant gradient g, what velocity does momentum settle at?
mlmaths:09.55.s: Step 1, at steady state v=0.9v−ηg. Step 2, so 0.1v=−ηg and v=−10ηg. Momentum moves 10 times faster than plain gradient descent on a steady slope.

mlmaths:09.56.q: Find the minimum-norm vector w with a⊤w=1 for a fixed non-zero a. What is the minimum of ∥w∥2?
mlmaths:09.56.s: Step 1, ∇∥w∥2=2w and ∇(a⊤w−1)=a, so 2w=λa. Step 2, substitute into a⊤w=1: λ∥a∥2/2=1, so λ=2/∥a∥2 and w⋆=a/∥a∥2. Step 3, ∥w⋆∥2=1/∥a∥2.

mlmaths:09.57.q: Minimise (x−3)2 subject to x≤1. Find x⋆ and μ.
mlmaths:09.57.s: Step 1, the unconstrained minimum x=3 breaks the constraint, so the wall is tight: x⋆=1. Step 2, stationarity: 2(1−3)+μ=0, so μ=4≥0. Valid.

mlmaths:10.01.q: Roll one fair die. A is "even" and B is "at least 4". Find P(A∪B) and P(A∣B).
mlmaths:10.01.s: Step 1, P(A)=P(B)=0.5 and A∩B={4,6}, so P(A∩B)=1/3. Step 2, P(A∪B)=0.5+0.5−1/3=2/3. Step 3, P(A∣B)=(1/3)/(1/2)=2/3: among {4,5,6}, two are even.

mlmaths:10.02.q: A screening test has sensitivity 99% and specificity 95%. The condition affects 1% of the people tested. A person tests positive: what is the probability they have the condition?
mlmaths:10.02.s: Step 1, P(+∣D)=0.99, P(+∣¬D)=0.05, P(D)=0.01. Step 2, P(+)=0.99×0.01+0.05×0.99=0.0594. Step 3, P(D∣+)=0.0099/0.0594≈0.167. Only about one positive in six is real.

mlmaths:10.03.q: One die. Are "even" and "at least 4" independent? Are two separate fair coin flips?
mlmaths:10.03.s: Step 1, P(even∩at least 4)=1/3 but P(even)P(at least 4)=1/4. Not independent. Step 2, P(both heads)=0.25=0.5×0.5. Independent.

mlmaths:10.04.q: 10,000 samples fall into bins of width 0.1. One bin holds 400 samples. What density does its bar estimate?
mlmaths:10.04.s: Step 1, the fraction in the bin is 400/10,000=0.04. Step 2, divide by the width: 0.04/0.1=0.4.

mlmaths:10.05.q: X has density p(x)=cx2 on [0,1]. Find c and P(X>0.5).
mlmaths:10.05.s: Step 1, ∫01cx2 dx=c/3=1, so c=3. Step 2, P(X>0.5)=∫0.513x2 dx=1−0.125=0.875.

mlmaths:10.06.q: For p(x)=3x2 on [0,1], find F(x) and P(0.5<X≤0.8).
mlmaths:10.06.s: Step 1, F(x)=∫0x3t2 dt=x3. Step 2, F(0.8)−F(0.5)=0.512−0.125=0.387.

mlmaths:10.07.q: Latency is exponential with mean 200 ms. Find the median and the p99.
mlmaths:10.07.s: Step 1, F(x)=1−e−x/200. Step 2, median: e−m/200=0.5, so m=200ln⁡2≈139 ms. Step 3, p99: e−x/200=0.01, so x=200ln⁡100≈921 ms.

mlmaths:10.08.q: Give a formula to sample X with density 3x2 on [0,1] from a uniform U.
mlmaths:10.08.s: Step 1, F(x)=x3. Step 2, solve u=x3: X=U1/3.

mlmaths:10.09.q: Z∼𝒩(0,1) and Y=max⁡(0,Z). What are P(Y=0) and P(Y>1)?

mlmaths:10.10.q: X∼Uniform(0,1) and Y=X2. Find FY and pY.
mlmaths:10.10.s: Step 1, FY(y)=P(X≤y)=y for 0<y≤1. Step 2, pY(y)=12y, which is unbounded near 0 but integrates to 1.
mlmaths:10.10.t: Functions of a Random Variable: the CDF Method

mlmaths:10.11.q: X∼𝒩(0,1) and Y=eX. Find pY.
mlmaths:10.11.s: Step 1, g−1(y)=ln⁡y with derivative 1/y. Step 2, pY(y)=1y2πe−(ln⁡y)2/2 for y>0.

mlmaths:10.12.q: X∼𝒩(70,102). What is P(X>90)?

mlmaths:10.13.q: Z∼𝒩(0,I2) and X=AZ with A=(2003). How does pX(0) compare with pZ(0)?
mlmaths:10.13.s: Step 1, det⁡A=6, so the map stretches area by 6. Step 2, pX(0)=pZ(0)/6=12π/6≈0.0265.
mlmaths:10.13.t: Transformations in Several Dimensions and Normalising Flows

mlmaths:10.14.q: Loss 𝔼[z2] with z=μ+σε. What is ∂/∂μ, and what does the per-sample estimate average to?
mlmaths:10.14.s: Step 1, exactly 𝔼[z2]=μ2+σ2, so the derivative is 2μ. Step 2, per sample ∂z2/∂μ=2z, which averages to 2μ.

mlmaths:10.15.q: X=10 with probability 0.1 and X=0 otherwise. Find 𝔼X.

mlmaths:10.16.q: A classifier gets each of 100 test examples right with probabilities p1,…,p100, possibly correlated. What is the expected number correct?
mlmaths:10.16.s: Step 1, write the count as ∑i𝟏[example i right]. Step 2, each indicator has mean pi. Step 3, by linearity the expected count is p1+⋯+p100, whatever the correlation.

mlmaths:10.17.q: For a fair die, compute 𝔼[X2] and compare it with (𝔼X)2.
mlmaths:10.17.s: Step 1, 𝔼[X2]=(1+4+9+16+25+36)/6=91/6≈15.17. Step 2, (𝔼X)2=3.52=12.25. They differ.

mlmaths:10.18.q: X=10 with probability 0.1, else 0. Find the variance and standard deviation.
mlmaths:10.18.s: Step 1, 𝔼X=1 and 𝔼X2=10. Step 2, Var⁡X=10−1=9, so σ=3.

mlmaths:10.19.q: Per-example gradient components have variance 4. What is the standard deviation of a batch mean with B=64? With B=256?
mlmaths:10.19.s: Step 1, 4/64=0.0625, standard deviation 0.25. Step 2, 4/256=0.015625, standard deviation 0.125. Four times the batch halves the noise.

mlmaths:10.20.q: An exponential distribution has skewness 2. Which is larger, its mean or its median?
mlmaths:10.20.s: Step 1, positive skew means a long right tail. Step 2, the tail pulls the mean up, so the mean (1/λ) is larger than the median (ln 2/λ).

mlmaths:10.21.q: X is 1 or 3 with equal probability. Check Jensen for x2 and for log⁡x.
mlmaths:10.21.s: Step 1, (𝔼X)2=4≤𝔼X2=5. Step 2, 𝔼log⁡X=(ln⁡3)/2≈0.549≤log⁡2≈0.693.

mlmaths:10.22.q: X=10 with probability 0.1, else 0. What does Chebyshev say about P(∣X−1∣≥9), and what is the truth?
mlmaths:10.22.s: Step 1, σ=3, so 9 is k=3 standard deviations. Chebyshev gives at most 1/9≈0.11. Step 2, the truth: ∣X−1∣≥9 only when X=10, probability 0.1. The bound is nearly tight here.

mlmaths:10.23.q: How many test examples guarantee, with probability 95%, that measured accuracy is within 0.03 of the truth?
mlmaths:10.23.s: Step 1, set 2e−2n(0.03)2=0.05. Step 2, n=ln⁡(40)/(2×0.0009)≈2049.4, so 2,050 examples.

mlmaths:10.24.q: Two equal groups: means 160 and 180, each with variance 25. What is the total variance?
mlmaths:10.24.s: Step 1, within: 25. Step 2, between: the means 160 and 180 have variance 102=100. Step 3, total 125, standard deviation about 11.2.
