mlmaths:10.25.q: An email is spam with probability 0.3. Give the mean and variance of the indicator X.
mlmaths:10.25.s: Step 1, mean p=0.3. Step 2, variance 0.3×0.7=0.21.

mlmaths:10.26.q: How many ways can exactly 2 of 5 emails be spam?

mlmaths:10.27.q: 5 emails, each spam with probability 0.3. What is the probability exactly 2 are spam?
mlmaths:10.27.s: Step 1, (52)=10 ways. Step 2, each has probability 0.32⋅0.73=0.03087. Step 3, total ≈0.309.

mlmaths:10.28.q: Each training run succeeds with probability 0.25. What is the chance the first success is run 3, and the expected number of runs?

mlmaths:10.29.q: A service averages 3 failed jobs per hour. What is the chance of no failures in an hour, and of 8 or more?
mlmaths:10.29.s: Step 1, P(0)=e−3≈0.050. Step 2, P(K≥8)≈0.012, about once every 84 hours by chance.

mlmaths:10.30.q: 1000 requests with error rate 1%. Compare the binomial and Poisson probabilities of zero errors.
mlmaths:10.30.s: Step 1, binomial: 0.991000≈4.32×10−5. Step 2, Poisson(10): e−10≈4.54×10−5. Close.
mlmaths:10.30.t: The Poisson as a Limit of the Binomial

mlmaths:10.31.q: A model outputs π=(0.7,0.2,0.1). What is the probability it assigns to the true class 2 (the second one)?
mlmaths:10.31.s: Step 1, it is π2=0.2. Step 2, with one-hot y=(0,1,0), this is ∏kπkyk=0.2.

mlmaths:10.32.q: Logits z=(2,1,0), true class 0. Compute the cross-entropy.
mlmaths:10.32.s: Step 1, e2+e1+e0≈11.11. Step 2, π0=7.39/11.11≈0.665. Step 3, loss −log⁡0.665≈0.408.

mlmaths:10.33.q: Roll a fair die 6 times. What is the chance each face appears exactly once?
mlmaths:10.33.s: Step 1, 6!1!6(1/6)6=720/46656. Step 2, that is about 0.0154.

mlmaths:10.34.q: Hourly errors have mean 3 and variance 12. Is a Poisson model reasonable?
mlmaths:10.34.s: Step 1, a Poisson has variance equal to its mean, 3. Step 2, the data's variance is 4 times that, so the counts are overdispersed and a negative binomial fits better.

mlmaths:10.35.q: What range [−a,a] gives variance 2/512 (He initialisation, nin=512)?

mlmaths:10.36.q: Waiting time has mean 10 minutes. You've waited 10 already. What is the chance of waiting at least 5 more?
mlmaths:10.36.s: Step 1, memorylessness: it is P(X>5)=e−5/10. Step 2, ≈0.61, the same as from the start.

mlmaths:10.37.q: Test scores are 𝒩(70,102). What fraction lies between 50 and 90?
mlmaths:10.37.s: Step 1, 50 and 90 are 2 standard deviations from the mean. Step 2, about 95%.

mlmaths:10.38.q: Give the He standard deviation for nin=512.

mlmaths:10.39.q: What is the mean of Beta(2, 8)? Of Gamma with k=2, θ=3?

mlmaths:10.40.q: Prior Beta(1, 1). You see 3 clicks in 10 views. Give the posterior and its mean.
mlmaths:10.40.s: Step 1, Beta(1 + 3, 1 + 7) = Beta(4, 8). Step 2, mean 4/12≈0.333, versus the raw 0.3.

mlmaths:10.41.q: A residual is 10 standard deviations. How much extra negative log-density does it cost under a Gaussian, a Laplace and a Student-t3?
mlmaths:10.41.s: Step 1, Gaussian: 102/2=50. Step 2, Laplace: 10. Step 3, t3: about 7.

mlmaths:11.01.q: A classifier's accuracy is 90% and the positive rate in the data is 10%. Can you work out its precision from these two numbers alone?
mlmaths:11.01.s: Step 1, precision depends on how predictions and truth combine, cell by cell. Step 2, the two numbers are summaries of each variable separately, so they don't fix the joint table. Precision cannot be determined.

mlmaths:11.02.q: With P(0,0)=0.4, P(0,1)=0.2, P(1,0)=0.1, P(1,1)=0.3, find P(X=Y) and P(X=1 or Y=1).
mlmaths:11.02.s: Step 1, P(X=Y)=0.4+0.3=0.7. Step 2, P(X=1 or Y=1)=1−P(0,0)=0.6.

mlmaths:11.03.q: For the table (0.4,0.2;0.1,0.3), find both marginals.
mlmaths:11.03.s: Step 1, rows: pX=(0.6,0.4). Step 2, columns: pY=(0.5,0.5).

mlmaths:11.04.q: For the table (0.4,0.2;0.1,0.3), find P(Y=1∣X=1) and P(X=1∣Y=1).
mlmaths:11.04.s: Step 1, row X=1 is (0.1,0.3) with sum 0.4, so P(Y=1∣X=1)=0.75. Step 2, column Y=1 is (0.2,0.3) with sum 0.5, so P(X=1∣Y=1)=0.6.

mlmaths:11.05.q: Is the table (0.4,0.2;0.1,0.3) independent?
mlmaths:11.05.s: Step 1, the marginals are (0.6,0.4) and (0.5,0.5). Step 2, independence would need p(0,0)=0.3, but it is 0.4. Not independent.

mlmaths:11.06.q: 90 true positives, 10 false negatives, 60 false positives, 840 true negatives. Find recall, precision and accuracy.
mlmaths:11.06.s: Step 1, recall 90/100=0.9. Step 2, precision 90/150=0.6. Step 3, accuracy (90+840)/1000=0.93.

mlmaths:11.07.q: (X,Y) is uniform on the triangle 0≤y≤x≤1. What is its density?
mlmaths:11.07.s: Step 1, the triangle has area 1/2. Step 2, a constant density with total 1 must be 2 on the triangle.

mlmaths:11.08.q: For the uniform density 2 on 0≤y≤x≤1, find pX and pY.
mlmaths:11.08.s: Step 1, at fixed x, y runs from 0 to x: pX(x)=∫0x2 dy=2x. Step 2, at fixed y, x runs from y to 1: pY(y)=2(1−y).

mlmaths:11.09.q: For the uniform triangle, find p(y∣x=0.5) and 𝔼[Y∣X=0.5].
mlmaths:11.09.s: Step 1, p(0.5,y)=2 on [0,0.5] and pX(0.5)=1. Step 2, so p(y∣0.5)=2 on [0,0.5]: uniform, mean 0.25.

mlmaths:11.10.q: p(x,y)=e−x−y for x,y≥0. Are X and Y independent? Find P(X+Y≤1).
mlmaths:11.10.s: Step 1, it splits as e−x⋅e−y on a quadrant, so yes: two independent Exponential(1) variables. Step 2, P(X+Y≤1)=1−2e−1≈0.264.

mlmaths:11.11.q: A coin has unknown heads probability θ with a uniform prior. You see 7 heads in 10 flips. What is the posterior?
mlmaths:11.11.s: Step 1, the posterior is proportional to θ7(1−θ)3. Step 2, that is Beta(8, 4), with mean 8/12≈0.667.

mlmaths:11.12.q: A regression model predicts mean 3 and σ=0.5 at some x. What range covers about 95% of y there?

mlmaths:11.13.q: For the table (0.4,0.2;0.1,0.3), find 𝔼[XY] and compare it with 𝔼X 𝔼Y.
mlmaths:11.13.s: Step 1, only cell (1,1) has xy≠0, so 𝔼[XY]=0.3. Step 2, 𝔼X 𝔼Y=0.4×0.5=0.2. The gap, 0.1, is the covariance.
mlmaths:11.13.t: Expectations of Functions of Two Variables

mlmaths:11.14.q: For the table (0.4,0.2;0.1,0.3), find 𝔼[Y∣X=0] and 𝔼[Y∣X=1].
mlmaths:11.14.s: Step 1, row 0 rescaled is (2/3,1/3), mean 1/3. Step 2, row 1 rescaled is (0.25,0.75), mean 0.75.

mlmaths:11.15.q: In the uniform triangle, 𝔼[Y∣X]=X/2 and pX(x)=2x. Find 𝔼Y.
mlmaths:11.15.s: Step 1, 𝔼[X/2]=12𝔼X. Step 2, 𝔼X=∫012x2 dx=2/3. Step 3, 𝔼Y=1/3.

mlmaths:11.16.q: Data 1,2,3,10. Compare MSE at the mean and the median, and absolute error at both.
mlmaths:11.16.s: Step 1, the mean is 4, MSE 12.5; the median is 2.5, MSE 14.75. Step 2, absolute error: 3 at the mean, 2.5 at the median. Each loss is minimised by its own centre.
mlmaths:11.16.t: Conditional Expectation as the Best Predictor

mlmaths:11.17.q: X has covariance (4223). What are Var⁡X1, Var⁡X2 and Cov⁡(X1,X2)?
mlmaths:11.17.s: Step 1, the diagonal gives 4 and 3. Step 2, the off-diagonal gives 2.

mlmaths:11.18.q: μ=(1,2), Σ=(4223). Find the mean and variance of X1−X2.
mlmaths:11.18.s: Step 1, a=(1,−1), mean a⊤μ=−1. Step 2, Σa=(2,−1), so a⊤Σa=2+1=3.

mlmaths:11.19.q: X∼𝒩(0,I100). What are 𝔼∥X∥2 and the typical length?
mlmaths:11.19.s: Step 1, tr⁡I=100. Step 2, typical length about 100=10.

mlmaths:11.20.q: Why do random ±1 vectors work for z?
mlmaths:11.20.s: Step 1, each entry has mean 0 and variance 1, and the entries are independent. Step 2, so Cov⁡(z)=I, and the quadratic-form formula gives tr⁡(MI)=tr⁡M.

mlmaths:11.21.q: Hours studied and exam scores: (1,50),(2,60),(3,65),(4,85). Compute the covariance (divide by n).
mlmaths:11.21.s: Step 1, means 2.5 and 65. Step 2, products of deviations: 22.5,2.5,0,30. Step 3, average 13.75.

mlmaths:11.22.q: For the study data, Cov⁡=13.75, σX≈1.118, σY≈12.75. Find ρ.
mlmaths:11.22.s: Step 1, ρ=13.75/(1.118×12.75). Step 2, ≈0.965, a strong positive linear relationship.

mlmaths:11.23.q: Show Cov⁡(X,X2)=0 for standard normal X.
mlmaths:11.23.s: Step 1, Cov⁡=𝔼[X3]−𝔼X 𝔼[X2]. Step 2, 𝔼[X3]=0 by symmetry and 𝔼X=0, so the covariance is 0.

mlmaths:11.24.q: Two models with error variance 1. What is the variance of their average for ρ=0, 0.8 and 1?
mlmaths:11.24.s: Step 1, Var⁡=14(1+1+2ρ)=(1+ρ)/2. Step 2, that gives 0.5, 0.9 and 1.

mlmaths:11.25.q: Σ=(10.80.81). Along which directions do the contours stretch, and by how much?
mlmaths:11.25.s: Step 1, eigenvalues 1.8 and 0.2 with eigenvectors (1,1) and (1,−1). Step 2, spread 1.8≈1.34 along the diagonal and 0.2≈0.45 across it.

mlmaths:11.26.q: X∼𝒩(1,4) and Y∼𝒩(2,9) independently. What is the distribution of 2X−Y?
mlmaths:11.26.s: Step 1, mean 2−2=0. Step 2, variance 4×4+9=25. So 2X−Y∼𝒩(0,25).

mlmaths:11.27.q: μ=(1,2,3), Σ=(410120.500.51). Find the marginal of (X1,X3).
mlmaths:11.27.s: Step 1, keep entries 1 and 3: μ=(1,3). Step 2, Σ=(4001). Step 3, the zero off-diagonal means X1 and X3 are independent.

mlmaths:11.28.q: (X,Y) has means 0, variances 1 and correlation 0.8. Find the distribution of Y given X=1.
mlmaths:11.28.s: Step 1, mean 0+0.8×1=0.8. Step 2, variance 1−0.82=0.36, standard deviation 0.6.

mlmaths:11.29.q: Give the Cholesky factor of (10.80.81) and the sampling formula.
mlmaths:11.29.s: Step 1, L=(100.80.6), since 0.82+0.62=1. Step 2, x1=z1, x2=0.8z1+0.6z2.

mlmaths:12.01.q: A die has variance 35/12. What is the standard deviation of the mean of 25 rolls?
mlmaths:12.01.s: Step 1, Var⁡Xˉ=(35/12)/25. Step 2, standard deviation 35/12/5≈0.342.

mlmaths:12.02.q: Which is the better estimator of a normal population's centre from 11 points: the mean or the median?
mlmaths:12.02.s: Step 1, both are centred on μ. Step 2, for normal data the median's variance is about π/2≈1.57 times the mean's, so the mean is better.

mlmaths:12.03.q: Test accuracy is 0.9 on 1000 examples. What is its standard error?
mlmaths:12.03.s: Step 1, each example is a Bernoulli with variance 0.9×0.1=0.09. Step 2, SE=0.09/1000≈0.0095, about one percentage point.

mlmaths:12.04.q: Data 2,4,6. Compute the variance dividing by n and by n−1.
mlmaths:12.04.s: Step 1, mean 4, squared deviations 4,0,4, sum 8. Step 2, 8/3≈2.67 and 8/2=4.

mlmaths:12.05.q: A running average of die rolls is at 3.9 after 10 rolls. Do later rolls "make up" for the high start?
mlmaths:12.05.s: Step 1, no: each roll is independent with mean 3.5. Step 2, the early excess is not cancelled but diluted, since it is divided by an ever larger n.

mlmaths:12.06.q: Xi∼Exponential(1), n=100. Use the CLT to estimate P(Xˉ>1.2).
mlmaths:12.06.s: Step 1, Xˉ≈𝒩(1,0.01), standard deviation 0.1. Step 2, 1.2 is 2 standard deviations up: P≈0.023. The exact answer is about 0.028.

mlmaths:12.07.q: An estimator has bias −0.2 and variance 0.512. Another has bias 0 and variance 0.8. Which has lower MSE?
mlmaths:12.07.s: Step 1, first: 0.04+0.512=0.552. Step 2, second: 0.8. The biased one wins.
mlmaths:12.07.t: Bias, Variance and Mean Squared Error

mlmaths:12.08.q: Estimate μ from 5 samples with σ=2 using cXˉ. What c minimises the MSE when μ=1?
mlmaths:12.08.s: Step 1, MSE =(c−1)2μ2+c2σ2/n=(c−1)2+0.8c2. Step 2, set the derivative to zero: 2(c−1)+1.6c=0, so c=1/1.8≈0.56.

mlmaths:12.09.q: 100 users each contribute 50 nearly identical rows. Is the effective sample size 5000?
mlmaths:12.09.s: Step 1, no: rows from one user carry mostly the same information. Step 2, the effective size is closer to 100, so the standard error is about 7 times larger than σ/5000 suggests.

mlmaths:12.10.q: Coin data H, H, T, H. Compare L(0.5) and L(0.75).
mlmaths:12.10.s: Step 1, L(0.5)=0.54=0.0625. Step 2, L(0.75)=0.753×0.25≈0.105. The data favour 0.75.

mlmaths:12.11.q: Derive the MLE of p from k successes in n trials.
mlmaths:12.11.s: Step 1, ℓ(p)=klog⁡p+(n−k)log⁡(1−p). Step 2, ℓ′(p)=k/p−(n−k)/(1−p)=0 gives p^=k/n.

mlmaths:12.12.q: Data 2,4,6. Give the Gaussian MLEs.

mlmaths:12.13.q: Show that minimising the Gaussian negative log-likelihood with fixed σ is minimising MSE.
mlmaths:12.13.s: Step 1, each example's NLL is 12log⁡(2πσ2)+(y−f(x))2/(2σ2). Step 2, the first term is constant and the second is squared error times a constant.

mlmaths:12.14.q: Find I(p) for a Bernoulli and the approximate variance of p^.
mlmaths:12.14.s: Step 1, 𝔼[−∂2log⁡p]=1/p+1/(1−p)=1p(1−p). Step 2, Var⁡p^≈p(1−p)/n.
mlmaths:12.14.t: Fisher Information and the Accuracy of the MLE

mlmaths:12.15.q: Beta(2, 2) prior, 3 heads in 3 flips. Compare the MLE and the MAP estimate.
mlmaths:12.15.s: Step 1, MLE 3/3=1. Step 2, the posterior is Beta(5, 2) with peak (5−1)/(5+2−2)=0.8.

mlmaths:12.16.q: A model assigns probabilities 0.1, 0.05, 0.2 and 0.02 to four true tokens. What is its perplexity?
mlmaths:12.16.s: Step 1, the average NLL is −14(ln⁡0.1+ln⁡0.05+ln⁡0.2+ln⁡0.02)≈2.705. Step 2, perplexity e2.705≈14.95.

mlmaths:12.17.q: You compute a 95% interval [0.88,0.92]. Is there a 95% probability the true accuracy is in it?
mlmaths:12.17.s: Step 1, in the frequentist sense, no: the truth is fixed and the interval either contains it or not. Step 2, the 95% is the long-run hit rate of the procedure that produced it.

mlmaths:12.18.q: Ten training runs: mean 5.0, s=2.0. Give the 95% t interval.
mlmaths:12.18.t: Intervals for a Mean: z and t

mlmaths:12.19.q: Zero errors in 200 test cases. What error rate can you rule out?
mlmaths:12.19.s: Step 1, the Wald interval is [0,0], which claims certainty. Step 2, the rule of three gives an upper bound of 3/200=1.5%.

mlmaths:12.20.q: How many examples measure a 90% accuracy to within ±1 point?
mlmaths:12.20.s: Step 1, n=1.962×0.09/0.012≈3457.4. Step 2, round up to 3,458.

mlmaths:12.21.q: Why resample with replacement rather than without?
mlmaths:12.21.s: Step 1, without replacement every resample of size n is the original data. Step 2, with replacement some rows repeat and others drop out, which mimics drawing a fresh sample.

mlmaths:12.22.q: A gets 900 of 1000 right, B gets 910. They disagree on 10 examples, all won by B. Is B better?
mlmaths:12.22.s: Step 1, under "no difference" each disagreement is a fair coin. Step 2, 10 out of 10 has probability about 0.002: strong evidence that B is better.
mlmaths:12.22.t: Comparing Two Models on One Test Set

mlmaths:13.01.q: A teammate flags outliers in a column of per-user purchase amounts by removing rows with |z| > 3, recomputes the mean and standard deviation, and repeats until nothing is removed. What can go wrong, and what would you do instead?
mlmaths:13.01.s: Purchase amounts are right-skewed with a heavy tail, so the first pass is distorted by masking: the biggest values inflate the standard deviation and can hide each other, so some true outliers survive. Iterating then has the opposite failure: each pass shrinks $s$, so ordinary large but legitimate purchases start crossing the threshold and the procedure keeps eating the right tail, biasing the mean and total revenue downwards. Instead, compute fences from order statistics (Tukey's $Q_3 + 1.5\,\mathrm{IQR}$ or a MAD-based robust z with a cutoff near 3.5), which the outliers cannot distort, then inspect what is flagged. Remove only values shown to be errors; for genuine whales, report a robust summary (median, trimmed mean) alongside the mean, or winsorize for modelling, rather than deleting revenue that really happened.
mlmaths:13.01.t: Describing data: location, spread and shape

mlmaths:13.02.q: You measure average session length on 2,000 sessions coming from 200 users (10 sessions each) and compute the SE as s divided by the square root of 2,000. Why is this probably too small, and how would you get a defensible SE?
mlmaths:13.02.s: The formula assumes 2,000 independent observations, but sessions from the same user are correlated: a heavy user has consistently long sessions. With positive within-user correlation the variance of the mean is inflated by a design effect of roughly $1 + (m-1)\rho$ for $m = 10$ sessions per user and intra-user correlation $\rho$; with $\rho = 0.3$ that is 3.7, so the true SE is almost twice the naive one and the effective sample size is closer to 540 than 2,000. A defensible SE treats the user as the unit: compute each user's mean (or total sessions and total time, then use the delta method for the ratio), take the SE across the 200 users, or run a bootstrap that resamples users rather than sessions. Session length is also right-skewed, so check that 200 users is enough, or use a log transform or the bootstrap.

mlmaths:13.03.q: Two models are scored on the same 40 test prompts. A Welch two-sample t-test on the two score columns gives p = 0.30, while a paired t-test gives p = 0.004. Explain how both can be correct calculations and which one answers the question.
mlmaths:13.03.s: Both are arithmetically right but they test different designs. Welch treats the columns as independent groups, so its SE includes the large prompt-to-prompt variation: some prompts are easy for both models, some hard for both. That shared variation swamps a small, consistent difference, giving p = 0.30. The paired test works on per-prompt differences; prompt difficulty cancels because it affects both models, so the SE of the mean difference is far smaller and the same mean gap becomes clearly significant. Since both models saw the same prompts, the observations are paired and the paired test is the correct one; Welch's independence assumption is false here and wastes the design. You should still check that the differences are not dominated by a few prompts (look at their distribution, or use a permutation or sign test) and report the mean difference with its interval.
mlmaths:13.03.t: Hypothesis testing: z, t and p-values

mlmaths:13.04.q: You compare error-type distributions (5 error categories) between two model versions using every logged error: 12,000 errors from version 1 and 11,500 from version 2, collected from 300 users. The chi-square test of independence gives p = 1e-9. What would you check before concluding the versions fail differently?
mlmaths:13.04.s: First, independence: the 23,500 errors come from only 300 users, and a few heavy users with their own peculiar inputs can generate thousands of correlated errors, so the chi-square treats clustered events as independent and the p-value is far too small. Re-run the analysis with the user as the unit, for example per-user error-type proportions compared with a permutation test that shuffles version labels across users, or a user-level bootstrap. Second, confounding: did the same users and traffic mix see both versions, or did version 2 roll out to different segments or later dates? Third, effect size: with 23,500 counts tiny shifts are significant, so inspect standardised residuals $(O-E)/\sqrt E$ per cell to see which categories moved and by how much, and judge whether that matters. Finally, check expected counts in rare categories.
mlmaths:13.04.t: Tests for counts, groups and correlation

mlmaths:13.05.q: You bootstrap the p99 latency of 400 requests to get a 95% confidence interval, and the interval looks oddly narrow and lumpy, sitting on just a few distinct values. Explain why, and what you would do instead.
mlmaths:13.05.s: The p99 of 400 points is determined by the top 4 or 5 order statistics. Every bootstrap resample is built only from the observed values, so its p99 can only land on (or interpolate between) the few largest observations; the replicates take a handful of distinct values and cannot reach beyond the observed maximum. The bootstrap is known to be unreliable for extremes and high quantiles because the empirical distribution has no tail beyond the sample. Options: collect far more requests so the p99 rests on hundreds of tail points; report a lower, better-supported quantile such as p90; use a distribution-free order-statistic interval for the quantile, based on the binomial count of points below it; or fit a tail model (for example a generalized Pareto above a threshold) if extrapolation is needed. Also check that requests are independent; bursts of slow requests would call for a block bootstrap.

mlmaths:13.06.q: A test with 20 secondary metrics runs for two weeks. The primary metric is flat (p = 0.4), but 'time on page for Android users in Germany' is up 12% with p = 0.01. The PM wants to ship. What is your analysis?
mlmaths:13.06.s: The headline result is the primary metric, and it shows no detectable effect. The German Android finding is one of a very large number of metric-by-segment combinations that could have been examined (20 metrics times many segments), so at least one p near 0.01 is expected by chance; with, say, 200 implicit comparisons, a Bonferroni threshold would be 0.00025, and Benjamini-Hochberg would almost certainly not reject a lone 0.01. The segment was also chosen after seeing the data, which invalidates the nominal p-value. The 12% lift is likely inflated by the same selection. Correct move: treat it as a hypothesis, not a result. Do not ship on it; if the segment matters, run a new test pre-registered on that segment and metric, sized by a power calculation, and confirm SRM and guardrails as usual.
mlmaths:13.06.t: A/B testing: design, power and multiple testing

mlmaths:14.01.q: You train linear regression by gradient descent on two features: one in [0, 1], the other in [0, 1000]. Any learning rate above 1e-6 diverges, and at 1e-6 the weight of the first feature barely moves after 10,000 steps. Explain both symptoms with the eigenvalue picture and give the fix.
mlmaths:14.01.s: The Hessian of mean squared error is $X^\top X/n$, whose eigenvalues are roughly the second moments of the features: about 0.33 for the [0, 1] feature and about $3\times10^5$ for the [0, 1000] feature. Stability requires $\eta < 2/L \approx 6.7\times10^{-6}$, so larger rates diverge along the large-scale feature's direction. At $\eta = 10^{-6}$ the small-scale direction contracts by $1 - 10^{-6}\cdot0.33$ per step, so after 10,000 steps it has moved only about 0.3% of the way: the condition number is around $10^6$. Standardise both features (zero mean, unit variance) so the curvatures are comparable; $\kappa$ drops to near 1 (or to whatever the feature correlation implies), a step size near 1 becomes stable, and convergence takes tens of steps. Centring also removes the large coupling with the intercept.

mlmaths:14.02.q: A model trains well with plain SGD at learning rate 0.1. A colleague switches on momentum 0.9 with the same learning rate and the loss immediately diverges. Explain why, and what learning rate would be a sensible first try with momentum.
mlmaths:14.02.s: With momentum the steady-state step is $\eta/(1-\beta)$, so at $\beta = 0.9$ the same $\eta = 0.1$ behaves like a plain step of about 1.0, ten times larger. If 0.1 was near the stability edge for the sharpest directions, ten times that is far past it and the iterates blow up. The larger stability region of heavy ball ($\eta < 2(1+\beta)/L$) only buys a factor of about 1.9, not 10. A sensible first try keeps the effective step similar: $\eta \approx 0.1\cdot(1 - 0.9) = 0.01$, then tune upward. The same logic says that changing beta in any recipe should come with a learning-rate retune, since beta and eta together set the effective step.

mlmaths:14.03.q: You fine-tune a model with Adam plus an L2 penalty and notice that the large embedding rows for frequent tokens keep growing while rarely seen rows shrink towards zero. Explain the mechanism, and how switching to AdamW changes it.
mlmaths:14.03.s: With L2 inside Adam, the penalty gradient $\lambda\theta$ is added to the data gradient and then divided by $\sqrt{\hat v}$. Frequent tokens have large, frequent gradients, so their $\hat v$ is large and the penalty term is scaled down to almost nothing: their rows are effectively unregularised and grow. Rare tokens get few data gradients, so $\hat v$ is small and the same penalty is amplified, pulling those rows strongly to zero on every step even though there is little data to oppose it. The regularisation strength therefore depends on gradient statistics rather than being uniform. AdamW applies decay outside the adaptive scaling, $\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\lambda\theta$, so every row shrinks by the same fraction per step regardless of its gradient history. You would then retune $\lambda$, often excluding embeddings, biases and normalisation parameters from decay.
mlmaths:14.03.t: Adaptive methods: AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam, AdamW

mlmaths:14.04.q: Your cosine-scheduled run is configured for 100k steps, but you have to stop at 60k. A colleague suggests simply taking the 60k checkpoint. Why is that checkpoint likely worse than a run configured for 60k from the start, and how would a warmup-stable-decay schedule have avoided the problem?
mlmaths:14.04.s: At 60% of a cosine schedule the learning rate is still about $\eta_{min} + 0.5(\eta_{max}-\eta_{min})(1+\cos(0.6\pi)) \approx 35\%$ of the peak. The model is therefore still bouncing around in the large noise ball that a high learning rate produces; the annealing phase, where the rate falls towards the floor and the loss drops substantially as iterates settle, never happened. A run configured for 60k would have spent its final steps at a low rate and reached a lower loss. Under warmup-stable-decay the rate is constant on the plateau and decay is a short separate phase, so you can take the 60k plateau checkpoint and run a decay phase of 10-20% of the steps, getting nearly the result of a dedicated 60k run. The general lesson: with cosine, the schedule commits you to $T$ in advance; WSD decouples the stopping decision from the schedule.
mlmaths:14.04.t: Learning-rate schedules: step, cosine, warmup, one-cycle

mlmaths:14.05.q: You need to fit a logistic regression with 50,000 sparse features on 2 million rows that fit in memory. Compare plain gradient descent, Newton's method and L-BFGS for this job and say which you would use.
mlmaths:14.05.s: Gradient descent is cheap per iteration, one pass over the data, but logistic-regression Hessians with many correlated sparse features are badly conditioned, so it needs thousands of passes and a carefully tuned step. Newton's method would converge in perhaps 10 to 20 iterations, but each needs the 50,000 by 50,000 Hessian: 2.5 billion entries (20 GB in fp64) and a factorisation of about $4\times10^{13}$ flops, which is impractical (an iterative solver with Hessian-vector products, truncated Newton, would be the workable form). L-BFGS uses only full gradients, which are exact because the data fit in memory, keeps about $m = 10$ curvature pairs (1 million numbers), uses a Wolfe line search, and typically converges in tens to a few hundred passes without step-size tuning. I would use L-BFGS, which is why scikit-learn makes it the default, with an L2 penalty to make the problem strongly convex; if an L1 penalty were required, a proximal or coordinate method (14.06) would replace it.

mlmaths:14.06.q: You fit a lasso model with PyTorch by adding lam * w.abs().sum() to the loss and running Adam. The validation score is fine, but none of the 2,000 weights is exactly zero, although the lasso solution should have only about 50 non-zeros. Explain why and how to get the sparse solution.
mlmaths:14.06.s: The gradient of $|w_i|$ is $\pm1$ (the framework picks a subgradient at zero), so each step pushes small weights towards zero but overshoots: a weight at 0.001 is pushed past zero and then pushed back, oscillating with an amplitude set by the step size and never landing exactly on 0. Adam makes it worse by normalising each coordinate's step to about $\eta$, so tiny weights keep moving by $\eta$ around zero. The optimiser approximates the lasso objective's value but not its exact zeros. To get the sparse solution, use a method that handles the non-smooth term exactly: proximal gradient (ISTA or FISTA) with soft-thresholding after each gradient step on the smooth loss, or coordinate descent as in scikit-learn's Lasso. Both produce exact zeros. A pragmatic alternative is to threshold the trained weights and refit, but the prox step is the principled fix.
mlmaths:14.06.t: Regularisation as optimisation: penalties, constraints, proximal steps

mltk:01.01.q: X is a C-ordered float32 array of shape (100000, 256). Give X.strides and X.T.strides. Why does X.T cost almost nothing, while X.T.reshape(-1) allocates about 100 MB?
mltk:01.01.s: X.strides is (1024, 4): one row is 256 x 4 = 1024 bytes and neighbours within a row are 4 bytes apart. X.T has shape (256, 100000) and strides (4, 1024). Creating it only writes a new header with the axes and strides swapped, over the same buffer, so the cost does not depend on the array size. reshape(-1) has to return elements in C order of X.T, which means walking down the columns of X: element 0 of row 0, then element 0 of row 1, and so on. In the buffer those elements are 1024 bytes apart, then the next run starts 4 bytes after the first. A single stride cannot describe that sequence for a 1-D result, so NumPy must copy the data into a new contiguous buffer: 100000 x 256 x 4 bytes is about 102 MB.

mltk:01.02.q: You run `X = data[data[:, 0] > 0]` and then `X[:, 1] = 0`. Does `data` change? What changes if you instead write `X = data[5:100]`? And why does `data[data[:, 0] > 0, 1] = 0` behave differently from both?
mltk:01.02.s: With the boolean mask, `X` is a copy because the mask is an advanced index. Setting `X[:, 1] = 0` writes into that new buffer and `data` is unchanged. With `X = data[5:100]`, `X` is a basic slice: a view with a new offset over the same buffer, so `X[:, 1] = 0` zeroes column 1 of rows 5 to 99 of `data`. The single expression `data[data[:, 0] > 0, 1] = 0` is one `__setitem__` call on `data` itself, with the mask selecting rows and `1` selecting the column, so it modifies exactly the masked rows of `data`. No intermediate copy is created. The rule is that indexing a view or copy and then assigning is two operations, while assigning through one combined index is one.

mltk:01.03.q: A softmax over each row of `S` (shape (B, T)) is written as `np.exp(S) / np.exp(S).sum(axis=1)`. When does this raise, when does it silently give the wrong answer, and what is the fix?
mltk:01.03.s: `np.exp(S).sum(axis=1)` has shape (B,). Broadcasting aligns it with the last axis of (B, T), so it lines up with the T columns, not the B rows. If B != T the shapes (B, T) and (B,) are incompatible on the last axis and NumPy raises an error. If B == T (for example a square attention matrix) the shapes match, and element (i, j) is divided by the sum of row j instead of row i. No error is raised, and the rows no longer sum to 1. The fix is `keepdims=True`, giving shape (B, 1), which broadcasts across each row: `e = np.exp(S - S.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)); e / e.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)`. The max shift also prevents overflow.

mltk:01.04.q: A colleague computes binary cross-entropy as `-(y*np.log(sigmoid(z)) + (1-y)*np.log(1-sigmoid(z))).mean()` on float32 logits. For which values of z does this break, how, and how would you rewrite it stably?
mltk:01.04.s: For large positive z (above about 17 in float32) sigmoid(z) rounds to exactly 1.0, so `np.log(1 - sigmoid(z))` is `log(0) = -inf`. If the label is 0, the loss is infinite, and its gradient is `nan`. For large negative z, sigmoid(z) underflows towards 0 (the naive `1/(1+np.exp(-z))` returns exactly 0 below about -89 in float32, when the exponential overflows), giving the same problem on the other term when y = 1. The stable form works in logit space: $\log\sigma(z) = -\log(1+e^{-z})$ and $\log(1-\sigma(z)) = -\log(1+e^{z})$, so the loss is `np.logaddexp(0, z) - y*z`, equivalently `np.maximum(z, 0) - y*z + np.log1p(np.exp(-np.abs(z)))`. No exponent is ever large and positive, nothing rounds to 0 inside a log, and the result is accurate for any z.

mltk:01.05.q: Sensor data `X` has shape (days, sensors, 24) with hourly readings and some NaNs. Write the calls for (a) each sensor's mean over all days and hours, and (b) for each day, the hour at which the average over sensors peaked. What happens in (b) if one day is entirely NaN, and how would you handle it?
mltk:01.05.s: (a) Collapse days and hours, keep sensors: `np.nanmean(X, axis=(0, 2))`, shape (sensors,). (b) First average over sensors for each day and hour: `H = np.nanmean(X, axis=1)`, shape (days, 24). Then collapse the hour axis to a position: `np.nanargmax(H, axis=1)`, shape (days,). If one day is entirely NaN, `nanmean` gives a NaN row with a RuntimeWarning, and `nanargmax` raises ValueError because that row has no valid entry. Handle it explicitly: compute `ok = ~np.isnan(H).all(axis=1)`, fill the bad rows with `-np.inf` (`np.where(np.isnan(H), -np.inf, H)`), take `argmax`, and then set the result for days where `ok` is False to a sentinel such as -1. That way the missing day is visible and is never confused with a real peak at hour 0.

mltk:01.06.q: You have token embeddings `X` of shape (B, T, D) and want multi-head form (B, H, T, D/H). Explain why `X.reshape(B, H, T, D // H)` is wrong, give the correct sequence of calls, and say which step copies memory.
mltk:01.06.s: `reshape` regroups elements in C order. For each batch item, the T x D block is read row by row and cut into H consecutive chunks of T x D/H values. That mixes tokens: the first `head` ends up holding the first T/H tokens' full embeddings rather than the first D/H features of every token. The heads must split the feature axis D, so: `X.reshape(B, T, H, D // H)`, which is a view because it only splits the last axis of a contiguous array, then `.transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)` to get (B, H, T, D/H), also a view since it only permutes strides. Nothing has copied yet. A copy happens only when a later operation needs contiguous memory, for example `np.ascontiguousarray`, a reshape that merges the transposed axes, or handing the array to code that requires C order.

mltk:01.07.q: A ridge regression implementation computes `w = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X + lam * np.eye(d)) @ X.T @ y` with X of shape (1,000,000, 50). Comment on its cost and accuracy, and propose a better version. When would you prefer lstsq instead?
mltk:01.07.s: The expensive part is `X.T @ X`, about $n d^2 = 2.5 \times 10^9$ multiply-adds, which is fine. The inverse is only 50 x 50, so its cost is negligible, but it is still the wrong tool: `np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X + lam * np.eye(d), X.T @ y)` is cheaper and more accurate, and because the matrix is symmetric positive definite, a Cholesky solve (`scipy.linalg.cho_factor` and `cho_solve`) is better still. Also note the evaluation order: `inv(...) @ X.T @ y` multiplies a 50 x 50 matrix by the 50 x 1,000,000 `X.T` first; computing `X.T @ y` first avoids that large intermediate. Accuracy depends on $\kappa(X)^2$ shrunk by the ridge term. When lam is tiny or zero and features are badly scaled or collinear, use `lstsq` on the augmented system `[X; sqrt(lam) I] w = [y; 0]`, which works with $\kappa(X)$ rather than its square.
mltk:01.07.t: Linear algebra and random numbers in NumPy

mltk:02.01.q: A colleague's training script reads `events.csv` with a bare `pd.read_csv(path)`. It worked for months, but after a new export the `item_id` column comes out as `float64` instead of `int64`, a later join on `item_id` against an items table (where it is `int64`) now matches fewer rows, and some ids print as `1.2345678e+07`. What probably changed in the file, why did pandas react this way, and how would you make loading robust?
mltk:02.01.s: The new export almost certainly contains at least one empty or missing `item_id`. NumPy's `int64` has no missing value, so pandas promotes the whole column to `float64` to hold `NaN`. Floats print large integers in scientific notation and, beyond 2^53, cannot represent every integer exactly, so some ids can change value; and the missing rows can never match. The fix is to stop relying on inference: pass `dtype={"item_id": "Int64"}` (nullable integer, missing becomes `pd.NA`) or read ids as `"string"` since they are labels, list the expected missing markers in `na_values`, and restrict to known columns with `usecols`. Then decide explicitly what a missing id means (drop the row, or route it to an 'unknown' bucket) and count how many rows are affected, rather than letting the join silently drop them. The same schema dictionary should be used wherever this file is read, including serving.

mltk:02.02.q: You sort a validation DataFrame by `timestamp`, filter it to rows with `segment == "new_users"`, call `preds = model.predict(val[FEATURES])` and then write `val.loc[:, "pred"] = preds` followed by `metrics = val.groupby("day").apply(...)`. Separately, a teammate computes `val_sorted.loc[0:99]` to look at "the first 100 rows". Which of these steps are correct, which are not, and why?
mltk:02.02.s: Assigning a NumPy array with `val.loc[:, "pred"] = preds` is correct: an array has no index, so pandas assigns it by position in the frame's current row order, which is the order `val[FEATURES]` was passed to the model. The risky variant would be building `pd.Series(preds)` without an index and assigning that: its labels run 0..n-1 while `val`'s index holds the original labels from before sorting and filtering, so alignment would put predictions on the wrong rows or leave NaNs. Either keep raw arrays, or wrap with `pd.Series(preds, index=val.index)`. The teammate's `val_sorted.loc[0:99]` is wrong: `.loc` slices by label, inclusive of the end, and after sorting the labels are no longer in order, so it returns every row positioned between label 0 and label 99 wherever they fell, possibly thousands of rows or none. The positional intent is `val_sorted.iloc[:100]` or `val_sorted.head(100)`. If the filtered frame is also modified later, write with `.loc` on `val` itself rather than through a chained selection, because under Copy-on-Write chained writes are discarded.

mltk:02.03.q: You inherit a fraud dataset of card transactions. `amount` is `object` dtype, about 3% of `merchant_country` values are `""` or `"N/A"`, there are 40,000 rows sharing a `transaction_id` with another row, and a notebook caps `amount` at the 99.5th percentile and fills missing `merchant_country` with the mode, both computed on the whole table before a random train/test split. List what you would check and change, in order, and explain the leakage risks.
mltk:02.03.s: First fix types: inspect why `amount` is text (currency symbols, thousands separators, words like 'refund'), clean with `.str` methods and convert with `pd.to_numeric(errors="coerce")`, then count and examine the values that became NaN rather than dropping them blindly. Next make missing explicit: map `""` and `"N/A"` to NaN (and check whether `read_csv` already turned `"N/A"` into NaN by default), and add a `merchant_country_missing` indicator because missingness may itself be a fraud signal. Then the duplicates: check whether rows sharing a `transaction_id` are exact copies (a double load, so drop) or versions of one transaction (an authorisation and a settlement, say), in which case keep the authoritative one with `sort_values` plus `drop_duplicates(subset="transaction_id", keep=...)`. If duplicates remain and the split is random, the two copies of a transaction can land on either side, inflating test scores, so deduplicate before splitting and prefer a time-based split for fraud. Finally move the fitted steps after the split: compute the 99.5th percentile cap and the mode of `merchant_country` on the training rows only and apply those values to test and serving. Computing them on the whole table leaks test-set information into training features; the effect is usually small for a mode but can matter for caps when the test period has a different amount distribution.

mltk:02.04.q: You build a click-through model on impression logs with columns `user_id`, `ad_id`, `ts` and `clicked`. A teammate adds `ad_ctr = df.groupby("ad_id")["clicked"].transform("mean")` and `user_n_impr = df.groupby("user_id")["ad_id"].transform("size")` on the full log, then does a random 80/20 split. Validation AUC jumps from 0.71 to 0.93. Explain what each feature leaks, and how you would compute them correctly.
mltk:02.04.s: `ad_ctr` is a target encoding computed over all rows, including the row's own `clicked` value and the validation rows. Rare ads are the worst case: an ad with one impression gets `ad_ctr` equal to its own label, and an ad with a few impressions gets a value strongly correlated with each row's label, so the model reads the answer off the feature. `user_n_impr` uses the full log, including impressions that happen after each row's timestamp, which leaks future activity (users who keep getting impressions are by construction active later), and it is computed partly from validation rows. The random split makes it worse because the same users and ads appear on both sides. Correct versions: split by time first (train on earlier days, validate on later ones); compute `ad_ctr` from training-period rows only, with smoothing such as `(clicks + m * global_ctr) / (impressions + m)`, and map it onto validation rows by `ad_id`, filling unseen ads with the global rate; within the training set use out-of-fold or leave-one-out encoding so a row never sees its own label. For `user_n_impr`, count only impressions strictly before each row's `ts`, e.g. `df.sort_values("ts").groupby("user_id").cumcount()`, which is also exactly what can be computed at serving time.

mltk:02.05.q: You train a model to predict whether a support ticket escalates. `tickets` has one row per ticket with `customer_id` and `created_at`. `accounts` is a nightly export with one row per customer per day (`customer_id`, `snapshot_date`, `plan`, `open_tickets`). You write `tickets.merge(accounts, on="customer_id")`. What goes wrong, and what join should you write instead?
mltk:02.05.s: `accounts` has many rows per customer, so the merge is many-to-many: each ticket is repeated once per snapshot of its customer, which explodes the row count (a customer with 400 daily snapshots and 5 tickets yields 2,000 rows). Even after deduplicating, every ticket would carry feature values from all dates, including snapshots taken after the ticket was created, so `open_tickets` would count the ticket itself and later tickets: target leakage. The default `how="inner"` also drops tickets from customers missing from the export. The correct join is point in time: sort both frames by time and use `pd.merge_asof(tickets.sort_values("created_at"), accounts.sort_values("snapshot_date"), left_on="created_at", right_on="snapshot_date", by="customer_id", direction="backward", allow_exact_matches=False)`, so each ticket gets the latest snapshot strictly before it was created (both time columns as datetimes with the same time zone; a snapshot dated the same day could already reflect the ticket, so excluding exact matches is safer, or compare against the previous day's date). Add a `tolerance` so very stale snapshots become missing, assert that the output has exactly `len(tickets)` rows, and count tickets that found no snapshot. The serving path must use the same rule: the latest snapshot available at prediction time.

mltk:02.06.q: Your fraud features include `n_tx_<category>`, built per user by `pivot_table` over the last 30 days of transactions with `aggfunc="count", fill_value=0`, and `avg_amount_<category>` built the same way with `aggfunc="mean", fill_value=0`. In production, the scoring service rebuilds these columns from the live 30-day window and passes `wide.values` to the model. What can go wrong, and how do you fix both the features and the serving path?
mltk:02.06.s: Three problems. First, the column set depends on which categories happen to occur in the window: the live data may lack categories seen in training (columns disappear) or contain new ones (columns appear), and because the service passes `wide.values` by position, every feature after the first difference is shifted onto the wrong model weight with no error. Fix it by saving the training column list and doing `wide.reindex(columns=TRAIN_COLUMNS, fill_value=...)` before scoring, mapping unseen categories to an `other` bucket before pivoting, and selecting by name rather than position. Second, `fill_value=0` for `avg_amount_<category>` conflates 'no transactions in this category' with 'transactions averaging zero'; leave these as NaN (and impute consistently) or rely on the count column to disambiguate. Counts filled with 0 are correct. Third, column order from `pivot_table` is sorted by category value, which can differ between environments if category labels are normalised differently (case, whitespace); apply the same normalisation function in both places. A test that builds features for a fixed sample in both the training pipeline and the serving code and compares them column by column catches all three, which is the core of a training-serving skew check.

mltk:02.07.q: You predict whether a user will make a purchase in the next 7 days, scoring every Monday at 00:00 UTC. For training you create one row per user per Monday with features `purchases_30d = rolling("30D").count()` over the user's purchase events, computed with `groupby("user_id")` on a frame indexed by purchase time, then merged onto the Monday rows by `(user_id, date)`. The label is purchases in `[Monday, Monday + 7 days)`. Identify the leakage and other bugs in this setup and describe a correct construction.
mltk:02.07.s: The rolling count is evaluated at each purchase event, not at the Monday scoring time, so merging on `(user_id, date)` only works for Mondays on which the user purchased, and then the window includes purchases made on Monday itself, i.e. inside the label window: direct leakage. For other Mondays the merge finds no row, so the feature is missing or gets filled with 0, which is also wrong. The correct construction computes features at the scoring times: build the grid of `(user_id, monday)` rows, then for each one count purchases in `[monday - 30 days, monday)`. One way is `pd.merge_asof` from the Monday grid onto a per-user cumulative count of events with `allow_exact_matches=False`, then subtracting the cumulative count as of `monday - 30 days`; another is resampling purchases to daily counts per user, computing `rolling(30)` on the regular daily series, shifting by one day so the window ends on Sunday, and selecting the Mondays. The label must be computed from events in `[monday, monday + 7 days)` only. Split train and validation by Monday dates, not randomly, with at least a 7-day gap so the last training labels do not overlap the first validation features. Check the result by recomputing a few rows by hand and by confirming the same code runs at serving time with only data up to Sunday 23:59.

mltk:02.08.q: A preprocessing step takes 40 minutes on 20 million rows. It reads a CSV, then runs `df["bucket"] = df.apply(lambda r: "high" if r["score"] > 0.8 and r["country"] in EU else "low", axis=1)`, then `df["device"] = df["device"].astype("category")` and finally writes `df["device"].cat.codes` as a model feature. The serving service applies the same code to each incoming batch. Identify the performance and correctness problems and rewrite the logic.
mltk:02.08.s: Performance: `apply(axis=1)` calls a Python function and builds a row Series 20 million times; it is almost certainly where the 40 minutes go. The vectorised form is `df["bucket"] = np.where((df["score"] > 0.8) & df["country"].isin(EU), "high", "low")`, which runs in well under a second; store it as a category too. Reading the CSV with explicit `dtype` and `usecols` (or switching to Parquet) and casting low-cardinality text to `category` will also cut memory and parse time. Correctness: `astype("category")` infers categories from whatever data it sees and sorts them, so in serving each batch gets its own category list and `cat.codes` can map the same device to different integers between training and serving, or between batches. The model then receives meaningless codes without any error. Fix it by building `DEVICE_DTYPE = pd.CategoricalDtype(train_categories)` once on the training data, saving it with the model, and applying `astype(DEVICE_DTYPE)` in both pipelines; unseen devices become NaN (code -1), which should be handled explicitly, for example by mapping to an 'other' category that exists in training. Putting both steps in one function used by training and serving, with a test comparing their outputs on the same rows, guards against the skew.

mltk:03.01.q: A table `requests(id, model, status, latency_ms)` has NULL latency for timed-out requests. `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM requests WHERE latency_ms < 500 OR latency_ms >= 500` returns a smaller number than the table's row count. Explain why, and say what this means for a query reporting the share of requests that were 'fast' (under 500 ms).
mltk:03.01.s: For a row with NULL latency both comparisons are UNKNOWN, and UNKNOWN OR UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN, so WHERE drops the row. The two conditions look complementary, but under three-valued logic they cover only rows with a known latency; the missing count is exactly the timed-out requests. For the 'fast share', the denominator matters. If you compute it over rows with `latency_ms IS NOT NULL`, timeouts disappear and the service looks faster than it is. Timeouts are the slowest requests, so they should normally count as not fast: compute the numerator with `latency_ms < 500` (which is never TRUE for NULL) and the denominator with `COUNT(*)` over all requests, and report the timeout count separately so the choice is visible.

mltk:03.02.q: `runs(run_id, model_id, gpu_hours)` has one row per run and `evals(run_id, benchmark, score)` has 0 to 5 rows per run. An analyst writes `SELECT r.model_id, SUM(r.gpu_hours), AVG(e.score) FROM runs r LEFT JOIN evals e ON e.run_id = r.run_id GROUP BY r.model_id`. Which numbers are wrong, why, and how would you fix the query?
mltk:03.02.s: The join fans out: a run with k evals appears k times (and once if it has none, thanks to the LEFT JOIN). `SUM(r.gpu_hours)` therefore counts each run's hours once per eval, so models with many evals are overcharged; the total is inflated by the eval count per run. `AVG(e.score)` is correct as an average over eval rows (NULLs from runs without evals are ignored), but runs with more benchmarks get more weight, which may or may not be intended. Fix by aggregating each side to one row per key before joining: compute gpu hours per model from `runs` alone, compute the score average per model (or per run first, then per model) from `evals` joined to `runs`, then join the two per-model results on `model_id`. Each side is then one-to-one at the join.

mltk:03.03.q: A dashboard computes weekly active users as the sum of seven daily `COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)` values, and the average session length per country as the average of per-city averages. Explain what each gets wrong, and write the shape of the correct query for each.
mltk:03.03.s: Summing daily distinct counts counts a user once for every day they were active, so a user active all week contributes 7. Weekly actives must be one distinct count over the whole week: `SELECT week, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) FROM events GROUP BY week`, with week derived from the timestamp. The average of per-city averages gives each city equal weight regardless of how many sessions it had, so a small city with unusual sessions distorts the country figure. The correct figure aggregates raw sessions directly, `SELECT country, AVG(session_length) FROM sessions GROUP BY country`, or, if only per-city summaries exist, weights by count: `SUM(city_avg * city_n) / SUM(city_n)`. Both mistakes come from treating non-additive statistics as if they could be combined from group results.

mltk:03.04.q: `SELECT day, SUM(gpu_hours) OVER (ORDER BY day) FROM usage` is meant to give cumulative GPU hours, but `usage` has one row per (team, day). What does the query return for a day with three rows, how does adding `ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING` change it, and what is the cleanest correct query?
mltk:03.04.s: With ORDER BY and no frame, the default is RANGE from the start to the current row, and in RANGE mode the current row includes all its peers. Each of the three rows for that day gets the same value: the cumulative total through the end of that day, including all three teams. With `ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING` the three rows get three different partial totals, in an arbitrary order among the ties, so the intermediate values depend on which team happens to come first. Neither is a clean per-day cumulative series. The clean query aggregates to one row per day first and then runs the window: `SELECT day, SUM(SUM(gpu_hours)) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) FROM usage GROUP BY day`, or equivalently a CTE with daily sums and a window over it. Per-team cumulative totals would add `PARTITION BY team` instead.

mltk:03.05.q: A query lists users who never bought anything: `SELECT user_id FROM users WHERE user_id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM orders)`. It worked for months, then started returning zero rows after guest checkout was launched. Explain the cause and give two correct rewrites.
mltk:03.05.s: Guest checkout probably writes orders with a NULL `user_id`. Once the subquery returns a NULL, `user_id NOT IN (...)` expands to a chain of `<>` comparisons joined by AND, one of which is `user_id <> NULL`, which is UNKNOWN. The condition can then be FALSE or UNKNOWN but never TRUE, so every row is filtered out. Rewrite 1: `SELECT u.user_id FROM users u WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.user_id)`, where NULL order rows simply never match. Rewrite 2: `SELECT u.user_id FROM users u LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.user_id WHERE o.user_id IS NULL`. Adding `WHERE user_id IS NOT NULL` inside the original subquery also works, but it leaves the trap ready for the next nullable column.

mltk:03.06.q: A fraud model is trained on `transactions` joined to `accounts` for features like `account_age_days`, `num_chargebacks` and `is_frozen`. Offline AUC is 0.97; in production it is 0.71. Identify at least two likely leaks in this setup and say how to rebuild the features point-in-time correctly.
mltk:03.06.s: First, `accounts` is a current-state table. `is_frozen` is very likely set *because* fraud was detected, so it encodes the label; it must be dropped or taken as of the transaction time, which would usually be false. Second, `num_chargebacks` counted over all history includes chargebacks filed after the transaction, often for that very transaction. It must count only chargebacks known before the transaction time, using the date the chargeback was recorded, not the date of the original purchase. Third, `account_age_days` computed from today's date rather than the transaction date gives every account a later age, distorting the feature. The rebuild: make the spine one row per transaction with its timestamp as the cutoff, compute each feature from history tables filtered to records available before that cutoff, and evaluate on a later time period than training.

mltk:03.07.q: A dashboard query, `SELECT * FROM predictions WHERE model_id = 'm7' AND CAST(created_at AS DATE) = '2025-05-01' ORDER BY created_at`, is slow despite an index on `(created_at, model_id)`. Explain why the index does not help and propose an index and a query rewrite that would.
mltk:03.07.s: Two problems. The filter casts `created_at`, so the condition is not a bare-column comparison and the planner cannot use the index's ordering on `created_at`. Even without the cast, the index puts `created_at` first, so it would still read that day's predictions for every model and discard the ones that are not `m7`. Rewrite the filter as a half-open range, `created_at >= '2025-05-01' AND created_at < '2025-05-02'`, and create an index on `(model_id, created_at)`: equality column first, range column second. The planner then seeks to model `m7`, reads one day's contiguous range, and returns rows already in `created_at` order, so no sort is needed. `SELECT *` still requires a table lookup per row; listing the needed columns and adding them to the index would make it covering.

mltk:04.01.q: A model runs in bfloat16 on the GPU. Inside `forward` you add a positional table built with `torch.arange(T)[:, None] / 10000 ** (torch.arange(0, d, 2) / d)` and then add it to the bfloat16 activations. Predict the device and dtype of the result, and say what goes wrong and how to fix it.
mltk:04.01.s: `torch.arange` creates int64 tensors on the CPU by default, and the division promotes to the default float dtype, float32. Adding a CPU float32 tensor to CUDA bfloat16 activations fails with a device-mismatch error (PyTorch only lets 0-dim CPU tensors mix with CUDA tensors). If you fix only the device, the addition succeeds, but both operands are dimensioned floats, so the result is promoted to float32: every activation after that point doubles in size and runs slower kernels. Build the table with `device=x.device`, cast it to `x.dtype` (or compute in float32 and cast once), and ideally compute it once in `__init__` and store it with `register_buffer` so that `model.to()` moves and casts it with the rest of the model.

mltk:04.02.q: You train with gradient accumulation over 8 micro-batches but write `loss = loss_fn(out, y); loss.backward()` without dividing by 8, and you also call `opt.zero_grad()` inside the micro-batch loop instead of before it. Describe precisely what gradient each optimiser step uses, and what each bug alone would do to training.
mltk:04.02.s: With `zero_grad()` inside the loop, each micro-batch's gradients are wiped before the next one is added, so when `opt.step()` runs, `.grad` holds only the last micro-batch's gradient. Training then behaves like batch size B/8 with 7/8 of the data's gradient signal thrown away, plus the noise of a small batch. Without that bug, forgetting the division by 8 makes the step use the sum rather than the mean of 8 micro-batch gradients: the direction is right but the magnitude is 8 times too large, equivalent to multiplying the learning rate by 8 for SGD. Adam largely normalises the scale away (it divides by the root of the second moment), though epsilon and weight decay interactions shift slightly, while gradient clipping thresholds become wrong by a factor of 8. Both fixes: zero once before the loop, and divide each micro-batch loss by the number of micro-batches (or by total tokens).

mltk:04.03.q: A colleague's Transformer stores its blocks as `self.blocks = [Block(d) for _ in range(12)]` and its causal mask as `self.mask = torch.tril(torch.ones(T, T))`. Training runs on CPU without errors but the loss barely moves. On GPU it crashes. Explain both symptoms and what saving a checkpoint would contain.
mltk:04.03.s: A plain list does not register the blocks as submodules, so `model.parameters()` returns only the embedding, final norm and head. The optimiser updates those, which is why loss moves a little, while the 12 blocks stay at their random initialisation, acting as fixed random features. On GPU, `model.to('cuda')` moves only registered state: the blocks' weights and the plain-attribute mask stay on the CPU, so the first block's matmul with CUDA activations fails with a device-mismatch error. A saved `state_dict()` would contain only the embedding, norm and head tensors; loading it into a corrected model with `strict=True` raises missing keys for every block. Fix: `nn.ModuleList` for the blocks and `register_buffer('mask', ..., persistent=False)` for the mask.

mltk:04.04.q: A sequence tagger produces logits of shape `(B, T, C)` with padded positions labelled -100. A teammate computes `nn.CrossEntropyLoss()(torch.softmax(logits, -1).permute(0, 2, 1), y)`. It runs. List what is right, what is wrong, and what the training curves will look like.
mltk:04.04.s: The permute is correct: it puts classes on dimension 1, giving `(B, C, T)` against targets `(B, T)`, and the default `ignore_index=-100` correctly drops padded positions from both the sum and the averaging count. The bug is the softmax: `CrossEntropyLoss` applies log-softmax itself, so it now treats probabilities in [0, 1] as logits. Softmax of values in [0, 1] is nearly uniform: even a perfect one-hot prediction gives a logit gap of only 1, so the loss is bounded below by ln(1 + (C-1)/e), about 1.46 for 10 classes instead of 0. Gradients pass through two softmaxes and are small. Curves show the loss starting near ln(C) and flattening well above zero while accuracy creeps up slowly, with no error raised. Remove the softmax and pass the raw logits.

mltk:04.05.q: You launch the same script on 4 GPUs. Each rank builds `DataLoader(ds, batch_size=32, num_workers=8)` over an `IterableDataset` that streams JSON lines from one big file. An epoch takes 32 times as many optimiser steps as you expected, and the training loss drops unusually fast. What is happening, and how do you fix it?
mltk:04.05.s: Nothing shards the stream. Each of the 4 ranks opens the whole file, and within each rank the 8 workers each iterate their own copy of the dataset from the first line, so every line is read once per worker per rank: 32 copies per epoch. You get 32 times the expected steps, and every batch is repeated 32 times, so the model memorises the data and the training loss falls faster than real progress justifies. Samplers cannot help: `DataLoader` rejects a sampler such as `DistributedSampler` for an `IterableDataset`. Shard inside `__iter__` instead: combine the rank and world size from `torch.distributed` with `get_worker_info().id` and `num_workers` into a global reader index from 0 to 31, and have each reader yield only its own lines (line number modulo 32 equals its index), or split the file into shard files and give each reader its own set.

mltk:04.06.q: Your validation accuracy changes by about 1 point every time you re-run evaluation on the same checkpoint, and after the first evaluation the training loss starts falling faster than before. The model uses dropout and batch norm. What is wrong with the loop and what do you change?
mltk:04.06.s: Evaluation is running in training mode. With dropout active, every evaluation samples a different subnetwork, so accuracy varies between identical re-runs; in eval mode the forward pass is deterministic. Batch norm in training mode also normalises with the validation batches' own statistics and updates its running averages with validation data. The faster-falling training loss after evaluation is the second half of the bug: either evaluation switched to eval mode and never switched back, so training continues with dropout disabled and fits the training data more easily, or the running statistics were contaminated. The fix is a helper that calls `model.eval()` and runs under `torch.no_grad()`, then restores `model.train()` before returning, as in the evaluate function in this lesson.

mltk:04.07.q: You switch a working fp32 training script to fp16 autocast with `GradScaler`, and add gradient clipping at max_norm 1.0. Training is now much slower to converge, and the logged gradient norm before clipping is around 30,000 every step. What is the bug, why does it slow convergence, and why would the same code be fine with bfloat16 and the scaler disabled?
mltk:04.07.s: The gradients are clipped while still multiplied by the loss scale. `scaler.scale(loss).backward()` produces gradients S times too large (S is about 2^15 to 2^16 here, consistent with a logged norm near 30,000 for a true norm below 1), and clipping them to norm 1 then shrinks every update by a factor of roughly S/true-norm. `scaler.step()` later divides by S again, so the effective step is tiny: convergence slows as if the learning rate were cut by orders of magnitude. The fix is `scaler.unscale_(opt)` before `clip_grad_norm_`, so clipping sees true gradient magnitudes, and `scaler.step` knows not to unscale twice. With bfloat16 and `enabled=False`, `scale()` and `unscale_()` are identities, so the gradients are never scaled and clipping already sees true values.

mltk:04.08.q: A Transformer language model (vocabulary 32,000) trains fine for 3,000 steps, then the loss becomes nan at step 3,140 and stays nan. The gradient norm log shows values around 1 to 2, then 900 at step 3,138 and inf at 3,139. Describe a systematic way to find the cause, and name two plausible root causes and their fixes.
mltk:04.08.s: First reproduce cheaply: reload the last checkpoint before the spike, with the same data order, and replay steps 3,130 to 3,140 with per-layer gradient-norm logging, forward hooks asserting finite outputs, and anomaly detection on. That identifies the first layer and op that produce huge or non-finite values, and the exact batch. Inspect the batch: an all-padding or garbage sequence points at the data. Plausible causes: (1) attention logits growing until softmax saturates or fp16 overflows; fixes are bfloat16, query-key normalisation, lower peak learning rate or longer warmup. (2) A fully masked row producing softmax over all -inf, which gives nan; fix the masking or filter empty sequences. Also add global-norm clipping with `error_if_nonfinite=True` or skip non-finite steps so one bad batch cannot destroy the weights.

mltk:05.01.q: You port a NumPy preprocessing function to JAX. It builds `out = np.zeros(n)` and then loops `for i, j in enumerate(idx): out[j] += w[i]`, where `idx` has repeated entries and occasionally contains `n` (one past the end) as a sentinel. Rewrite it in JAX and explain what the rewritten version does with the repeats and the sentinel, compared with the original loop.
mltk:05.01.s: The idiomatic rewrite is `out = jnp.zeros(n).at[idx].add(w)`: one scatter-add with no Python loop, which also compiles under `jit`. Repeats behave like the original loop, because `.at[].add` accumulates every occurrence (unlike the vectorised NumPy `out[idx] += w`, which would keep only one write per position). The sentinel differs. The NumPy loop raises `IndexError` on `out[n]`, whereas JAX's scatter drops out-of-bounds updates by default, so sentinel entries are silently ignored. That happens to be the desired behaviour here, but it is better to make it explicit, for example `.at[idx].add(w, mode='drop')`, or to zero the weights of sentinel entries with `jnp.where(idx < n, w, 0)`, so a future change to the indexing mode or to the sentinel value cannot quietly change results. Note also that the result is float32 unless 64-bit mode is enabled, so if the NumPy version relied on float64 accumulation for very long sums, compare the results with a tolerance.

mltk:05.02.q: You want the largest eigenvalue of the loss Hessian for a 50-million-parameter model, to check whether your learning rate is near the stability limit $2/\lambda_{max}$. A colleague proposes `jnp.linalg.eigvalsh(jax.hessian(loss)(params))`. Explain why this fails and describe a JAX approach that works, including its cost per iteration.
mltk:05.02.s: The full Hessian has $(5\times10^7)^2 = 2.5\times10^{15}$ entries, about 10 petabytes in float32, so `jax.hessian` cannot even be materialised, let alone decomposed (and with a pytree of parameters it would be a nested block structure anyway). Power iteration only needs products $Hv$. Define `hvp = lambda v: jax.jvp(jax.grad(loss_of_params), (params,), (v,))[1]`, where `loss_of_params` closes over a fixed batch. Start with a random pytree `v` of the same structure as `params`, then repeat: `w = hvp(v)`, estimate $\lambda = \langle v, w\rangle$ (summing over all leaves), and set `v = w / ||w||`. Each iteration costs roughly one forward and two backward-like passes (a JVP through the gradient computation, about 2 to 3 times a gradient), and memory is a small multiple of one gradient. Wrap the step in `jax.jit` so it compiles once, run some tens of iterations until $\lambda$ stabilises, and use the same batch throughout because the Hessian depends on the data. The top eigenvalue is the one of largest magnitude, which near a minimum is usually the largest positive one.

mltk:05.03.q: A jitted beam-search decoder takes `max_len` and `beam_size` as arguments and loops `for t in range(max_len)` in Python, breaking out early when all beams have emitted an end token. It fails with a tracer error. A colleague deletes the early break and marks both arguments static; it now runs, but compiling takes four minutes and every new `max_len` compiles again. Explain both symptoms and how you would restructure it.
mltk:05.03.s: The early `break` needs a Python boolean computed from traced data (whether all beams finished), so under `jit` the comparison is a tracer and converting it to `bool` raises a `TracerBoolConversionError`. Deleting the break removes the error, but the Python loop over a static `max_len` is unrolled: the jaxpr contains `max_len` copies of the decoder step, so compile time grows with the length, and every new `max_len` value is a new static value and therefore a new compilation. The fix is to keep `max_len` and `beam_size` static (they determine shapes, so they should be), and replace the Python loop with a compiled loop. `lax.while_loop` with a condition `(t < max_len) & ~all_done` stops early on the device, with a carry holding fixed-shape buffers of size `(beam_size, max_len)` updated with `.at[:, t].set(...)`. Alternatively `lax.scan` over `max_len` steps with a `done` mask keeps going but freezes finished beams with `jnp.where`; scan is simpler when you might later differentiate through the loop, which `while_loop` does not support in reverse mode. Either way the body is traced once, so compile time no longer grows with `max_len`.

mltk:05.04.q: For DP-SGD you compute `jax.vmap(jax.grad(loss), in_axes=(None, 0, 0))(params, X, Y)` on a 350M-parameter model with batch 256 in float32, and the step runs out of memory on an 80 GB GPU even though a normal training step at batch 256 fits easily. Explain the memory difference and give two ways to make it fit while keeping exact per-example clipping.
mltk:05.04.s: A normal step reduces over the batch inside the backward pass, so it only ever holds one gradient pytree (350M floats, about 1.4 GB) plus activations. The vmapped version materialises one gradient per example: 256 x 1.4 GB is about 358 GB, far beyond 80 GB, before counting activations. Clipping only needs each example's norm and the clipped sum, so the full per-example tensor never has to exist at once. First option: split the batch into micro-batches of, say, 16 and loop over them with `lax.scan` (or `lax.map`), computing per-example gradients for 16 examples (about 22 GB), clipping them, and adding their sum into a running accumulator in the scan carry; at the end divide by 256 and add noise. Second option: a two-pass approach, computing per-example gradient norms cheaply (for dense layers the norm of an outer-product gradient factorises into norms of activations and output gradients, the 'ghost clipping' trick) and then running one ordinary backward pass on a loss reweighted by each example's clip factor, which gives the clipped sum with a single gradient-sized buffer. Reducing precision or using `jax.checkpoint` addresses activations, not the per-example gradient buffer, so they do not fix this on their own.

mltk:05.05.q: Your training state is `(params, opt_state)` and you checkpoint it by flattening with `jax.tree.leaves` and saving the list of arrays. After a refactor that renamed `'mlp'` to `'ffn'` in the parameter dict, restoring the checkpoint with `jax.tree.unflatten(treedef, leaves)` succeeds, but the loss starts much higher than when you saved. What happened, and how should the checkpoint be stored instead?
mltk:05.05.s: Dict leaves are flattened in sorted key order, so renaming `'mlp'` to `'ffn'` moves that subtree to a different position in the flattened list (for instance from after `'ln'` to before it). The saved list is still in the old order. If several subtrees have the same structure and leaf shapes (for example the MLP weights and another block with matching shapes), unflattening the old list into the new treedef assigns arrays to the wrong parameters without any shape error, and the Adam moments get scrambled in the same way. The model then starts from a partly permuted set of weights, so the loss jumps. A positional list of leaves is not a safe checkpoint format. Store leaves keyed by their path, for example from `jax.tree_util.tree_flatten_with_path`, or use a checkpointing library such as Orbax that saves the tree structure with names, then restore by name and fail loudly on any key that is missing or unexpected. A rename should be handled by an explicit key mapping during restore.

mltk:05.06.q: A colleague's data-augmentation function is `vmap`ped over the batch as `jax.vmap(augment, in_axes=(None, 0))(key, images)` and the key is split once per step. They report that augmentations look random across steps but the model ignores them. What is going on, and what is the correct call?
mltk:05.06.s: With `in_axes=None` the key is broadcast, so every image in the batch receives the same random crop, flip and colour jitter within a step. Across steps the key changes, so the augmentation looks random when you inspect one image over time, but within a batch all examples are transformed identically. That greatly reduces the diversity of augmentations per gradient step (and with batch-level statistics such as batch norm, an identical transform is partly normalised away). The fix is to give each example its own key: `keys = jax.random.split(step_key, images.shape[0])` and `jax.vmap(augment)(keys, images)`, with `in_axes=0` for both. A useful check is to augment a batch made of one image repeated B times and confirm that the outputs differ.

mltk:05.07.q: You have 16 GPUs as 2 nodes of 8 with fast NVLink inside a node and slower networking between nodes. You want tensor parallelism plus data parallelism for a model whose layers are too large for one GPU's memory with optimiser state. Propose a mesh shape and axis order, the PartitionSpecs for a dense layer's weight `(d_in, d_out)`, the activations `(B, T, d)` and the batch, and say which collectives cross nodes.
mltk:05.07.s: Use a mesh of shape `(2, 8)` with axes `('data', 'model')`, ordered so that the 8 devices of one node form the `'model'` axis; `jax.make_mesh` tries to match axes to the physical topology, but you should check that each `'model'` group is one node by inspecting `mesh.devices`. Tensor parallelism communicates inside every layer, so it belongs on the fast NVLink axis, while data parallelism communicates once per step for gradients, so it can cross the slower inter-node link. For a column-parallel layer the weight is `P(None, 'model')` and for the following row-parallel layer `P('model', None)`; to also reduce optimiser-state memory, add FSDP on the other dimension, for example `P('data', 'model')`, at the cost of all-gathers across nodes. The batch is `P('data', None)` for token ids `(B, T)`, and activations `(B, T, d)` are `P('data', None, None)` between blocks and `P('data', None, 'model')` inside the MLP. Communication over `'model'` (the all-reduce after each row-parallel matmul) stays inside a node. Only the gradient all-reduce over `'data'` (or, with FSDP, the weight all-gathers and gradient reduce-scatters) crosses nodes, and XLA can overlap it with the backward pass.

mlcore:01.01.q: A team trains a fraud model by minimising log loss, reports 0.3% training error, and ships. On live traffic the model flags almost nothing. Name two distinct places in the learning setup where this could have gone wrong, and how you would tell them apart.
mlcore:01.01.s: One is the **generalisation gap**: the class is flexible enough to memorise the training set, so low empirical risk says little about true risk. You would see it by evaluating on a held-out split drawn from the same period: if held-out error is far above 0.3%, the model overfit. The other is a violation of the **i.i.d. assumption**: live traffic comes from a different distribution (new fraud patterns, a different country mix, a feature computed differently in production). Then held-out error from the old data can look fine while live performance collapses; comparing feature distributions between training and live data (or evaluating on a later time slice) exposes it. A third suspect is the **loss/metric mismatch**: with 0.3% fraud, predicting "not fraud" always already gives 0.3% error, so the reported number may simply be the base rate.

mlcore:01.02.q: A gradient-boosted model has 2% training error and 2.5% validation error, but the product needs 1%. A colleague proposes collecting ten times more data. Using the bias-variance view, argue whether this is likely to help and what you would try instead.
mlcore:01.02.s: Training and validation error are close (2% vs 2.5%), so variance is small: the model is not overfitting much. The dominant problem is **bias** (or irreducible noise): even on data it has seen, the model reaches only 2%. More data mainly reduces variance, so ten times more rows would likely shave a little off the 0.5% gap and leave the 2% floor. Better options attack bias: add capacity (deeper trees, more rounds, less regularisation), and above all add informative features, because if the 2% is close to the Bayes error for the current features no model can beat it. A useful check is human or oracle error on a sample: if experts also miss about 2% with the same inputs, only new information (features or labels of better quality) will help.

mlcore:01.03.q: You build a model that predicts machine failure from sensor readings sampled every minute on 40 machines, and random 5-fold CV gives 97% accuracy. Explain why that number is suspect and design a split that answers the real question "will this work on next month's data from the same fleet" and, separately, "will it work on a new machine".
mlcore:01.03.s: Minute-level readings are strongly autocorrelated, so a random split puts almost identical neighbouring minutes in train and validation; the model can interpolate between them instead of learning failure signals. Both machine identity and time leak. For **next month on the same fleet**, split by time: train on months 1..t, validate on month t+1, and roll forward (time-series CV), with a gap between the windows if features use lookback windows so no window spans the cut. For **a new machine**, group by machine id: leave-one-machine-out or GroupKFold over the 40 machines, so each validation machine is unseen; ideally also keep the time ordering inside. Expect both numbers to be well below 97%; the gap between them tells you how much the model relies on machine-specific behaviour. Fit any scaling or feature selection inside each training fold.

mlcore:01.04.q: You fit L1-regularised logistic regression on 500 features, two of which are near-duplicates (correlation 0.99) and both truly predictive. What will the lasso likely do with them, why, and how does switching to L2 or elastic net change the outcome?
mlcore:01.04.s: The lasso will usually keep one of the pair and set the other to exactly zero, and which one survives can flip between bootstrap samples. Because the two features carry almost the same information, the loss is nearly unchanged if weight moves from one to the other, while the L1 penalty $|w_1| + |w_2|$ is the same for any split with the same total, so the corner solution (one weight zero) is as cheap as any split and the constant L1 push removes the weaker one. L2 penalises $w_1^2 + w_2^2$, which for a fixed total is smallest when the weight is shared equally, so ridge gives both about half the weight and is stable. Elastic net mixes the two: the L2 part encourages grouping (both kept with similar weights) while the L1 part still zeros out the many irrelevant features.

mlcore:01.05.q: Your new recommender beats a random-item baseline by 40% on hit rate@10, and your manager is pleased. What baseline is missing, why could it change the conclusion, and what would a learning curve add to the decision about whether to keep investing?
