Also check that A does not gain unfairly from mapping rare words to a cheap <unk>; bits per byte on raw text avoids both issues.

dlcore:06.03.q: Under BM25 with k1 = 1.2 and b = 0.75, why doesn't a 10,000-word document that mentions 'python' 20 times automatically outrank a 200-word document that mentions it 5 times, when the average document length is 500 words? Work out the term-frequency factor for each.
dlcore:06.03.s: The tf factor is tf(k1+1) / (tf + k1(1 - b + b|d|/avgdl)). Long doc: |d|/avgdl = 20, so the length term is 1.2 × (0.25 + 0.75 × 20) = 1.2 × 15.25 = 18.3; factor = 20 × 2.2 / (20 + 18.3) = 44 / 38.3 ≈ 1.15. Short doc: |d|/avgdl = 0.4, length term = 1.2 × (0.25 + 0.3) = 0.66; factor = 5 × 2.2 / (5 + 0.66) = 11 / 5.66 ≈ 1.94. The short document scores higher for this term: saturation caps how much repeated mentions can add (the factor can never exceed 2.2), and length normalisation recognises that 20 mentions in 10,000 words is a lower density than 5 in 200. Raw TF-IDF without normalisation would have favoured the long document.

dlcore:06.04.q: You need word vectors for a domain of clinical notes full of rare drug names, abbreviations and misspellings. Compare word2vec and fastText for this, including one way fastText could mislead you.
dlcore:06.04.s: word2vec learns one vector per vocabulary entry, so misspellings and rare drug names either fall below the minimum count and get no vector, or get noisy vectors from very few contexts; every unseen variant at test time has nothing. fastText builds each word from character n-gram vectors, so 'amoxicilin' (misspelt) shares most n-grams with 'amoxicillin' and lands near it, and inflections and unseen words get usable vectors. It also shares statistical strength across words with common pieces. The risk is that surface similarity is not semantic similarity: drug names that differ by a few characters but are clinically unrelated (sound-alike or look-alike medications) will get similar vectors, and short abbreviations with few n-grams can collide. Check nearest neighbours for critical terms before trusting them.

dlcore:06.05.q: A NER model's per-token argmax output for five words is: O, B-LOC, I-PER, I-PER, O. How would a lenient BIO decoder, a strict decoder, and Viterbi decoding with transition constraints each handle this, and how does each outcome affect entity-level F1 if the gold answer is a single PER entity over words 2-4?
dlcore:06.05.s: A lenient decoder closes LOC at word 2 and starts a new PER entity at word 3 from the stray I-PER, giving LOC(2) and PER(3-4). A strict decoder keeps LOC(2) and discards the I-PER tokens, since they lack a B-PER. Viterbi with constraints forbids B-LOC followed by I-PER and finds the best valid sequence; if the PER logits on words 3-4 are strong, it is likely to choose B-PER I-PER I-PER for words 2-4, or B-LOC O O if the LOC evidence on word 2 dominates. Against the gold PER(2-4): lenient produces two false positives and one miss (P = 0, R = 0); strict produces one false positive and one miss; only the constrained decode can produce an exact match, giving P = R = F1 = 1 for this sentence. Structured decoding converts per-token evidence into consistent spans.

dlcore:06.06.q: Suppose you pretrain BERT but replace every chosen token with [MASK] (100/0/0 instead of 80/10/10). What goes wrong when you fine-tune and use the model, and what specific job does the 10% 'left unchanged' bucket do?
dlcore:06.06.s: With 100% [MASK], the model only ever has to make predictions at [MASK] positions, so it can learn that ordinary visible tokens never need a carefully built representation of their own identity: the useful computation is focused on [MASK] slots. At fine-tuning and inference there are no [MASK] tokens, so every input looks unlike pretraining, and the representations of real tokens are less suited to the downstream task (a pretrain-finetune mismatch). The 10% random replacement means any visible token might be wrong, so the model must keep a contextual representation for every position. The 10% unchanged bucket means a visible token is sometimes also the correct answer, which teaches the model that the observed word is informative and anchors each position's representation toward the actual token, which is exactly the situation at fine-tuning time.

dlcore:06.07.q: You raise the beam width of a translation model from 5 to 50. Model log-probability of the outputs goes up, but BLEU goes down and outputs get noticeably shorter. Explain why, and what you would change.
dlcore:06.07.s: Beam search maximises the total log-probability, a sum of negative terms, so every extra token lowers the score; short hypotheses that end early have an advantage. A narrow beam rarely finds those short, high-probability hypotheses, but a 50-wide beam explores enough to find them. It is succeeding at search while exposing a mismatch between the model's probability and translation quality. BLEU drops because the outputs omit content (lower n-gram matches) and because the brevity penalty e^(1 - r/c) applies once candidates are shorter than the references. Fixes: add length normalisation (divide by length to the power α, about 0.6-1.0, or GNMT's penalty), possibly a coverage penalty, and tune both the beam width and α on a dev set; often a beam of 4-8 with normalisation is best.

dlcore:07.01.q: You train a VAE on MNIST with the loss `F.mse_loss(x_hat, x) + kl.mean()`, where `mse_loss` averages over all 784 pixels and the KL is summed over 20 latent dimensions. Samples from the prior all look like the same grey blob. What happened, and how do you fix it?
dlcore:07.01.s: Averaging the reconstruction error over 784 pixels makes it about 784 times smaller than the per-image negative log-likelihood, while the KL is still summed over latent dimensions. The KL therefore dominates: the cheapest solution is to set $q(z\mid x)$ equal to the prior for every input (KL = 0), so $z$ carries no information and the decoder learns to output the mean image. This is posterior collapse caused by mis-weighting, not by the model. Fix it by summing the reconstruction loss over pixels per image (equivalently, choosing a sensible decoder variance) and averaging over the batch, so both terms are per-example log-densities. KL warm-up or a free-bits floor helps if collapse persists. Check by watching per-dimension KL: active dimensions should sit well above zero.

dlcore:07.02.q: Halfway through training, your GAN's discriminator loss drops to almost zero and stays there, and generated samples stop improving. Explain what the generator's gradient looks like in this state under the minimax loss and under the non-saturating loss, and name two changes that would restore a useful signal.
dlcore:07.02.s: A near-zero discriminator loss means $D(G(z))\approx 0$ for fakes, so the logit is very negative. Under the minimax loss $\log(1-D)$ the gradient with respect to the logit is $\sigma(l)\approx 0$, so the generator receives essentially nothing. The non-saturating loss $-\log D$ gives a logit gradient near 1, but that only helps if $D$'s gradient with respect to the image is informative; when real and fake supports are disjoint and $D$ is a sharp classifier, $\partial D/\partial x$ can be tiny or point in unhelpful directions. Restoring signal means constraining $D$: add a gradient penalty (WGAN-GP on interpolates, or R1 on reals) or spectral normalisation so $D$ stays smooth, and/or weaken it (fewer $D$ steps, lower $D$ learning rate, augmentation of $D$'s inputs). Switching to a Wasserstein-style critic also keeps the loss informative when supports do not overlap.

dlcore:07.03.q: A colleague removes the $\sqrt{1-\beta_t}$ factor and uses $x_t=x_{t-1}+\sqrt{\beta_t}\,\epsilon_t$ with the same linear $\beta$ schedule, still starting sampling from $\mathcal N(0, I)$. Using the Gaussian addition rule, what is the distribution of $x_T$ given $x_0$, and why does sampling now go wrong?
dlcore:07.03.s: Without the shrink, each step adds independent noise with variance $\beta_t$ and leaves the signal untouched, so $x_T = x_0 + \sqrt{\sum_t\beta_t}\,\epsilon$. For the linear schedule $\sum\beta_t \approx 1000\cdot(10^{-4}+0.02)/2\approx 10.05$, so $x_T\sim\mathcal N(x_0, 10.05\,I)$. Two problems follow. The signal is never removed: the SNR at $T$ is about $\|x_0\|^2/10$ per pixel, not zero, so $x_T$ still depends on the image. And the total variance is about 11 (data variance plus 10), not 1. Starting the reverse chain from $\mathcal N(0, I)$ therefore feeds the model inputs from a distribution it never saw at $t=T$: wrong scale and no image component. This is the 'variance exploding' family, which can work, but only if you sample from $\mathcal N(0,\sigma_\text{max}^2 I)$ with $\sigma_\text{max}$ much larger than the data scale, as in score SDE and EDM models.

dlcore:07.04.q: You switch a working model from $\epsilon$-prediction to zero-terminal-SNR, so at $t=T$ the input is pure noise. Training still uses $\epsilon$-MSE, and samples come out as washed-out mush. Explain what the network learns at $t=T$ and what goes wrong when the sampler converts $\hat\epsilon$ into $\hat x_0$.
dlcore:07.04.s: At $t=T$ with $\bar\alpha_T=0$, the input is $x_T=\epsilon$ exactly. The $\epsilon$-MSE optimum is therefore the identity: the network copies its input and learns nothing about the data at that step, while the loss there is trivially zero. The sampler, however, needs $\hat x_0$ (or a mean) and computes $\hat x_0=(x_t-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\hat\epsilon)/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}$, which is $0/0$ at $t=T$ and wildly amplified near it: any small error in $\hat\epsilon$ is divided by a tiny $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}$. The first, most important steps, which set global layout and brightness, are thus driven by noise or by whatever clipping you apply. Switching the target to $v$ (or $x_0$) fixes it: at $t=T$, $v=-x_0$, so the network must predict the data mean given no information, a well-posed and well-scaled target, and conversion to $\hat x_0$ involves no division by $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}$.
dlcore:07.04.t: Diffusion: the denoiser and its objective

dlcore:07.05.q: A DDIM sampler with 20 steps on a pixel-space model produces good images. Your teammate switches to DDPM ancestral sampling but keeps the same 20-step subsequence, using $\sigma_t^2=\beta_t$ from the original 1000-step schedule at each visited step. Images become noisy and grainy. Why?
dlcore:07.05.s: Ancestral DDPM is derived for consecutive steps with small $\beta_t$: the reverse step's variance and the coefficient on $\hat\epsilon$ assume the chain removes only one step's worth of noise. On a 20-step subsequence each jump spans about 50 original steps, but the update still removes noise using one step's $\beta_t$ and adds $\sigma_t z$ sized for a single step. The mean therefore removes far too little noise per jump while fresh noise keeps being injected, so the sample arrives at $t=0$ with leftover noise. To use a subsequence with a stochastic sampler you must recompute the effective $\beta$ between visited steps, $1-\bar\alpha_t/\bar\alpha_{t'}$, and the matching posterior variance, which is what DDIM's general formula with $\eta=1$ does automatically.
dlcore:07.05.t: Diffusion: sampling with DDPM and DDIM

dlcore:07.06.q: A flow-matching model trained with the straight path $x_t=(1-t)x_0+t x_1$ is sampled with 4 Euler steps and looks fine; a DDPM-trained model sampled with 4 DDIM (Euler) steps looks blurry and wrong. Both are well trained. Explain the difference in terms of the ODE each sampler integrates.
dlcore:07.06.s: Both samplers integrate an ODE whose marginals match the data, but the trajectories differ. DDPM's probability-flow ODE follows curved paths: early on, the estimate $\hat x_0$ is a blurry average of many plausible images, and the trajectory bends as the prediction sharpens. A 4-step Euler integration takes large straight steps along the tangent at each point, so it overshoots the curve and ends somewhere off the data manifold, often near the blurry average. The flow-matching velocity field is trained on straight noise-to-data pairs, so its marginal trajectories are much less curved, and a straight Euler step along the tangent stays close to the true path. Euler's error scales with curvature times step size squared, so straighter paths tolerate far larger steps. Remedies for the diffusion model are a higher-order solver, step spacing concentrated where curvature is high, or distillation.

dlcore:07.07.q: You fine-tune a text-to-image model on a new dataset but forget to keep the 10 percent caption dropout. At sampling time with $w=7.5$, images are noisy and incoherent, while $w=1$ looks reasonable. Explain why, and what you would do short of retraining from scratch.
dlcore:07.07.s: CFG needs $\epsilon_\theta(x_t,\varnothing)$ to be a good unconditional prediction. Without caption dropout during fine-tuning, the network never sees the null condition on the new data, and its null-branch behaviour drifts as the shared weights change: the unconditional prediction becomes arbitrary and no longer approximates the unconditional score. At $w=1$ the null branch cancels out ($\hat\epsilon=\epsilon_c$), so samples look fine. At $w=7.5$ the sampler extrapolates 6.5 times the difference between a sensible and a meaningless prediction, which injects large, structured error at every step. The fix is to continue fine-tuning with caption dropout restored (typically 10 to 20 percent), which re-teaches the null branch on the new data. As a stopgap, use a low $w$, or take the unconditional branch from the original pre-fine-tuning model, accepting some mismatch.

dlcore:08.01.q: A robot task has a 500-step time limit. Your value-learning code treats step 500 as terminal, so the target there is just $r$. Training converges, but the robot behaves badly near the end of each episode and values for identical states differ depending on the time step. Explain the bug using the definition of return and the Markov property, and give the fix.
dlcore:08.01.s: The state the agent observes does not include time, so under the Markov assumption a given state should have one value regardless of when it is reached. Treating the time-limit cutoff as terminal tells the learner that the return from that state is just the last reward, while the same state reached earlier has a long future. Values for identical states then conflict and the learned values near the cutoff are biased low; the policy acts as if the world ends, for example taking risky actions or stopping effort. The cutoff is a truncation, not a property of the environment. Fix: keep separate `terminated` and `truncated` flags and bootstrap with $r+\gamma V(s')$ on truncation (only true terminals use $r$ alone). Alternatively, if the time limit really is part of the task, add the remaining time to the state so the problem is Markov again.

dlcore:08.02.q: On a 10,000-state gridworld with $\gamma=0.99$, value iteration takes about 1,800 sweeps to converge, while policy iteration converges in 6 iterations. Which is faster in wall-clock time, and what does the answer depend on? Suggest a middle ground.
dlcore:08.02.s: It depends on the cost of each policy-iteration evaluation. If evaluation is done exactly by solving the linear system, each iteration costs $O(|S|^3)\approx 10^{12}$ operations for a dense matrix (much less if $P_\pi$ is sparse, as in a gridworld where each state has a few successors and a sparse solver works well), versus about $|S|\cdot|A|\cdot$(successors) per value-iteration sweep. With sparse transitions, 6 sparse solves are often cheaper than 1,800 sweeps; with dense transitions, value iteration wins. If evaluation is iterative, each policy-iteration step itself needs hundreds of sweeps at $\gamma=0.99$, so the total sweep counts become comparable. The middle ground is modified policy iteration: run a fixed small number $m$ of evaluation sweeps (say 10 to 50) between greedy improvements. It keeps policy iteration's fast policy convergence without paying for exact evaluation of early, poor policies.

dlcore:08.03.q: In a 1,000-step episodic task where the only reward arrives at the end, you compare Monte Carlo with TD(0) for value prediction, each run for the same small number of episodes. Which learns faster for states near the start, and why? How would TD($\lambda$) with $\lambda=0.9$ change the picture?
dlcore:08.03.s: TD(0) propagates the final reward back by only one state per visit: after the first episode only the second-to-last state has learned anything, and information reaches the start only after on the order of 1,000 episodes along the path (sooner if trajectories overlap and $\alpha$ is large). Monte Carlo updates every visited state with the actual return after each episode, so states near the start get a useful, if noisy, signal immediately. With a sparse, delayed reward and few episodes, MC learns the early states faster; TD's lower variance only pays off once values have propagated. TD($\lambda$) with $\lambda=0.9$ spreads each TD error back over recently visited states with weight $(\gamma\lambda)^k$, so the final reward reaches tens of steps back in one episode (the trace falls to 1 percent after about 44 steps for $\gamma\lambda=0.9$). It propagates much faster than TD(0) while keeping lower variance than full MC; for very long chains, $\lambda$ closer to 1 or n-step returns help further.

dlcore:08.04.q: You train a tabular Q-learning agent from a fixed log of transitions collected by a cautious human operator who never visits states near a hazard. The learned greedy policy confidently routes through the hazard region and fails. Q-learning is off-policy and 'learns $Q^*$ from any data', so what went wrong?
dlcore:08.04.s: Off-policy convergence to $Q^*$ requires that the behaviour data keep visiting every relevant state-action pair. The operator never visited the hazard region, so $Q$ there stays at its initial values and is never corrected by real rewards. If initial values are zero or optimistic and rewards elsewhere are negative per step, untried actions near the hazard look as good as or better than tried ones, and the max in the Q-learning target propagates those unearned values back to states that were visited. The greedy policy then exploits estimation error rather than real knowledge. This is the core failure of offline RL: distribution shift between the data and the learned policy. Remedies include collecting data that covers the region, initialising unvisited values pessimistically, or constraining the policy to actions well supported by the data (conservative or behaviour-regularised methods).

dlcore:08.05.q: An e-commerce team runs Thompson sampling over 5 page layouts, but conversions are reported in daily batches, so the algorithm picks the layout for every visitor of the day before seeing any of that day's results. They want to switch to UCB1 'because it is deterministic and easier to audit'. What happens to UCB1 under daily batching, and why does Thompson sampling cope better?
dlcore:08.05.s: UCB1 is deterministic given its counts. Within a day the counts do not change, so every visitor that day gets the same layout: the one with the highest upper bound at the start of the day. Exploration then happens one arm per day instead of continuously, so it takes many days to try the arms enough, and a whole day of traffic can be spent on an arm that a few hundred visitors would have ruled out. Regret grows with batch size. Thompson sampling draws a fresh posterior sample per visitor, so within one day traffic is spread across layouts in proportion to the probability that each is best, which is natural, well-calibrated batch exploration. If auditability matters, keep Thompson sampling with logged seeds and per-visitor assignment probabilities (which also enables unbiased offline evaluation), or use a batched UCB variant that spreads each batch across arms.

dlcore:08.06.q: Your actor-critic implementation computes `loss = -(logp * (returns - values)).mean() + 0.5 * ((returns - values)**2).mean()` with a single shared network, and training is unstable: the policy seems to chase the critic. What is the bug, and what else would you check in this loss?
dlcore:08.06.s: The advantage `returns - values` is not detached, so the policy term backpropagates into the critic. Gradient descent on $-\log\pi\cdot(R-V)$ with respect to $V$ pushes $V$ up whenever $\log\pi$ is negative (always, for a stochastic policy), and in general moves the critic to make the policy loss small rather than to predict returns. With a shared body, the policy and value objectives then fight through the same features. Fix: `adv = (returns - values).detach()`, optionally normalised per batch, and use the non-detached values only in the value loss. Other checks: add an entropy bonus (missing here) so the policy does not collapse; make sure `returns` are computed with bootstrapping from $V(s_{T})$ at truncation and none at true terminals; consider GAE instead of raw returns for lower variance; and check the relative scale of the value loss, since on a shared network a large value loss can swamp the policy gradient.

dlcore:08.07.q: After DPO training, your model's win rate against the reference improves, but you notice the log-probability of the chosen answers on the training set went down, not up. Is this a bug? Explain using the DPO loss, and say what risk it signals.
dlcore:08.07.s: It is not necessarily a bug. The DPO loss depends only on the margin $\beta[(\log\pi(y_w)-\log\pi_\text{ref}(y_w))-(\log\pi(y_l)-\log\pi_\text{ref}(y_l))]$. It can be increased by pushing the rejected answer's likelihood down faster than the chosen one's, even while both fall. The chosen and rejected answers for a prompt are usually similar, sharing most tokens, so gradients that push down $y_l$ also push down $y_w$; the loss is satisfied as long as $y_l$ falls more. The risk is that probability mass leaves both answers and goes somewhere the data says nothing about, possibly to off-distribution or degenerate outputs, which is a form of over-optimisation that the implicit KL does not fully prevent with a finite dataset. Monitor chosen and rejected log-probabilities and KL from the reference; mitigations include a higher $\beta$, early stopping, adding an SFT (negative log-likelihood) term on chosen answers, or on-policy variants that refresh the pairs.

dlcore:09.01.q: Your Go engine sometimes reports that a move capturing an opponent group is illegal as suicide. The bug report shows the placed stone had no empty neighbours at the moment it was placed. Explain the bug in terms of the order of rule checks, and explain why this specific order is what the rules require.
dlcore:09.01.s: The engine checks the new stone's liberties before removing captured opponent groups. When a stone is placed into a point surrounded by opponent stones, its group may have zero liberties at that instant, but if that placement takes the last liberty of an adjacent opponent group, that group is removed first, which empties points next to the new stone and gives it liberties. The rules define a move as: place the stone, remove all opponent groups with no liberties, then check your own group. Only if your group still has no liberties after captures is the move suicide (illegal under Chinese rules). Capturing therefore always takes precedence, which is what makes moves that fill an opponent's last liberty from 'inside' legal. Fix the order: place, scan the up-to-four adjacent opponent groups and remove any with no liberties, then flood-fill your own group, then run the superko check on the resulting board.
dlcore:09.01.t: Game trees and the rules of Go

dlcore:09.02.q: A teammate's MCTS converts each leaf value to the root player's perspective once and adds that same number to every edge on the path; selection at every node then maximises $Q+U$. Search looks fine when it only expands the root's children, but deeper searches approve moves that lose to a simple reply. What game is the search actually solving, and why does the depth-1 case hide it?
dlcore:09.02.s: At nodes where the opponent is to move, the edges now store the root player's value, and selection picks the edge that maximises it. The search therefore models an opponent who chooses the reply that is best for the root player: it is solving a cooperative game, not minimax. A move whose only refutation is one strong reply looks excellent, because the search assumes the opponent will never play that reply. With only the root's children expanded, every selection happens at a root-player node, where maximising the root player's value is correct, so the bug is invisible; it appears as soon as the tree contains opponent decisions. The fix is to store each edge's value from the perspective of the player who chose it: back up $v$ from the leaf player's view and negate it at every level, so that each node's maximisation is that node's player looking after their own interests.

dlcore:09.03.q: Why is the policy target the MCTS visit distribution $\pi$ rather than a one-hot vector on the move actually played? Give two concrete reasons, considering how the move is chosen in self-play and what the network learns from each target.
dlcore:09.03.s: First, the played move is sampled from $\pi$ (with temperature, and for the first 30 moves stochastically), so a one-hot target would add sampling noise: an exploratory move with 3 percent of the visits would be taught as if it were the search's choice. The full distribution is the less noisy, expected version of that target. Second, $\pi$ carries much more information: it ranks all moves the search considered, says how close the alternatives were and spreads probability across equally good moves, so the network learns calibrated priors rather than overconfident ones. That matters because those priors steer future searches; a peaked, wrong prior starves good moves of visits under PUCT. More generally, the visit distribution is the output of a policy improvement operator (the search), and matching it with cross-entropy is distillation of that improved policy, the same role the greedy improvement step plays in policy iteration.

dlcore:09.04.q: To save compute, you cut self-play to 50 MCTS simulations per move while keeping everything else the same. Training loss goes down nicely, but playing strength plateaus early. Use the policy-iteration view of the loop to explain why, and say what you would change if compute really is limited.
dlcore:09.04.s: The loop improves only as far as search improves on the network. With 50 simulations on a 362-move board, the search barely explores beyond the network's top few priors, so the visit distribution $\pi$ is close to $p$ itself. Training $p$ towards $\pi$ then teaches the network what it already believes: the policy improvement step has almost no effect, and the loss falls because the target is easy, not because play improves. Value targets also come from weak, near-raw-network games, so $v$ learns to evaluate a weak policy. With limited compute, keep a strong improvement signal where it matters: KataGo's playout-cap randomisation runs a full search (say 600 or more simulations) on a random fraction of moves and records only those as policy targets, while the remaining moves use a cheap search just to keep the game going. Also reduce other costs first: a smaller network, resignation with false-positive checks, and a larger replay window to reuse data.

air-fanout-v1:01.01.q: A colleague says a 3-layer network with no activation functions is "more expressive" than one linear layer because it has more parameters. Is that right, and how would you show it in one line?
air-fanout-v1:01.01.s: No. Composing affine maps gives an affine map: W3​(W2​(W1​x+b1​)+b2​)+b3​=Wx+b with W=W3​W2​W1​. The extra parameters only change the optimisation, not the set of functions. Non-linear activations between layers are what add expressiveness.

air-fanout-v1:01.02.q: Your finite-difference gradient check uses h=10−12 in float32 and disagrees with autograd by 100%. Autograd is correct. What went wrong, and what should h be?
air-fanout-v1:01.02.s: Round-off. In float32 (about 7 significant digits), f(x+h)−f(x) with h=10−12 is mostly rounding noise, then divided by a tiny h. Use the central difference (f(x+h)−f(x−h))/2h with h≈10−3 to 10−4 in float32, or do the check in float64 with h≈10−6.

air-fanout-v1:01.03.q: Two 768-dimensional embeddings have a dot product of 40. Can you say whether they are similar? What would you compute instead?
air-fanout-v1:01.03.s: Not without their lengths: a large dot product can come from long vectors pointing in different directions. Compute cosine similarity, u⋅v/(∥u∥∥v∥), which is in [−1,1] and ignores length. If the vectors are already unit-normalised, as many embedding APIs return them, the dot product is the cosine.

air-fanout-v1:01.04.q: Gradient descent on f(x,y)=x2+100y2 with one learning rate oscillates wildly in y while barely moving in x. Explain using the gradient, and name two fixes.
air-fanout-v1:01.04.s: The gradient is (2x,200y): curvature in y is 100 times that in x. A learning rate small enough to be stable in y (<0.01) makes x crawl. Fixes: per-parameter adaptive steps (Adam, RMSProp), momentum to damp the oscillation, or rescaling the inputs (preconditioning, normalisation) so the curvatures match.

air-fanout-v1:01.05.q: A layer maps a batch X of shape (32, 512) with a weight matrix stored as (256, 512). Write the forward pass and give the output shape and the number of multiply-adds.
air-fanout-v1:01.05.s: Y=XW⊤ (as in nn.Linear), shape (32, 256). Each of the 32×256 outputs is a 512-term dot product, so 32⋅256⋅512≈4.19M multiply-adds, about 8.4M FLOPs.

air-fanout-v1:01.06.q: Derive dzd​σ(z) for the sigmoid and explain why it caused vanishing gradients in deep sigmoid networks.
air-fanout-v1:01.06.s: σ′(z)=σ(z)(1−σ(z)), which is at most 0.25 (at z=0) and near 0 when ∣z∣ is large. Backprop multiplies one such factor per layer, so 10 layers scale the gradient by at most 0.2510≈10−6. ReLU's derivative is 1 for positive inputs, which avoids this.

air-fanout-v1:01.07.q: For L=(σ(wx+b)−y)2, write ∂L/∂w by the chain rule, and say which quantities from the forward pass backprop must store.
air-fanout-v1:01.07.s: With z=wx+b, a=σ(z): ∂L/∂w=2(a−y)⋅a(1−a)⋅x. Backprop needs x, and a (from which σ′(z)=a(1−a) follows). Storing such activations is why training uses much more memory than inference.

air-fanout-v1:01.08.q: In your hand-written backprop, a node used twice in the graph (e.g. y = x * x) gets the wrong gradient. What is the bug?
air-fanout-v1:01.08.s: Gradients from every use must be accumulated (+=), not assigned. For y=x⋅x, each branch contributes x⋅yˉ​, giving 2xyˉ​; assignment keeps only one branch and returns half. It is the same reason PyTorch accumulates into .grad and you call zero_grad().

air-fanout-v1:01.09.q: What is the Jacobian of softmax, and why does no framework ever build it explicitly during backprop?
air-fanout-v1:01.09.s: ∂si​/∂zj​=si​(δij​−sj​), i.e. diag(s)−ss⊤, a V×V matrix. For a 150k vocabulary that is 22.5 billion entries per token. Backprop only needs the vector-Jacobian product zˉ=s⊙(sˉ−(sˉ⋅s)), which costs O(V); with cross-entropy it simplifies further to s−onehot(y).

air-fanout-v1:01.10.q: In an LSTM gate, ct​=ft​⊙ct−1​+it​⊙gt​. What is ∂ct​/∂ct−1​, and why does that matter?
air-fanout-v1:01.10.s: It is diag(ft​): an element-wise scaling by the forget gate. When ft​≈1, gradients flow back through time almost unchanged, which is how LSTMs avoid the vanishing gradients of plain RNNs, whose recurrence multiplies by a full weight matrix and a squashing derivative each step.

air-fanout-v1:01.11.q: A language model's validation loss is 2.0 nats per token. What is its perplexity, and how many bits per token is that?
air-fanout-v1:01.11.s: Perplexity =e2.0≈7.39: on average as uncertain as a uniform choice among about 7.4 tokens. In bits, 2.0/ln2≈2.89 bits per token. Comparing losses across models with different tokenisers needs bits per byte or per character, not per token.

air-fanout-v1:01.12.q: In RLHF, the KL penalty is computed as KL(πθ​∥πref​), not the reverse. What behaviour does this direction encourage?
air-fanout-v1:01.12.s: Reverse KL (expectation under the policy) is mode-seeking: it heavily penalises putting probability where the reference has almost none, but does not penalise ignoring some of the reference's modes. The policy stays on text the reference finds plausible, while being free to concentrate on a subset of good answers.

air-fanout-v1:01.13.q: A 4096×4096 weight update has singular values that drop to near zero after the first 16. What does that tell you, and which method exploits it?
air-fanout-v1:01.13.s: The update is approximately rank 16: it can be written as BA with B of shape 4096×16 and A 16×4096, about 131k numbers instead of 16.8M. LoRA trains exactly such a low-rank update; truncated SVD of the full update gives the best rank-16 approximation (Eckart–Young).

air-fanout-v1:01.14.q: You keep an EMA of model weights with decay 0.999 and evaluate it after 500 steps. Why is it bad, and what are two fixes?
air-fanout-v1:01.14.s: The EMA's effective window is about 1/(1−0.999)=1000 steps, and it started at the random initial weights, which still carry weight 0.999500≈0.61. Fix with bias correction (divide by 1−βt, as Adam does) or a warm-up decay such as min(0.999,(1+t)/(10+t)); or start the EMA later.

air-fanout-v1:01.15.q: Why do 4-bit quantised LLM weights need a separate scale per small group (e.g. 64 weights), rather than one scale per tensor?
air-fanout-v1:01.15.s: 4 bits give only 16 levels. One outlier weight in a tensor sets the scale for all, so most weights round to the same few levels. Per-group scales let each group use its own range, at the cost of storing one scale (often float16) per group, about 0.25 extra bits per weight for groups of 64.

air-fanout-v1:02.01.q: In attention, scores are QK⊤/d​. With d=128 and query and key entries roughly i.i.d. with unit variance, what is the standard deviation of a raw dot product, and why divide?
air-fanout-v1:02.01.s: The sum of 128 unit-variance products has variance 128, so standard deviation 128​≈11.3. Logits that large make softmax nearly one-hot, with tiny gradients. Dividing by d​ brings the standard deviation back to about 1.

air-fanout-v1:02.02.q: A naive softmax returns NaN on logits [1000, 1001, 1002]. Why, and what is the fix? What are the correct probabilities?
air-fanout-v1:02.02.s: exp(1000) overflows to infinity, and inf/inf is NaN. Subtract the maximum first: softmax is unchanged by a constant shift, so compute exp([-2,-1,0]). The result is about [0.090, 0.245, 0.665].

air-fanout-v1:02.03.q: Your regression loss ((pred - y)**2).mean() trains to a poor fit with no error. pred has shape (N,) and y has shape (N, 1). What happened?
air-fanout-v1:02.03.s: Broadcasting turned pred - y into an (N, N) matrix of every prediction minus every target, so the loss compares each prediction with all targets. Make shapes match (y.squeeze(1) or pred[:, None]) and assert pred.shape == y.shape; F.mse_loss warns about this case.

air-fanout-v1:02.04.q: You add L1 regularisation to a linear model and many weights become exactly 0; with L2 they become small but not zero. Explain using the gradients.
air-fanout-v1:02.04.s: The L1 penalty's gradient is λsign(w), a constant push towards 0 however small w is, so weights reach and stay at 0 (with proximal or subgradient methods). L2's gradient 2λw shrinks as w shrinks, so weights approach 0 but never get there.

air-fanout-v1:03.01.q: torch.tensor(np_array) and torch.from_numpy(np_array) both work. You modify the NumPy array afterwards. Which tensor changes, and which choice is right for a data loader?
air-fanout-v1:03.01.s: from_numpy shares memory, so it changes; torch.tensor copies, so it does not. In a data loader, from_numpy avoids a copy, but make sure the array is not reused or mutated later (and that its dtype is what the model expects, e.g. float32 not float64).

air-fanout-v1:03.02.q: You compute attention scores with q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) for q, k of shape (B, H, T, d). What is the output shape, and how does the memory grow with sequence length?
air-fanout-v1:03.02.s: (B, H, T, T). Memory grows as T2: at T = 32k, one head's float16 score matrix is about 2 GB. FlashAttention avoids storing it by computing softmax in tiles.

air-fanout-v1:03.03.q: After x = x.transpose(1, 2), x.view(B, -1) raises an error but x.reshape(B, -1) works. Why, and what does reshape do differently?
air-fanout-v1:03.03.s: Transpose only changes strides, so the tensor is no longer contiguous in memory, and view cannot reinterpret it without copying. reshape returns a view when possible and otherwise copies (as x.contiguous().view(...) would). Be aware that the copy costs memory and time.

air-fanout-v1:03.04.q: A model expects (N, 1, 28, 28) but your batch is (N, 28, 28). Give two correct one-liners, and one common wrong fix.
air-fanout-v1:03.04.s: x.unsqueeze(1) or x[:, None]. Wrong: x.view(N, 28, 28, 1) (channels-last) or x.reshape(N, 1, 28, 28) applied to data that was actually laid out differently, both of which run without error and feed the model scrambled pixels.

air-fanout-v1:03.05.q: You set y = x[:, :10] then y.zero_(). Is x changed? What about y = x[:, [0, 2, 4]]?
air-fanout-v1:03.05.s: Basic slicing returns a view, so x is changed. Indexing with a list (advanced indexing) returns a copy, so x is unchanged. This difference causes silent bugs in data augmentation code.

air-fanout-v1:03.06.q: You have a list of 8 tensors, each (3, 224, 224). Which call gives a batch of shape (8, 3, 224, 224), and what does torch.cat along dim 0 give instead?
air-fanout-v1:03.06.s: torch.stack(lst) adds a new dimension: (8, 3, 224, 224). torch.cat(lst, 0) joins along the existing first axis: (24, 224, 224), which a model would misread as 24 single-channel images.

air-fanout-v1:03.07.q: Build a boolean causal mask for T = 5 in one line, and say how it is applied to attention scores.
air-fanout-v1:03.07.s: mask = torch.tril(torch.ones(5, 5, dtype=torch.bool)). Then scores.masked_fill(~mask, float('-inf')) before softmax, so position i gives zero weight to positions after i.

air-fanout-v1:03.08.q: Your tensor pipeline runs on CPU at 1 s per batch; moving it to the GPU makes it slower. Name the two most likely causes.
air-fanout-v1:03.08.s: Data moving between host and device every step (e.g. .cpu(), .numpy() or .item() inside the loop, or building tensors on the CPU then copying), and tensors too small for the GPU to beat its kernel-launch overhead. Profile with torch.profiler, batch the work, and keep tensors on one device.

air-fanout-v1:03.09.q: Write a vectorised one-liner for pairwise squared Euclidean distances between X (N, d) and Y (M, d), and name its numerical risk.
air-fanout-v1:03.09.s: (X**2).sum(1)[:, None] + (Y**2).sum(1)[None] - 2 * X @ Y.T. Cancellation can give small negative values for near-identical points; clamp at 0 before taking a square root. torch.cdist does this for you.

air-fanout-v1:04.01.q: A Keras model ending in Dense(10) with SparseCategoricalCrossentropy() trains to only 85% on MNIST where you expected 92%. What is the likely one-word bug?
air-fanout-v1:04.01.s: from_logits. The loss defaults to from_logits=False, treating raw logits as probabilities. Set from_logits=True, or add a softmax to the last layer.

air-fanout-v1:04.02.q: Your CNN gets 99% on MNIST but 60% on the same digits shifted 6 pixels. Convolution is translation-equivariant, so why does this happen?
air-fanout-v1:04.02.s: Equivariance holds for convolution layers, but pooling with stride, the final flatten and the dense layer tie features to positions. A 6-pixel shift moves features to other dense-layer inputs never seen at those positions in training. Global average pooling and shift augmentation make the model far more tolerant.

air-fanout-v1:04.03.q: Old TF1 code calls sess.run(train_op, feed_dict={x: batch}). Translate this into TF2 in words, and say why print(loss) inside the TF1 model showed no number.
air-fanout-v1:04.03.s: In TF2, the training step is a normal Python function (optionally @tf.function) called with the batch as an argument; there is no session or placeholder. In TF1, model code only built a graph, so print showed a symbolic Tensor; values existed only when sess.run executed it.

air-fanout-v1:04.04.q: You test a model with dropout and batch norm and get different predictions on every call for the same input. What did you forget in PyTorch, and in Keras?
air-fanout-v1:04.04.s: PyTorch: model.eval() (and torch.no_grad()). Keras: calling the model with training=False (or using predict/evaluate, which do so). Without it, dropout stays active and batch norm uses batch statistics.

air-fanout-v1:04.05.q: Your MNIST arrays are sorted by label. With fit(..., validation_split=0.2), training accuracy is 95% but validation accuracy is near 0%. Why?
air-fanout-v1:04.05.s: validation_split takes the last 20% of the arrays before any shuffling, so validation holds only the last classes (mostly 8s and 9s), which the model never trains on. Shuffle the arrays first, or pass an explicit stratified validation_data.

air-fanout-v1:04.06.q: You save a fine-tuned PyTorch model with torch.save(model, path) and a teammate cannot load it after refactoring the class's module path. What should you have saved?
air-fanout-v1:04.06.s: model.state_dict(): a dictionary of tensors with no dependence on the class's import path. Rebuild the model from code and call load_state_dict. Save the optimizer state and step too if training will resume.

air-fanout-v1:04.07.q: Five copies of a model, trained from the same seed on the same data in the same order, are averaged. How much does the ensemble help, and what would you change?
air-fanout-v1:04.07.s: Nothing: identical training gives identical models, so correlation ρ=1 and the variance term ρσ2 does not shrink. Vary the seed, data order or bootstrap sample, or the architecture, so members make different errors.

air-fanout-v1:04.08.q: Your CIFAR-10 model reaches 99% training accuracy and 75% test accuracy. Give the three changes most likely to close the gap, in order of cost.
air-fanout-v1:04.08.s: Data augmentation (random crops with padding and horizontal flips), weight decay with a learning-rate schedule, and a better architecture with batch norm and residual connections (a small ResNet reaches 93% or more). Augmentation alone typically gives the largest gain for the least effort.

air-fanout-v1:04.09.q: You feed raw 0–255 pixels to a pre-trained Keras InceptionV3 and get confident nonsense. What is missing, and why is there no error?
air-fanout-v1:04.09.s: inception_v3.preprocess_input, which scales pixels to [−1,1]. Any float tensor of the right shape is a valid input, so the model runs, but on inputs far outside its training distribution.

air-fanout-v1:04.10.q: You cache frozen-backbone features once, then add random flips and crops to the training images to fight overfitting. Accuracy does not change. Why?
air-fanout-v1:04.10.s: The cached features were computed from un-augmented images, so the head never sees the augmentation. With augmentation, run the frozen backbone inside the training loop (or cache several augmented copies).

air-fanout-v1:04.11.q: A frame classifier built from 40 phone videos scores 99% on a random frame-level split and 65% on videos filmed the next day. Explain and fix.
air-fanout-v1:04.11.s: Leakage: neighbouring frames of the same video are near-duplicates, so the test set repeated training images, and the model may have learnt backgrounds. Split by video (GroupShuffleSplit), and test on videos from new locations and lighting.

air-fanout-v1:04.12.q: You unfreeze all of VGG16 and fine-tune at learning rate 1e-3 with a new random head. Validation accuracy drops below the frozen-backbone baseline. What two mistakes did you make?
air-fanout-v1:04.12.s: You unfroze before training the head, so large random-head gradients wrecked the pre-trained features, and you used a learning rate about 100 times too high for fine-tuning. Train the head first with the base frozen, then unfreeze the top layers at about 1e-5.

air-fanout-v1:04.13.q: A model has 95% clean accuracy and 2% accuracy under FGSM with ε=8/255. A reviewer suggests JPEG-compressing inputs as a defence and FGSM accuracy rises to 60%. Should you claim robustness?
air-fanout-v1:04.13.s: No. Input transformations often mask gradients rather than remove adversarial examples. Evaluate with an adaptive attack that knows the defence (e.g. PGD through a differentiable JPEG approximation, or BPDA, Athalye et al., 2018). Expect accuracy to fall back sharply.

air-fanout-v1:04.14.q: After adversarial training against one fixed universal noise pattern, accuracy on that noise is 98%. What does this say about robustness to other attacks?
air-fanout-v1:04.14.s: Very little: the network learned to ignore one pattern. Robustness needs the inner maximisation to be solved fresh for each batch (e.g. PGD within an ε-ball), and evaluation with attacks not used in training.

air-fanout-v1:04.15.q: Activation maximisation for a channel produces high-frequency static. Without changing the network, list three changes that make the image interpretable.
air-fanout-v1:04.15.s: Random jitter, rotation and scaling of the image each step (transformation robustness); a regulariser such as total variation or periodic blurring; and optimising in a decorrelated or Fourier parameterisation instead of raw pixels.

air-fanout-v1:04.16.q: You show a saliency map for a digit classifier in a report. How do you check that it reflects the model and not just the image?
air-fanout-v1:04.16.s: Run the model-randomisation test (Adebayo et al., 2018): randomise the trained weights and recompute the map. If it looks the same, the map is mostly an edge detector on the input. Also compare to a label-randomised model.

air-fanout-v1:04.17.q: Your DeepDream output on a 4000×3000 photo runs out of GPU memory and shows a grid of seams. What two techniques fix both?
air-fanout-v1:04.17.s: Process the image in tiles, which bounds memory, and apply a random shift (roll) to the image before each step and undo it after, so tile boundaries move and seams average out. Octaves (multiple scales) also let you work at low resolution first.

air-fanout-v1:04.18.q: Why does a Gram matrix capture style but not content? Answer in terms of what is summed away.
air-fanout-v1:04.18.s: Gij​=∑p​Fip​Fjp​ sums over all spatial positions p, so it records which channels co-activate but not where. Texture and colour statistics survive; the arrangement of objects, which is content, is discarded.

air-fanout-v1:04.19.q: You time y = x @ x for an 8192×8192 matrix on a GPU with time.time() around it and get 0.05 ms. Why is that impossible, and how do you time it properly?
air-fanout-v1:04.19.s: The matmul is 2⋅81923≈1.1 TFLOP, so 0.05 ms would need about 22 PFLOP/s, far beyond any GPU. CUDA launches asynchronously, so the timer measured only the launch. Warm up, call torch.cuda.synchronize() before stopping the timer (or .numpy() in TF), and average several runs. Expect over 100 ms in float32 on a Colab T4.

air-fanout-v1:04.20.q: Your DQN's Q-values grow without bound during training on CartPole. Name three likely causes.
air-fanout-v1:04.20.s: No target network (or updating it every step), forgetting the (1 - done) mask so terminal states bootstrap from the next episode, and the max operator's overestimation (fix with Double DQN). A too-high learning rate or missing reward clipping can also contribute.

air-fanout-v1:04.21.q: You inherit TF1 Estimator code that must run on current TensorFlow. What is your plan?
air-fanout-v1:04.21.s: tf.estimator was removed in TF 2.16, so port it: turn model_fn's network into a Keras model, input_fn into a tf.data pipeline, the train op into compile/fit or a custom train_step, and model_dir into ModelCheckpoint and TensorBoard callbacks. Check the port by matching metrics on a fixed checkpoint or a short run.

air-fanout-v1:04.22.q: Your GPU utilisation is 30% while training from a tf.data pipeline that decodes JPEGs. What three changes do you try first?
air-fanout-v1:04.22.s: map(..., num_parallel_calls=tf.data.AUTOTUNE) for decoding and augmentation, .prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE) at the end, and .cache() after decoding if the dataset fits in memory (or pre-serialise to TFRecords). Then check that shuffling's buffer is not doing expensive work.

air-fanout-v1:04.23.q: You tune 40 trials and report the best validation accuracy as your result, beating a baseline from a paper by 0.4%. What is wrong with the comparison?
air-fanout-v1:04.23.s: The best-of-40 validation score is optimistically biased, and the baseline was probably not tuned with the same budget. Report the chosen configuration's test score, over several seeds, and tune the baseline with the same search.

air-fanout-v1:04.24.q: Your GRU sentiment model gets 50% on IMDB while bag-of-words logistic regression gets 88%. The reviews are padded at the end to length 500. What is the likely bug?
air-fanout-v1:04.24.s: Post-padding without masking: the GRU reads hundreds of padding zeros after the review and its final state forgets the text. Use mask_zero=True on the embedding, or pre-padding, or take the state at each review's true last token.

air-fanout-v1:04.25.q: Your seq2seq model translates short sentences well and long ones badly, with the second half often unrelated to the source. What is the architectural cause and the standard fix?
air-fanout-v1:04.25.s: The whole source is compressed into one fixed-size encoder vector, which cannot hold long sentences. Attention (Bahdanau et al., 2014) lets the decoder read all encoder states at each step.

air-fanout-v1:04.26.q: Your captioning model's BLEU went up 2 points but human raters prefer the old model. Which do you trust, and why might they disagree?
air-fanout-v1:04.26.s: The human judgement, for the final decision. BLEU rewards n-gram overlap with reference captions, so generic, common phrasings score well while correct but differently worded or more specific captions score low. Report both, and add a semantic or model-based metric.

air-fanout-v1:04.27.q: A GRU forecasting next-day temperature reaches MAE 1.8 °C. Persistence ("tomorrow equals today") has MAE 1.9 °C. Your split was random by day. How good is the model?
air-fanout-v1:04.27.s: Unknown and probably worse than it looks: a random split leaks future information, and even so it barely beats persistence. Re-split by time, fit scalers on the training period only, and compare again to persistence and seasonal-naive baselines.

air-fanout-v1:05.01.q: A single sigmoid neuron trained with squared error learns very slowly when its output starts near 0 or 1, even if badly wrong. Why, and which loss fixes it?
air-fanout-v1:05.01.s: The gradient contains σ′(z)=a(1−a), near 0 when the output saturates. Cross-entropy with a sigmoid cancels that factor: ∂L/∂z=a−y, so a confidently wrong neuron gets a large gradient.

air-fanout-v1:05.02.q: A layer maps 4096 inputs to 11,008 outputs with bias. How many parameters does it have, and what standard deviation would He initialisation use for its weights?
air-fanout-v1:05.02.s: 4096⋅11008+11008=45,099,776 parameters. He initialisation uses standard deviation 2/4096​≈0.0221.

air-fanout-v1:05.03.q: Your from-scratch 4-layer network's loss stays at exactly ln10≈2.303 on a 10-class problem from the first step. Name two likely causes.
air-fanout-v1:05.03.s: All weights initialised to zero (every unit identical, so outputs are uniform), or gradients not reaching the weights: no update step, a missing zero_grad making updates cancel, or a ReLU layer whose units are all dead because of a large negative bias. Check that parameter norms change after one step.

air-fanout-v1:05.04.q: How does RMSNorm differ from LayerNorm, and why do most LLMs use it?
air-fanout-v1:05.04.s: RMSNorm divides by mean(x2)+ϵ​ and multiplies by a learned scale; it does not subtract the mean and has no bias. It is cheaper (one reduction instead of two) and works as well in practice for transformers.

air-fanout-v1:05.05.q: Training diverges in the first 200 steps at learning rate 3e-4 but is fine at 1e-4, which then trains too slowly. What schedule change would you try?
air-fanout-v1:05.05.s: Linear warm-up from near 0 to 3e-4 over the first few hundred to a few thousand steps, then cosine or linear decay. Early steps have large, noisy gradients and Adam's second-moment estimates are not yet reliable; warm-up avoids huge early updates.

air-fanout-v1:05.06.q: You use torch.optim.Adam(params, weight_decay=0.1) and find that large-gradient weights are barely regularised. Why, and what should you use?
air-fanout-v1:05.06.s: In Adam, L2 weight decay is added to the gradient and then divided by v^​, so weights with large gradient variance are decayed less. AdamW decouples decay: w←w−ηλw separately from the adaptive step, so every weight decays at the same rate.

air-fanout-v1:05.07.q: Your from-scratch MLP matches PyTorch's forward pass exactly but its gradients differ by a factor of exactly the batch size. What is the bug?
air-fanout-v1:05.07.s: The loss is summed over the batch in one implementation and averaged in the other. Use the mean in both (divide the output gradient by N), or compare against reduction='sum'.

air-fanout-v1:06.01.q: Attention weights are often presented as an explanation of a model's prediction. Give one reason to be cautious.
air-fanout-v1:06.01.s: Attention weights show where one layer's head read from, not how much that information affected the output; values pass through many layers, residual connections and MLPs afterwards. Different attention patterns can give the same prediction (Jain and Wallace, 2019). Use attribution or ablation methods for causal claims.

air-fanout-v1:06.02.q: Your self-attention outputs at position 3 change when you edit the token at position 7, in a model meant to be causal. Where is the bug, and how do you test for it?
air-fanout-v1:06.02.s: The causal mask is missing, wrong (e.g. upper instead of lower triangle), or applied after softmax. Test: perturb future tokens and assert outputs at earlier positions are unchanged to numerical precision.

air-fanout-v1:06.03.q: Your GPT's initial training loss on a 50,257-token vocabulary is 10.8. What should it be with a correct initialisation, and what does 10.8 suggest?
air-fanout-v1:06.03.s: About ln50257≈10.82, the loss of a uniform prediction. 10.8 is therefore correct. A much higher value (say 30) means the initial logits are too large, often because the output projection or embeddings are initialised with too much variance.

air-fanout-v1:07.01.q: Your RL agent's reward curve rises steadily, but the behaviour, when you watch it, does something unintended and pointless. What is this called and what do you do?
air-fanout-v1:07.01.s: Reward hacking (specification gaming): the agent maximises the reward as written, not as meant. Fix the reward or the environment, add constraints, and always inspect rollouts, not just curves.

air-fanout-v1:07.02.q: REINFORCE learns very slowly with high-variance gradients. Which single change usually helps most, and why does it not bias the gradient?
air-fanout-v1:07.02.s: Subtract a baseline b(s), typically a learned value estimate, from the return: use (Gt​−b(st​))∇logπ(at​∣st​). Because Ea​[∇logπ(a∣s)]=0, the baseline term has zero expectation, so the gradient stays unbiased while its variance falls.

air-fanout-v1:07.03.q: Why does DQN need a replay buffer, while on-policy methods such as PPO do not use one?
air-fanout-v1:07.03.s: Q-learning is off-policy: its target r+γmaxQ(s′,a′) is valid for data from any behaviour policy, so old transitions can be reused, and sampling them randomly breaks temporal correlation. PPO's objective assumes data from the current (or very recent) policy, so stale data would bias it.

air-fanout-v1:07.04.q: In PPO the importance ratio rt​=πθ​(at​∣st​)/πold​(at​∣st​) is clipped to [1−ϵ,1+ϵ]. What failure does clipping prevent?
air-fanout-v1:07.04.s: Large policy updates from a batch collected under the old policy. Without clipping, maximising rt​At​ pushes rt​ far from 1, where the old samples no longer estimate the new policy's performance, and the policy can collapse. Clipping removes the incentive to move further once the ratio leaves the band.
air-fanout-v1:07.04.t: PPO, LLM Reasoning, Importance Ratio, Advantage

air-fanout-v1:07.05.q: GRPO normalises each answer's reward by the mean and standard deviation of its group. What happens to a prompt where all 8 sampled answers are correct?
air-fanout-v1:07.05.s: All advantages are 0 (and the standard deviation is 0, so implementations add an ϵ), so the prompt contributes no learning signal. Batches dominated by all-right or all-wrong prompts waste compute, which is why methods such as DAPO filter them out.
air-fanout-v1:07.05.t: Qwen 3 GSPO & DeepSeek GRPO — LLM Reasoning

air-fanout-v1:08.01.q: In grouped-query attention with 32 query heads and 8 KV heads, by what factor does the KV cache shrink compared with full multi-head attention, and what is the trade-off?
air-fanout-v1:08.01.s: By 4, because each KV head is shared by 4 query heads. The trade-off is a small quality loss compared with full MHA, usually negligible at scale, in exchange for much cheaper long-context inference.

air-fanout-v1:08.02.q: DeepSeek V3 has 671B parameters but activates about 37B per token. What does that mean for training compute and for serving memory?
air-fanout-v1:08.02.s: Compute per token scales with the 37B active parameters, so training and inference FLOPs are like a ~37B dense model. Memory is not: all 671B parameters must be stored and loaded across GPUs, so serving needs as many devices as a 671B model, and expert routing adds communication.

air-fanout-v1:08.03.q: Your from-scratch Qwen 3 matches Hugging Face logits for 3 tokens but diverges for 300. Which two components do you check first?
air-fanout-v1:08.03.s: RoPE (layout of rotated pairs, base θ=106, and position indices) and the attention mask or KV-cache indexing, both of which only show errors as positions grow. Also check QK-Norm is applied before RoPE.

air-fanout-v1:08.04.q: You train a 125M-parameter model on 2.5B tokens. Roughly how far is that from Chinchilla-optimal, and is that a problem?
air-fanout-v1:08.04.s: Chinchilla suggests about 20 tokens per parameter, i.e. 2.5B tokens for 125M parameters, so it is about compute-optimal. If the model will be used a lot for inference, training on more tokens than that (as Llama does) is better value.

air-fanout-v1:09.01.q: Your new method beats the baseline by 0.3 points, from one seed each. A reviewer asks if it is real. What do you run?
air-fanout-v1:09.01.s: Several seeds per method (at least 3 to 5), with the same tuning budget for both. Report the mean and a confidence interval or standard deviation; if the difference is within seed variation, say so. Add an ablation showing which part of the method causes the gain.
air-fanout-v1:09.01.t: Code, Write & Publish AI Research Paper

air-fanout-v1:10.01.q: A company wants its support bot to know its 200-page product manual. Should you fine-tune? Justify.
air-fanout-v1:10.01.s: Usually not first. Facts that change and need citing are better served by retrieval (RAG) over the manual. Fine-tune when you need a consistent format, tone or skill that prompting cannot reliably produce, or to make a smaller model match a larger one on a narrow task.

air-fanout-v1:10.02.q: You fine-tune a 7B model with QLoRA on a 16 GB GPU. Where does most of the memory saving come from, and what still takes memory?
air-fanout-v1:10.02.s: The frozen base weights are stored in 4-bit (about 3.5 GB instead of 14 GB in bf16), and only the small LoRA matrices have gradients and optimiser state. Activations still take memory, which grows with sequence length and batch size; gradient checkpointing reduces them.

air-fanout-v1:10.03.q: Your fine-tuning set has 5,000 examples, 30% of which are near-duplicates generated from one template. What is the risk and the fix?
air-fanout-v1:10.03.s: The model overfits to that template's phrasing and the effective dataset is smaller than it looks. Deduplicate (exact and near-duplicate, e.g. MinHash), rebalance, and keep a held-out set with no duplicates of training items.

air-fanout-v1:10.04.q: Your LoRA fine-tune's training loss falls to 0.2 in epoch 3, while validation loss starts rising after epoch 1. What do you do, and which number do you report?
air-fanout-v1:10.04.s: Stop at about epoch 1 (or lower the learning rate and use 1 to 2 epochs): the model is memorising. Pick the checkpoint by validation loss or, better, by evaluation of held-out generations, and report the test-set evaluation of that checkpoint.

air-fanout-v1:10.05.q: Your fine-tuned model looks great in the notebook but gives worse answers in your vLLM deployment. What is the most common cause?
air-fanout-v1:10.05.s: A chat-template mismatch: the deployment formats prompts differently (system prompt, special tokens, generation prompt) from training. Also check sampling settings and that the LoRA adapter was actually merged or loaded.

air-fanout-v1:11.01.q: A hiring manager clones your research repo and cannot reproduce your main number. List the four things that most often cause this.
air-fanout-v1:11.01.s: Unpinned dependencies, data not versioned or not available, configuration not recorded with the run (parameters, seed, commit), and manual steps not in code. Fix with a lock file, DVC, logged configs and commit hashes, and a single pipeline command.

air-fanout-v1:11.02.q: You discover an AWS key was committed three commits ago and pushed to a public repo. What do you do, in order?
air-fanout-v1:11.02.s: Revoke and rotate the key immediately in AWS, check its usage logs for misuse, then remove it from history (e.g. git filter-repo) and force-push, and add it to .gitignore or move it to secrets. Deleting the file in a new commit alone leaves the key in history.

air-fanout-v1:11.03.q: A teammate's training component mutates its config object to change the output path, and a later stage writes into the wrong folder. Which Python feature prevents this?
air-fanout-v1:11.03.s: Frozen dataclasses (@dataclass(frozen=True)): assignment to a field raises an error, so a stage cannot change shared settings. Return new values in an artifact object instead.

air-fanout-v1:11.04.q: What exactly does a .dvc file in Git contain, and where is the data?
air-fanout-v1:11.04.s: A small YAML file with the data's content hash (md5), size and path. The data itself is in the DVC cache and in the remote (S3, GCS, etc.). dvc pull uses the hash to fetch the right version for the current Git commit.

air-fanout-v1:11.05.q: You change only train.max_depth in params.yaml and run dvc repro. Which stages rerun, and how does DVC know?
air-fanout-v1:11.05.s: Only train and the stages that depend on its outputs (such as evaluation); ingestion and preparation are skipped. DVC compares the hashes of each stage's dependencies, code and declared parameters against dvc.lock.
air-fanout-v1:11.05.t: ML Pipeline with DVC & AWS S3

air-fanout-v1:11.06.q: Two runs in MLflow have the same parameters but different metrics. What is missing from your logging?
air-fanout-v1:11.06.s: Whatever else changed: the random seed, the code version (Git commit), the data version (DVC hash), or library versions. Log all of them with every run.

air-fanout-v1:11.07.q: Which tests are worth running in CI for an ML repository on every pull request, given CI runners are small and slow?
air-fanout-v1:11.07.s: Unit tests for data processing and shapes, a smoke test that trains for a few steps on a tiny sample and checks the loss falls, a test that loads the model and predicts on fixed inputs, plus linting. Full training belongs in a separate, scheduled or manual job.

air-fanout-v1:11.08.q: Your Docker image for a FastAPI model server is 9 GB and rebuilds take 15 minutes for one-line code changes. What two Dockerfile changes help most?
air-fanout-v1:11.08.s: Order layers so dependencies are installed (copy requirements.txt, then pip install) before copying the code, so code changes reuse the cached layer; and use a slim base with CPU-only wheels or a multi-stage build, and a .dockerignore excluding data, checkpoints and .git.

air-fanout-v1:11.09.q: For the vehicle insurance model, the sales team can call 1,000 of 50,000 customers per week. Which metric should guide model selection?
air-fanout-v1:11.09.s: Precision (or the conversion rate) among the top 1,000 ranked customers, i.e. precision@k, along with ROC-AUC or PR-AUC as ranking quality. Accuracy is misleading because most customers are negative.

air-fanout-v1:11.10.q: You add 0.0.0.0/0 to MongoDB Atlas network access so your cloud app can connect. What is the risk and what would you do in a real system?
air-fanout-v1:11.10.s: The database is reachable from the whole internet, protected only by the password. In a real system, restrict access to the app's IP addresses or use private networking (VPC peering or private endpoints), and use a least-privilege database user.

air-fanout-v1:11.11.q: Ingestion reads 400,000 rows, of which 12% are positive. After a random (unstratified) split, the test set has 10.5% positives. Why does this matter, and what is the fix?
air-fanout-v1:11.11.s: Train and test distributions differ, so test metrics, especially recall and precision, are biased and noisier. Use stratify=df[target] with a fixed seed.

air-fanout-v1:11.12.q: A teammate applies SMOTE to the full dataset, then splits into train and test, and recall jumps from 0.45 to 0.80. What is wrong?
air-fanout-v1:11.12.s: Synthetic test points are interpolated from training points, so test data leaks into training and the test distribution is artificial. Split first, resample only the training set, and evaluate on the untouched test set.

air-fanout-v1:11.13.q: The evaluation component accepts any new model with a higher F1 than production. Over a month, models are swapped 20 times with no real improvement. Why, and what do you change?
air-fanout-v1:11.13.s: F1 differences between runs are often within noise, so "higher" is frequently random. Require a minimum gain (e.g. 0.02), evaluate on a larger fixed holdout, and check the gain across seeds or with a bootstrap confidence interval.

air-fanout-v1:11.14.q: Your FastAPI endpoint loads the model inside the request handler. Latency is 2 s per request. Fix it, and name one more thing the endpoint needs.
air-fanout-v1:11.14.s: Load the model once at start-up (module level or the lifespan handler) and reuse it. Also add input validation with a Pydantic schema and a /health endpoint for probes.

air-fanout-v1:11.15.q: Your deploy workflow pushes images tagged latest and runs docker pull latest on EC2. A bad build reaches production. How do you roll back, and what should you change?
air-fanout-v1:11.15.s: With only latest, you must rebuild an old commit. Tag images with the commit SHA, deploy by SHA, and roll back by redeploying the previous SHA. Add a health check after deployment that fails the job.

air-fanout-v1:11.16.q: What is the difference between a Pod, a Deployment and a Service, in one sentence each?
air-fanout-v1:11.16.s: A Pod runs one or more containers together on a node; a Deployment keeps a desired number of identical Pods running and manages rolling updates; a Service gives those Pods a stable address and load-balances traffic between them.

air-fanout-v1:11.17.q: After kubectl apply, pods are Running but requests fail for 30 seconds after each restart. What is missing?
air-fanout-v1:11.17.s: A readiness probe. Without it, Kubernetes sends traffic as soon as the container starts, before the model has loaded. Add a readiness probe on /health that returns success only once the model is ready.

air-fanout-v1:11.18.q: Why should latency be recorded as a Prometheus histogram rather than an average gauge?
air-fanout-v1:11.18.s: Averages hide the slow tail that users notice. A histogram's buckets allow percentiles (histogram_quantile(0.95, ...)) to be computed and aggregated across pods; averages cannot be combined into percentiles.

air-fanout-v1:11.19.q: You deploy Prometheus and Grafana on your cluster, but your app's metrics never appear. Name two likely causes.
air-fanout-v1:11.19.s: Prometheus is not configured to scrape the app: no scrape config or ServiceMonitor, or a ServiceMonitor missing the label the Prometheus instance selects; or the Service's port name or path does not match where /metrics is served.

air-fanout-v1:11.20.q: In an end-to-end MLOps capstone, which component is the single most important for a reviewer to trust your reported model performance?
air-fanout-v1:11.20.s: The data split and evaluation: a fixed, versioned test set never used in training, preprocessing fitting or model selection, with the evaluation run by the pipeline rather than by hand.

air-fanout-v1:11.21.q: Your CI job logs runs to DagsHub's MLflow, but they appear under the wrong experiment and without the Git commit. What do you fix?
air-fanout-v1:11.21.s: Call mlflow.set_experiment(...) explicitly in the code, and set the commit as a tag (e.g. from GITHUB_SHA) if MLflow does not detect the repository in CI. Pass tracking URI and credentials as environment variables from secrets.

air-fanout-v1:11.22.q: The app loads models:/clf@champion and a separately saved vectoriser file. After promoting a new model, predictions become nonsense. Why?
air-fanout-v1:11.22.s: The new model was trained with a different vectoriser (vocabulary), but the app still loads the old one. Log the preprocessing object with the same MLflow run (or package them in one pipeline model) and load both from that version.

air-fanout-v1:11.23.q: Your CI's model performance test always passes, even when a teammate introduces a bug that clearly hurts the model in production. What is the likely flaw?
air-fanout-v1:11.23.s: The test uses data the model was trained or tuned on, or a threshold far below normal performance. Use a fixed, untouched holdout and a threshold close to the champion's score (no regression beyond a small margin).

air-fanout-v1:11.24.q: You finish the EKS lesson and delete your Deployments. A week later your AWS bill is still growing. What is still running?
air-fanout-v1:11.24.s: The EKS control plane (billed hourly), worker nodes, and possibly the load balancer created by a LoadBalancer Service and EBS volumes. Delete the Service first, then eksctl delete cluster, and check the console and CloudFormation for leftovers.

air-fanout-v1:11.25.q: Write a PromQL query for the 95th-percentile prediction latency over 5 minutes across all pods, from a histogram named predict_seconds.
air-fanout-v1:11.25.s: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(predict_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le)). Summing by le first aggregates the buckets across pods before computing the quantile.

air-fanout-v1:12.01.q: At a fixed number of tokens per batch, you double the sequence length and halve the batch size. How do compute per token and gradient noise change?
air-fanout-v1:12.01.s: Attention's score computation per token roughly doubles, because it scales with sequence length; MLP and projection compute per token is unchanged. Gradient noise depends mainly on tokens per batch, which is unchanged, though tokens within one sequence are correlated, so the effective batch is slightly smaller. The gain is learning longer-range dependencies.
air-fanout-v1:12.01.t: Train LLM — Sequence Length vs Batch Size

air-fanout-v1:12.02.q: You replace a 4d-hidden ReLU MLP with SwiGLU and keep the hidden size at 4d. Is the comparison fair? What hidden size should you use?
air-fanout-v1:12.02.s: No: SwiGLU has three matrices, so it has 50% more parameters and compute. Use a hidden size of about 38​d to match parameters, e.g. 11,008 for d=4096 after rounding.
air-fanout-v1:12.02.t: SwiGLU: two projections and a gate

air-fanout-v1:12.03.q: TRM gets 45% on ARC-AGI-1 with 7M parameters. Why is it not fair to say it is "smarter than" a large LLM evaluated on the same benchmark?
air-fanout-v1:12.03.s: TRM is trained specifically on that benchmark's training tasks with heavy augmentation, while the LLMs are general models evaluated without task-specific training. The result shows the power of recursion on small data for structured puzzles, not general reasoning ability.

air-fanout-v1:13.01.q: You are asked to cost a run: a dense decoder with 48 layers, hidden size 6144, vocabulary 50,000 (untied embeddings), context 2048, trained on 600B tokens on 256 H100s (989 TFLOP/s bf16 peak) at 45 percent MFU. Estimate the parameter count, the training FLOPs with and without the attention term, the wall-clock time, and the model-state memory. Can any single GPU hold the full optimiser state?
air-fanout-v1:13.01.s: Parameters: blocks $12 \times 48 \times 6144^2 = 21.7$B, embeddings $2 \times 50{,}000 \times 6144 = 0.61$B, so $N \approx 22.4$B. Training FLOPs: $6 \times 22.4\text{B} \times 600\text{B} = 8.05 \times 10^{22}$. The attention term is $12 \times 48 \times 2048 \times 6144 \times 600\text{B} = 4.35 \times 10^{21}$, about 5.4 percent extra, consistent with $T/(6d) = 2048/36{,}864 = 5.6$ percent; short contexts make attention cheap relative to the weights. Total about $8.48 \times 10^{22}$ FLOPs. Throughput: $256 \times 989 \times 10^{12} \times 0.45 = 1.14 \times 10^{17}$ FLOP/s, so about $7.4 \times 10^5$ seconds, roughly 8.6 days, before restarts and evaluation overhead. Model state at 16 bytes per parameter: $16 \times 22.4\text{B} = 358$ GB. No single 80 GB GPU can hold it; even before activations you need the state split at least five ways, and in practice sharded across all 256 GPUs (about 1.4 GB each under full sharding) or split by tensor and pipeline parallelism. The first planning decision is therefore how to partition state, not how big a batch to use.

air-fanout-v1:13.02.q: You must fine-tune a 13B model with full Adam on 32 GPUs (4 nodes of 8, 80 GB each, about 50 GB/s per GPU between nodes). Profiling shows activations need about 35 GB per GPU at your chosen micro-batch. Which ZeRO stages fit, and what does each cost in gradient-synchronisation time per optimiser step if nothing is overlapped?
air-fanout-v1:13.02.s: Per-GPU model state with $\Psi = 13$B and $N_d = 32$: plain DP $16 \times 13 = 208$ GB (impossible); ZeRO-1 $4 \times 13 + 12 \times 13/32 = 52 + 4.9 = 56.9$ GB, plus 35 GB of activations is 92 GB, which does not fit; ZeRO-2 $2 \times 13 + 14 \times 13 / 32 = 26 + 5.7 = 31.7$ GB, plus 35 GB is about 67 GB, which fits with some headroom for buffers and fragmentation; ZeRO-3 $208/32 = 6.5$ GB, plus 35 GB is 41.5 GB, which leaves room for a larger micro-batch. Communication: bf16 gradients are 26 GB, so a ring reduce-scatter plus all-gather moves $2 \times \frac{31}{32} \times 26 = 50.4$ GB per rank, about 1.0 s at 50 GB/s for ZeRO-1 or ZeRO-2. ZeRO-3 adds a second parameter all-gather, about 1.5 times as much, roughly 1.5 s. ZeRO-2 is the natural choice; pick ZeRO-3 (or FSDP `FULL_SHARD`, or `HYBRID_SHARD` so the parameter gathers stay inside a node) if you want the memory for a bigger micro-batch and the step compute is long enough to hide the extra traffic. Gradient accumulation also helps: synchronisation happens once per optimiser step, not once per micro-batch.

air-fanout-v1:13.03.q: You have 512 GPUs (64 nodes of 8) for a 70B dense model, a global batch of 512 sequences of 4096 tokens, and micro-batch size 1. Compare layout A (TP 8, PP 8, DP 8) with layout B (TP 8, PP 4, DP 16): number of micro-batches per replica, bubble fraction with 1F1B, and model-state memory per GPU (16 bytes per parameter, before any ZeRO). Why would putting TP 16 across two nodes be a poor third option?
air-fanout-v1:13.03.s: Layout A: each of 8 replicas gets 512/8 = 64 sequences, so $m = 64$ and the bubble is $(8-1)/(64+7) = 7/71 \approx 9.9$ percent. Each GPU holds 1/64 of the model, so state is $70\text{B} \times 16 / 64 = 17.5$ GB. Layout B: 16 replicas get 32 sequences each, $m = 32$, bubble $3/35 \approx 8.6$ percent. Each GPU holds 1/32 of the model: $70 \times 16 / 32 = 35$ GB, and each stage holds twice as many layers, so its activations (up to about $p$ micro-batches of its layers under 1F1B) are larger too. B has a slightly smaller bubble and more data parallelism but roughly twice the state; it fits only if activations stay under about 40 GB, and ZeRO-1 across the 16 data-parallel ranks can recover most of the optimiser share (12 of the 16 bytes). TP 16 across two nodes would put four all-reduces per layer of a $1 \times 4096 \times 8192$ bf16 activation (about 67 MB each) on the inter-node network, on the critical path of every layer, which typically costs far more than the bubble savings. Keep tensor parallelism within the NVLink domain.

air-fanout-v1:13.04.q: To save memory a teammate stores weights and Adam moments in bf16, with no fp32 master copy. The learning rate decays to $3 \times 10^{-5}$ by the end of training and typical weights have magnitude around 0.02. Adam's per-step updates are roughly the learning rate in size. What happens to the updates, and what would you change? Separately, the same run uses full activation checkpointing; by how much does that inflate the FLOPs per token, and what would you try first instead?
air-fanout-v1:13.04.s: A bf16 weight of about 0.02 lies in the binade $[2^{-6}, 2^{-5})$ = [0.0156, 0.0313), where consecutive bf16 values are $2^{-6} \times 2^{-7} = 2^{-13} \approx 1.22 \times 10^{-4}$ apart. An update of $3 \times 10^{-5}$ is below half that gap ($6.1 \times 10^{-5}$), so it is rounded away: the weight does not move, and late training stalls while the loss curve flattens for no visible reason. Larger updates are quantised to multiples of the gap, so even those that survive are distorted (an update of $10^{-4}$ becomes a step of $1.22 \times 10^{-4}$). The fix is fp32 master weights (adds 4 bytes per parameter, usually recovered by sharding them with ZeRO), or if memory forbids it, stochastic rounding or Kahan-compensated updates in bf16. Keep the Adam second moment in fp32 too, since it is used in a square root and a division. On recomputation: full checkpointing adds one forward pass, about $2N$ on top of $6N$, so 33 percent more FLOPs per token. Try selective recomputation of the attention core, or simply FlashAttention, which removes the quadratic activation term at a few percent cost, plus sequence parallelism if tensor parallelism is in use; fall back to full checkpointing only for layers that still do not fit.

air-fanout-v1:13.05.q: You have a training budget of $2 \times 10^{23}$ FLOPs and expect to serve $10^{13}$ tokens over the model's lifetime. Compute the Chinchilla-style compute-optimal size and token count at 20 tokens per parameter, then the tokens a 7B model would see with the same budget. Compare lifetime FLOPs (training plus about $2N$ per served token). What would you need to check before committing to the 7B option?
air-fanout-v1:13.05.s: Compute-optimal: $N = \sqrt{2 \times 10^{23}/120} = 40.8$B parameters, $D = 20N = 816$B tokens. A 7B model with the same budget sees $2 \times 10^{23}/(6 \times 7 \times 10^9) = 4.76$T tokens, about 680 tokens per parameter.
