Serving cost: $2 \times 40.8\text{B} \times 10^{13} = 8.2 \times 10^{23}$ FLOPs versus $2 \times 7\text{B} \times 10^{13} = 1.4 \times 10^{23}$. Lifetime totals: about $1.02 \times 10^{24}$ for the 41B model versus $3.4 \times 10^{23}$ for the 7B, three times cheaper overall, because serving dominates. The catch is quality: the 7B model is off the compute-optimal point, so at equal training compute its loss is somewhat higher (the approach-3 fit predicts 1.988 versus 1.980, under half a percent, but do not trust the fit's third digit). Before committing, check that the extra tokens exist at the same quality (4.76T unique tokens, or acceptable repetition), validate with your own IsoFLOP or over-training points at smaller scale that the loss gap is as small as predicted, and check downstream metrics rather than loss alone. If the gap matters, spending part of the inference savings on more training tokens for the 7B model is usually the better trade.

air-fanout-v1:13.06.q: Your near-duplicate step uses 100 MinHash values as 20 bands of 5 rows, and reviewers complain that it removes many documents that are merely on the same topic. You want to treat pairs with Jaccard similarity of about 0.8 and above as duplicates. Compute the candidate probability at Jaccard 0.5, 0.7, 0.8 and 0.9 for 20 x 5 and for 10 x 10, and recommend a configuration. What else would you check before rerunning the whole corpus?
air-fanout-v1:13.06.s: For 20 bands of 5 rows, $P = 1 - (1 - s^5)^{20}$: 0.47 at $s = 0.5$, 0.975 at 0.7, and essentially 1 at 0.8 and 0.9. The threshold $(1/20)^{1/5} \approx 0.55$ is far too low, which explains the topical false positives: nearly half of pairs at Jaccard 0.5 are flagged. For 10 bands of 10 rows, $P = 1 - (1 - s^{10})^{10}$: 0.01 at 0.5, 0.25 at 0.7, 0.68 at 0.8 and 0.99 at 0.9, with threshold $(1/10)^{1/10} \approx 0.79$. That matches the target, at the cost of missing about a third of pairs right at 0.8; more hashes (for example 14 bands of 8 rows, or more bands at 10 rows) sharpen the curve if recall near the threshold matters. Before rerunning: verify on a labelled sample of candidate pairs by computing their true Jaccard similarity; confirm the shingle size (word 5-grams behave very differently from character 5-grams); decide whether to deduplicate per snapshot or globally (FineWeb found per-snapshot better); keep a stable order so the same document survives each run; and run a small-model ablation on deduplicated versus original data, since the end goal is better models, not fewer documents.

air-fanout-v1:13.07.q: In an RLVR run with GRPO you sample 64 prompts per step with 8 completions each. Logs show 20 prompts where all 8 completions are correct and 12 where all 8 are wrong. Meanwhile pass@1 on your held-out maths benchmark has risen from 40 to 70 percent in 200 steps, while two similar benchmarks moved by 2 points. What fraction of the batch is producing gradient, what would you change in sampling, and what do you suspect about the benchmark jump?
air-fanout-v1:13.07.s: Groups with identical rewards have zero advantage for every completion, so 32 of 64 prompts (256 of 512 completions, half the rollout compute) produce no policy gradient beyond any KL term. Filter prompts by pass rate: drop or down-sample those the model already always solves or always fails, and refill the batch until it holds enough mixed groups (sampling more prompts per step and discarding degenerate groups, or keeping a running per-prompt pass-rate estimate to drive a curriculum). Revisit the hardest prompts later, since a few lucky successes are the most informative signal. On the benchmark: a 30-point jump in 200 steps on one benchmark while similar benchmarks barely move suggests contamination or a verifier artefact rather than skill. Check long n-gram overlap (13-grams, say) between the RL and SFT prompt sets and the benchmark questions and answers; check whether the evaluation's answer extraction or template changed; and read a sample of newly-correct outputs to see whether they reason or recite. Report pass@1 averaged over several samples at fixed decoding settings, so the comparison is not sampling noise.

aieng:01.01.q: How is an AI engineer's job different from an ML engineer's? Give two concrete differences.
aieng:01.01.s: ML engineers mostly train and tune models from data; AI engineers start from a pretrained foundation model and adapt it with prompts, retrieval, tools and sometimes fine-tuning. Evaluation is also different: ML work measures accuracy on labelled data, while AI engineering has to judge open-ended outputs with rubrics, LLM judges or human review. A third difference is cost: inference per token dominates instead of training compute.

aieng:01.02.q: Name the three layers of the AI stack and give one component you'd find in each.
aieng:01.02.s: Application layer: prompts, retrieval/context construction, guardrails, evaluation (e.g. a RAG pipeline). Model layer: model selection, fine-tuning, distillation, quantization (e.g. a LoRA fine-tune). Infrastructure layer: inference serving, GPUs, vector databases, caching and monitoring (e.g. vLLM or a vector DB).

aieng:01.03.q: Your chat request has a 2,000-token prompt and gets a 300-token answer. Describe what the server does, and which part dominates time-to-first-token.
aieng:01.03.s: The server tokenizes the prompt, then runs prefill: all 2,000 tokens go through the model in one parallel pass, filling the KV cache and producing the first token, so prefill dominates TTFT. Then decode runs 300 sequential forward passes, each sampling one token from the output distribution and appending to the KV cache, streaming tokens back until EOS or max_tokens. Decode dominates total latency.
aieng:01.03.t: One model call, end to end

aieng:02.01.q: Explain how a sentence becomes a single embedding vector in a modern embedding model, and why the same model must be used at index and query time.
aieng:02.01.s: The text is tokenized, a transformer encoder produces a contextual vector per token, and a pooling step (usually mean pooling or the [CLS] token) collapses them into one fixed-length vector, often L2-normalized. The model was trained contrastively so related texts are close. Each model defines its own vector space, so query vectors are only comparable with document vectors from the same model and version.

aieng:02.02.q: When is cosine similarity equivalent to dot product, and why do most embedding pipelines normalize vectors?
aieng:02.02.s: Cosine similarity equals dot product when both vectors have unit length, since cosine is the dot product divided by the product of norms. Pipelines normalize so the cheapest operation (dot product) gives cosine rankings, L2 ordering also matches, and vector length no longer biases results.

aieng:02.03.q: You have 2 million product descriptions in Postgres with price and category filters. Would you add pgvector or a dedicated vector DB? Justify with workload numbers.
aieng:02.03.s: 2M x 768 floats is about 6 GB, which fits on one Postgres node with an HNSW index. Data and filters (price, category) already live in Postgres, so pgvector keeps joins, transactions and one system to operate. A dedicated vector DB is only justified at hundreds of millions of vectors, thousands of QPS, heavy filtered search or multi-tenant isolation.

aieng:02.04.q: A 768-dim float32 vector is compressed with PQ into 96 subvectors with 256 centroids each. What is the new size and compression ratio?
aieng:02.04.s: Each of the 96 subvectors is stored as one byte (256 centroids = 8 bits), so the vector becomes 96 bytes. The original is 768 x 4 = 3,072 bytes, so the compression ratio is 32x (plus a small shared codebook).

aieng:02.05.q: Compare int8 scalar quantization and binary quantization on size, speed and accuracy for 1024-dim vectors.
aieng:02.05.s: int8 SQ stores 1024 dims in 1,024 bytes (4x smaller than float32), uses fast integer dot products, and loses very little accuracy. Binary stores 1 bit per dim, 128 bytes (32x smaller), uses Hamming distance via XOR and popcount (fastest), but loses more accuracy, so you oversample candidates and rescore them with higher-precision vectors.

aieng:02.06.q: Why can't you just do exact k-NN over 50 million vectors per query, and what metric do you use to judge an approximate index?
aieng:02.06.s: Exact k-NN must compute distances to all 50M vectors per query (tens of billions of operations and reading ~150 GB of floats), giving high latency and very low QPS. ANN indexes skip most vectors. They're judged by recall@k (fraction of the true top-k found) versus latency/QPS and memory, measured against exact search as ground truth.

aieng:02.07.q: Explain how HNSW finds a nearest neighbour, and name the parameters that trade recall for speed and memory.
aieng:02.07.s: HNSW stores vectors in a multi-layer proximity graph. A query enters at the sparse top layer, greedily hops to the neighbour closest to the query until no improvement, drops to the next layer and repeats; at layer 0 it explores a candidate list of size efSearch and returns the top k. M controls links per node (recall vs memory), efConstruction controls build quality, and efSearch controls query-time recall vs latency.
aieng:02.07.t: Indexing techniques that make vector search scale

aieng:02.08.q: Walk through a query in a RAG system from user text to the chunks placed in the prompt. Where would you add a reranker, and why there?
aieng:02.08.s: The query text is embedded with the same model as the corpus; filters (tenant, date) are applied via pre-filtering or filtered index traversal; ANN runs on each shard and results are merged into a global top 50-100; candidates are optionally rescored with full vectors, then a cross-encoder reranks them; the top few chunks' text is fetched and inserted into the prompt with citations. The reranker goes after ANN because it is accurate but too slow to run on the whole corpus.
aieng:02.08.t: Search execution from query to result

aieng:02.09.q: In Milvus, what happens between an insert and the moment the new vector is searchable with an index? Name the components involved.
aieng:02.09.s: The proxy receives the insert and writes it to the log broker (durable at that point). Query nodes consume the log so the data is searchable in a growing segment via brute force. Data nodes batch log entries into segments and flush to object storage; once a segment is sealed, the index coordinator schedules an index node to build the ANN index, after which query nodes load the indexed sealed segment.

aieng:03.01.q: An LLM is 'just predicting the next token'. Explain what that means and give one capability and one failure that follow from it.
aieng:03.01.s: Given the tokens so far, the model outputs a probability distribution over its vocabulary for the next token; generation samples one, appends it, and repeats. Capability: because predicting text well requires modelling its structure, it can translate, summarise or write code without task-specific training. Failure: it produces the most plausible continuation, not a verified one, so it can hallucinate confident false facts (and knows nothing after its training cut-off unless given context).
aieng:03.01.t: What a large language model does

aieng:03.02.q: What loss does pretraining minimise, and what did the Chinchilla paper change about how big models are trained?
aieng:03.02.s: Pretraining minimises cross-entropy loss on next-token prediction: the negative log-probability of the actual next token at each position, averaged over the corpus. Chinchilla showed that for a fixed compute budget, earlier models were too large and trained on too little data; compute-optimal training scales data with parameters, roughly 20 tokens per parameter (70B params on 1.4T tokens beat a 280B model).
aieng:03.02.t: How LLMs learn and generate text

aieng:03.03.q: You need reliable JSON extraction for one feature and varied marketing copy for another. What decoding settings would you use for each and why?
aieng:03.03.s: JSON extraction: temperature 0 or near it (greedy-like, repeatable), plus schema/grammar-constrained decoding so every token keeps the output valid, and enough max_tokens to avoid truncation. Marketing copy: temperature ~0.8-1.0 with top-p ~0.9 (optionally a small repetition penalty) to sample diverse but coherent text, possibly generating several candidates. Greedy/beam search makes copy bland and repetitive; high temperature makes JSON unreliable.

aieng:03.04.q: A support bot answers in the wrong tone and also doesn't know your product's latest pricing. Which technique fixes each problem, and why not the other way round?
aieng:03.04.s: Stale pricing is a knowledge problem: use retrieval (RAG) to put current pricing into the prompt at query time; fine-tuning would freeze facts that change and can't be updated without retraining. Wrong tone is a behaviour problem: fix it with a better system prompt and examples, and if that's not enough, supervised fine-tuning (e.g. LoRA) on example replies in the right tone. RAG doesn't reliably change style.

aieng:03.05.q: Your RAG bot gives wrong answers. List the steps you'd check, in order, to find whether retrieval or generation is at fault.
aieng:03.05.s: 1) Check the answer exists in the source corpus. 2) Inspect how the relevant document was chunked (is the needed fact in one coherent chunk with enough context?). 3) Check retrieval: is that chunk in the top-k for this query (recall@k, try hybrid/rerank)? 4) Check the chunk actually reached the prompt (no truncation). 5) Only then check generation: did the model stay faithful to the retrieved text, or ignore/contradict it? Steps 1-4 failing means retrieval; only 5 is generation.

aieng:04.01.q: Why does a transformer need positional information at all, and what is the main advantage of RoPE over learned absolute position embeddings?
aieng:04.01.s: Self-attention is permutation-invariant: it compares tokens by content only, so without position information word order is lost. RoPE rotates query and key vectors by angles proportional to their positions, so their dot product depends only on relative distance. Unlike learned absolute embeddings it adds no parameters, generalises better to relative structure, and can be rescaled (interpolation, NTK, YaRN) to extend context beyond the training length.

aieng:04.02.q: Write the scaled dot-product attention formula and explain what Q, K and V are and why the scores are divided by sqrt(d_k).
aieng:04.02.s: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V. Q, K and V are linear projections of the token vectors: queries say what a token looks for, keys what each token can be matched on, values the information passed on. Scores are query-key dot products, softmaxed into weights that mix the values. Dividing by sqrt(d_k) keeps score variance near 1; otherwise large dot products make softmax nearly one-hot and gradients vanish.

aieng:04.03.q: Draw (in words) one decoder block of a modern LLM like Llama, naming each sub-layer in order and where the residual connections go.
aieng:04.03.s: Input from the residual stream -> RMSNorm -> causal multi-head self-attention (with RoPE on queries/keys) -> add the output back to the residual stream -> RMSNorm -> feed-forward MLP (SwiGLU) -> add back to the residual stream -> next block. Residual connections wrap both the attention and the MLP sub-layers; after the last block a final norm and the LM head produce logits.

aieng:04.04.q: Compute the KV cache size for one 8,000-token sequence on a model with 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head dim 128, in fp16.
aieng:04.04.s: Per token: 2 (K and V) x 32 layers x 8 KV heads x 128 head dim x 2 bytes = 131,072 bytes = 128 KB. For 8,000 tokens: 8,000 x 128 KB = 1,024,000 KB, about 1 GB (0.98 GiB) per sequence.

aieng:04.05.q: Name two limits of RNNs that attention removed, and one new cost that attention introduced.
aieng:04.05.s: Attention removed the RNN's fixed-size hidden-state bottleneck (any token is one step from any other, so long-range dependencies don't fade) and the sequential training constraint (all positions are processed in parallel, enabling large-scale GPU training). The new cost: compute and memory quadratic in sequence length, plus a KV cache that grows with every token at inference.

aieng:05.01.q: Write the 4x4 causal mask for a 4-token sequence and explain how it is applied and why it makes parallel training possible.
aieng:05.01.s: Mask (0 = allowed, -inf = blocked): row0 [0,-inf,-inf,-inf], row1 [0,0,-inf,-inf], row2 [0,0,0,-inf], row3 [0,0,0,0]. It is added to the scaled QK^T scores before softmax, so future positions get weight 0. Since each output position only depends on earlier tokens, every position is a valid next-token prediction, so one forward pass trains all n positions in parallel without leaking the answer.

aieng:05.02.q: A model has d_model = 4096 and 32 heads. What is each head's dimension, and how do multi-head outputs get back to size 4096?
aieng:05.02.s: Head dimension = 4096 / 32 = 128. Q, K and V are reshaped into 32 heads of 128 dims; each head computes attention independently; the 32 outputs (each seq x 128) are concatenated back to seq x 4096 and multiplied by the output projection W_O (4096 x 4096) to mix information across heads.

aieng:05.03.q: For batch 2, sequence 10, d_model 512, 8 heads, vocab 32,000: give the tensor shape after embedding, after splitting into heads, the attention score matrix, and the final logits.
aieng:05.03.s: After embedding: (2, 10, 512). After splitting into heads: (2, 8, 10, 64) for each of Q, K, V (d_head = 512/8 = 64). Attention scores QK^T: (2, 8, 10, 10). Final logits: (2, 10, 32000).
aieng:05.03.t: Trace the shapes through a transformer

aieng:06.01.q: Why did pre-vLLM servers waste most of their KV cache memory, and how does paging fix it?
aieng:06.01.s: They pre-allocated one contiguous KV region per request sized to the maximum sequence length, so space reserved for tokens never generated, early finishes (internal fragmentation) and unusable gaps between allocations (external fragmentation) left only ~20-38% of memory holding real tokens. PagedAttention splits the cache into fixed-size blocks allocated on demand and tracked by a per-sequence block table, so memory needn't be contiguous, waste is limited to the last partial block (<4%), and blocks can be shared copy-on-write across sequences.

aieng:06.02.q: Mixtral 8x7B has about 47B parameters but uses about 13B per token. Explain why, and what that means for GPU memory versus compute.
aieng:06.02.s: Mixtral has 8 expert MLPs per layer but routes each token to only the top 2. Attention and embedding weights are shared, so total parameters are ~47B (not 8x7B=56B), while each token only touches shared weights plus 2 experts, about 13B active parameters. All ~47B must be held in GPU memory, but compute (FLOPs) per token is similar to a 13B dense model.

aieng:06.03.q: FlashAttention does the same maths as standard attention. Where does its speedup come from, and why does it also save memory?
aieng:06.03.s: The speedup comes from cutting reads and writes to slow GPU HBM: attention is memory-bound, and standard attention writes and re-reads the full T x T score and softmax matrices. FlashAttention tiles Q, K, V into SRAM-sized blocks, computes scores, an online (running max/sum) softmax and the output block by block, and writes only the final output. Since the T x T matrix is never materialised (and is recomputed in the backward pass instead of stored), memory is linear rather than quadratic in sequence length.

aieng:06.04.q: A GPU has 24 GB free for KV cache. Per-token KV size is 128 KB, block size is 16 tokens. How many blocks exist, and how many 1,000-token requests fit with paging vs with 4,096-token contiguous reservations?
aieng:06.04.s: Block = 128 KB x 16 = 2 MB, so 24 GB / 2 MB = 12,288 blocks. A 1,000-token request needs ceil(1000/16) = 63 blocks, so paging fits 12,288 / 63 = 195 requests. Contiguous 4,096-token reservations cost 4,096 x 128 KB = 512 MB each, so only 24 GB / 512 MB = 48 fit: about 4x fewer, with ~76% of reserved memory unused.

aieng:07.01.q: A 70B model in fp16 needs how much memory for weights? What about int8 and 4-bit, and what do you risk at 4-bit?
aieng:07.01.s: Weights = params x bytes: 70B x 2 bytes = 140 GB in fp16; 70B x 1 byte = 70 GB in int8; 70B x 0.5 byte = ~35 GB at 4-bit (a bit more for per-block scales). At 4-bit, rounding error and outliers can hurt quality, mostly on maths, code, long-context and rare languages, so you'd use outlier-aware methods (GPTQ, AWQ) and test on your own evals.

aieng:07.02.q: With a sliding window of 4,096 tokens, can a token in layer 30 of a 32-layer model use information from 50,000 tokens back? Explain.
aieng:07.02.s: In principle yes: each layer passes information one window back, so after ~30 layers the receptive field is about 30 x 4,096 = ~123k tokens, which covers 50,000. But the information must be relayed indirectly through about 13 window hops, getting compressed at each, so precise recall from that far back is unreliable. Direct attention only reaches 4,096 tokens per layer; that's why models mix in full-attention layers.

aieng:07.03.q: Why do soft labels from a teacher carry more information than hard labels, and what does temperature do in distillation?
aieng:07.03.s: A hard label only says which answer is right; the teacher's full distribution also says how plausible each wrong answer is (which classes or tokens are similar), so each example gives the student much more signal ('dark knowledge'). Temperature T > 1 divides the logits before softmax, flattening the distribution so those small probabilities become large enough to learn from; the student is trained to match the teacher's softened distribution via KL divergence (scaled by T^2).

aieng:07.04.q: Why can a big model verify 5 drafted tokens in about the same time it takes to generate 1, and how does speculative decoding keep the output distribution unchanged?
aieng:07.04.s: Decode is memory-bandwidth bound: one step reads all the weights to produce one token, so a forward pass over 5 positions reads the weights once and only adds cheap compute, taking about the same time. Drafts are accepted left to right with probability min(1, p_target/p_draft) (or exact match in greedy mode); at the first rejection a replacement is sampled from the residual distribution max(0, p_target - p_draft). This rejection-sampling rule makes the output exactly distributed as the target model's.

aieng:07.05.q: Your chatbot has slow first tokens on long documents, but streaming speed is fine. Which bottleneck is it, and which two optimizations would you try first?
aieng:07.05.s: Slow first token but fine streaming means prefill is the bottleneck: processing the long prompt is compute-heavy (attention cost grows with length). First fixes: prefix/prompt caching so repeated documents or system prompts aren't re-prefilled, and cutting the context sent (retrieve relevant chunks instead of whole documents). Also ensure FlashAttention and chunked prefill. Quantization and speculative decoding mainly help decode, so they're not the first choice here.
aieng:07.05.t: Match the optimization to the bottleneck

aieng:08.01.q: Compare RLHF with a learned reward model to RL with verifiable rewards (as in DeepSeek-R1). What signal does each optimise, and what can go wrong?
aieng:08.01.s: RLHF optimises a learned reward model trained on human preference comparisons (via PPO with a KL penalty, or directly via DPO); it handles open-ended qualities like helpfulness but can be reward-hacked (verbosity, sycophancy) because the reward model is only a proxy. RL with verifiable rewards optimises a programmatic check, such as the correct final maths answer or passing tests; the signal is objective and drove emergent long reasoning in R1, but it only covers checkable tasks and can be gamed if the checker is weak (e.g. right answer from wrong reasoning, which process rewards address).

aieng:08.02.q: Why does writing out intermediate steps improve accuracy for a next-token predictor? Give a mechanical explanation, not 'it thinks harder'.
aieng:08.02.s: A transformer does a fixed amount of computation per output token. Writing intermediate steps gives the model more forward passes (more total compute) before the answer, and stores partial results in the context where later tokens can attend to them instead of having to compute everything implicitly in one pass. So multi-step problems get decomposed into steps that each fit in one pass.

aieng:08.03.q: Describe the message flow when a model answers 'What's the weather in Paris?' using a get_weather tool. Who executes the tool?
aieng:08.03.s: The app sends the user message plus the get_weather tool definition (name, description, JSON schema) to the model. The model returns a structured tool call get_weather(city='Paris') instead of text. The application (not the model) executes the function/API, then sends the result back as a tool-result message. The model reads it and writes the final answer, or calls another tool.

aieng:08.04.q: Tree of Thoughts solved 74% of Game of 24 puzzles vs 4% for chain of thought with GPT-4. What does ToT do differently that explains the gap?
aieng:08.04.s: Chain of thought follows one path and can't recover if an early arithmetic choice leaves an unsolvable state. ToT generates several candidate next steps at each stage, has the model evaluate each partial state (sure/maybe/impossible to reach 24), keeps the best few (BFS with breadth 5) and prunes or backtracks from dead ends. Exploring and evaluating alternatives is what lifts success from 4% to 74%, at the cost of many more model calls.

aieng:08.05.q: A reasoning model gets a maths answer wrong, then when asked 'are you sure?' changes a correct answer to a wrong one on another problem. Which failure is the second, and what's a better way to verify?
aieng:08.05.s: The second case is self-correction backfiring: asked to re-check without any new information, the model flips a correct answer because pushback alone shifts its output (intrinsic self-correction often lowers accuracy). Better: verify with an external signal, e.g. recompute with a calculator or code, check against a solver or tests, or use a separate verifier/process reward model, and only revise when that check fails, passing the concrete error back.

aieng:09.01.q: An agent's quality drops after 40 tool calls in a long session. Name three context engineering techniques you'd apply and what each fixes.
aieng:09.01.s: 1) Clear/trim old tool results: raw outputs from many calls ago add noise and cost, causing context rot. 2) Compaction: summarise history into decisions, current state and next steps and continue in a fresh context, so the window isn't dominated by stale turns. 3) Structured external notes (task list/progress file) the agent reads and updates, so goals and state survive compaction. Also: sub-agents for exploratory sub-tasks that return short summaries, and just-in-time retrieval instead of loading everything.

aieng:09.02.q: When should you build a fixed workflow instead of an autonomous agent? Give two criteria and an example of each.
aieng:09.02.s: Use a workflow when the steps are known and fixed in advance (e.g. a weekly report: fetch metrics, summarise, format), and when errors are costly or hard to detect, so predictability matters. Use an agent when the number and order of steps depend on what's discovered (e.g. debugging an unfamiliar codebase) and when results can be checked by real feedback such as tests, so the loop can self-correct.

aieng:09.03.q: Explain the M x N integration problem MCP solves, and name MCP's three server-side primitives with an example of each.
aieng:09.03.s: Without a standard, each of M AI apps needs a custom integration for each of N services (M x N). MCP defines one protocol, so each service ships one server and each app one client implementation (M + N). Server primitives: tools (model-invoked actions, e.g. create_issue on GitHub), resources (app-controlled data read into context, e.g. a file or DB schema), and prompts (user-selected templates, e.g. a 'summarise this PR' workflow).

aieng:09.04.q: Write a checkable plan for an agent that triages new GitHub issues: list its tools, stopping conditions, human checkpoints and how you'd evaluate it.
aieng:09.04.s: Goal: label type and priority, suggest an owner and flag duplicates for each new issue. Tools: read (get_issue, search_issues, list_labels, read CODEOWNERS) and low-risk writes (add_labels, post_comment, assign); no close permission. Stop: labels and comment done, or a max of ~15 tool calls/budget, or low confidence -> label needs-triage. Checkpoints: closing duplicates or anything external needs maintainer approval. Evaluation: replay ~100 past triaged issues, measure label accuracy, priority accuracy, duplicate precision, steps and cost per issue; read failed traces and classify as context, tool, reasoning or budget failures before changing anything.
aieng:09.04.t: Build an agent plan you can check

ieng:IN.01.q: In two sentences, explain the difference between training a model and serving it, and name one metric an inference engineer owns.
ieng:IN.01.s: Training adjusts a model's weights using huge batches of data, usually offline, and is judged by final model quality. Inference runs the frozen weights on live requests, one token at a time, and is judged by latency, throughput and cost. An inference engineer owns metrics such as time to first token, tokens per second per GPU, or cost per million tokens.

ieng:IN.02.q: List the layers a single chat request passes through from the user's HTTP call to GPU kernels, and name one optimization that lives at each layer.
ieng:IN.02.s: Client and API gateway (rate limiting, auth), router or load balancer (cache-aware routing), inference engine scheduler (continuous batching), KV cache manager (paged allocation, prefix caching), model runtime (CUDA graphs, torch.compile), kernels (FlashAttention, quantized GEMM), and hardware (GPU memory and NVLink). Each layer has its own optimizations and its own metrics.
ieng:IN.02.t: The Inference Stack: Model to GPU to Production

ieng:IN.03.q: Describe what distinguishes a level-2 (engine user) from a level-4 (engine builder) inference engineer, with one concrete task each.
ieng:IN.03.s: A level-2 engineer runs an existing engine like vLLM, tunes flags such as max batched tokens and GPU memory fraction, and benchmarks against an SLO, for example picking the cheapest GPU that meets p95 TTFT. A level-4 engineer changes the engine itself, for example writing a new attention kernel or modifying the scheduler, and proves the gain with profiles and ablations.

ieng:00.01.q: A 70B-parameter model is stored in BF16. How much memory do the weights need, and what is the decode speed ceiling on a GPU with 3.35 TB/s of bandwidth at batch size 1?
ieng:00.01.s: 70 billion parameters times 2 bytes is 140 GB, so it does not fit on one 80 GB GPU. If it did, each decode step must read all weights once, so the ceiling is about 3.35 TB/s divided by 140 GB, roughly 24 tokens per second at batch 1, ignoring KV reads and overheads.

ieng:00.02.q: In a transformer layer with hidden size 4096, a batch of 8 sequences each 512 tokens long enters a linear layer with weight shape [4096, 11008]. What are the input and output shapes, and how many FLOPs does the matmul take?
ieng:00.02.s: Input is [8, 512, 4096], output is [8, 512, 11008]. FLOPs are 2 x 8 x 512 x 4096 x 11008, about 370 GFLOPs.

ieng:00.03.q: Why does attention divide scores by the square root of the head dimension, and why do implementations subtract the max before softmax?
ieng:00.03.s: Dot products of random vectors grow with dimension, so dividing by sqrt(d) keeps score variance near 1 and stops softmax saturating into a near one-hot distribution. Subtracting the max keeps exp() from overflowing; it does not change the result because softmax is invariant to adding a constant to every input.

ieng:00.04.q: You run a benchmark twice and get p99 latency of 820 ms and 1,140 ms. What does this tell you, and what would you do before reporting a number?
ieng:00.04.s: The p99 is unstable, likely because too few requests were measured or the system was not at steady state. Run longer (thousands of requests), discard warm-up, repeat several times, and report the median of runs with a spread or confidence interval rather than one number.

ieng:00.05.q: Name three PyTorch settings or habits that matter for inference but not for training, and say why.
ieng:00.05.s: Use torch.inference_mode() (or no_grad) so autograd does not store activations. Load weights directly in BF16 or FP16 on the GPU instead of FP32 on CPU, halving memory and load time. Synchronize with torch.cuda.synchronize() before taking timings, because CUDA calls are asynchronous and timing without it measures only kernel launch.

ieng:00.06.q: Sketch one decoder layer of a modern LLM like Llama and say which part dominates parameters and which part grows with context length.
ieng:00.06.s: Input goes through RMSNorm, then self-attention (Q, K, V projections, RoPE on Q and K, attention, output projection), plus a residual add; then RMSNorm, a gated MLP (gate, up, down projections with SiLU), plus a residual add. The MLP holds most parameters (around two thirds). Attention's KV cache and attention compute grow with context length.

ieng:00.07.q: You rent a cloud GPU box. List the first five commands you run and what each tells you.
ieng:00.07.s: nvidia-smi (GPU model, driver, CUDA version, memory, processes); nproc and free -h (CPU cores and RAM); df -h (disk space for model weights); python -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.is_available(), torch.version.cuda)" (PyTorch sees the GPU); and tmux new -s work so long jobs survive an SSH drop.

ieng:00.08.q: nvidia-smi reports "CUDA Version: 12.4" but your PyTorch wheel was built for CUDA 12.8 and fails to see the GPU. Explain why and how to fix it.
ieng:00.08.s: nvidia-smi shows the highest CUDA version the installed driver supports, not an installed toolkit. A PyTorch build for CUDA 12.8 needs a driver new enough for 12.8. Either upgrade the NVIDIA driver or install a PyTorch build for a CUDA version the driver supports, such as 12.4 or earlier.

ieng:00.09.q: Write the checklist your setup must pass before you trust any benchmark from it.
ieng:00.09.s: GPU visible to PyTorch with the expected name and memory; driver and CUDA versions recorded; model weights cached on fast local disk; a pinned environment (container or lockfile); a tmux session; a script that prints environment info into every result file; and a smoke test that generates tokens from a small model.
ieng:00.09.t: Lab: Build Your Inference Engineering Setup

ieng:01.01.q: You have one 24 GB GPU. Pick a model size and precision for a chat assistant and justify it with memory math.
ieng:01.01.s: An 8B instruct model in BF16 needs about 16 GB for weights, leaving roughly 6 to 7 GB for KV cache and activations, which is enough for modest concurrency at a few thousand tokens of context. A 14B model would need 28 GB in BF16 and only fits if quantized to 8-bit or 4-bit. So an 8B BF16 model, or a larger model in FP8/INT4 if quality needs it.

ieng:01.02.q: Why does the same sentence produce a different number of tokens in two models, and why does that matter for cost and latency comparisons?
ieng:01.02.s: Each model has its own tokenizer and vocabulary, so it splits text into different pieces; larger vocabularies tend to use fewer tokens per word. Since compute, memory and pricing scale with tokens, comparing models by requests or words without counting tokens per model gives misleading cost and speed comparisons.

ieng:01.03.q: Explain why streaming improves perceived latency without changing total generation time.
ieng:01.03.s: Without streaming the user waits for the whole response. With streaming, tokens are sent as soon as each is generated, so the user starts reading after the first token (TTFT) instead of after the last. Total end-to-end time is the same or slightly longer, but the wait the user feels is much shorter.

ieng:01.04.q: nvidia-smi shows 100% GPU utilization during decode at batch size 1. Does this mean the GPU is fully used? Explain.
ieng:01.04.s: No. nvidia-smi's utilization counts the fraction of time at least one kernel was running, not how much of the GPU's compute or bandwidth it used. A batch-1 decode can keep a tiny kernel running constantly and show 100% while using a small fraction of the SMs and tensor cores. Use SM occupancy, achieved bandwidth or a profiler to judge real usage.

ieng:01.05.q: Your FastAPI server wraps model.generate. Two users send requests at the same time. What happens and why is it a problem?
ieng:01.05.s: With a single model and a blocking generate call, requests run one at a time: the second user waits for the first request to finish, so latency grows linearly with queue length. The GPU also runs at batch size 1, wasting most of its capacity. Real engines batch concurrent requests together at every step.

ieng:01.06.q: Describe the three measurements your lab report must include and why each matters.
ieng:01.06.s: TTFT and per-token latency for a single request (the best-case baseline), latency as concurrency rises from 1 to 8 (shows queueing in a naive server), and peak GPU memory with the model loaded (shows headroom for KV cache). Together they show the baseline and why a real engine is needed.
ieng:01.06.t: Lab: Build a Reproducible GPU Inference Server

ieng:02.01.q: For one decode step of a 32-layer model, list the operations in order from token id to next-token logits.
ieng:02.01.s: Embedding lookup for the new token; then for each of 32 layers: RMSNorm, Q/K/V projections, RoPE on Q and K, append K and V to the cache, attention over all cached keys and values, output projection, residual add, RMSNorm, gate and up projections, SiLU and multiply, down projection, residual add; then a final RMSNorm and the LM head matmul to vocabulary logits.

ieng:02.02.q: In decode, why do we only compute Q for the new token, but need K and V for every previous token?
ieng:02.02.s: The new token is the only one asking a question about the past, so it alone needs a query. Its answer is a weighted mix of all earlier tokens' values, weighted by how its query matches their keys, so all past K and V are required. Past tokens' K and V do not change when new tokens arrive because of the causal mask, which is why they can be cached.
ieng:02.02.t: Q, K, V & Causal Attention During Inference

ieng:02.03.q: Why is the MLP typically the largest compute cost in decode at short context, and how does SwiGLU change the weight count compared with a plain two-matrix MLP?
ieng:02.03.s: The MLP processes every token through large matrices (hidden to about 2.7 to 4 times hidden and back), and at short context attention over the cache is cheap, so the MLP's matmuls dominate both FLOPs and weight bytes. SwiGLU uses three matrices (gate, up, down) instead of two, and shrinks the intermediate width to about 8/3 of hidden to keep total parameters similar.

ieng:02.04.q: Explain what happens in order when you set temperature 0.7, top-p 0.9 and a repetition penalty, and which step can be expensive at large batch sizes.
ieng:02.04.s: The engine takes the logits for the last position, applies the repetition penalty to tokens already seen, divides by temperature 0.7, applies softmax, sorts tokens by probability and keeps the smallest set summing to 0.9, renormalizes and samples. Sorting the full vocabulary for top-p across many sequences can be noticeably expensive, so engines use specialized sampling kernels.

ieng:02.05.q: Write pseudocode for a generation loop without a KV cache and state its cost per step as the sequence grows.
ieng:02.05.s: ids = prompt; for step in range(max_new): logits = model(ids)[-1]; tok = sample(logits); ids.append(tok); if tok == eos: break. Each step reprocesses the whole sequence, so step t costs work proportional to (prompt + t), and total cost grows quadratically with output length.
ieng:02.05.t: Build a Tiny Autoregressive Generation Loop

ieng:02.06.q: For one generated token, list where it spends time from HTTP arrival to the client receiving it, and which parts are on the GPU.
ieng:02.06.s: Network and HTTP parsing (CPU), tokenization of the prompt (CPU), queueing in the scheduler (CPU), prefill or decode forward pass (GPU: matmuls, attention, norms), sampling (GPU), detokenization (CPU), and SSE write and network back to the client (CPU). Only the forward pass and sampling run on the GPU.
ieng:02.06.t: Visual Lab: Trace One Token End-to-End

ieng:03.01.q: Without a cache, how many token-positions of work does generating 100 tokens after a 900-token prompt take, compared with a cached approach?
ieng:03.01.s: Without a cache, step t processes 900 + t positions, so total is about 100 x 900 + (0+...+99), roughly 95,000 token-positions. With a cache, prefill processes 900 positions once and each of the 100 decode steps processes one new position, about 1,000 total. Roughly 95 times less work, ignoring attention reads.

ieng:03.02.q: Why is prefill usually compute bound while decode is memory bound? Use arithmetic intensity in your answer.
ieng:03.02.s: In prefill, a matmul processes thousands of prompt tokens against each weight read, so arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte) is high and tensor cores stay busy; time is set by FLOPs. In decode each weight is used for only one token per sequence, so intensity is low and time is set by how fast weights and KV cache can be read.

ieng:03.03.q: Decode at batch 1 runs at 40 ms per token. At batch 32 it runs at 48 ms per token. Explain why throughput rose so much.
ieng:03.03.s: Decode is memory bound: each step reads all weights once regardless of batch size, and that read dominates time. At batch 32 the same weight read serves 32 sequences, so step time rises only slightly (more KV reads and some compute) while tokens per step rise 32 times. Throughput goes from 25 to about 670 tokens per second.

ieng:03.04.q: What tensors does a per-layer KV cache hold, with what shapes, and what changes in the attention call once you use it?
ieng:03.04.s: Per layer, a key tensor and a value tensor of shape [batch, kv_heads, max_len, head_dim], plus a current length per sequence. In decode the model computes Q, K and V for only the new token, writes K and V at position len, then attends with Q against K[:, :, :len+1] and V[:, :, :len+1]. Input to the model becomes one token per sequence instead of the full sequence.

ieng:03.05.q: Break down the memory on an 80 GB GPU running an 8B BF16 model in vLLM with gpu_memory_utilization 0.9.
ieng:03.05.s: vLLM targets 72 GB in total. Weights take about 16 GB. Activations and temporary buffers for the largest batch take a few GB (measured by a profiling run), CUDA graphs and the CUDA context take around 1 to 2 GB. Whatever remains, roughly 50 GB, becomes the KV cache pool. The other 8 GB is left unused as a safety margin.

ieng:03.06.q: Compute KV cache bytes per token for a model with 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head dim 128, in BF16. How many 8k-token conversations fit in 40 GB?
ieng:03.06.s: Per token: 2 (K and V) x 32 layers x 8 heads x 128 dim x 2 bytes = 131,072 bytes, about 128 KB. An 8k-token sequence needs about 1 GB. So 40 GB holds about 40 such sequences at full length.
ieng:03.06.t: Calculate KV Memory, Context & Concurrency Limits

ieng:03.07.q: Your measured max concurrency is 30% lower than your KV formula predicted. Name three plausible reasons.
ieng:03.07.s: Activation and CUDA graph memory took more than assumed, leaving a smaller KV pool; block-level allocation wastes the unused part of each sequence's last block; and the engine reserves blocks for the maximum possible output length or keeps a watermark of free blocks to avoid preemption. Prompt lengths in the test may also be longer than the assumed average.
ieng:03.07.t: Lab: Cached vs Uncached Generation & Model Fit

ieng:04.01.q: A request has TTFT 300 ms, produces 200 tokens, and finishes at 4.3 s. Compute TPOT and explain how ITL differs from TPOT.
ieng:04.01.s: TPOT = (4.3 - 0.3) / (200 - 1), about 20 ms per token. ITL is the gap between each pair of consecutive tokens; TPOT is their average for the request. ITL keeps the distribution, so you can see stalls (for example a 400 ms gap when a long prefill ran) that the average hides.

ieng:04.02.q: Explain the difference between a closed-loop benchmark at concurrency 32 and an open-loop benchmark at 10 requests per second, and which one can reveal queueing collapse.
ieng:04.02.s: Closed loop keeps exactly 32 requests in flight: a new one starts only when one finishes, so load self-limits and latency cannot run away. Open loop sends requests on a schedule (10 per second, often Poisson) regardless of completions, like real users. If the server is slower than the arrival rate, the queue grows without bound and latency explodes. Only open loop reveals that collapse.

ieng:04.03.q: Why can a benchmark of 128-token prompts with 128-token outputs mislead you about a RAG product, and what workload would you use instead?
ieng:04.03.s: RAG prompts are long (often 2k to 8k tokens of retrieved context) with short outputs, so prefill dominates and TTFT is the key metric; a short-in, short-out benchmark mostly measures decode and hides prefill cost and interference. Use prompt and output lengths sampled from real logs, include shared system prompts so prefix caching is exercised, and test a mix with chat traffic.

ieng:04.04.q: List four things you must hold constant or record to make two benchmark runs comparable.
ieng:04.04.s: The exact model revision, dtype and engine version and flags; the hardware and driver; the workload file (prompts, lengths, seed, arrival pattern); and the warm-up procedure and measurement window. Also record GPU clocks or power limits, and whether prefix caching was cold or warm.

ieng:04.05.q: Your p50 TTFT improved by 20% after enabling a feature, but p99 got 40% worse. Should you ship it? What would you check?
ieng:04.05.s: It depends on the SLO, which is usually written against a tail percentile, so the worse p99 probably fails it. Check which requests became slow (long prompts? specific arrival bursts?), whether the change is reproducible across runs, and whether the p99 is measured on enough samples. Often a scheduling change helps typical requests at the expense of long ones.

ieng:04.06.q: A server does 5,000 tokens/s at 64 concurrency, but only 70% of requests meet the TTFT SLO. Another does 4,000 tokens/s with 99% meeting it. Which is better and how would you express it?
ieng:04.06.s: The second, for a latency-sensitive product. Goodput counts only requests that meet the SLO: roughly 3,500 good tokens/s for the first vs 3,960 for the second. Report goodput (or max request rate at which 99% meet the SLO) rather than raw throughput.

ieng:04.07.q: You want to compare two engines fairly with an existing tool. What settings must match across both runs?
ieng:04.07.s: Same model weights and dtype, same tokenizer and chat template, same dataset with identical prompt and output lengths (fixed output via ignore_eos or max_tokens), same arrival pattern and rate or concurrency, same hardware, same warm-up and duration, and the same client tool measuring through the same OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Also align prefix caching and sampling settings.

ieng:04.08.q: What should the output of your harness contain so that someone else can reproduce and trust a result?
ieng:04.08.s: A results file with the environment report (hardware, driver, versions), full engine config, workload definition and seed, load pattern, raw per-request timing records (send, first token, every token, end, token counts, errors), and computed summaries: TTFT, TPOT, ITL and E2E percentiles, throughput, goodput against a stated SLO, plus charts over load.
ieng:04.08.t: Project: Build Your Inference Benchmark Harness

ieng:05.01.q: Why measure a single request on an idle server before any load test, and what two numbers do you take from it?
ieng:05.01.s: It gives the best case the hardware and engine can deliver with no queueing or interference, so every later result can be expressed as degradation from it. Take TTFT for your typical prompt length and TPOT for steady decode. If these alone miss the SLO, no amount of scheduling will fix it; you need a smaller model, faster hardware or a different engine configuration.

ieng:05.02.q: Describe the curves you expect for throughput and TPOT as concurrency rises from 1 to 256 on a real engine, and where the knee usually comes from.
ieng:05.02.s: Throughput rises almost linearly at first, then bends and flattens; TPOT stays near baseline at low concurrency, then climbs. The knee appears when decode stops being purely bandwidth bound (compute starts to matter), when the KV cache fills and the engine queues or preempts, or when batched prefills start interfering with decode.

ieng:05.03.q: How does doubling prompt length affect TTFT, max concurrency and decode speed, and why?
ieng:05.03.s: TTFT roughly doubles (more at long context because attention prefill is quadratic). Max concurrency roughly halves because each sequence holds twice the KV cache. Decode TPOT rises somewhat because each step's attention reads twice as much KV per sequence; at short context the weight read dominates so the effect is small, at long context it becomes large.

ieng:05.04.q: Name the three boundaries you look for when stressing one GPU and the signal for each.
ieng:05.04.s: Saturation: throughput stops increasing as load rises. SLO failure: the chosen percentile of TTFT or TPOT crosses its target, or goodput starts falling. Memory boundary: the engine starts preempting requests, queueing because KV blocks are exhausted, or crashes with out-of-memory. Each happens at a different load and you operate below the lowest.
ieng:05.04.t: Find Saturation, SLO Failure & OOM Boundaries

ieng:05.05.q: Summarize what an operating envelope chart shows and how a product team would use it.
ieng:05.05.s: For each workload shape (prompt and output length), it shows the maximum request rate or concurrency at which the SLO still holds, plus the throughput there and the binding constraint (SLO, compute or KV memory). A product team uses it to know how much traffic one GPU can take for their prompt sizes, and when they need more replicas or a different model.
ieng:05.05.t: Lab: Map the GPU Operating Envelope

ieng:06.01.q: List four specific inefficiencies of serving with model.generate behind an HTTP server.
ieng:06.01.s: Requests run one at a time or in static batches, so the GPU is underused and short requests wait for long ones. KV cache is pre-allocated or grown per request, wasting and fragmenting memory. Python and kernel-launch overhead dominate small decode steps without CUDA graphs. There is no shared-prefix reuse, so identical system prompts are recomputed for every request.
ieng:06.01.t: Why Plain PyTorch Serving Breaks Down

ieng:06.02.q: Name five vLLM startup flags you would set deliberately and what each controls.
ieng:06.02.s: --model (weights), --dtype or --quantization (precision), --max-model-len (longest sequence, which caps KV per request), --gpu-memory-utilization (fraction of GPU memory vLLM may use, which sizes the KV pool), and --max-num-seqs or --max-num-batched-tokens (scheduler limits on batch size and tokens per step). Also --tensor-parallel-size for multi-GPU.

ieng:06.03.q: What fields in a streamed chat completion response would you use to compute TTFT and token counts, and what is the stream_options usage flag for?
ieng:06.03.s: Each SSE chunk carries choices[0].delta.content; the time of the first chunk with non-empty content gives TTFT. Token counts come from the usage object; with stream_options {"include_usage": true} the server sends a final chunk containing prompt_tokens and completion_tokens, so you do not have to re-tokenize to count.

ieng:06.04.q: During a load test you see num_requests_waiting rising and KV cache usage at 99%. What is happening and what are two fixes?
ieng:06.04.s: The KV cache is full, so the scheduler cannot admit new sequences and they queue, raising TTFT. Fixes: free KV space (quantize the KV cache to FP8, quantize weights, raise gpu-memory-utilization, lower max-model-len if long requests reserve too much), or add capacity (another replica) and route traffic away; also check if requests are generating longer outputs than expected.

ieng:06.05.q: Describe the path of a chat request through vLLM from HTTP arrival to the first streamed token.
ieng:06.05.s: The API server receives the request, applies the chat template and tokenizes, and hands it to the engine core as a new request in the waiting queue. On the next step the scheduler allocates KV blocks and schedules its prompt tokens (possibly in chunks). The model runner builds input tensors and runs the forward pass with the attention backend writing K and V into the allocated blocks. The sampler picks the first token, the output processor detokenizes, and the API server streams it as an SSE chunk.

ieng:06.06.q: You see vLLM win by 15 times at concurrency 64 but only 1.5 times at concurrency 1. Explain both numbers.
ieng:06.06.s: At concurrency 1 the gain comes only from lower per-step overhead and better kernels (CUDA graphs, fused attention), since both run one sequence. At concurrency 64, vLLM batches all sequences into every decode step and uses paged KV memory to fit them, while the naive server processes them one at a time, so throughput scales with batch size for vLLM and stays flat for the naive server.

ieng:07.01.q: With static batching, a batch has requests needing 20, 50 and 500 output tokens. What happens to the GPU and to the first two requests?
ieng:07.01.s: All three start together and the batch runs until the 500-token request finishes. The first two finish early but their slots stay idle (padding) for the remaining steps, so GPU work is wasted, and new requests cannot join until the whole batch ends, so they wait. Users of short requests may also wait if results are returned only when the batch completes.

ieng:07.02.q: What is the scheduling unit in iteration-level scheduling, and what does that enable?
ieng:07.02.s: One model iteration (one forward pass that produces one token per running sequence). After every iteration the scheduler can remove finished sequences and add waiting ones, so the batch composition changes step by step, finished slots are refilled immediately, and new requests start without waiting for others to finish.

ieng:07.03.q: Describe continuous batching in one paragraph and give its main effect on throughput and on TTFT.
ieng:07.03.s: Continuous batching keeps a running batch that changes every step: finished sequences leave immediately, and waiting requests join as soon as there is a slot and KV memory, with their prefill folded into the next step. This keeps the GPU's batch full, raising throughput several times over static batching, and lowers TTFT because new requests do not wait for a batch to finish.

ieng:07.04.q: What does max_num_batched_tokens limit, and what happens to TTFT and ITL if you set it very low or very high?
ieng:07.04.s: It caps how many tokens (decode tokens plus prompt tokens) one step may process. Very low: long prompts are split into many small chunks, so TTFT rises, but decode steps stay short and ITL stays smooth. Very high: big prefills run in one step, lowering TTFT for that request but causing long steps and ITL spikes for everyone else, plus a higher activation memory peak.
ieng:07.04.t: Token Budgets, Max Sequences & Max Batched Tokens

ieng:07.05.q: A client disconnects mid-stream. What should the engine do and why does it matter for capacity?
ieng:07.05.s: The engine should detect the disconnect, abort the request, stop generating for it and free its KV blocks immediately. Otherwise it keeps spending decode steps and KV memory on tokens nobody will read, reducing capacity for live users. In busy chat products a meaningful share of requests are abandoned, so this matters.

ieng:07.06.q: What inputs and outputs should a minimal continuous-batching simulator have to answer "what happens to TTFT if I halve max_num_batched_tokens?"
ieng:07.06.s: Inputs: a request trace (arrival time, prompt length, output length), a cost model for step time as a function of decode tokens and prefill tokens, KV capacity in tokens, and scheduler parameters (token budget, max seqs, chunked prefill on or off). Outputs: per-request TTFT, TPOT, E2E, and per-step batch composition, so you can compare percentiles across settings.

ieng:07.07.q: You must hit p95 TTFT under 800 ms and p95 TPOT under 40 ms at the highest possible rate. Which knobs do you sweep and in what order?
ieng:07.07.s: First set max_num_batched_tokens (with chunked prefill on) to the smallest value meeting the TTFT target at the expected load. Then raise max_num_seqs until TPOT p95 approaches 40 ms. Then increase request rate until either target breaks, and record that as capacity. Re-check prefix caching and gpu_memory_utilization if KV becomes the limit.

ieng:08.01.q: Name the three kinds of memory waste in contiguous per-request KV allocation.
ieng:08.01.s: Reservation waste: space reserved up to max length that the sequence never uses. Internal fragmentation: unused space at the end of each allocation once the sequence finishes short. External fragmentation: free memory split into gaps between allocations, none large enough for a new sequence even when the total free is sufficient.

ieng:08.02.q: With block size 16 and a sequence of 1,000 tokens, how many blocks are used and how much is wasted? How does a block table find token 517?
ieng:08.02.s: ceil(1000/16) = 63 blocks; the last holds 8 tokens so 8 slots are wasted (under 1%). Token 517 is in logical block 517 // 16 = 32 at offset 517 % 16 = 5. The block table maps logical block 32 to some physical block id, and the kernel reads slot 5 of that physical block.

ieng:08.03.q: What does a PagedAttention kernel need as input that a standard attention kernel does not, and what does it cost?
ieng:08.03.s: It needs the block table for each sequence (mapping logical to physical blocks) and the sequence lengths, and reads K and V from non-contiguous blocks. The cost is extra indexing and less perfectly contiguous memory access, which makes the kernel slightly slower per byte than ideal contiguous attention, but the memory saved allows much larger batches, which is a big net win.

ieng:08.04.q: Two requests share a 1,000-token system prompt. How does block sharing work, and what happens when one of them writes a new token into a shared, partially filled block?
ieng:08.04.s: Both block tables point to the same physical blocks for the shared prefix, with a reference count of 2 on each. Full blocks are read-only and can be shared freely. If the last shared block is partially filled and a request must append to it, copy-on-write duplicates that block for the writer so the other request's view is unchanged. Blocks are freed when their reference count drops to zero.

ieng:08.05.q: When is recomputation a better preemption strategy than swapping to CPU, and when is swapping better?
ieng:08.05.s: Recomputation is better when the preempted sequence is short or the GPU has spare compute, since redoing a short prefill is fast and needs no PCIe transfer or CPU memory. Swapping is better for long sequences, where recomputing a long prefix costs much more than copying the KV over PCIe, provided there is CPU memory and PCIe bandwidth to spare.

ieng:08.06.q: What invariants should your allocator's tests check?
ieng:08.06.s: Every physical block is either free or owned with refcount at least 1, never both; the sum of free and used blocks equals the pool size; a sequence's block table covers exactly ceil(len / block_size) blocks; freeing a sequence decrements refcounts and returns blocks only at zero; and no two sequences write to the same block without copy-on-write.
ieng:08.06.t: Visual Lab: Build a Paged KV Allocator

ieng:09.01.q: What makes a baseline "tunable" rather than just a first measurement?
ieng:09.01.s: It is fully pinned (model, engine version, every flag written down), measured on the target workload with the harness at several loads, and recorded with engine metrics. That way each later change touches one variable and can be compared directly, and you know which constraint (TTFT, TPOT, KV memory) binds first.

ieng:09.02.q: List four ways to increase KV capacity on a single GPU and the cost of each.
ieng:09.02.s: Raise gpu_memory_utilization (less safety margin against OOM); quantize the KV cache to FP8 (small quality risk, kernel support needed); quantize weights to FP8 or INT4 to free space (quality risk); lower max_model_len or max_num_batched_tokens to reduce reserved or activation memory (limits long requests or TTFT). Disabling CUDA graphs saves a little memory but costs speed.

ieng:09.03.q: Why should you run production at less than the measured SLO-safe maximum load, and how much headroom is typical?
ieng:09.03.s: Real traffic bursts, prompt mixes shift, and hardware or replicas fail, so running at the measured maximum means any spike breaks the SLO. Teams typically plan to run at 60 to 80% of the measured SLO-safe capacity, leaving room for bursts and for autoscaling to react.

ieng:09.04.q: What would a convincing before-and-after report for single-GPU optimization contain?
ieng:09.04.s: The baseline and final configs (full flags), the workload and SLO, a goodput vs load chart for both, a table of each change with its individual effect, engine metrics explaining each gain, quality checks for any precision change, and the final SLO-safe capacity with planned headroom.

ieng:10.01.q: Describe an experiment that shows long-prompt interference and the metric that reveals it.
ieng:10.01.s: Run a steady stream of short chat requests and measure ITL. Then inject occasional 16k-token prompts while keeping the chat load constant. Without chunked prefill, each long prompt's prefill runs in a single step lasting hundreds of milliseconds, so ITL p99 for the chat users jumps sharply while their p50 barely moves. The ITL tail (and per-step time trace) reveals it.

ieng:10.02.q: How does chunked prefill fix interference, and what is the cost of a chunk size that is too small?
ieng:10.02.s: It splits a long prompt into chunks of at most N tokens and processes one chunk per step alongside the ongoing decodes, so each step stays bounded and decoding users keep getting tokens. A chunk that is too small means many steps to finish the prompt, which raises that request's TTFT and loses some prefill efficiency, since small matmuls use the GPU less well and attention over previous chunks must be re-read each step.
ieng:10.02.t: Chunked Prefill & Choosing the Chunk Size

ieng:10.03.q: How would you measure how much prefill work in your traffic is repeated?
ieng:10.03.s: From logs, tokenize each request's prompt and compute, for each request, the length of the longest prefix matching any earlier request (at block granularity, e.g. 16 tokens). The sum of matched tokens divided by total prompt tokens is the maximum achievable prefix hit rate; it is an upper bound because cache size and eviction limit what is actually kept.

ieng:10.04.q: How does block-hash-based prefix caching decide that a new request can reuse cached KV, and why must the hash include the parent block?
ieng:10.04.s: The prompt is split into full blocks; each block's hash is computed from its tokens plus the hash of the previous block. The engine looks up each hash in a table of cached blocks and reuses blocks until the first miss. Including the parent hash is required because a block's K and V depend on all earlier tokens, so identical tokens after different prefixes produce different KV.

ieng:10.05.q: In a multi-turn chat, why does prefix caching help each new turn, and what can break it between turns?
ieng:10.05.s: Each turn resends the whole conversation, so everything before the new user message matches the previous turn's prompt plus its generated reply, which is already in the cache. It breaks if the earlier cache entries were evicted (long gaps or memory pressure), if the request lands on a different replica, or if the client changes earlier content (trimming history, re-rendering the template differently).
ieng:10.05.t: Shared Prompts, RAG Context & Multi-Turn Reuse

ieng:10.06.q: What does a radix tree give SGLang's prefix cache that a flat hash table of blocks does not, and what is cache churn?
ieng:10.06.s: A radix tree stores cached sequences as shared paths, so finding the longest matching prefix is a single walk, sharing is explicit, and eviction can remove leaves (least recently used) without breaking parents still in use. It also helps schedule requests that share a prefix together. Cache churn is when entries are evicted before they are reused, because the working set is larger than the cache, so you pay to store KV that never hits.

ieng:10.07.q: For a workload of chat plus long RAG prompts with a shared system prompt, which two features do you enable and what do you measure to prove each helped?
ieng:10.07.s: Chunked prefill, proven by lower ITL p99 for chat users when long prompts arrive; and prefix caching, proven by the prefix hit rate metric and lower TTFT for requests with the shared system prompt or repeated documents. Measure each alone and together against the same workload and SLO.
ieng:10.07.t: Lab: Optimize a Mixed Long-Prompt Workload

ieng:11.01.q: Why does quantizing weights from BF16 to INT4 speed up decode on almost any GPU, but may not speed up prefill?
ieng:11.01.s: Decode is memory bound, so reading 4 times fewer weight bytes per step directly cuts step time, even if the GPU dequantizes to BF16 before the math. Prefill is compute bound, and if the hardware has no INT4 tensor core path, the math still runs in BF16 plus dequantization overhead, so prefill may be no faster or even slower.

ieng:11.02.q: Compare per-tensor, per-channel and per-group scaling for weight quantization, and say which INT4 methods usually use.
ieng:11.02.s: Per-tensor uses one scale for the whole matrix: cheap but outliers force a coarse scale for everything. Per-channel uses one scale per output channel: better accuracy, still cheap. Per-group uses one scale per small group (e.g. 128 weights) along the input dimension: best accuracy at low bits but more scale storage and dequant work. INT4 methods like GPTQ and AWQ typically use per-group scaling with group size 128.

ieng:11.03.q: In one sentence each, what problem do GPTQ, AWQ and SmoothQuant solve?
ieng:11.03.s: GPTQ quantizes weights layer by layer, adjusting remaining weights to compensate for rounding error using second-order information from calibration data. AWQ finds the small fraction of weight channels that matter most (by activation magnitude) and scales them up before quantizing so they lose less precision. SmoothQuant moves outlier magnitude from activations into weights with a per-channel scale, so both can be quantized to 8 bits.

ieng:11.04.q: Why can a W4A16 model be faster than BF16 at batch 1 but slower at batch 256?
ieng:11.04.s: At batch 1 the matmul is memory bound, so reading 4-bit weights cuts time nearly 4 times and dequantization hides under memory latency. At batch 256 the matmul becomes compute bound; the math still runs in BF16 and dequantizing each weight tile adds instructions, so the kernel can run slower than a plain BF16 GEMM.

ieng:11.05.q: What are the two benefits of an FP8 KV cache, and what can go wrong?
ieng:11.05.s: It halves KV memory, roughly doubling the number of tokens that fit (more concurrency or longer context), and it halves bytes read by decode attention, speeding long-context decode. Things that can go wrong: quality loss if scales are poor (especially for keys with outlier channels), attention kernels without FP8 support falling back to slow paths, and calibration needed for per-tensor scales.

ieng:11.06.q: After switching to FP8 weights, throughput at batch 1 improved 1.7 times but SLO-safe capacity improved only 1.2 times. Give plausible explanations.
ieng:11.06.s: At the operating load the batch is large and closer to compute bound, where FP8 gains are smaller than at batch 1; capacity may be limited by TTFT (prefill) or the scheduler rather than decode speed; and freed memory may not translate into more concurrency if KV was not the binding constraint. Overheads outside GEMMs (attention, sampling, CPU) also do not get faster.

ieng:11.07.q: Why is perplexity on generic text not enough to approve a quantized model for production?
ieng:11.07.s: Perplexity measures average next-token prediction on some text, which can stay nearly unchanged while specific capabilities (math, code, long context, instruction following, rare languages) degrade. You should also run task evals that match your product, compare outputs on real prompts, and check long-context and structured-output behavior.

ieng:11.08.q: What is a Pareto frontier in this context, and how do you choose a point on it?
ieng:11.08.s: Each configuration (precision of weights and KV, method) gives a point with quality, capacity (or cost) and memory. A configuration is on the frontier if no other one is better on all axes. You choose the cheapest point on the frontier that meets your quality threshold and SLO.
ieng:11.08.t: Project: Build the Quality/Speed/Memory Pareto Frontier

ieng:12.01.q: Outline a profiling workflow that goes from "the server is slow" to a specific fix.
ieng:12.01.s: Reproduce with a fixed workload and measure the symptom. Check engine metrics to rule out queueing or memory pressure. Capture a system-level timeline (Nsight Systems or the PyTorch profiler) of steady-state steps to find GPU idle gaps and which kernels dominate. Drill into the top kernels with Nsight Compute to see whether they are memory or compute bound and how close to peak. Form a hypothesis, change one thing, and re-measure.
ieng:12.01.t: Stop Guessing: Build a Profiling Workflow

ieng:12.02.q: What does the PyTorch memory snapshot show that torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated does not?
ieng:12.02.s: It records every allocation and free with its size, time and Python stack trace, so you can see which code allocated memory, how the peak was formed, and where fragmentation occurs in the caching allocator. max_memory_allocated only reports a single peak number.

ieng:12.03.q: In an Nsight Systems timeline of a decode step you see many short kernels separated by gaps of 5 to 10 microseconds. What is the likely cause and fix?
ieng:12.03.s: The GPU is waiting for the CPU to launch each kernel: launch overhead dominates because each kernel finishes faster than the next can be issued. Fixes are CUDA graphs (record the whole step once and replay it with one launch), kernel fusion to reduce the number of kernels, and moving scheduling work off the critical path.

ieng:12.04.q: Nsight Compute reports a decode attention kernel at 85% of DRAM bandwidth and 8% of compute throughput. What does that tell you and what would make it faster?
ieng:12.04.s: The kernel is memory bound and already near the bandwidth limit, so tuning its compute will not help. It can only get faster by moving fewer bytes: quantizing the KV cache (FP8), using GQA-aware kernels that read each KV head once for all its query heads, or avoiding redundant reads.

ieng:12.05.q: In a profile of prefill and decode for the same model, which kernels' share of time changes most, and why?
ieng:12.05.s: In prefill, large GEMMs dominate and attention grows with prompt length squared, both compute bound. In decode, GEMMs remain large in share but become memory bound and much shorter per token, attention becomes a bandwidth-bound read of the KV cache, and small kernels (norms, RoPE, sampling) plus launch overhead take a much larger share of the step.

ieng:12.06.q: Order the GPU memory levels from fastest and smallest to slowest and largest, and say where a FlashAttention kernel keeps its tiles.
ieng:12.06.s: Registers (per thread), shared memory and L1 (per SM, ~200 KB), L2 cache (tens of MB, shared), HBM global memory (tens of GB). FlashAttention loads tiles of Q, K and V from HBM into shared memory and registers, computes on them there, and writes only the output back to HBM, avoiding storing the full attention matrix in HBM.
ieng:12.06.t: GPU Execution, Memory Hierarchy & Kernel Launches

ieng:12.07.q: An H100 has about 990 TFLOPs of dense BF16 and 3.35 TB/s of HBM bandwidth. What arithmetic intensity is the ridge point, and is a batch-8 decode GEMM above or below it?
ieng:12.07.s: Ridge = 990e12 / 3.35e12, about 295 FLOPs per byte. A BF16 GEMM with M = 8 does 2 x 8 x K x N FLOPs while reading about 2 x K x N bytes of weights, so intensity is about 8 FLOPs per byte, far below the ridge. It is memory bound.
ieng:12.07.t: Compute-Bound vs Memory-Bound & the Roofline Model

ieng:12.08.q: What sections does a good bottleneck report have?
ieng:12.08.s: Symptom and workload; environment; engine metrics summary; timeline breakdown of a steady-state step (kernel groups, idle time); top kernels with roofline position and efficiency; diagnosis naming the bottleneck class; ranked recommendations with estimated gain; and the verification plan.

ieng:13.01.q: Why does it matter that adjacent threads in a warp read adjacent memory addresses?
ieng:13.01.s: The hardware combines a warp's memory requests into as few memory transactions as possible. If 32 threads read 32 consecutive 4-byte values, that is one or a few 128-byte transactions (coalesced). If they read scattered addresses, the warp needs many transactions, wasting bandwidth, which is the main limit for memory-bound inference kernels.
ieng:13.01.t: GPU Threads, Warps, Blocks & Memory Access

ieng:13.02.q: How does Triton's programming model differ from CUDA's, and what does that save you?
ieng:13.02.s: In CUDA you write code per thread and manage thread indexing, shared memory and synchronization yourself. In Triton you write code per program instance operating on blocks (tiles) of data with tensor-like operations, and the compiler handles thread mapping, coalescing, shared memory and much of the tiling detail. You keep control of tile sizes and data layout while writing far less low-level code.

ieng:13.03.q: Explain why tiling a matrix multiply reduces HBM traffic.
ieng:13.03.s: Without tiling each output element reads a full row of A and column of B from HBM, so the same data is read many times. With tiling, a block loads a tile of A and a tile of B into shared memory or registers once and uses each loaded element for many output elements in its tile. Traffic drops roughly by the tile size factor, raising arithmetic intensity.

ieng:13.04.q: For a vector add kernel on 100 million BF16 elements, what is the best possible time on a 3.35 TB/s GPU and how do you check whether your kernel achieves it?
ieng:13.04.s: It reads two arrays and writes one: 3 x 100M x 2 bytes = 600 MB. At 3.35 TB/s the minimum is about 0.18 ms. Time the kernel with CUDA events or triton.testing.do_bench and compute achieved bandwidth as bytes moved divided by time; a good kernel reaches 80 to 90% of peak.

ieng:13.05.q: Why is a fused RMSNorm kernel faster than PyTorch's sequence of x.pow(2).mean(), rsqrt, multiply, multiply?
ieng:13.05.s: The unfused version launches several kernels and writes and reads intermediate tensors to HBM between them, moving the data several times. A fused kernel loads each row once, computes the mean square, scale and gain multiply in registers, and writes the output once, so it moves about the minimum bytes and launches one kernel.

ieng:13.06.q: What does rotary position embedding do to Q and K, and why is it a good candidate for fusion with the QKV projection output?
ieng:13.06.s: RoPE rotates each pair of dimensions of Q and K by an angle proportional to the token position, so dot products depend on relative position. It is purely elementwise on the projection output, so applying it right after the QKV GEMM (or while writing K into the KV cache) avoids an extra HBM read and write of Q and K.

ieng:13.07.q: Your Triton kernel is 3 times faster than PyTorch in a micro-benchmark but the end-to-end step improves only 2%. Why?
ieng:13.07.s: The op was only a small fraction of step time, so even a large speedup on it barely moves the total (Amdahl's law). The micro-benchmark may also have used shapes or conditions (warm caches, large sizes) unlike the real model, or the real engine already used a fused or optimized version, so the baseline in the step was faster than eager PyTorch.

ieng:13.08.q: How would you pick which kernel in a real engine to optimize for this challenge?
ieng:13.08.s: Profile a representative workload, list kernels by share of step time, and for each estimate headroom from its roofline position (how far below its memory or compute ceiling it runs). Choose the kernel with the largest share times headroom that you can realistically improve, such as a fused norm, a sampling kernel, or a decode attention variant at your shapes.
ieng:13.08.t: Challenge: Optimize a Real Inference Kernel

ieng:14.01.q: How much HBM traffic does naive attention generate for one head with sequence length 8k and head dim 128 in BF16, compared with the inputs?
ieng:14.01.s: Q, K and V are each 8k x 128 x 2 bytes = 2 MB, 6 MB total. The score matrix is 8k x 8k x 2 bytes = 128 MB, written and read back at least twice (scores, softmax output), so hundreds of MB of extra traffic, about 50 to 100 times the inputs. That traffic dominates naive attention time.

ieng:14.02.q: Explain how online softmax lets you process attention in blocks of keys without storing all scores.
ieng:14.02.s: For each query row you keep a running max m, a running sum of exponentials l, and a running output accumulator. For each new block of keys you compute block scores, update the max, rescale the old sum and accumulator by exp(old_m - new_m), add the new block's exponentials and weighted values, and move on. At the end you divide the accumulator by l. Only one block of scores exists at a time.

ieng:14.03.q: FlashAttention does more FLOPs than standard attention in the backward pass, yet it is faster. Why, and what changed in FlashAttention-2 and 3?
ieng:14.03.s: It is faster because attention is limited by HBM traffic, not FLOPs; FlashAttention keeps tiles in on-chip memory and never writes the score matrix, so it moves far fewer bytes, even if it recomputes some values. FlashAttention-2 improved parallelism and work partitioning across warps and along the sequence. FlashAttention-3 targets Hopper, using asynchronous data movement (TMA), warp specialization and FP8 support to raise tensor core utilization.

ieng:14.04.q: Why is a FlashAttention kernel tuned for prefill a poor fit for decode, and what technique helps long-context decode?
ieng:14.04.s: Prefill kernels tile over many queries per sequence, so each loaded K/V tile is reused by a big Q tile and tensor cores stay busy. In decode there is one query per sequence (or a few per KV head with GQA), so there is little reuse and too few query tiles to fill the GPU at small batch. Split-KV (flash-decoding) partitions the long KV sequence across many thread blocks, computes partial results in parallel, and reduces them, keeping all SMs busy.
