ieng:14.05.q: What does an engine's "attention backend" setting choose, and what should you consider when switching backends?
ieng:14.05.s: It chooses which kernel library implements attention for prefill, decode and mixed batches with the engine's KV layout, for example FlashAttention, FlashInfer, or Triton-based kernels. When switching, check hardware support, dtype support (FP8 KV), features (paged KV, sliding window, MLA, cascade attention), correctness on your model, and performance at your shapes (batch, context, GQA ratio).

ieng:14.06.q: What grid of conditions should an attention backend comparison cover?
ieng:14.06.s: Prefill-heavy and decode-heavy workloads; short (1k) and long (32k) contexts; small and large batch sizes; BF16 and FP8 KV; and, if relevant, shared-prefix traffic. Measure both kernel time from a profile and end-to-end TTFT, TPOT and throughput, and verify outputs match.

ieng:15.01.q: At batch size 1 decode, kernel time is 6 ms but step time is 11 ms. Where do the other 5 ms go?
ieng:15.01.s: CPU-side overhead: Python interpreting the model code, PyTorch dispatching each op, building kernel arguments and launching hundreds of kernels, plus scheduler work and synchronization between steps. The GPU sits idle between kernels waiting for launches. Compilation and CUDA graphs target exactly this.

ieng:15.02.q: What does torch.compile do to a model's forward pass at a high level?
ieng:15.02.s: TorchDynamo captures the Python code into an FX graph of tensor operations (falling back to Python where it cannot), AOTAutograd prepares the graph, and TorchInductor lowers it to optimized code, fusing elementwise and reduction ops into generated Triton kernels and calling libraries like cuBLAS for matmuls. The result runs fewer, larger kernels with less Python overhead.

ieng:15.03.q: What is a graph break, give two causes, and how do dynamic shapes cause recompilation?
ieng:15.03.s: A graph break is where TorchDynamo cannot trace the Python code, so it ends the current graph, runs that code eagerly, and starts a new graph; fusion across the break is lost. Causes: data-dependent control flow (if on a tensor value), calls to unsupported functions or .item(). With static shapes, a new input shape (different batch size or sequence length) triggers a new compilation; marking dimensions dynamic avoids that at some optimization cost.

ieng:15.04.q: What constraints does CUDA graph capture impose, and how do engines handle variable batch sizes with it?
ieng:15.04.s: A captured graph replays fixed kernels with fixed memory addresses and shapes; no CPU-side logic, host syncs or new allocations can happen inside it, and inputs must be copied into the same static buffers before replay. Engines capture one graph per batch size from a chosen set (e.g. 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 ... 512), and at runtime pad the batch up to the nearest captured size.

ieng:15.05.q: You capture CUDA graphs for 67 batch sizes and compile with max-autotune. Startup now takes 6 minutes and KV capacity dropped 3%. When is that worth it?
ieng:15.05.s: It is worth it for long-lived replicas with stable traffic, where steady-state speed matters over hours and startup is rare. It is not worth it when you autoscale often or need fast recovery, because every new replica takes 6 minutes before serving; there, capture fewer sizes, use default compile, or cache compiled artifacts.

ieng:15.06.q: Which three configurations do you compare and what do you expect at batch 1 vs batch 128?
ieng:15.06.s: Eager, torch.compile without graphs, and torch.compile with CUDA graphs. At batch 1, eager is slowest; compile helps through fusion; graphs give the biggest gain by removing launch overhead. At batch 128, all three are closer because kernels are long and overhead is a small share; compile still helps somewhat through fusion.
ieng:15.06.t: Lab: Compile and Capture an Inference Workload

ieng:16.01.q: Why can a model verify 5 proposed tokens in about the same time it takes to generate 1?
ieng:16.01.s: Decode is memory bound: a step's time is dominated by reading the weights. Feeding 5 tokens instead of 1 through the same forward pass reads the weights once and does 5 times the (still small) compute, so the step takes nearly the same time, while producing logits for all 5 positions at once.

ieng:16.02.q: Walk through one round of draft-model speculative decoding with k = 4.
ieng:16.02.s: The small draft model generates 4 tokens autoregressively from the current context (4 cheap passes). The target model runs one forward pass on the context plus those 4 tokens, producing distributions for 5 positions. Starting from the first, each draft token is accepted or rejected by comparing draft and target probabilities. At the first rejection, a corrected token is sampled and the rest discarded; if all 4 are accepted, a fifth token is sampled from the target's last distribution. The round yields between 1 and 5 tokens.
ieng:16.02.t: Draft Models, Target Models & Parallel Verification

ieng:16.03.q: State the acceptance rule for speculative sampling and explain why it preserves the target model's output distribution.
ieng:16.03.s: For a draft token x with draft probability q(x) and target probability p(x), accept with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)). If rejected, sample from the normalized residual max(0, p - q). Combining the two cases gives exactly p(x) for every token, so the final output is distributed as if sampled from the target alone. With greedy decoding, the rule reduces to accepting while the draft token equals the target's argmax.

ieng:16.04.q: Why does speculative decoding give big speedups at batch 1 and can slow things down at batch 128?
ieng:16.04.s: At batch 1 decode is memory bound and the GPU has lots of idle compute, so verifying k extra tokens per sequence is almost free. At batch 128 decode is close to compute bound; each verified token costs real compute, and rejected draft tokens are wasted work that could have served other users. Throughput can drop even if per-request latency improves slightly.

ieng:16.05.q: Why does prompt-lookup (n-gram) speculation work well for code editing and summarization, and poorly for open-ended chat?
ieng:16.05.s: It drafts by finding the last few generated tokens elsewhere in the prompt and copying what followed. Code editing and summarization often reproduce long spans of the input, so drafts are frequently right. Open-ended chat produces new text not present in the prompt, so matches are rare and drafts are mostly rejected.

ieng:16.06.q: How do Medusa heads and EAGLE differ in what they use to predict future tokens?
ieng:16.06.s: Medusa adds several extra decoding heads on the target model's last hidden state, each predicting the token at a further offset (t+1, t+2, ...), and verifies candidate combinations with tree attention. EAGLE trains a small autoregressive head that operates at the feature level, taking the target's hidden states (plus the sampled tokens) to predict the next features and tokens, which gives higher acceptance than independent heads.

ieng:16.07.q: What is the trade-off between a drafter that proposes positions one at a time and one that fills a whole block in a single pass, and how does dynamic draft length help?
ieng:16.07.s: A sequential drafter conditions each guess on the previous one, so later guesses are more accurate, but it adds k serial steps to every round. A block (parallel) drafter fills all k positions in one pass, so drafting latency is flat, but guesses are less coordinated and acceptance can drop for later positions. Dynamic speculation picks the draft length per step or per request from confidence and load, drafting long when guesses are likely accepted and the GPU has spare compute, short or not at all otherwise.

ieng:16.08.q: Which variables define the map of where speculation helps, and what is the output?
ieng:16.08.s: Method (draft model, n-gram, EAGLE-style), draft length, concurrency, task type (code, chat, RAG) and temperature. The output is a table or heatmap of TPOT and throughput change versus no speculation for each cell, plus acceptance rates, and a recommendation of which method and k to use per workload and load level.
ieng:16.08.t: Lab: Map Where Speculative Decoding Wins

ieng:17.01.q: Name four ways an engine comparison is commonly unfair.
ieng:17.01.s: Different defaults (one has prefix caching or chunked prefill on, the other off); different precision or quantization; tuning one engine and not the other; different workloads or output lengths (EOS not ignored); different versions or hardware; and measuring with each engine's own benchmark tool, which may define metrics differently.

ieng:17.02.q: Name two architectural ideas that distinguish SGLang from vLLM historically, and one area where both have converged.
ieng:17.02.s: SGLang introduced RadixAttention, a radix-tree prefix cache with cache-aware scheduling, and a frontend language for structured LLM programs; it also emphasized a lightweight, overlap-friendly scheduler. vLLM introduced PagedAttention and a block-based KV manager with hash-based prefix caching. Both now support continuous batching, chunked prefill, prefix caching, speculative decoding, structured output and multi-GPU parallelism.

ieng:17.03.q: What does TensorRT-LLM trade for its performance, compared with vLLM or SGLang?
ieng:17.03.s: It ties you more closely to NVIDIA hardware and its toolchain, can require building or converting engines for a specific model, precision and GPU (with longer build steps and less flexibility to change shapes), and has a steeper setup. In return it offers highly tuned kernels, strong FP8 and FP4 support and in-flight batching on NVIDIA GPUs.

ieng:17.04.q: Why would you choose llama.cpp over vLLM, and when would you not?
ieng:17.04.s: For local or edge deployment: laptops, phones, CPUs, Apple Silicon or small GPUs, single-user use, minimal dependencies, and aggressive quantization formats (GGUF k-quants). Not for high-concurrency datacenter serving, where vLLM or SGLang's batching, paged KV and multi-GPU support give far higher throughput.

ieng:17.05.q: Pick one dimension where engines differ and describe how you would test whether that difference matters for your workload.
ieng:17.05.s: Prefix caching: vLLM uses block-hash caching, SGLang a radix tree with cache-aware scheduling. Build a workload with realistic shared prefixes (multi-turn chat with system prompts), run both engines with identical settings under load, and compare hit rate, TTFT p95 and goodput. Then repeat with no shared prefixes to confirm the difference comes from caching.

ieng:17.06.q: What columns and rows should an engine selection matrix have, and how do you turn it into a decision?
ieng:17.06.s: Rows are candidate engines; columns are must-have requirements (model and hardware support, features), measured performance on your workloads (goodput under SLO, TTFT, TPOT), operational factors (startup time, metrics, deployment tooling, stability), and team factors (familiarity, ability to modify). Filter out engines failing must-haves, then weight the remaining columns by importance and pick the highest score, recording the reasoning.
ieng:17.06.t: Project: Build an Engine Selection Matrix

ieng:18.01.q: Give three distinct reasons to use more than one GPU for a model, and the parallelism each typically leads to.
ieng:18.01.s: The model does not fit in one GPU's memory (tensor or pipeline parallelism); you need lower latency per token than one GPU can give, by spreading each layer's work (tensor parallelism); or you need more total throughput than one replica (data parallelism, i.e. more replicas). Very long contexts can also need context parallelism.
ieng:18.01.t: Why and When to Scale Beyond One GPU

ieng:18.02.q: How would you check how the GPUs in a node are connected, and why does it matter for tensor parallelism?
ieng:18.02.s: Run nvidia-smi topo -m, which shows for each GPU pair whether they connect through NVLink (NV#), a PCIe switch (PIX/PXB) or across CPU sockets (SYS). Tensor parallelism does all-reduces every layer, so it needs high bandwidth and low latency; over NVLink it scales well, over PCIe or across sockets the communication can dominate step time.

ieng:18.03.q: In Megatron-style tensor parallelism of an MLP, which matrix is split by columns, which by rows, and where is the all-reduce?
ieng:18.03.s: The first matrices (gate and up projections) are split by columns, so each GPU computes part of the intermediate activations with no communication. The down projection is split by rows, so each GPU produces a partial sum of the full output. One all-reduce sums those partial outputs at the end of the MLP. Attention is split by heads in the same way, with one all-reduce after the output projection.

ieng:18.04.q: Estimate the all-reduce cost per decode step for a 80-layer model with hidden size 8192 at batch 32 with TP 4 over NVLink at 400 GB/s effective bus bandwidth.
ieng:18.04.s: Each all-reduce moves 32 x 8192 x 2 bytes = 512 KB. A ring all-reduce sends about 2 x (TP-1)/TP of the data per GPU, about 768 KB, taking roughly 2 microseconds at 400 GB/s plus around 10 to 20 microseconds of latency. Two per layer times 80 layers is 160 all-reduces, roughly 2 to 3.5 ms per step, mostly latency. That is significant against a 15 to 25 ms step.

ieng:18.05.q: You run an 8B model with TP 1 on one GPU and TP 2 on two GPUs. TPOT improves 1.5 times but throughput per GPU drops. Is that a bad result?
ieng:18.05.s: Not necessarily. TP 2 cuts per-step weight reads in half, so latency improves, but communication overhead means two GPUs give less than double the throughput of one. If your SLO needs the lower TPOT, TP 2 is right; if you only need throughput and TP 1 meets the SLO, two TP-1 replicas give more total throughput per GPU.

ieng:18.06.q: Why does pipeline parallelism add little communication but can hurt latency, and how do engines keep all stages busy?
ieng:18.06.s: Each stage holds a contiguous set of layers and only sends the activations of the tokens in flight to the next stage once per step, which is small. But a single request must pass through all stages sequentially, so per-token latency does not improve and adds transfer hops. Engines keep stages busy by having several micro-batches in flight, so while stage 2 processes batch A, stage 1 processes batch B.

ieng:18.07.q: For serving, what is data parallelism and when is it combined with expert parallelism?
ieng:18.07.s: In serving, data parallelism means running several full replicas of the model, each handling different requests, with no communication between them during a step. For large MoE models, attention can be data parallel (each replica holds its own KV and requests) while the expert layers are spread across all GPUs with expert parallelism, so a DP group shares the experts through all-to-all communication.

ieng:18.08.q: How does ring attention let several GPUs process one very long prompt, and what does each GPU store?
ieng:18.08.s: The sequence is split into chunks, one per GPU; each GPU holds Q, K and V for its chunk. GPUs pass K and V blocks around a ring; at each step every GPU computes attention between its queries and the KV block it currently holds, accumulating with online softmax, while sending that block on. After P steps every query has seen all keys. Each GPU stores only its chunk's KV plus one block in transit.

ieng:18.09.q: For a 70B model on one 8-GPU H100 node serving chat traffic, which configurations would you test and how do you choose?
ieng:18.09.s: TP 8 as one replica, TP 4 x 2 replicas, and TP 2 x 4 replicas if weights in FP8 fit (70 GB over 2 GPUs leaves some KV room). Measure SLO-safe goodput for the node, TPOT at low load, and KV capacity per replica. Choose the configuration with the highest node goodput that meets the TPOT SLO.
ieng:18.09.t: Lab: Choose and Benchmark a Parallelism Strategy

ieng:19.01.q: A MoE model has 235B total parameters and 22B active per token. What does each number mean for memory and for decode speed?
ieng:19.01.s: All 235B parameters must be stored (470 GB in BF16), so memory and GPU count are set by the total. Each token only uses about 22B parameters, so compute per token is like a 22B dense model. At small batch decode, only the selected experts' weights are read, so bandwidth cost per token is also near 22B; at large batch, different tokens select different experts, so most experts are read every step.
ieng:19.01.t: How MoE Inference Differs From Dense Models

ieng:19.02.q: Describe top-k routing for one token, and what "expert activation statistics" you would collect during serving.
ieng:19.02.s: The router computes a score per expert from the token's hidden state (a small linear layer), applies softmax (or sigmoid), picks the top-k experts, and normalizes their weights; the token's MLP output is the weighted sum of those experts' outputs. Collect per-layer counts of tokens routed to each expert per step and over time, to see load balance, hot experts, and how activation depends on the workload.

ieng:19.03.q: With 256 experts per layer over 32 GPUs, how does expert parallelism work, and what does placement decide?
ieng:19.03.s: Each GPU holds 8 experts per layer. After routing, tokens are sent with all-to-all to the GPUs holding their chosen experts, computed there, and sent back with another all-to-all. Placement decides which experts live on which GPU: grouping often co-activated experts, spreading hot experts, or replicating popular ones changes communication volume and load balance.

ieng:19.04.q: Why does one hot expert slow down the whole MoE layer under expert parallelism, and name two mitigations.
ieng:19.04.s: All GPUs must finish their experts before the combine all-to-all completes and the next layer starts, so the GPU with the most tokens sets the layer time; others wait idle. Mitigations: replicate hot experts on more GPUs and split their tokens (as in redundant-expert schemes), and rebalance placement periodically from observed statistics; capacity limits that drop or reroute overflow tokens also exist but can affect quality.

ieng:19.05.q: Why does MoE need grouped GEMM kernels, and why is all-to-all latency critical for decode?
ieng:19.05.s: Each expert gets a different, often small, number of tokens; launching one GEMM per expert wastes time and underuses the GPU. A grouped GEMM runs all experts' matmuls in one kernel with per-group sizes. In decode, few tokens per step means small messages, so all-to-all time is dominated by latency, and with two all-to-alls per MoE layer over dozens of layers it can rival compute time; low-latency all-to-all kernels and overlapping with compute are needed.

ieng:19.06.q: What would you measure in an MoE profile to decide between more TP and more EP?
ieng:19.06.s: The share of step time in MoE layers versus attention; per-expert GEMM sizes and efficiency; all-to-all (EP) versus all-reduce (TP) time; load imbalance across GPUs; and KV capacity per replica. If expert GEMMs are tiny and all-reduce heavy under TP, EP with larger per-expert batches may win; if all-to-all latency dominates at small scale, TP may be better.
ieng:19.06.t: Lab: Profile and Optimize an MoE Workload

ieng:20.01.q: Describe how TTFT, TPOT and max concurrency change as context goes from 4k to 128k tokens on one GPU.
ieng:20.01.s: TTFT grows faster than linearly because attention prefill cost grows with length squared, so 128k can take tens of seconds. TPOT grows roughly linearly with context because each decode step reads the whole KV cache, which eventually outweighs weights. Max concurrency falls inversely with context: 32 times longer context means about 32 times fewer sequences fit.

ieng:20.02.q: For a 128k-token prompt, roughly what fraction of prefill FLOPs is attention for an 8B model with 32 layers and hidden size 4096?
ieng:20.02.s: Linear layers cost about 2 x 8B x 128k, about 2e15 FLOPs. Attention scores and weighted sum cost about 4 x layers x seq^2 x hidden / 2 for causal, roughly 2 x 32 x (128k)^2 x 4096, about 4.4e15 FLOPs. So attention is around two thirds of prefill FLOPs at this length.

ieng:20.03.q: Compare FP8 KV, sliding-window attention and KV eviction (like H2O or StreamingLLM) as ways to fit long contexts.
ieng:20.03.s: FP8 KV halves memory with little quality loss and keeps all tokens. Sliding-window attention (a model architecture choice) keeps only the last W tokens' KV for some or all layers, bounding memory, but only works if the model was trained that way. KV eviction methods drop tokens judged unimportant (keeping attention sinks and heavy hitters) to fit a budget; they work with existing models but are lossy and can miss details needed later.

ieng:20.04.q: When does offloading KV to CPU memory make sense, and what limits it?
ieng:20.04.s: When KV could be reused later (multi-turn chats, repeated documents, preempted requests) but there is not enough GPU memory to keep it; recomputing a long prefix costs more than reloading it. It is limited by PCIe (or NVLink-C2C) bandwidth for moving KV back, by CPU memory capacity, and by the latency it adds to TTFT if loading is not overlapped with compute.

ieng:20.05.q: How can an engine hide the latency of loading KV from CPU memory for a request with a cached prefix?
ieng:20.05.s: Start the transfer as soon as the request is scheduled (or even when it arrives), and overlap it with other work: copy layer by layer so attention for layer 1 can start while later layers load, or schedule the request for a later step and run other requests meanwhile. Use asynchronous copies on separate CUDA streams and pinned host memory.

ieng:20.06.q: Why might "cache everything, evict LRU" be a poor policy for a lower KV tier, and what would you use instead?
ieng:20.06.s: Most prefixes are never reused, so caching everything spends bandwidth writing one-off KV and pushes out valuable entries (cache pollution). Better: admit only entries likely to be reused (seen more than once, long prefixes, active conversations), weigh eviction by size and recompute cost rather than recency alone, and route requests so each replica sees a stable subset of prefixes.

ieng:20.07.q: What result would show that your tiered KV setup is worth it?
ieng:20.07.s: On a multi-turn or repeated-document workload whose total KV exceeds GPU memory, TTFT p95 and goodput improve compared with GPU-only caching, with hit rate in the CPU tier showing where the gain comes from, and with no regression on a workload with no reuse.
ieng:20.07.t: Lab: Push Context Beyond GPU Memory

ieng:21.01.q: Give two reasons to run prefill and decode on separate GPU pools.
ieng:21.01.s: They interfere when colocated: long prefills stall decode steps (ITL spikes) and decode batches slow prefills, so it is hard to meet both TTFT and TPOT SLOs. And they have different resource profiles (prefill compute bound, decode memory bound), so separate pools can use different parallelism, batch sizes or even hardware, and be scaled independently to match the traffic's ratio of prompt to output tokens.

ieng:21.02.q: Traffic is 5 requests/s with 3,000-token prompts and 300-token outputs. A prefill GPU processes 20,000 tokens/s within TTFT SLO; a decode GPU sustains 2,500 output tokens/s within TPOT SLO. How many of each do you need?
ieng:21.02.s: Prefill demand is 5 x 3,000 = 15,000 tokens/s, so 0.75 GPUs: round up to 1 (plus headroom, so 1 to 2). Decode demand is 5 x 300 = 1,500 tokens/s, so 0.6 GPUs: 1. With headroom for bursts, about 2 prefill and 1 to 2 decode GPUs. The ratio shifts as prompt and output lengths change.

ieng:21.03.q: What must a decode worker receive from the prefill worker to continue a request, and in what order should things happen?
ieng:21.03.s: The KV cache for all prompt tokens (every layer), the first generated token (or the logits to sample it), the request's sampling parameters and state, and position information. Order: router sends request to prefill; prefill computes KV and first token; KV is transferred to blocks the decode worker allocated; decode worker adds the request to its running batch and continues generating; the first token can be streamed by prefill or decode.

ieng:21.04.q: Estimate the KV transfer time for a 4,000-token prompt of a 70B-class model (320 KB per token) over 400 Gb/s RDMA, and compare with its prefill time.
ieng:21.04.s: KV size is 4,000 x 320 KB = 1.28 GB. At 50 GB/s, about 26 ms. Prefill of 4,000 tokens for a 70B model on a TP-8 H100 node takes roughly 300 to 600 ms. Transfer is small relative to prefill, especially if overlapped layer by layer.

ieng:21.05.q: Under what conditions does colocated serving with chunked prefill beat disaggregation?
ieng:21.05.s: At low load, where interference is small and disaggregation's fixed overheads (KV transfer, extra hop, underused separate pools) dominate; with short prompts, where prefill is cheap and interference minor; when the network between pools is slow; or when traffic's prefill/decode ratio swings faster than pools can be rebalanced, leaving one pool idle.
ieng:21.05.t: Measure Transfer Cost & the Crossover Point

ieng:21.06.q: Which signals would you use to autoscale the prefill pool and the decode pool separately?
ieng:21.06.s: Prefill pool: queued prompt tokens or prefill queue wait time, and TTFT percentile against SLO. Decode pool: KV cache usage, running sequences per worker, and TPOT percentile against SLO. Scale each when its signals approach thresholds; request rate alone is insufficient because the prompt/output mix changes.

ieng:21.07.q: What is the minimum setup to demonstrate disaggregation's benefit, and what chart proves it?
ieng:21.07.s: At least two GPUs (one prefill, one decode) connected by a fast link, versus the same two GPUs as colocated replicas with chunked prefill, serving a workload with long prompts and a tight TPOT SLO. The proving chart is goodput (or SLO attainment) versus request rate for both setups, plus ITL p99 showing the interference removed.
ieng:21.07.t: Project: Reproduce a Disaggregated Serving Architecture

ieng:22.01.q: What goes into a production inference container image, and what should stay out of it?
ieng:22.01.s: In: a pinned engine version with its CUDA and PyTorch stack, your server wrapper or config, health and metrics endpoints, and startup scripts. Out: model weights (pull from a model store or mount a cache volume, so images stay small and models can change independently), secrets (inject at runtime), and environment-specific settings (pass as config).

ieng:22.02.q: Break down the cold start of a new 70B replica and name the biggest lever to shorten it.
ieng:22.02.s: Container pull (seconds to minutes), weight download (140 GB at 1 to 2 GB/s from object storage is over a minute, often several), loading weights into GPU memory (tens of seconds), compilation and CUDA graph capture (tens of seconds to minutes), and warm-up. The biggest lever is usually weight movement: keep weights on fast local NVMe or a nearby cache, use streaming loaders, and avoid re-downloading.

ieng:22.03.q: Why should readiness be reported only after warm-up requests, not after the model loads?
ieng:22.03.s: The first requests after load trigger lazy compilation, kernel autotuning, allocator growth and cache population, so they can be many times slower. If the load balancer sends real traffic as soon as weights load, those users get very slow responses or timeouts. Running synthetic warm-up requests first and then reporting ready keeps real users on warmed replicas.

ieng:22.04.q: Describe a graceful shutdown sequence for an inference replica during a rolling deploy.
ieng:22.04.s: Mark the replica not ready so the load balancer stops sending new requests; keep serving in-flight requests until they finish or a drain timeout (longer than typical E2E latency) passes; abort remaining requests with a clear error so clients can retry; flush metrics and logs; then exit and free the GPU.

ieng:22.05.q: What should a "deployment version" of an LLM service pin, beyond the model name?
ieng:22.05.s: The exact weights revision (hash), tokenizer and chat template, quantization recipe and calibration, engine version and image hash, all engine flags (parallelism, scheduler, KV dtype, speculation), and default sampling parameters. Any of these can change outputs or performance, so they should be versioned together and recorded with every result and log.

ieng:22.06.q: Compare shadow traffic and a canary for testing a new quantized model, and what you would watch in each.
ieng:22.06.s: Shadow traffic sends a copy of real requests to the new version without returning its responses to users; it is safe and shows performance and output differences, but not user reaction. A canary sends a small share of real users to the new version and returns its responses; it shows real quality signals (feedback, retries, task success) but carries risk. Watch latency, errors, output length, and quality metrics in both; in the canary, also user-facing signals and a fast rollback trigger.

ieng:22.07.q: You must serve 12 fine-tuned variants of the same 8B base, each with low traffic. What are your options?
ieng:22.07.s: Serve the base once with LoRA adapters and multi-LoRA batching, so all variants share weights and run in the same batches (best if fine-tunes are LoRA). If they are full fine-tunes, pack several models per GPU when memory allows, or use model swapping with fast loading for rarely used ones. Giving each variant its own GPU wastes capacity at low traffic.

ieng:22.08.q: List the production-readiness checks your server must pass.
ieng:22.08.s: Pinned, versioned config and image; weights cached for fast start; startup, readiness and liveness probes with warm-up; graceful drain within the grace period; metrics exported and dashboards built; request logging with version id; load test at expected and peak load meeting the SLO; a canary and rollback procedure tested; and a cold start time measured and documented.

ieng:23.01.q: Why is round-robin load balancing a poor fit for LLM replicas?
ieng:23.01.s: Requests vary hugely in cost (prompt and output length), so equal request counts produce very unequal load: one replica can be stuck with several long generations while another is idle. Round robin also ignores KV cache state and prefix locality. Least-outstanding-requests or token-aware balancing does better.

ieng:23.02.q: What is "herding" in queue-aware routing and how do you prevent it?
ieng:23.02.s: When many routers see the same replica as least loaded (from metrics a few seconds old), they all send to it at once, overloading it while others go idle; the pattern then flips. Prevent it with power-of-two-choices (sample two replicas at random, pick the better), local tracking of requests each router has just sent, and short metric staleness windows.

ieng:23.03.q: How do you balance cache affinity against load balance when routing?
ieng:23.03.s: Score each candidate replica by expected cache hit (length of prompt prefix it likely holds) and by its load. Send the request to the replica with the best hit if its load is under a threshold; otherwise fall back to the least-loaded replica (and let the cache build there). Consistent hashing on a prefix key (like session id or system-prompt hash) gives affinity with bounded imbalance.

ieng:23.04.q: Why is GPU utilization a poor autoscaling signal for LLM servers, and what would you use?
ieng:23.04.s: nvidia-smi utilization is near 100% whenever any kernel runs, even at low load, and does not track how close the server is to its SLO. Better signals are queue depth (waiting requests or tokens), KV cache usage, in-flight requests per replica relative to measured capacity, and SLO-related latencies (TTFT p95), possibly combined with predicted traffic.
ieng:23.04.t: Autoscale From Requests, Tokens & Queue Pressure

ieng:23.05.q: Your replicas take 5 minutes to become ready, and traffic can double in 2 minutes. What capacity strategy do you need?
ieng:23.05.s: Reactive autoscaling alone will miss the SLO during spikes, since new capacity arrives after the spike. You need standing headroom (run below capacity), a pool of warm standby replicas (loaded and warmed but receiving little traffic), and faster startup (local weight caches, compile caches). Load shedding or degraded modes cover what remains.

ieng:23.06.q: What does Ray Serve add on top of an inference engine like vLLM?
ieng:23.06.s: It provides the serving layer: deployments with replicas and autoscaling, request routing between them, composition of multiple models or steps in one application, multi-node placement of engine replicas (including tensor and pipeline parallel across nodes), and an OpenAI-compatible front end, all in Python on a Ray cluster.

ieng:23.07.q: How does Kubernetes give a pod a GPU, and what does KServe add for model serving?
ieng:23.07.s: The NVIDIA device plugin advertises GPUs as an extended resource (nvidia.com/gpu); a pod requests a whole number of them and the scheduler places it on a node with free GPUs, with the container runtime exposing those devices. KServe adds a model-serving abstraction (InferenceService) with standard runtimes, autoscaling (including scale to zero), canary rollouts and a consistent inference API on top.

ieng:23.08.q: How do you judge whether your autoscaling setup passed the lab?
ieng:23.08.s: Replay a traffic trace with a ramp and a spike, and measure SLO attainment over time (for example per minute), total GPU-hours used, and cold starts. It passes if SLO attainment stays above target (say 99%) through the trace except a bounded window during the spike, with GPU-hours lower than a static deployment sized for peak.
ieng:23.08.t: Lab: Hold an SLO Under Changing Traffic

ieng:24.01.q: Name the four dashboard panels you would build first for an LLM service.
ieng:24.01.s: Request rate and error rate by model; TTFT and TPOT percentiles (p50, p95, p99) against SLO lines; token throughput (prompt and generation tokens per second); and engine saturation (running and waiting requests, KV cache usage, preemptions) per replica.

ieng:24.02.q: Which GPU-level metrics can warn about hardware problems before a crash?
ieng:24.02.s: Xid errors in driver logs, ECC error counts (correctable rising, uncorrectable any), retired or remapped memory pages, NVLink error counters, thermal throttling and clock drops, and power anomalies. DCGM exposes most of these as metrics; rising correctable errors or row remapping often precede failures.

ieng:24.03.q: What spans would a trace of one RAG chat request contain, and which attributes are specific to LLM serving?
ieng:24.03.s: Spans for gateway auth, retrieval, reranking, prompt assembly, routing, engine queue wait, prefill, decode, and streaming back, plus tool calls if any. LLM-specific attributes: model and version, prompt tokens, cached prompt tokens, output tokens, TTFT, TPOT, replica id, preemptions, and finish reason.

ieng:24.04.q: Why is rejecting some requests early better than accepting all of them during overload?
ieng:24.04.s: Accepted requests beyond capacity queue up, so every request's latency grows, many time out after consuming GPU time, and goodput collapses. Rejecting excess requests quickly (with a retryable status) keeps latency within SLO for the admitted ones and gives clients a clear signal to back off or retry elsewhere.

ieng:24.05.q: A client retries any request that takes over 10 seconds. What problem does this create for an LLM service?
ieng:24.05.s: Long generations legitimately exceed 10 seconds, so the client cancels and resends them, and if cancellation does not propagate, the server keeps generating the old one too. Load multiplies exactly when the server is slow, causing a retry storm. Fix with timeouts tied to expected E2E (or streaming idle timeouts), propagated cancellation, retry budgets, and backoff.

ieng:24.06.q: A replica crashes with CUDA OOM during a long prompt. Describe immediate and long-term responses.
ieng:24.06.s: Immediate: the orchestrator restarts the replica, the router stops sending to it while it is down, and in-flight requests fail with a retryable error so clients retry elsewhere. Long-term: find the triggering request (prompt length, batch composition), cap max prompt length or max batched tokens to bound activation memory, lower gpu memory utilization if needed, and add a test that reproduces the case.
ieng:24.06.t: OOM, Worker, GPU & Cache Failure Recovery

ieng:24.07.q: Name three chaos experiments worth running on an LLM fleet and the expected safe outcome for each.
ieng:24.07.s: Kill one replica under load: router stops sending within seconds, SLO dips briefly, in-flight requests retry successfully. Inject a slow replica (throttle its GPU or add latency): queue-aware routing shifts traffic away and p99 stays bounded. Send a burst of very long prompts: admission control and chunked prefill keep other users within SLO and no OOM occurs.

ieng:24.08.q: List four security concerns specific to multi-tenant LLM inference.
ieng:24.08.s: Cross-tenant data leakage through shared prefix caches (timing attacks revealing whether another tenant's prompt is cached, or bugs reusing KV across tenants); prompt and output data exposure in logs or traces; abuse and resource exhaustion (huge prompts, max tokens) as denial of service; and model weight theft or tampering. Also prompt injection affecting tool-using agents.

ieng:24.09.q: What should the final report of this project contain?
ieng:24.09.s: The service setup and SLO; a list of injected faults with hypotheses; for each, observed impact (SLO attainment, errors, recovery time) with charts; the weaknesses found and fixes applied; re-run results after fixes; and a runbook entry for each failure type.
ieng:24.09.t: Project: Break and Recover the Service

ieng:25.01.q: A GPU costs $2.50 per hour and sustains 3,000 output tokens/s at the SLO while running at 70% average utilization. What is the cost per million output tokens?
ieng:25.01.s: Effective throughput is 3,000 x 0.7 = 2,100 tokens/s, or 7.56 million tokens per hour. $2.50 / 7.56 is about $0.33 per million output tokens. Input tokens add cost too; a complete model would attribute GPU time to both prefill and decode.
ieng:25.01.t: Cost per Request & Cost per Million Tokens

ieng:25.02.q: Why compare configurations by goodput per dollar instead of throughput per dollar?
ieng:25.02.s: Throughput per dollar rewards overloading the GPU, which raises raw tokens/s but makes many requests miss the SLO. Those tokens have less or no value to the product. Goodput per dollar counts only tokens from requests that met the SLO, so it measures what you are actually buying.

ieng:25.03.q: Which GPU specs predict decode performance and which predict prefill performance, and why does the answer to "which GPU is cheapest" depend on the workload?
ieng:25.03.s: Decode is predicted by memory bandwidth and memory capacity (for KV and batch size); prefill by dense tensor throughput in your precision (BF16, FP8, FP4). A decode-heavy workload favors GPUs with the best bandwidth per dollar and enough memory; a prefill-heavy RAG workload favors the best FLOPs per dollar. So the cheapest GPU changes with prompt and output lengths.

ieng:25.04.q: You expect a peak of 120 requests/s. One replica's SLO-safe capacity for your workload is 9 req/s, and you plan to run at 70%. How many replicas do you need, and what else would you add?
ieng:25.04.s: Planned per-replica load is 9 x 0.7 = 6.3 req/s, so 120 / 6.3 is about 19.05, round up to 20 replicas. Add N+1 or N+2 for failures (one or two replicas down), so 21 to 22, and check that the workload mix assumed in the benchmark matches forecast traffic.

ieng:25.05.q: Your traffic has a daily peak 4 times the overnight minimum. What strategies reduce the cost of capacity sitting idle overnight?
ieng:25.05.s: Autoscale down overnight (keeping enough warm capacity for morning ramps); fill idle GPUs with deferrable batch jobs (offline inference, evals, embeddings) at lower priority; shift workloads across regions or time zones; and use cheaper commitment pricing for the baseline and on-demand for peaks.
ieng:25.05.t: Peak Load, Failure Headroom & Idle Capacity

ieng:25.06.q: Describe the steps to find the cheapest serving system for a given workload and SLO.
ieng:25.06.s: Fix the workload and SLO; shortlist models (sizes, quantizations) that pass quality; shortlist hardware by per-dollar ratios; benchmark each feasible combination for SLO-safe capacity; compute replicas needed for forecast peak with headroom and spares; compute monthly cost including idle and autoscaling assumptions; pick the cheapest, and document the runner-up and sensitivities.
ieng:25.06.t: Project: Build the Cheapest System That Meets the SLO

ieng:26.01.q: How does grammar-constrained decoding guarantee valid JSON, and what does it cost per step?
ieng:26.01.s: A grammar (from a JSON schema or regex) is compiled into a state machine. At each step, the engine computes which vocabulary tokens are allowed from the current state and masks the rest to minus infinity before sampling, so only valid continuations can be chosen. The cost is computing that mask each step (precomputation and caching keep it small) and occasionally constraining the model away from its preferred tokens, which can affect quality.

ieng:26.02.q: How can one engine batch requests for 50 different LoRA adapters in the same step?
ieng:26.02.s: The base model weights are shared; each request carries an adapter id. For each linear layer, the base matmul runs on the whole batch, then a batched low-rank kernel (like SGMV or BGMV) applies each request's own A and B matrices to its tokens and adds the result. Adapters live in GPU memory (or are swapped in from CPU) in a pool, so many can be active at once.

ieng:26.03.q: Why do images often dominate TTFT in vision-language models, and what can you cache?
ieng:26.03.s: Each image is encoded by a vision encoder into hundreds or thousands of tokens, and both encoding and the prefill over those image tokens take time, often more than the text prompt. You can cache the encoder output per image (by hash) and, through the prefix cache keyed with image hashes, the KV for image tokens, so repeated images skip both steps.

ieng:26.04.q: How do agent workloads differ from chat for an inference service?
ieng:26.04.s: Agents make many sequential calls per task, each with a long, growing prompt (instructions, tool definitions, history, tool outputs) and often short outputs, and the next call waits for the previous one plus tool execution. So prefix reuse is very high, TTFT and E2E per call matter more than streaming speed, and total task latency is the sum of many calls. Bursty fan-out (parallel tool calls) is also common.

ieng:26.05.q: A reasoning model generates 5,000 thinking tokens before a 200-token answer. What does this do to capacity and what levers exist?
ieng:26.05.s: Output tokens grow 25 times, so decode time, KV memory per request (the thinking stays in context) and cost all rise sharply; concurrency per GPU falls and E2E latency becomes tens of seconds. Levers: decode speed optimizations (speculative decoding, quantization), thinking budgets or effort settings, larger KV capacity (FP8 KV, offload), and streaming the thinking or a summary so users see progress.

ieng:26.06.q: How should you configure an engine differently for offline batch inference compared with interactive serving?
ieng:26.06.s: Drop latency SLOs and maximize throughput: very large batches (high max_num_seqs and max_num_batched_tokens), no chunked prefill concerns, sort or group inputs by length to reduce waste, maximize prefix sharing by grouping requests with common prefixes, use the offline engine API instead of HTTP, and run at full GPU memory utilization. Checkpoint progress for restartability.

ieng:26.07.q: What makes rollout generation in RL training different from production serving?
ieng:26.07.s: Rollouts generate many samples per prompt (for example 8 to 64) with high temperature and often long outputs; weights change every training step, so the inference engine must reload or sync weights quickly; the generation phase blocks training, so the slowest rollout (long tail of lengths) stalls the whole step; and throughput per training step matters, not per-user latency.

ieng:26.08.q: Why does diffusion inference behave so differently from LLM decode in terms of batching and bottlenecks?
ieng:26.08.s: A diffusion model runs a fixed number of denoising steps over the whole image or latent at once, each step a full forward pass of a large network on many spatial tokens. Work per step is large and compute bound, with no growing KV cache. Latency is roughly steps times step time, and batching helps less because each step is already compute heavy.

ieng:26.09.q: How would you choose the number of denoising steps for a production image service?
ieng:26.09.s: Generate images for a fixed prompt set at several step counts (for example 4, 8, 20, 30, 50) with your sampler and model, measure quality with automatic metrics (FID or CLIP-based scores) and human or model preference ratings, and measure latency and cost. Choose the smallest step count whose quality is within your acceptance threshold of the best, possibly offering different budgets per tier.

ieng:26.10.q: How do you scope an elective project on a specialized workload so it produces a clear result?
ieng:26.10.s: Pick one workload (for example multi-LoRA, structured output, VLM, agents, reasoning, batch, RL rollouts or diffusion), define its realistic traffic and metric of success, build a baseline on a standard engine, apply two or three targeted optimizations from the lesson, and report the measured gain against the baseline with quality checks.
ieng:26.10.t: Elective Project: Choose One Specialized Workload

ieng:27.01.q: Which top-level areas of the vLLM repository would you read first to understand request handling, and why?
ieng:27.01.s: The entrypoints (OpenAI-compatible API server) to see how requests arrive; the engine and engine core (the main loop and process structure); the core scheduler and KV cache manager (which requests run and where their KV goes); the worker and model runner (input preparation, forward pass, CUDA graphs); and the attention backends and model definitions. That order follows a request.

ieng:27.02.q: What artifacts should you produce from tracing one request through the engine?
ieng:27.02.s: A sequence diagram of the request across processes and components, with function names; the data structures it is converted into at each stage (request object, scheduled batch, model input tensors, outputs); timestamps of each stage from logs or a profile; and notes on where queueing, allocation, execution and detokenization happen.

ieng:27.03.q: What state does the scheduler keep per request, and how does it decide how many tokens a request gets this step?
ieng:27.03.s: Per request: status (waiting, running, preempted, finished), number of tokens computed so far, number of prompt and output tokens, assigned KV blocks, and sampling parameters. Each step it gives running requests their decode token (or next prefill chunk), then fills remaining token budget with waiting requests' prompt tokens, limited by free KV blocks and max sequences; it preempts if decode cannot get blocks.

ieng:27.04.q: Where in the code would you confirm how prefix cache hits are found and how evicted blocks are chosen?
ieng:27.04.s: In the KV cache manager and block pool: the function that computes block hashes for a request's tokens, the lookup that walks those hashes against the cached-block map to find the longest hit, and the free-block queue that orders cached blocks with zero references for eviction (least recently used first). Tests for the block pool show these behaviors directly.

ieng:27.05.q: How does the model runner turn a scheduled batch into one forward pass, and where does the attention backend get per-request information?
ieng:27.05.s: It flattens all scheduled tokens across requests into one input-id tensor with matching positions, builds metadata (query start offsets per request, sequence lengths, block tables, slot mappings for where new KV goes), pads to a captured CUDA graph size if applicable, and calls the model. Each attention layer reads that metadata, built once per step by the backend's metadata builder, to run paged attention over each request's blocks.

ieng:27.06.q: Give an example of a well-scoped modification for this project and how you would evaluate it.
ieng:27.06.s: Example: change the scheduler to prioritize requests with the most prefix cache hits (longest-prefix-first) within a fairness bound. Evaluate on a shared-prefix workload and a random workload, measuring hit rate, TTFT p50 and p95, and fairness (max wait time), comparing against the unmodified engine with identical settings, plus a profile to confirm no added scheduler overhead.
ieng:27.06.t: Project: Modify and Profile One Engine Component

ieng:28.01.q: What interface should your mini engine's model runner expose so that later lessons can add batching and paging without rewriting it?
ieng:28.01.s: A function that takes a flat batch of token ids with positions and per-sequence metadata (which tokens belong to which sequence, where their KV lives) and returns logits for the last token of each sequence. Keep the model code free of request logic so the scheduler and KV manager can change independently.
ieng:28.01.t: Build the Model Runner & Generation Loop

ieng:28.02.q: What tests prove your KV cache is correct?
ieng:28.02.s: Greedy generation with and without the cache produces identical tokens for several prompts and lengths; logits at each decode step match a full recompute within tolerance; positions continue correctly after the prompt (RoPE); and step time stays nearly flat as the sequence grows.

ieng:28.03.q: How do you batch sequences of different lengths in decode without padding attention for the short ones?
ieng:28.03.s: Flatten one new token per sequence into a batch for all linear layers, and run attention per sequence (a loop or a variable-length kernel) using each sequence's own cache length. Only attention needs to know lengths; the matmuls just see a [num_seqs, hidden] matrix.

ieng:28.04.q: What changes in your engine loop when you move from static to continuous batching?
ieng:28.04.s: The loop no longer processes a fixed batch to completion. Each step it removes finished sequences, admits waiting requests if there is KV space and token budget, schedules their prefill (whole or chunked) alongside current decodes, runs one forward pass over the mixed batch, and emits tokens. Requests carry state (computed tokens, status) so they can join and leave at any step.

ieng:28.05.q: What changes in the attention path when you switch from contiguous to paged KV?
ieng:28.05.s: New K and V are written to slots given by a slot mapping (physical block id x block size + offset) rather than a contiguous position, and attention gathers K and V through each sequence's block table. You need either a gather step before standard attention (simple, slower) or a paged attention kernel (FlashInfer, FlashAttention with block tables, or your own Triton kernel).

ieng:28.06.q: How should the engine loop and the HTTP server communicate so streaming does not slow the GPU loop?
ieng:28.06.s: Run the engine loop in its own thread or process and the HTTP server in an async event loop. The server puts new requests on a queue to the engine and receives generated tokens via per-request output queues (or a shared output channel); detokenization and SSE writes happen on the server side, so the engine loop never waits on network I/O.

ieng:28.07.q: Which metrics should your mini engine export so you can compare it with vLLM?
ieng:28.07.s: Running and waiting requests, KV blocks used and free, prefix cache hit tokens and queries, preemptions, prompt and generation token counters, and histograms for TTFT, TPOT and E2E, all in Prometheus format at /metrics.

ieng:28.08.q: Your mini engine reaches 40% of vLLM's throughput. How do you find out where the gap comes from?
ieng:28.08.s: Profile both on the same workload and compare step time breakdowns: kernel time for attention and GEMMs, small-op count (fusion), GPU idle gaps (CPU overhead, no CUDA graphs), scheduling overhead per step, and batch sizes achieved (KV capacity). Then close the biggest gap first, for example by adding CUDA graphs or a better attention kernel, and re-measure.
ieng:28.08.t: Project: Benchmark Your Engine Against vLLM

ieng:29.01.q: What three questions should you answer after a first pass over an inference systems paper?
ieng:29.01.s: What problem and bottleneck does it target (and under what workload)? What is the core mechanism, in one or two sentences? What baseline and setup produced the headline number (hardware, model, batch size, metric), and does that setting match yours?
ieng:29.01.t: How to Read an Inference Systems Paper

ieng:29.02.q: Why is reconstructing the paper's baseline the most important step of a reproduction?
ieng:29.02.s: The headline result is a ratio against a baseline. If your baseline differs (version, flags, hardware), the ratio is meaningless: you might show a large gain against a weak baseline or none against a strong one. Matching the paper's baseline numbers first proves your setup is comparable before you test the technique.
ieng:29.02.t: Choose a Paper & Reconstruct the Baseline

ieng:29.03.q: A paper evaluates on "ShareGPT at 4 requests per second." What details must you pin down to recreate this workload?
ieng:29.03.s: Which ShareGPT version and filtering, how conversations were turned into prompts (first turn only or full history), tokenizer used to compute lengths, any length truncation or filtering, output length handling (use dataset output lengths with ignore_eos or let the model decide), number of requests, arrival distribution (Poisson with which seed), and warm-up.

ieng:29.04.q: Your reproduced speedup is 1.6 times where the paper claims 2.3 times. How do you decide if this counts as a successful reproduction?
ieng:29.04.s: Check whether the direction and rough magnitude hold and whether the gap can be explained: different hardware, a stronger baseline, workload differences, or missing tuning. If you can trace the gap to a documented difference and the mechanism still shows a clear, repeatable gain, it is a partial reproduction worth reporting. If the gain disappears entirely under matched conditions, report that too.

ieng:29.05.q: Why profile a technique after reproducing its speedup?
ieng:29.05.s: To confirm the speedup comes from the mechanism the paper claims (for example fewer bytes moved or less idle time) rather than an unrelated side effect, to find where the remaining time goes, and to understand which hardware or workload properties the gain depends on, which predicts where it will fail.

ieng:29.06.q: What is an ablation, and design one for a technique that combines three ideas.
ieng:29.06.s: An ablation removes or varies one component at a time to measure its individual contribution. For a technique combining A, B and C: run baseline, each of A, B and C alone, each pair, and all three, on the same workload, so you can see which components matter, whether they interact, and whether one gives most of the gain.

ieng:29.07.q: Give three axes along which you would search for where an inference technique stops helping, with an example.
ieng:29.07.s: Load (concurrency or request rate): speculative decoding helps at low load and stops helping at high load. Workload shape (prompt and output lengths, prefix sharing): prefix caching does nothing without shared prefixes. Hardware and scale (GPU type, interconnect, model size): disaggregation stops paying on slow networks or at small scale.
ieng:29.07.t: Find Where the Technique Stops Working

ieng:29.08.q: What should a published reproduction report contain to be useful to others?
ieng:29.08.s: The paper and claim reproduced; full setup (hardware, versions, flags, workload file); baseline match; main result with spread; profile showing the mechanism; ablations; the map of where it helps and stops helping; a comparison against a current engine's default (does the gap still exist?); and code and data to rerun it.
ieng:29.08.t: Project: Compare Against Modern Engines & Publish

ieng:30.01.q: Write a one-paragraph workload and SLO definition for a hypothetical support-chat product.
ieng:30.01.s: Support chat for a SaaS product: requests have a 2,500-token shared system prompt plus 500 to 3,000 tokens of conversation history and retrieved docs, outputs average 250 tokens (p95 600). Peak 80 requests per second, average 30, with 2x bursts. SLO: p95 TTFT under 800 ms, p95 TPOT under 40 ms, 99% attainment. Quality: at least 95% of the BF16 reference model's score on our 400-question support eval, and 100% valid JSON for tool calls.
ieng:30.01.t: Define the Workload, Quality Target & SLO

ieng:30.02.q: What evidence should support your model, hardware and engine choices?
ieng:30.02.s: Model: eval scores against the quality bar for each candidate size and precision. Hardware: memory fit and per-dollar ratios matched to whether the workload is prefill or decode heavy, plus a quick benchmark. Engine: a fair comparison on your workload (goodput under SLO) and required features, recorded in a selection matrix.

ieng:30.03.q: What makes the capstone baseline good enough to measure all later optimizations against?
ieng:30.03.s: It is fully pinned and scripted (one command reproduces it), uses the capstone workload file, measures the SLO metrics and goodput across a rate sweep, records engine and GPU metrics, and its run-to-run variance is known, so later gains can be judged against noise.

ieng:30.04.q: How do you decide which optimization phase to do first after profiling?
ieng:30.04.s: Identify the binding constraint at the expected load (SLO metric that fails first, KV pressure, or throughput ceiling), break down step time and engine state to find its cause, and estimate each candidate fix's gain on SLO-safe capacity. Start with the fix with the largest expected gain per unit of effort and risk.

ieng:30.05.q: Which three optimizations from this phase are most likely to help a support-chat workload with a shared system prompt?
ieng:30.05.s: Prefix caching (with sticky or prefix-aware routing) to skip the shared system prompt and conversation history; chunked prefill with a tuned token budget to keep TPOT stable when long histories arrive; and FP8 KV or memory tuning to raise concurrency without preemptions.

ieng:30.06.q: How do you make sure a precision change in the capstone does not break the quality bar?
ieng:30.06.s: Run the capstone quality eval (and format checks for tool calls) on the quantized configuration with production sampling settings and the same engine, compare against the BF16 reference with confidence intervals, and accept only if it stays above the bar set in 30.01. Also spot-check long-context and edge cases relevant to the product.

ieng:30.07.q: Under what results from earlier phases would you move the capstone to multi-GPU replicas or disaggregation?
ieng:30.07.s: Move to tensor parallelism if single-GPU TPOT cannot meet the SLO or KV capacity is insufficient after other optimizations. Consider disaggregation if long prompts cause decode interference that chunked prefill cannot fix at the required load and the network between GPUs is fast. Otherwise stay with single-GPU replicas, which are simplest and usually most efficient.

ieng:30.08.q: What routing, autoscaling and observability setup fits the capstone's support-chat workload?
ieng:30.08.s: Session-affinity or prefix-aware routing with load bounds, so conversation histories hit the cache; autoscaling on waiting requests and KV usage relative to measured capacity, with headroom for cold-start time and a small warm pool for bursts; and dashboards for traffic, TTFT/TPOT vs SLO, saturation and errors, with burn-rate alerts and request tracing including cached-token counts.

ieng:30.09.q: What final capacity and cost numbers should the capstone report?
ieng:30.09.s: Per-replica SLO-safe capacity for the workload; replicas needed at peak with headroom and failure spares; monthly GPU cost under the autoscaling policy and the resulting cost per million tokens and per conversation; and results of failure tests (recovery time, SLO impact) that justify the spare capacity.

ieng:30.10.q: What questions should you be ready to answer when defending your capstone system?
ieng:30.10.s: Why this model, precision, GPU and engine (with evidence); what the binding constraint was and how each optimization moved it; why you did or did not use multi-GPU or disaggregation; how the system behaves under bursts and failures; what it costs per request and how that scales; what quality risks remain; and what you would do next with more time or budget.
ieng:30.10.t: Publish and Defend the Complete System

ieng:31.01.q: A colleague's 2-D kernel uses `int row = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x; int col = blockIdx.y * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y;` with `dim3 block(32, 8)` on a row-major 4096 x 4096 float matrix. Results are correct but the kernel is about 5x slower than expected. Explain why, and what else could go wrong for other matrix shapes.
ieng:31.01.s: With `x` mapped to rows, the 32 threads of a warp (consecutive `threadIdx.x`) handle 32 different rows of the same column. In row-major storage those elements are 4096 floats apart, so each warp load touches 32 separate memory segments instead of one contiguous 128-byte span, wasting most of every memory transaction. Swapping the mapping so that `threadIdx.x` indexes columns makes each warp read contiguous memory. For other shapes, the grid must also be sized per axis with ceiling division and the bounds check must test both `row < rows` and `col < cols`; with non-square matrices, mixing up which grid dimension covers rows and which covers columns either leaves part of the matrix unprocessed or launches threads outside it. Very tall matrices can also exceed the 65535-block limit on `grid.y` if rows are mapped to y.

ieng:31.02.q: A row-wise L2-normalisation kernel for a 65536 x 1024 float matrix assigns one thread per row; each thread loops over its 1024 columns to compute the norm, then again to scale. It achieves about 150 GB/s on a GPU with 2 TB/s peak. Diagnose it and describe a better mapping.
ieng:31.02.s: With one thread per row, the 32 threads of a warp read the same column index of 32 different rows in each loop iteration. Rows are 4 KB apart, so every warp load touches 32 sectors and uses only 4 bytes of each 32-byte sector: 12.5% efficiency at best, and caches cannot absorb a working set this large. Map a warp (or a block) to each row instead: threads stride across the row's columns with step 32, so each warp load reads 128 consecutive bytes. Each thread accumulates a partial sum of squares, the warp combines partials with shuffle reductions, and then the same threads scale their elements, ideally from registers so the row is read once. Using `float4` loads further cuts instruction count. This mapping should approach 80 to 90% of peak bandwidth, around ten times faster.

ieng:31.03.q: You tile a matrix transpose with 32 x 32 blocks: each thread reads `in[y][x]` into `tile[ty][tx]`, synchronises, then writes `out[x'][y'] = tile[tx][ty]` with the output indices swapped so the global write is coalesced. It is faster than the naive transpose but still well below copy bandwidth. Why, and what one-line change fixes it?
ieng:31.03.s: The global reads and writes are now coalesced, but the shared-memory read `tile[tx][ty]` is a column access: the 32 threads of a warp have consecutive `tx`, so they read 32 words that are each a full row (32 floats) apart. All 32 words map to the same bank, so the warp's access is replayed 32 times, serialising every shared-memory read. Declaring the tile as `__shared__ float tile[32][33]` pads each row by one word, shifting successive rows by one bank, so a column read touches 32 different banks and completes in a single pass. With the padding, the transpose typically runs close to the speed of a simple device-to-device copy.

ieng:31.04.q: Your loss-averaging kernel sums 50 million FP32 values with one `atomicAdd` per thread into a single global float. It is slow and a unit test comparing the result bitwise to a reference fails intermittently. Explain both problems and the design you would use instead.
ieng:31.04.s: Speed: every one of 50 million threads performs an atomic on the same address, and atomics to one address are serialised at the L2, so throughput collapses to that of a single memory location instead of the full bandwidth. Bitwise failures: floating-point addition is not associative, and the order in which atomics land varies between runs, so the rounding differs in the last bits. Replace it with a hierarchical reduction: each thread accumulates many elements in a register via a grid-stride loop, each block reduces its threads with warp shuffles and a small shared-memory step, and each block writes one partial to an array. A second, single-block pass reduces the partials in a fixed order. That reads the data once at near-peak bandwidth and is deterministic. If one launch matters more than determinism, one atomic per block (a few thousand) is fast but still non-deterministic.

ieng:31.05.q: You need per-expert token counts for an MoE layer with 8 experts and 1 million tokens per step, computed on the GPU. A first version does one global `atomicAdd` per token on an array of 8 integers and is surprisingly slow. Explain why, and design a faster kernel. Is the result deterministic?
ieng:31.05.s: With only 8 counters, a million atomics are concentrated on 8 addresses, so the L2 serialises them: throughput is limited to about 8 concurrent updates, regardless of how many threads run. Use privatisation: each block keeps 8 counters in shared memory (or per warp, to cut shared contention further), threads accumulate with shared-memory atomics or, better, each thread first counts its own grid-stride elements in 8 registers and adds them once. After a barrier, each block issues at most 8 global atomics. With 1024 blocks that is 8192 global atomics instead of a million. Warp-level `__match_any_sync` or ballot-based aggregation can reduce shared atomics further when many lanes pick the same expert. The result is deterministic, because integer addition is associative and the final counts do not depend on the order of the atomics; only floating-point accumulations would vary.

ieng:31.06.q: A softmax kernel for attention scores of shape (batch x heads x 2048 queries) x 2048 keys in FP16 uses one thread per row and three passes over each row. Profiling shows 15% of peak bandwidth. Redesign it and estimate the best achievable time if the score tensor has 2^28 elements on a 2 TB/s GPU.
ieng:31.06.s: One thread per row makes a warp read 32 different rows at the same column: uncoalesced, with 32 sectors per request. Three passes also triple the reads. Assign one warp per row instead: each lane takes elements lane, lane+32, ... (or uses 16-byte vector loads of 8 FP16 values for coalescing), keeps its 64 values in registers, computes the max and the sum of exponentials with warp-shuffle reductions (or a single online-softmax reduction carrying (max, sum) pairs), then writes the normalised values from registers. The row is read once and written once. Traffic is 2^28 elements x 2 bytes x 2 (read + write) = 1 GiB, so the floor is about 1.07 GB / 2 TB/s = 0.54 ms; a good kernel reaches roughly 85 to 90% of peak, around 0.6 ms. Better still is to avoid materialising the scores at all by fusing softmax into attention, as FlashAttention does.

ieng:31.07.q: A custom attention-score kernel uses 128 registers per thread with 256-thread blocks and no shared memory. Nsight Compute reports 25% occupancy, 35% of peak memory bandwidth and 20% of peak compute, with warps mostly stalled waiting on global loads. Explain the occupancy figure and give two different ways to improve performance.
ieng:31.07.s: At 128 registers per thread, a 256-thread block needs 32,768 registers, so only 2 blocks (16 warps) fit within an SM's 65,536 registers: 16 of 64 warps is 25% occupancy. With neither memory nor compute near its roof and warps stalled on loads, the kernel is latency-bound: there are too few loads in flight to cover HBM latency. One fix is to increase thread-level parallelism: cap registers with `__launch_bounds__(256, 4)` or restructure to use fewer, aiming for 4 blocks per SM, and check that this does not cause spills. The other is to increase instruction-level parallelism and reuse without raising occupancy: issue several independent loads per thread before using them (unrolling, vectorised 16-byte loads), stage tiles in shared memory with double buffering so loads for the next tile overlap computation on the current one, and reuse loaded data across several outputs per thread. Either way, re-measure against the roofline after each change.

sdsd:01.01.q: For "design a URL shortener", list 3 functional requirements and 3 questions you'd ask the interviewer.
sdsd:01.01.s: Functional: shorten a URL, redirect a short URL to the original, optionally set a custom alias or expiry. Questions: How many new links per day and how many redirects? Do links expire? Can two users shortening the same URL get the same short link? Do we need click analytics? How short must the code be? Must redirects work during a regional outage?

sdsd:01.02.q: Draw boxes and arrows for a URL shortener (client, API, service, DB) without naming any vendor.
sdsd:01.02.s: Client sends requests to an API service behind a load balancer. On create, the service takes a unique ID from an ID generator, base-62 encodes it, and writes (code → URL) to a database. On redirect, it reads the code from a cache, falls back to the database on a miss, and returns an HTTP redirect. Arrows: client to API (HTTP, sync), API to cache and database (sync reads and writes), API to ID generator (sync).

sdsd:01.03.q: Turn "it should be fast" into a measurable requirement.
sdsd:01.03.s: Example: "p99 latency for loading the home feed is under 200 ms, measured at the server, at 50k requests per second." It names the operation, the percentile, the threshold and the load, so a design can be checked against it and monitored in production.

sdsd:01.04.q: Name one case where you'd accept stale data and one where you wouldn't.
sdsd:01.04.s: Accept stale data for a post's like count or a "people you may know" list: being a few seconds behind harms nobody and lets you serve it cheaply from a cache or replica. Don't accept it when checking a bank balance before a withdrawal or seat availability at the moment of booking, because acting on an old value causes overdrafts or double bookings; there you read from the primary or check inside a transaction.

sdsd:01.05.q: How many minutes of downtime per month does 99.9% allow? 99.99%?
sdsd:01.05.s: 99.9% allows about 43 minutes of downtime a month (0.1% of 43,200 minutes is 43.2 minutes in a 30-day month; about 43.8 in an average month). 99.99% allows about 4.4 minutes a month, ten times less, which is short enough that failover and rollback must be automatic.

sdsd:01.06.q: 100M daily users, 10 writes each, 1 KB per write. Estimate write QPS and storage per year.
sdsd:01.06.s: Writes per day = 100M users × 10 = 10⁹. Average write QPS = 10⁹ / ~10⁵ s ≈ 10,000 to 12,000 per second, so plan for about 20,000 to 30,000 at a 2 to 3x peak. Storage = 10⁹ × 1 KB = 1 TB per day, about 365 TB per year of raw data, or roughly 1 PB a year with 3 replicas. That rate is beyond one relational primary, so writes need partitioning or a write-optimised store.

sdsd:01.07.q: Why can one NGINX worker handle thousands of connections when a thread-per-request server struggles?
sdsd:01.07.s: Each NGINX worker uses non-blocking sockets and an event loop over epoll, so an idle connection costs only a file descriptor, kernel buffers and a small state machine, and the worker spends CPU only on sockets the kernel reports as ready. With one worker per core there are few context switches. A thread-per-request server spends a full thread (stack memory, scheduling, context switches) on every connection even while it just waits, so it runs out of memory or thread-pool slots at thousands of connections while the CPU sits mostly idle.
sdsd:01.07.t: How a server handles many requests

sdsd:01.08.q: Why is horizontal scaling easy for stateless web servers and hard for a database?
sdsd:01.08.s: Stateless web servers keep no data of their own (sessions and files live in shared stores), so any server can handle any request, and scaling out is just adding servers behind a load balancer. A database holds state that must stay correct and consistent across copies, so adding machines means replication, which brings lag, failover risk and no extra write capacity, or sharding, which means splitting data by key, cross-shard queries and transactions, rebalancing and hot shards.

sdsd:01.09.q: List 2 costs microservices add that a monolith doesn't have.
sdsd:01.09.s: Any two of: every cross-service call adds network latency and can fail or time out, so you need timeouts, retries and circuit breakers; there are no ACID transactions across services, so you need sagas, compensating actions and eventual consistency; the operational overhead of deploying, monitoring, logging and tracing many services; and harder refactoring, since moving logic between services needs versioned APIs and data migrations.

sdsd:01.10.q: What does a repository let you swap out in tests?
sdsd:01.10.s: You can swap the real database-backed repository for an in-memory fake (for example one wrapping a set or a dictionary) that implements the same small interface. Business logic tests then run in microseconds without a database, network, fixtures or cleanup, and a few separate integration tests check the real SQL adapter.

sdsd:01.11.q: When would you use a jsonb column instead of adding a new column?
sdsd:01.11.s: Use a jsonb column for optional, sparse or per-tenant attributes that vary from row to row and are mostly read together with the record, such as product specifications that differ by category or user-defined custom fields, especially when new attributes appear often and you don't want a migration for each. Add a real column instead for fields you filter, sort or join on heavily, need constraints or foreign keys on, or update often on their own, since the database can type, enforce and index those far better.

sdsd:01.12.q: Name 2 design choices that change cost by 10x or more.
sdsd:01.12.s: Examples of 10x choices: storing cold data in an archive or infrequent-access tier instead of SSD-backed databases or hot object storage (10 to 100 times cheaper per GB); keeping traffic in one zone and serving media through a CDN instead of paying cross-region or internet egress from origin; replacing per-request orchestration or per-item storage calls (like a billable workflow step per second of video) with in-process work; sampling logs and traces instead of keeping all of them; and running steady workloads on committed, spot or owned hardware instead of on-demand.

sdsd:01.13.q: Before adding a cache or queue, what 2 numbers should you know first?
sdsd:01.13.s: Know the current load and its growth (for example peak requests or writes per second, data size, and monthly growth rate), and where the bottleneck actually is, measured (for example database CPU at peak, or the p99 time of the slow query). Without both you can't show the new component solves a real problem, or that a simpler fix such as an index or a bigger instance wouldn't.

sdsd:02.01.q: Design the endpoints for creating, reading and listing short URLs. How do you paginate the list?
sdsd:02.01.s: POST /v1/urls {long_url, custom_alias?, expires_at?} creates a link and returns 201 with the code (409 if the alias is taken). GET /{code} redirects with 302 to the long URL, or 404. GET /v1/urls?page_size=20&page_token=... lists the caller's own links (owner taken from the auth token), newest first, and returns next_page_token. Use cursor pagination keyed on (created_at, code), encoded as an opaque token, because each page is an index seek that stays fast at any depth and does not skip or repeat rows when links are created or deleted while paging.

sdsd:02.02.q: When should service A call B synchronously, and when should it publish an event instead?
sdsd:02.02.s: Call B synchronously when A cannot continue without B's answer, such as authorising a payment before confirming an order or reading a price to show the user, and protect the call with a timeout, a circuit breaker and a fallback. Publish an event when A is announcing something that others react to, such as OrderPlaced triggering email, analytics and the warehouse, because then B's outages and slowness don't affect A, the broker buffers work while B catches up, and new consumers can subscribe without changing A.

sdsd:02.03.q: Why do many companies use REST at the edge and gRPC between internal services?
sdsd:02.03.s: Public clients like browsers, mobile apps and third-party developers need something universal, cacheable by standard HTTP caches and CDNs, and easy to debug with everyday tools, which is REST over HTTP with JSON. Between internal services the company controls both ends, so it can use gRPC's compact protobuf encoding, generated typed clients, HTTP/2 multiplexing, deadlines and streaming to cut latency, CPU and bandwidth at very high call volumes and to catch contract mistakes at compile time.

sdsd:02.04.q: Why do video calls and games use UDP while file downloads use TCP?
sdsd:02.04.s: In a call or game, data is only useful if it is fresh. TCP would hold back every later packet until a lost one is retransmitted, causing freezes and forcing extra buffering delay, whereas UDP delivers whatever arrives and the app conceals small gaps or simply uses the next update. A file download needs every byte in the right order and doesn't care about a few milliseconds of delay, so TCP's handshake, retransmission, ordering and congestion control are exactly right.

sdsd:02.05.q: List 3 things an API gateway does that a plain L4 load balancer doesn't.
sdsd:02.05.s: A plain Layer 4 load balancer sees only IP addresses and ports, so it cannot: (1) authenticate users by verifying tokens or API keys, (2) route requests by URL path or header to different services, or (3) apply per-user or per-key rate limits and quotas. Gateways also validate requests, translate REST and JSON into gRPC, combine responses from several services into one, and add consistent logging, metrics and tracing.

sdsd:02.06.q: When does least-connections beat round robin?
sdsd:02.06.s: Least connections beats round robin when requests vary widely in cost or duration, or when connections are long-lived, like WebSockets or streaming. Round robin keeps handing new work to a server that is stuck on slow requests, so requests queue behind them while other servers sit idle and p99 latency soars; least connections sees that server's high in-flight count and routes around it, which keeps queues short, balances live connections, and keeps tail latency low.

sdsd:02.07.q: Why route requests for the same key to the same backend? What breaks if one backend gets too hot?
