sdsd:02.07.s: Routing the same key to the same backend keeps that server's cache warm for it (a high hit rate without every server caching everything), keeps per-key state such as a session or chat room in one place, and matches requests to the shard that owns the data. If one backend gets too hot, for example because a viral key lives on it, its queue grows and latency and errors rise for every key it owns, even cold ones, and it may fall over and push its load onto a neighbour. Fixes are replicating or salting the hot key, a local cache in front, or consistent hashing with bounded loads so overflow spills to the next server on the ring.

sdsd:02.08.q: You add a field to an event. What must be true so old consumers keep working?
sdsd:02.08.s: The new field must be optional (with a default, typically null), and old consumers must ignore fields they don't recognise instead of rejecting the event. Then events in the new format still parse for them (forward compatibility), while new consumers can still read old events in the log that lack the field (backward compatibility). No existing field may change its name, type or meaning, and a schema registry enforcing the compatibility mode should check the new schema before it ships.

sdsd:02.09.q: A payment request times out. Why can't the client just retry, and how do idempotency keys fix it?
sdsd:02.09.s: A timeout cannot tell the client whether the request never reached the server or whether the charge completed and only the reply was lost, so a blind retry may charge the customer twice. With an idempotency key, the client generates a unique key for the payment and sends the same key on every attempt. The server stores the key, the request parameters and the result atomically with the charge, and when the key arrives again it returns the stored result instead of charging again (or an error if the parameters differ), so retries become safe.

sdsd:02.10.q: Batching raises throughput. What does it cost you, and which knob controls that?
sdsd:02.10.s: Batching costs latency: items that arrive early wait for the batch to fill or for the timer to fire, so per-item latency rises and becomes more uneven. It also adds memory use, a larger blast radius when a batch fails (or harder per-item error handling), and possible loss of an unsent batch on a crash. The knob is the maximum wait time (such as Kafka's linger.ms or DataLoader's batch schedule), usually paired with a maximum batch size so a full batch is sent immediately.

sdsd:02.11.q: A producer is 2x faster than its consumer. Name 3 ways to handle it.
sdsd:02.11.s: (1) Control the producer: signal it to slow down (flow control, a blocking bounded queue, 429 responses) or let the consumer pull at its own pace, which loses nothing. (2) Buffer in a bounded queue to absorb bursts, alarming on the age of the oldest item, accepting that a sustained 2x imbalance will still fill it. (3) Drop or sample excess items when only recent data matters, such as position updates or metrics. You can also scale out the consumer to match the producer's rate, if the bottleneck isn't a shared resource.

sdsd:02.12.q: If a request fans out to 100 servers and each has a 1% chance of being slow, what fraction of requests are slow?
sdsd:02.12.s: The request is slow if any one of the 100 servers is slow. The chance that all 100 are fast is 0.99^100 ≈ 0.366, so about 63% of requests are slow, even though each server is slow only 1% of the time. This is why tail latency on individual servers matters so much for fan-out systems, and why techniques like hedged requests (where a leaf call is slow only if both copies are slow) are used to cut it.

sdsd:02.13.q: Why is rejecting requests fast better than letting them all queue?
sdsd:02.13.s: If everything queues, every request waits longer until latency passes the client's timeout. The server then spends its capacity on requests whose clients have already given up and are retrying, so goodput drops towards zero while load keeps rising, and the system can stay stuck even after the spike passes. Rejecting excess requests fast is cheap, keeps the accepted ones within their deadlines so goodput stays at capacity, and tells clients to back off.

sdsd:03.01.q: Model users, posts and likes. Which columns get foreign keys and unique constraints?
sdsd:03.01.s: `posts.user_id` is a NOT NULL foreign key to `users.id`. `likes` has foreign keys to both `users.id` and `posts.id`, and a composite primary key (or unique constraint) on `(user_id, post_id)` so a user can like a post only once, even when two requests race. `users.email` gets a unique constraint so two accounts cannot share an email. Use surrogate BIGINT ids as primary keys. Add an index on `likes.post_id` (Postgres does not create one for a foreign key) for counting likes and fast post deletion, and an index on `posts(user_id, created_at)` for profile pages. Choose ON DELETE behaviour deliberately, for example CASCADE for likes or RESTRICT plus batched cleanup for very large relationships.

sdsd:03.02.q: Why would a company build a KV store on top of SQL instead of adopting a NoSQL product?
sdsd:03.02.s: Because the storage engine is proven and the team already knows how to run it: crash recovery, replication, backups, failover and 3 a.m. debugging are solved problems. Storing values as blobs means new fields need no migrations, and building the layer yourself lets you choose the trade-offs, such as eventually consistent secondary indexes, buffered writes during failover, and append-only cells that double as a change log for triggers. A new NoSQL product brings unfamiliar failure modes, and at the time few products met requirements like accepting writes during failover or built-in change notification. The cost is that you own sharding, routing and index repair, and lose joins and cross-shard transactions.

sdsd:03.03.q: Why does an index on (a, b) help WHERE a = ? but not WHERE b = ?
sdsd:03.03.s: An index on (a, b) is sorted by a first and by b only within each value of a, like a phone book sorted by surname then first name. For WHERE a = ? the database descends the tree to the one contiguous block of entries with that a and reads only those. Rows with a given b are scattered: there is one small run of them inside every distinct value of a, so there is no single place in the sort order to seek to. The database would have to read the whole index (or the whole table), so the planner usually does a full scan instead. Some engines can skip-scan across values of a, but that only helps when a has very few distinct values.

sdsd:03.04.q: Why is a B-tree lookup O(log n) with a very small n of disk reads in practice?
sdsd:03.04.s: Each B-tree node is a whole disk page holding hundreds of keys, so it has hundreds of children and the base of the logarithm is in the hundreds, not 2. A billion keys need only about 4 levels (300^4 is 8.1 billion). The root and upper branch levels are read by every lookup, so they stay permanently in the buffer pool (the top two levels are only a few MB). A lookup therefore costs one or two real disk reads (the leaf and the table row), often fewer. The cost is dominated by page reads, not comparisons, and the wide fanout keeps the page count tiny.

sdsd:03.05.q: When does the planner choose a sequential scan even though an index exists?
sdsd:03.05.s: When the planner estimates that a sequential scan is cheaper. That happens when the condition matches a large fraction of the table (roughly more than 5 to 20% of rows), because fetching each row through the index is a random page read priced at about 4 times a sequential one, so one sequential pass beats thousands of random reads. It also happens on tiny tables (a few pages), when the index cannot serve the condition as written (filtering only on a non-leading column of a composite index, a function on the column, a leading wildcard, a type mismatch), and when stale or misleading statistics make it overestimate how many rows will match.

sdsd:03.06.q: Give an example of a lost update and the isolation level or lock that prevents it.
sdsd:03.06.s: A lost update: a wallet holds 100. Transaction 1 reads 100 to deduct 30 and transaction 2 reads 100 to deduct 50. Transaction 1 writes 70 and commits, then transaction 2 writes 50 and commits, so the first deduction is silently lost (it should be 20). Read committed, the default in Postgres, does not prevent this because the computation happens in the application. Prevent it with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE so the second transaction waits for the row lock and then reads 70; or an atomic UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance - 30 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 30; or optimistic locking with a version column (UPDATE ... WHERE version = 7); or repeatable read or serializable isolation, where the second transaction's update fails with a serialisation error and is retried.

sdsd:03.07.s: Because Postgres implements MVCC by never overwriting rows: an UPDATE writes a new tuple and marks the old one with xmax, and a DELETE just marks it. Once no snapshot can see an old version it is dead, but it still occupies space in the table and every index, so heavily updated tables bloat and scans slow down. VACUUM removes dead tuples and makes the space reusable, refreshes planner statistics, updates the visibility map (which speeds later vacuums and enables index-only scans), and freezes old rows so that 32-bit transaction IDs can wrap around without old rows suddenly appearing to be in the future and vanishing. If freezing falls too far behind, Postgres stops accepting writes to protect data. Long-running or idle transactions block all of this.

sdsd:03.08.q: The server crashes after COMMIT returns but before data pages are flushed. How is the data recovered?
sdsd:03.08.s: Before COMMIT returned, the transaction's change was recorded in the write-ahead log and the log, including its commit record, was fsynced to durable storage; the data page itself was only changed in memory. When the server restarts, the database finds the last checkpoint and replays the WAL forward from it. For each record it compares the record's LSN with the LSN stored on the target page, and reapplies any change the page is missing (full-page images in the log repair any torn pages). Because the commit record is in the log, the transaction counts as committed, so the paid invoice is fully restored. Uncommitted transactions are replayed too but stay invisible under MVCC (or are undone in engines like InnoDB).

sdsd:03.09.q: How do two ticket servers avoid handing out the same ID?
sdsd:03.09.s: They split the number space so it can never overlap. Both servers set auto_increment_increment = 2, but server A uses auto_increment_offset = 1 and issues only odd numbers (1, 3, 5...) while server B uses offset 2 and issues only even numbers (2, 4, 6...). Each server uses REPLACE INTO on its one-row table plus LAST_INSERT_ID() to get the next number, so neither needs to know what the other has issued and there is no replication or coordination between them. Clients round-robin between the two and fail over to the other if one is down. The counters drift apart, so IDs are unique and roughly, not strictly, increasing. With N servers you use increment N and offsets 1 to N.

sdsd:03.10.q: In what order would you try read replicas, caching, vertical scaling and sharding?
sdsd:03.10.s: First measure which resource is exhausted. Then: 1) tune queries and indexes (cheapest, often fixes it); 2) cache hot reads in Redis or Memcached; 3) scale vertically to a bigger machine with more RAM and faster disks; 4) add read replicas for remaining read load, handling replication lag with read-your-writes. Caching, replicas and vertical scaling can be interleaved depending on the workload: read-heavy loads favour cache and replicas, while write-heavy loads get nothing from them and go to vertical scaling and then sharding sooner. Shard last, only when write volume or data size outgrows one primary, because it brings cross-shard queries and transactions, hot shards and rebalancing work. When sharding, choose a key that keeps related data together and create many logical shards.

sdsd:03.11.q: Why can a normal CREATE INDEX cause an outage on a busy table?
sdsd:03.11.s: A normal CREATE INDEX holds a lock that blocks every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on the table until the build finishes, and on a large table that is minutes to hours. On a busy table, writes pile up behind the lock, the application's connection pool fills with waiting requests, new requests time out and retries add load, so the application goes down even though the database is healthy. Worse, the build must first wait for any in-progress write transaction on the table, and new writes queue behind it while it waits (for ALTER TABLE, which needs an exclusive lock, even reads queue). CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY avoids blocking writes by building in two scans and waiting for old transactions, at the cost of a slower build, extra load, and the risk of leaving an INVALID index to clean up if it fails. Setting lock_timeout on migrations prevents the lock queue pile-up.

sdsd:03.12.q: List the steps to rename a column with zero downtime.
sdsd:03.12.s: 1) Add the new column as nullable with no default (a fast change, with a lock timeout). 2) Deploy code that writes both the old and new columns on every insert and update but still reads the old one (or add a trigger that copies writes). 3) Backfill existing rows into the new column in small, throttled, resumable batches. 4) Deploy code that reads the new column while still writing both, and verify by comparing the two. 5) Deploy code that stops writing the old column. 6) After a waiting period with no remaining readers, drop the old column. Each step works with the code versions running before and after it, and every step except the final drop can be rolled back.

sdsd:03.13.q: What breaks in unique constraints and queries when you soft delete rows?
sdsd:03.13.s: Unique constraints still see soft-deleted rows, so a deleted user's email or username cannot be reused (re-signup fails with a duplicate key) unless every unique constraint becomes a partial unique index WHERE deleted_at IS NULL, and restoring a row can then fail if someone else took the value. Every query and every join must remember WHERE deleted_at IS NULL, or deleted data leaks into results, counts and reports. Foreign keys no longer protect you: live children can point at a soft-deleted parent and ON DELETE CASCADE never fires. Tables and indexes fill with dead rows unless indexes are made partial, and the eventual hard purge must walk every dependent table in order.

sdsd:04.01.q: Name 2 workloads where NoSQL is a clear win and 2 where it isn't.
sdsd:04.01.s: NoSQL is a clear win for (1) very high-volume, append-heavy writes read back by key and time range, such as event logs, metrics or chat history in a wide-column store like Cassandra, where write rates exceed one machine and the database partitions for you; and (2) simple, latency-critical key lookups on ephemeral data, such as sessions, carts, rate-limit counters or live locations in Redis or DynamoDB. It is a poor fit for (1) payments, ledgers, inventory or bookings, which need multi-row ACID transactions and constraints, and (2) reporting or admin tools with ad hoc queries and joins across many entities, because NoSQL tables are designed around fixed queries.

sdsd:04.02.q: When would you pick a document store over a key-value store?
sdsd:04.02.s: Pick a document store when you need to query, filter or index by fields inside the record rather than only fetch it by its key (for example "find all carts containing product 123", or products by brand and price), when you want to update individual fields atomically without rewriting the whole value, or when records are nested objects with varying shapes that are read together, like a product catalogue or an order with its line items. If you only ever fetch and replace the whole value by one key, such as a session, cache entry or rate-limit counter, a key-value store like Redis is simpler and faster.

sdsd:04.03.q: Cassandra and ClickHouse are both "column" databases. How are they different?
sdsd:04.03.s: Cassandra is a wide-column store: rows are grouped into partitions by a hashed partition key spread across nodes and sorted inside each partition by clustering columns, and writes go through an LSM tree (commit log plus memtable), so it is built for huge write volumes and reading a known partition, an OLTP-style workload serving the application. ClickHouse is a columnar store: each column is stored separately and heavily compressed on disk, and queries are executed in vectorised batches, so analytical queries read only the few columns they need across billions of rows, an OLAP workload. Cassandra is bad at scans and aggregations; ClickHouse is bad at frequent single-row writes and updates. Cassandra serves the app; ClickHouse serves analytics.

sdsd:04.04.q: Which query is painful in SQL but natural in a graph database?
sdsd:04.04.s: Multi-hop and variable-length traversals, such as "friends of friends of friends who like jazz", the shortest path between two users, or finding every account connected to a known fraudster through any chain of shared cards or devices within 4 hops. In SQL each hop is another self-join on the edges table with fast-growing intermediate results, and a variable number of hops needs an awkward, hard-to-optimise recursive CTE. A graph database stores each node's relationships directly (index-free adjacency), so a query like MATCH (a)-[:FOLLOWS*1..3]->(b) follows pointers hop by hop with the hop count as a simple parameter, and offers path-finding built in.

sdsd:04.05.q: Pick a shard key for a chat app's messages table. What query does it make hard?
sdsd:04.05.s: Shard the messages table by conversation_id (hashed, with many logical shards). One conversation's messages then live together on one shard, ordered by time, so loading or paginating a chat, the most common query, touches a single shard, and with hundreds of millions of conversations the load spreads evenly (very large group chats can be bucketed by month). It makes queries across conversations hard: "all messages sent by user X", account export, moderation by sender and global search must fan out to every shard. Serve those from secondary stores keyed differently, such as a messages_by_user table sharded by sender_id and a search index, filled asynchronously from message events.

sdsd:04.06.q: A celebrity's post gets 1M likes a minute on one key. How do you spread it?
sdsd:04.06.s: One key cannot exceed one partition's limit (for example about 1,000 writes per second per DynamoDB partition), and 1 million likes a minute is about 16,700 per second. Split the counter into N shards (for example likes:post123:0 to likes:post123:63), send each like to a random shard, and sum the shards on read (cached for a couple of seconds) or roll them up periodically. Better still, buffer and batch: publish like events to a stream partitioned by post and random suffix, aggregate them for a second, and apply one increment per counter shard, so one write carries thousands of likes. Store who liked what separately under an evenly distributed key like (user_id, post_id), and show an approximate, slightly stale total.

sdsd:04.07.q: With modulo hashing, adding 1 server to 10 moves how many keys? With consistent hashing?
sdsd:04.07.s: With modulo hashing, going from 10 to 11 servers changes hash % N for about 10/11 of keys, so roughly 91% of keys move to a different server, and a cache's hit rate collapses. With consistent hashing, only the keys in the arcs taken over by the new server move, about 1/11, roughly 9% of keys, while every other key stays where it was; with virtual nodes those 9% come in small slices evenly from all 10 existing servers instead of from one neighbour.

sdsd:04.08.q: Why are auto-increment IDs a problem once you shard?
sdsd:04.08.s: Each shard has its own auto-increment counter starting at 1, so different shards hand out the same numbers, and IDs collide as soon as rows are referenced globally, moved between shards during rebalancing or merged in analytics. Fixing that with a single central counter puts a network round trip on every insert and makes one database a throughput bottleneck and single point of failure. Per-shard counters also lose any global creation order (ID 5,000 on one shard may be newer than ID 7,000 on another) and an ID no longer tells you which shard holds the row. The usual fix is Snowflake-style 64-bit IDs generated locally from a timestamp, a machine or shard number, and a sequence.

sdsd:04.09.q: Why does UUIDv4 hurt B-tree insert performance and UUIDv7 doesn't?
sdsd:04.09.s: A B-tree keeps keys sorted, so where an insert goes depends on the key's value. UUIDv4 values are random, so each insert lands on a random leaf page anywhere in the index. Once the index is larger than memory, most of those pages are not cached, so inserts cause random disk reads and churn the cache; full pages split in the middle and settle around 70% full, making the index bigger; and many distinct pages are dirtied, multiplying write-ahead log volume (full-page writes). UUIDv7 puts a 48-bit millisecond timestamp in its most significant bits, so each new key is larger than the previous ones and always goes to the rightmost leaf pages, which stay in memory and fill sequentially to nearly 100%, just like an auto-increment key, while still needing no coordination to generate.

sdsd:04.10.q: Break down the 64 bits of a Snowflake ID. How many IDs per ms per machine?
sdsd:04.10.s: 1 sign bit, always 0 so the ID is positive; 41 bits of milliseconds since a custom epoch (2^41 ms is about 69 years); 10 bits of machine ID (1,024 generators, often split into 5 bits of data centre and 5 bits of worker); and 12 bits of sequence that counts IDs within the same millisecond on that machine. So each machine can generate 2^12 = 4,096 IDs per millisecond, about 4 million per second; if it needs more within one millisecond it waits for the next millisecond and resets the sequence. The ID is built as (timestamp minus epoch) shifted left 22, OR machine shifted left 12, OR sequence.

sdsd:04.11.q: A machine's clock jumps backward 5 ms. What should a Snowflake generator do?
sdsd:04.11.s: It must not issue IDs with the earlier timestamps, because it may already have used those (timestamp, sequence) pairs, and reusing them would create duplicate IDs. For a small 5 ms jump it should either wait until the clock passes the last timestamp it used (Twitter's original approach, a delay of about 5 ms), or keep using the last timestamp and keep incrementing the sequence, waiting only if the 4,096 sequence values for that millisecond run out. It should record a metric and log the event, and refuse to generate (failing health checks and alerting) if a backward jump is large, such as more than 100 ms to a second. It should also persist its last timestamp so a restart after a backward step cannot reuse old timestamps.

sdsd:04.12.q: Why does page 10,000 with OFFSET get slower, and why doesn't keyset?
sdsd:04.12.s: With OFFSET the database has no way to jump to the Nth row, so it must produce every earlier row in order and discard it: page 10,000 of 20 rows reads about 200,000 index entries and rows to return 20, so cost grows linearly with depth (and inserts shift rows, causing duplicates and gaps). Keyset pagination remembers the last row's sort values and uses WHERE (sort_key, id) < (last values) ORDER BY sort_key, id with a matching composite index, so the database descends the B-tree straight to that position (3 or 4 page reads) and reads only the next 20 entries. The cost is the same on page 1 and page 10,000, and results stay stable because the position is defined by values, not by counting rows.

sdsd:04.13.q: A Bloom filter says "maybe present" or "definitely not". Why can't it say "definitely present"?
sdsd:04.13.s: Because the bits are shared between all items and never cleared. When you check an item, its k bits may all be 1 because other items set them, not because this item was added; the filter stores no record of which item set which bit, so it cannot distinguish the two cases and can only say "maybe" (a false positive, at a rate set by bits per item and the number of hash functions). The reverse is certain: if any of the k bits is 0, the item was definitely never added, because adding it would have set that bit to 1 and bits are never reset. The same sharing is why a standard Bloom filter cannot delete items.

sdsd:04.14.q: Logs older than 30 days are rarely read. What's your storage plan and the retrieval tradeoff?
sdsd:04.14.s: Keep the last 30 days hot: compressed log files in S3 Standard plus a search index, so incidents can be investigated in seconds. A lifecycle rule then moves files older than 30 days to a cheaper class: Glacier Instant Retrieval (or Standard-IA) for the next months, which still reads in milliseconds but charges per GB retrieved, then Glacier Deep Archive for long-term compliance, and finally expires them when the retention period (for example 7 years) ends. Compact hourly files into large compressed objects before archiving to avoid per-object and transition fees. The trade-off: storage becomes many times cheaper (Deep Archive is about 1/23 of Standard's price), but reading old logs costs retrieval fees, is no longer searchable without a restore and a separate query tool, and from Deep Archive takes up to 12 to 48 hours; objects also incur minimum storage durations of 90 to 180 days if deleted early.

sdsd:05.01.q: Compare cache-aside and write-through. Which one can serve stale data and when?
sdsd:05.01.s: Cache-aside loads data into the cache only on a read miss and relies on TTLs or deletes to remove old values, so it can serve stale data after a database update if the delete fails or a slow reader writes an old value back after the delete (the read-write race); the staleness lasts until the TTL expires. Write-through updates the cache on every write, so reads of recent writes are fresh, but writes are slower and the cache fills with data that may never be read. It can still serve stale data if one of its two writes fails or concurrent writes land in different orders, so both patterns need a TTL as a safety net.

sdsd:05.02.q: How does a client decide which cache node holds a key?
sdsd:05.02.s: The client hashes the key and maps the hash to a node using a scheme every client shares. With consistent hashing it places the key on a hash ring and picks the first node clockwise, so adding a node moves only about 1/N of keys. With Redis Cluster it computes CRC16(key) mod 16,384 to get a hash slot, looks up which node owns that slot in its cached slot map, sends the request there directly, and refreshes the map when a node replies MOVED. Alternatively a proxy such as mcrouter or Twemproxy does this hashing on the client's behalf, at the cost of an extra hop.

sdsd:05.03.q: Why does Redis use approximate LRU instead of exact LRU?
sdsd:05.03.s: Exact LRU needs every key linked into one ordered list that is updated on every access, which costs about 16 bytes of pointers per key (gigabytes across hundreds of millions of keys) and extra work on every read on Redis's single command thread. Redis instead keeps a small last-access clock in each key's existing header and, when it must evict, samples a few random keys (5 by default), keeps the most idle ones in a 16-entry candidate pool, and evicts the oldest. For real, skewed workloads this is almost as good as true LRU at a fraction of the memory and CPU cost.

sdsd:05.04.q: Why can't Redis delete every expired key the instant it expires?
sdsd:05.04.s: Deleting each key exactly at its expiry would need a timer per key or a continuously maintained sorted index over millions of keys, costing memory per key, work on every write and bursts of deletion work that would stall Redis's single command thread. Instead Redis deletes expired keys lazily when a command touches them, so clients never see them, and runs an active cycle about 10 times a second that samples around 20 volatile keys, deletes the expired ones and repeats while many are expired, within a CPU budget. Memory is reclaimed slightly late, but the work stays small and bounded.

sdsd:05.05.q: A hot key expires and 10,000 requests miss at once. Name 2 fixes.
sdsd:05.05.s: (1) Make only one request rebuild the value: a lease issued by the cache (Facebook's memcache leases, which cut one hot key's database load from 17,000 to 1,300 queries per second), a distributed lock such as SET rebuild:key token NX EX 5, or request coalescing in each process, while the other requests wait briefly and re-read or get a stale copy. (2) Refresh the key before it expires, with a background job, a soft TTL that serves the old value while one request refreshes, or probabilistic early expiration (XFetch), so the key never goes missing under load. Adding jitter to TTLs also stops many keys expiring at once, and a database concurrency cap is the last line of defence.

sdsd:05.06.q: Your cache cluster dies. Why might sending all traffic to the database take the database down too?
sdsd:05.06.s: The database was sized only for the small fraction of reads that miss the cache, so with a 95% hit rate, losing the cache sends 20 times its normal read load to it all at once. Arrivals exceed capacity, queues and latency grow, requests time out while the database keeps doing the abandoned work, retries multiply the load further, connections run out and application threads block, so the database collapses and takes the rest of the site with it, and a cold cache then slows recovery. Instead of falling back blindly, cap and shed database load, serve stale or degraded data, and keep the cache itself highly available.

sdsd:06.01.q: Why can't a node tell the difference between a crashed peer and a slow network?
sdsd:06.01.s: A node learns about a peer only through messages. If no reply arrives, the peer may have crashed, it may be alive but paused or overloaded (a long garbage collection pause, say), the request or the reply may have been lost or delayed, or the network may be partitioned. All of these look identical from outside: silence. Because real networks have no guaranteed upper bound on message delay or processing time, any timeout you choose can expire on a healthy but slow peer, so failure detection can only ever be a suspicion, and decisions taken on a timeout must be safe if the peer is still alive.

sdsd:06.02.q: What's the difference between linearizability and serializability?
sdsd:06.02.s: Linearizability is a guarantee about single operations on one object: each operation appears to take effect at one instant between its start and end, consistent with real time, so a read always sees any write that completed before the read began and the system behaves as if there were one copy. Serializability is a guarantee about transactions over many objects: the outcome equals some serial order of the transactions, which prevents anomalies like write skew but need not match real time, so a serializable system may legally return stale data. Strict serializability requires both properties together.

sdsd:06.03.q: With N=3 replicas, why do W=2 and R=2 guarantee you read the latest write?
sdsd:06.03.s: With N = 3 replicas, a successful write was acknowledged by some 2 of them and a read contacts some 2 of them. Two groups of 2 drawn from only 3 replicas cannot be disjoint, because that would need 4 different replicas (2 + 2 = 4 > 3), so by the pigeonhole principle at least one replica is in both groups. That replica holds the latest acknowledged write, and the reader picks the newest version among the answers by its version number or timestamp, so it returns the latest write. The same setting tolerates one replica being down for both reads and writes. Edge cases such as sloppy quorums and concurrent writes mean this is not full linearizability.

sdsd:06.04.q: Explain PACELC in one sentence. Why is it more useful than CAP?
sdsd:06.04.s: PACELC says that if there is a network partition a replicated system must choose between availability and consistency, and else, in normal operation, it must choose between lower latency and consistency. It is more useful than CAP because partitions are rare, while the latency cost of keeping replicas consistent (waiting for a leader, a quorum or another region) applies to every single request, so PACELC describes the trade-off users actually feel, explains why systems such as Cassandra weaken consistency even when nothing has failed, and lets you choose per operation.

sdsd:06.05.q: What can vector clocks detect that Lamport clocks can't?
sdsd:06.05.s: Vector clocks can detect that two events are concurrent: compare the vectors entry by entry, and if neither vector is less than or equal to the other in every entry, neither event could have caused the other, so they are concurrent (for example two conflicting updates made on different replicas during a partition). Lamport clocks only guarantee that a cause has a smaller timestamp than its effect; a smaller Lamport timestamp does not tell you whether the events were causally related or independent, because one integer cannot record what each process knew of the others.

sdsd:06.06.q: Why does Raft need a majority to commit, and what happens with 2 of 5 nodes down?
sdsd:06.06.s: Raft needs a majority because any two majorities of the same cluster overlap in at least one server: so two candidates cannot both win the same term (the shared server votes only once), and a committed entry, being on a majority, is held by at least one server in every future election majority, which refuses to vote for a candidate missing it, so every new leader has all committed entries. A minority cannot commit, because two minorities could then decide different values. With 2 of 5 nodes down, the 3 survivors are still a majority, so they elect a leader and keep committing writes, though every write now needs all three and there is no margin left; if a third node fails, nothing can commit until one returns, but nothing incorrect is ever returned.

sdsd:06.07.q: Two nodes both think they're the leader. What mechanism stops them corrupting data?
sdsd:06.07.s: A fencing token or epoch checked by the resource: each new leadership grant comes with a strictly higher number from the lock service or consensus system (a Raft term, an epoch, a ZooKeeper zxid), the leader includes it in every write, and the storage remembers the highest number it has seen and rejects any write carrying a lower one. So when the old leader resumes after a pause or partition and writes with its stale token, the write fails and it steps down. Conditional writes on an epoch or version column in the database achieve the same thing; checking one's own lease alone is not enough, because a pause can occur between the check and the write.

sdsd:06.08.q: Why must a lock have a lease (expiry)? What new problem does the lease create?
sdsd:06.08.s: Without a lease, a client that crashes, hangs or is partitioned while holding the lock would block every other client forever, because the lock service can never be sure it is dead, so the lock must expire unless renewed. The new problem is that expiry is decided by the lock service's sense of time, and a client paused by garbage collection, VM migration or a slow network may not notice its lease has gone: it can keep acting, even after checking the lease, while another client holds the lock, so two holders exist at once and can overwrite each other's work. Fencing tokens, increasing numbers checked by the resource, make that safe.

sdsd:06.09.q: How does a fencing token protect storage from a client whose lock expired?
sdsd:06.09.s: Each lock grant comes with a strictly increasing number (for example an etcd revision or ZooKeeper zxid). The client sends that token with every write, and the storage atomically remembers the highest token it has accepted for the resource and rejects any write carrying a lower one. So if a client's lock expired while it was paused and a newer client has already written with a higher token, the stale client's write is refused (for example a conditional UPDATE ... WHERE lock_token < 34 matches no rows), regardless of what the stale client believes about holding the lock.

sdsd:06.10.q: Why does a circuit breaker make the system fail faster, and why is that good?
sdsd:06.10.s: Once failures (errors, timeouts or slow calls) cross a threshold, the breaker opens and rejects calls immediately, in microseconds, instead of letting every call wait for a timeout. That is good because the request would fail anyway: failing fast frees the caller's threads and connections so it keeps serving everything that does not need the broken dependency, stopping a cascading failure; it gives the struggling dependency room to recover instead of being hammered by requests and retries; it gives users and upstream services an immediate error they can handle with a fallback such as cached or degraded data; and half-open trial calls close the breaker automatically once the dependency is healthy.

sdsd:06.11.q: How many rounds does gossip need to reach N nodes, roughly?
sdsd:06.11.s: About O(log N) rounds. Each round every node that has the information passes it to a few random peers, so the number of informed nodes roughly multiplies each round (for example roughly threefold with a fanout of 2) until nearly everyone knows, then a few extra rounds catch the stragglers. For 1,000 nodes that is on the order of 10 rounds and for a million about 20, while each node sends only a constant number of messages per round regardless of cluster size.

sdsd:06.12.q: Why store cluster metadata in a consensus-backed service rather than a normal database?
sdsd:06.12.s: Because every node must see the same answer to questions like "who is the leader" or "who owns this shard", even during server failures and failovers, and a wrong answer causes split brain and divergent data. A consensus-backed service commits each change to a majority before acknowledging it, so it never loses or reorders acknowledged updates when a server fails, unlike a single database or one with asynchronous replicas. It also provides sessions with ephemeral nodes or leases that tie membership to liveness automatically, watches that push change notifications instead of polling, and monotonically increasing version numbers (zxid, etcd revision) usable as fencing tokens. The cost is small capacity and slower writes, which is fine for metadata.

sdsd:06.13.q: How does a node find a key in a DHT without knowing every other node?
sdsd:06.13.s: Each node keeps a small routing table whose entries are spaced exponentially around the ID space: many contacts near itself and few far away (Chord's finger table points to the nodes 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on positions ahead; Kademlia's k-buckets hold up to k contacts for each range of XOR distance). To find a key, a node sends the lookup to the known node closest to the key without passing it (or, in Kademlia, asks the few closest known nodes for even closer ones), and that node does the same with its own table. Each hop at least halves the remaining distance, so the owner is found in about O(log N) hops (about 10 for a million nodes) while each node stores only O(log N) contacts.

sdsd:07.01.q: Why is sequential disk I/O so much faster than random I/O, even on SSDs?
sdsd:07.01.s: A random I/O pays a fixed cost before any data moves. On a hard disk that is a seek plus half a rotation, about 10 ms, against microseconds to transfer 4 KB, so a drive does only about 120 random operations a second but streams around 200 MB/s. An SSD has no arm, but flash is written in pages and erased only in large blocks and cannot be overwritten in place, so small random overwrites leave stale pages scattered everywhere and force the drive's garbage collector to copy live data before erasing (device write amplification, wear and latency spikes). Large sequential writes fill and later free whole blocks, and the OS and drive can prefetch, merge and parallelise them into large requests.

sdsd:07.02.q: When would you choose an LSM tree over a B-tree?
sdsd:07.02.s: Choose an LSM tree when the workload is write-heavy or the data is large: logging, metrics, time series, event stores, messaging, feeds. It turns every write into a sequential log append and memory insert, flushes large sorted files, compresses well (immutable files) and is gentle on SSDs, so it sustains far higher write rates than a B-tree doing random page rewrites. The price is reads that may check several files (mitigated by Bloom filters and caching), background compaction I/O and occasional latency spikes. Choose a B-tree when reads, especially point lookups and range scans with predictable latency, dominate, or when you need mature transactional behaviour.

sdsd:07.03.q: How do you update a file so a crash never leaves it half-written?
sdsd:07.03.s: Never modify the live file in place. Write the complete new version to a temporary file in the same directory, fsync it, atomically rename it over the original (POSIX rename within one filesystem is atomic, so readers see the old or new file, never a mix), then fsync the directory so the rename itself is durable; a crash at any point leaves either the full old file or the full new one, plus at most a stray temp file. For frequent small updates, append records framed with a length and a checksum to a log, acknowledge only after the covering fsync, and on recovery replay until the first record that fails its checksum and truncate that torn tail.

sdsd:07.04.q: Why put a magic number and version at the start of a file format?
sdsd:07.04.s: A magic number lets any program instantly tell this file type from every other and reject garbage, an empty file or the wrong file before misreading it, and a well-chosen one also exposes transfer damage such as line-ending conversion. A version number lets readers cope with format changes: new code can recognise and still read old layouts, and old code can detect a newer file and refuse it cleanly (or, with separate read and write versions as in SQLite, open it read-only) instead of interpreting the new bytes with the old layout and silently returning or writing corrupt data.

sdsd:07.05.q: How can a client read one record from a 10 GB object without downloading it all?
sdsd:07.05.s: Store an index that maps each record to a byte offset and length, either inside the object (typically a footer at the end, as Parquet and ZIP do, with its length in the last few bytes) or alongside it in a database. The client first fetches the index with a small range request (for example `Range: bytes=-8` to get the footer length, then the footer), looks up the record's offset and length, then sends `Range: bytes=start-end` and receives a `206 Partial Content` with only those bytes. Statistics in the index can also rule out whole blocks, and an ETag check (If-Range or If-Match) ensures the pieces come from the same version of the object.

sdsd:07.06.q: Why does never modifying a file in place make concurrency and rollback easier?
sdsd:07.06.s: If files never change, a reader can never see a partially written file or a mix of old and new rows; it simply reads the set of files listed in the version it started with, so it needs no locks and gets snapshot isolation for free. Writers do their heavy work without locks and coordinate only on one tiny atomic commit (put-if-absent of the next log entry, or compare-and-swap of a metadata pointer), retrying if another writer won and checking whether its changes conflict. Every old version is still a complete list of files that still exist, so rolling back means publishing an earlier file list, which takes seconds and copies nothing, as long as a vacuum has not yet deleted those older files.

sdsd:07.07.q: Append-only writes are fast. What do you pay for them later?
sdsd:07.07.s: You pay in space, because overwritten values and tombstones stay on disk until compaction removes them and compaction itself needs free headroom while inputs and outputs coexist. You pay in extra I/O and CPU, because compaction rereads and rewrites the same data many times (write amplification). You pay in read cost, because the newest value of a key may be in the memtable or any of several files, so reads need indexes, Bloom filters and caches, and missing keys are expensive. And you pay in latency spikes, because compaction competes with live traffic and, if it falls behind, the engine must throttle or stall writes.

sdsd:07.08.q: Bitcask keeps every key in RAM. What does that limit, and how does it handle deletes?
sdsd:07.08.s: Holding every key in the in-memory keydir limits the total number of keys (not the data volume) to what RAM can hold, at roughly the key size plus a few tens of bytes per key, so a node with 200 million 40-byte keys needs about 14 GB just for the index; and because the keydir is a hash table there is no key order, so no range scans or prefix listings. A delete appends a tombstone record and removes the key from the keydir, so later reads miss immediately; the background merge then copies only records the keydir still points at into new files, drops dead values and tombstones, deletes the old files and writes hint files of keys and offsets so the keydir can be rebuilt quickly on restart.

sdsd:07.09.q: Walk through a write in an LSM tree from API call to disk.
sdsd:07.09.s: The write is stamped with a sequence number, appended to the write-ahead log (optionally fsynced, usually batched with other writers via group commit) for durability, inserted into the in-memory sorted memtable (a skip list), and then acknowledged, with no SST file touched. When the memtable reaches its size limit it becomes immutable and a new memtable takes writes; a background thread flushes the immutable one in key order as a new sorted, immutable SST file in level 0 and records it in the MANIFEST, after which the old WAL segment is deleted. Background compaction later merges L0 files into L1 and each level into the next, roughly ten times larger, discarding older versions of the key; if flush or compaction falls behind, the engine slows or stops writes.

sdsd:07.10.q: Why does an LSM engine need a WAL if the memtable gets flushed to an SSTable anyway?
sdsd:07.10.s: The memtable lives only in RAM and is flushed only when it fills (or another trigger fires), which can be minutes and tens of megabytes after a write, so on its own every recent write would be lost in a crash. Flushing an SSTable per write would destroy the batching that makes LSM writes fast. The WAL is a cheap sequential append, fsynced in groups as configured, that records every write in order until the memtable holding it is safely in an SSTable; on restart the engine replays the WAL to rebuild the lost memtables, and a WAL file is deleted only once all memtables it covers have been flushed.

sdsd:07.11.q: Why are reads for missing keys the worst case in an LSM, and how do Bloom filters help?
sdsd:07.11.s: A lookup must return the newest version, so it checks the memtables, then every overlapping L0 file, then one file per level, from newest to oldest, stopping at the first match. A key that exists is usually found early, but a missing key has no match, so the search can never stop early and must check every place, which without help means one block read per file (about 10 reads for 10 files). A Bloom filter per SST file, held in memory, answers "definitely not here" or "maybe here" with no false negatives; at about 10 bits per key only about 1% of files that lack the key give a false "maybe", so most files are skipped without any disk I/O, and the per-file index block ensures any file that must be checked costs just one data block read.
sdsd:07.11.t: LSM read path: Bloom filters and sparse index

sdsd:07.12.q: Define write amplification. Why does leveled compaction have more of it than tiered?
sdsd:07.12.s: Write amplification is the total bytes physically written to storage (WAL, flush and every compaction rewrite) divided by the bytes the application wrote, so 20x means 1 GB of inserts causes 20 GB of disk writes. Leveled compaction keeps each level a single non-overlapping sorted run about ten times larger than the one above, so moving a file down one level means merging and rewriting it together with all the overlapping files of the next level, roughly ten times its size, and that happens again at every level as the data sinks, giving typically 10 to 30x. Tiered (universal) compaction lets several sorted runs of similar size accumulate and merges them only when enough pile up, so each byte is rewritten roughly once per tier and there are few tiers, giving lower write amplification at the cost of more runs to read and more duplicate data on disk.

sdsd:07.13.q: Why store images in object storage and only their metadata in a database?
sdsd:07.13.s: Images are large, written once and read whole, which object storage serves cheaply (dense disks, erasure coding, several times cheaper per GB), very durably and at huge parallel scale, directly to clients or a CDN through signed URLs. Databases are expensive per byte and suffer when filled with blobs: the buffer pool is polluted, the WAL, replicas and backups balloon, and every download has to stream through app servers. But databases are excellent at indexing, querying and transactionally updating small records such as owner, key, size, checksum and timestamps, which object storage cannot query. Storing metadata in the database (written after the bytes, with orphaned objects garbage-collected) and the bytes in object storage lets each do what it is good at.

sdsd:07.14.q: Name the main components behind an S3 PUT: front end, metadata, storage nodes. What does each do?
sdsd:07.14.s: The front end is a stateless fleet that terminates HTTP and TLS, authenticates and authorises the request, and routes it, choosing where the new data will go. The storage nodes (a fleet of hard disks, each managed by the ShardStore engine) durably store the object's erasure-coded shards, spread across disks, racks and Availability Zones as separate failure domains, and verify checksums. The metadata (namespace) service records the bucket and key, version, size, checksum and the locations of the shards, and also serves LIST; the metadata commit happens only after the shards are durable, and once it commits the object becomes visible to reads and the client gets 200 OK.

sdsd:07.15.q: Why does range partitioning support listing objects by prefix and hashing doesn't?
sdsd:07.15.s: With range partitioning, keys are stored in sorted order and each server owns a contiguous key range, so all keys sharing a prefix are adjacent and live in one range or a few neighbouring ones; a listing locates the first range from the partition map and reads keys in order from one or two servers, stopping after a page. Hashing deliberately scatters neighbouring keys to unrelated servers, so the system cannot know where keys with a given prefix live: it must send the listing to every node, have each find its matches, and merge-sort the results to return the first page in order, which costs requests on every node and is as slow as the slowest node.
sdsd:07.15.t: Range partitioning vs consistent hashing for storage

sdsd:07.16.q: What does a partition manager do when one range gets too hot?
sdsd:07.16.s: It first decides whether moving is enough: if the range's server is overloaded but the range itself could be handled by one server, it moves the range to a lightly loaded partition server (checkpoint, release lease, new owner loads the streams and replays a short commit log). If the range itself is too hot or too big, it orders a split: the owning server profiles the traffic, picks a split key that divides the load (not just the data), checkpoints, and creates two new partitions whose streams point at the same immutable extents, so no data is copied; the manager then updates the partition map table, moves one half to another server, and front ends route to the new owners. It repeats on later passes if a half is still hot, and merges cold neighbouring ranges to keep the partition count under control.

sdsd:07.17.q: Why keep object metadata separate from object bytes?
sdsd:07.17.s: Metadata is small, changes often (versions, tags, ACLs) and must be looked up by key and listed in sorted order, while bytes are huge, immutable and need cheap capacity, so each wants different hardware (SSD or RAM versus dense disks) and different structures (a sorted, partitioned index versus erasure-coded blobs). Separating them lets each scale on its own terms (metadata by object count, bytes by volume), lets LIST, HEAD and existence checks run without touching data, makes the metadata commit the single atomic moment an object becomes visible (bytes can be written first, safely invisible), lets repair and tiering move bytes by just updating a pointer, and makes garbage collection a matter of finding bytes no metadata row references. Haystack showed the cost of mixing them: three or more disk operations per photo on NFS versus one once metadata moved into memory.

sdsd:07.18.q: Why make the lowest storage layer append-only?
sdsd:07.18.s: With append-only extents, the only thing replicas can disagree about after a failure is how long the extent is, so the system can reconcile them simply: seal the extent at the smallest committed length (anything beyond it was never acknowledged, since acknowledgement requires all replicas) and force every replica to exactly that length, making them bitwise identical, then continue appending in a new extent. Sealed data never changes, so it can be erasure-coded, geo-replicated, cached, scrubbed and shared between streams without locks, which is what makes partition splits and merges metadata-only and recovery a matter of replaying logs. Appends are also sequential and disk-friendly. The cost is that deleted and overwritten data remains until higher layers compact live data and the stream manager garbage-collects unreferenced extents.

sdsd:07.19.q: 3x replication vs 10+4 erasure coding: compare storage overhead and repair cost.
sdsd:07.19.s: 3x replication stores 3 bytes per byte (200% overhead) and tolerates 2 failures; reads use any one copy, and repairing a lost copy just reads 1 unit from a surviving replica. 10 + 4 erasure coding stores 1.4 bytes per byte (40% overhead) and tolerates any 4 failures, so it is far cheaper for the same or better durability, but rebuilding one lost shard requires reading 10 shards from 10 other machines, so repair traffic after a disk failure is about 10 times higher, and healthy reads must gather 10 shards. That is why systems replicate fresh data on the write path and erasure-code large sealed data in the background.

sdsd:07.20.q: TCP already has checksums. Why also checksum data end to end?
sdsd:07.20.s: TCP's checksum only protects data on the wire between two TCP endpoints, and it is a weak 16-bit sum that misses whole classes of errors. Corruption also happens where TCP can't see it: in the sender's and receiver's memory, in proxies, load balancers and TLS terminators that end one connection and start another, in application and storage-engine bugs, and on disks (bad reads, misdirected or lost writes), as in the classic case of a gateway that swapped bytes in its own memory while every hop's checksum passed. At large scale these rare events happen daily. Only a checksum computed by the original sender from the data as it should be, carried with the data and verified by the final receiver (and rechecked on reads and at rest), confirms the data is intact end to end; lower-layer checks are still useful because they catch errors early and make end-to-end retries rare.

sdsd:08.01.q: A request takes 30 s to generate a PDF. How do you redesign it so the user isn't waiting?
sdsd:08.01.s: Turn it into an asynchronous job. The API validates the request, stores a job record with status "queued", puts the job ID on a durable queue and returns 202 Accepted with the ID in milliseconds. Workers take jobs off the queue under a lease (visibility timeout), heartbeat while generating the PDF, upload it to object storage and set the status to done with a link. The client polls GET /jobs/{id} every few seconds or receives a WebSocket, webhook or email notification. Failed attempts retry with exponential backoff and go to a dead-letter queue after a few tries, and the job is idempotent (output keyed by job ID) so a retry after a worker crash is safe.

sdsd:08.02.q: A task queue deletes messages when consumed; a stream keeps them. What does keeping them let you do?
sdsd:08.02.s: Keeping messages lets you replay history (reset a consumer group's offset to reprocess after a bug fix or rebuild a derived store such as a search index), add new consumers months later that read past events from the start of retention, and let several independent consumer groups read the same events at their own pace. Each consumer only tracks its own offset, so one slow or broken consumer does not affect the others, and the log doubles as an ordered audit trail for debugging.

sdsd:08.03.q: Why can't you write to the DB and then publish to Kafka in two separate steps safely?
sdsd:08.03.s: The two writes are not atomic, because no transaction spans the database and the broker. If you publish first and the database transaction then fails, consumers act on an order that never existed; if you commit first and the process crashes or the broker times out before publishing, the event is lost and nothing retries it. Two-phase commit is rarely available and couples the systems. The fix is the transactional outbox: insert the event into an outbox table in the same local transaction as the business row, and have a relay (polling or change data capture) publish it afterwards. The relay may publish twice, so consumers deduplicate by event ID.

sdsd:08.04.q: Lag is growing at 1,000 msgs/s. What are your options?
sdsd:08.04.s: First work out why: has the producer rate risen, or has processing slowed (often a slow dependency or a hot partition)? Then raise throughput: add consumers (and partitions, since Kafka parallelism is capped by partition count), batch writes and lookups, cache, and put timeouts and concurrency limits on slow dependencies. Drain time is backlog divided by spare capacity, so aim for well above 1,000 msg/s of headroom. While draining, process fresh messages first and move old ones to a backlog queue, expire messages that are no longer useful, isolate noisy tenants, apply backpressure or rate limits on producers, and send repeatedly failing messages to a dead-letter queue. Alert on the age of the oldest message.

sdsd:08.05.q: How do you ensure a scheduled job runs exactly once when the scheduler has 3 replicas?
sdsd:08.05.s: Elect one leader among the replicas (via Paxos, Raft or a renewable lease in etcd, ZooKeeper or the database, with a fencing token), or shard tasks so each has one owner, so only one replica launches a given task. Give each run a deterministic ID made of the task and its scheduled time, and insert it into an executions table with a unique constraint before launching, so a second scheduler's insert fails. A new leader checks which IDs already exist and launches only missing ones. Delivery to workers is still at least once, so the job itself is idempotent (outputs keyed by run ID, idempotency keys on external calls), which makes a rare duplicate harmless.

sdsd:08.06.q: Why does SKIP LOCKED let many workers pull from one table without blocking each other?
sdsd:08.06.s: Each worker claims rows with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, which writes a row lock owned by its transaction. Plain FOR UPDATE makes a second worker wait for that lock; SKIP LOCKED tells it to skip any row it can't lock immediately and keep scanning, so each worker grabs a different set of free rows at once with no blocking and no duplicates. The locks last until the worker's transaction commits (deleting or completing the rows) or rolls back after a failure or crash (releasing them for another worker), which gives acknowledgement and redelivery from ordinary transaction rules.

sdsd:08.07.q: A 5-step pipeline fails at step 4. What should the orchestrator do?
sdsd:08.07.s: Retry step 4 with exponential backoff as its retry policy sets, without rerunning steps 1 to 3, whose results are recorded durably. If the error is non-retryable or retries run out, mark the downstream step 5 as not run (upstream_failed), alert someone, and keep the run resumable so that after a fix it continues from step 4. If earlier steps had external side effects that must not stand on their own (a charge, a reservation), run compensating actions in reverse order, as in a saga. Every step should be idempotent so retries after a partial success are safe.

sdsd:08.08.q: Design "when an order over $500 is placed, notify the fraud team" so non-engineers can add rules.
sdsd:08.08.s: Publish product events such as OrderPlaced (via an outbox) to an event bus with a published schema of fields. Store rules as data: an event type, a constrained condition built from schema fields, operators and values (for example total > 500), and an action chosen from a fixed menu such as "notify the fraud channel". Non-engineers create rules in a UI with validation and a dry run that replays recent real events to show how often the rule would fire. A rule-evaluator service consumes events, looks up the active rules for that event type from a cache, evaluates them and enqueues matching actions, which workers execute with retries, rate limits and an idempotency key of event ID plus rule ID. Rules are versioned and audited, and chaining is disabled so behaviour stays understandable.

sdsd:08.09.q: Fan-out on write vs fan-out on read: which for a user with 50M followers?
sdsd:08.09.s: Fan-out on read for that user. Pushing every post into 50 million feeds means 50 million writes per post, minutes of delay at realistic worker throughput, a backlog that delays everyone else's posts, and wasted work for inactive followers. Store their posts once, keep them in a replicated hot cache, and merge them into each follower's feed when the feed is read. Keep fan-out on write for ordinary accounts so most of the feed is precomputed, which is the hybrid approach used by large social networks.

sdsd:08.10.q: 100 items, 100,000 buyers in 1 second. How do you avoid overselling?
sdsd:08.10.s: Put a CDN and a virtual waiting room or rate limit in front so only a manageable batch of users reaches checkout, each with an admission token. Decrement stock atomically and conditionally, for example with a Redis Lua script that checks stock > 0 and decrements in one step, or UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0 and check rows affected, so the count can never go below zero (a CHECK constraint and unique order constraint in the database act as a final guard). A successful decrement creates a reservation with a short TTL; an idempotent payment webhook confirms it, and an expired reservation returns the unit to stock for the next person in line. Once stock hits zero, set a sold-out flag so everyone after the 100th gets an immediate response without touching the counter.

sdsd:09.01.q: Name the stages from raw document to ranked result.
sdsd:09.01.s: Indexing: documents are acquired by crawling or ingestion (often CDC from the main database), parsed into fields, analysed (tokenised, lower-cased, accents folded, stemmed, maybe stop words removed) and written into an inverted index mapping each term to the documents that contain it, with frequencies and positions. Querying: the query goes through the same analysis plus spelling correction, synonym expansion and intent detection; the postings lists for its terms are looked up and combined into candidates and filtered; the candidates are scored with BM25 or similar; the top few hundred are re-ranked with a learned model using signals like popularity, freshness and clicks; and the final page is returned with snippets and highlights.

sdsd:09.02.q: Build the inverted index by hand for: "cat sat", "cat ran", "dog sat".
sdsd:09.02.s: Tokenise the documents: doc 1 gives cat, sat; doc 2 gives cat, ran; doc 3 gives dog, sat. Emit the pairs (cat,1) (sat,1) (cat,2) (ran,2) (dog,3) (sat,3), sort them by term then docID to get (cat,1) (cat,2) (dog,3) (ran,2) (sat,1) (sat,3), and group by term. The index is cat → [1, 2], dog → [3], ran → [2], sat → [1, 3], with document frequencies 2, 1, 1 and 2. Each postings list is sorted by docID, so a query like cat AND sat is answered by merging [1, 2] and [1, 3] to get [1].

sdsd:09.03.q: Why intersect the shortest posting list first?
sdsd:09.03.s: Because the intersection of several lists can never be longer than the shortest one. Starting with the rarest term (lowest document frequency, known from the dictionary before reading postings) makes the intermediate result small from the first step, so every later intersection only checks a few candidates against the longer lists, which can be jumped through with skip pointers or galloping search instead of read in full. Starting with a common term would walk millions of postings only to throw almost all of them away, for exactly the same answer.

sdsd:09.04.q: Why does IDF push down words like "the"?
sdsd:09.04.s: IDF is log(N / df), where N is the number of documents and df the number containing the term. A word like "the" appears in nearly every document, so df is close to N, the ratio is close to 1, and its logarithm is close to 0. Its tf-idf weight in every document is therefore near zero however many times it appears, so it barely changes any score or ranking. Rare terms that actually distinguish relevant documents get large weights, and the log keeps very rare terms from completely swamping the rest.

sdsd:09.05.q: What problem with TF-IDF does BM25's saturation (k1) fix?
sdsd:09.05.s: In tf-idf the score grows linearly with term frequency, so a document that repeats a word 50 times scores 50 times higher on that term than one that uses it once. That rewards keyword stuffing and over-weights long, repetitive documents, even though the 50th mention adds almost no evidence of relevance. BM25's term-frequency part, tf × (k1 + 1) / (tf + k1 × L), saturates: the first few occurrences raise the score a lot, later ones add less and less, and the contribution can never exceed k1 + 1 (2.2 with the default k1 = 1.2). Lower k1 saturates sooner; k1 = 0 counts only presence.

sdsd:09.06.q: What do champion lists trade away to make queries faster?
sdsd:09.06.s: They give up exactness. Only documents in at least one query term's precomputed top r list are scored, so a document that is a strong match for the whole query but not in the top r for any single term (for example ranked 600th for each word alone but best for both together) is never seen. The lists are chosen at index time without knowing the query, so they can't adapt to filters or term combinations; if r is smaller than the number of results needed, or many champions fail filters, the page may not fill; and the lists go stale until rebuilt.

sdsd:09.07.q: List the steps between a user's raw query and the index lookup.
sdsd:09.07.s: Normalise characters (lower-case, fold accents, unify Unicode and punctuation), tokenise (handling hyphens, symbols and languages without spaces), apply stemming or lemmatisation, correct spelling, segment the query into phrases such as "new york", recognise entities like brands, categories and price constraints, and classify the query's intent and category. Then rewrite it: expand synonyms, restrict parts to fields such as brand, turn constraints like "under $100" into structured filters, and relax it by dropping the least important term if it would match nothing. The resulting structured query is what is looked up in the index.

sdsd:09.08.q: Why are clicks a biased relevance signal? Name one bias.
sdsd:09.08.s: Clicks depend on where and how a result was shown, not only on how relevant it is. The main example is position bias: people click higher results much more often simply because they look at them first and often stop early, so a mediocre top result can collect more clicks than an excellent one at position 5. Other examples are presentation bias (images and ratings attract clicks), selection bias (results never shown get no clicks) and clickbait (a click followed by a quick return). Training on raw clicks would teach the model to keep ranking whatever was already on top, so clicks are reweighted by the probability each position was examined, combined with stronger signals like purchases, and supplemented with a little exploration.

sdsd:09.09.q: When is recall more important than precision?
sdsd:09.09.s: Recall matters more when missing a relevant document is costly and reading extra results is cheap by comparison: legal discovery (paralegals must find every relevant document), intelligence analysis, patent prior-art and medical systematic-review searches, compliance checks, finding one specific email in your own mailbox, and the first candidate-generation stage of a ranking pipeline, where anything not retrieved can never be ranked later. Web and shopping search usually favour precision because users only look at the first few results.

sdsd:09.10.q: Why is dual-writing to the DB and the search index risky? What's the safer pattern?
sdsd:09.10.s: Dual writes are not atomic: if the database write succeeds and the index write fails or the app crashes in between, the index stays wrong indefinitely, and concurrent updates can reach the index in a different order from the one in which they committed, leaving stale values; any script or code path that forgets the second write also causes drift. The safer pattern is log-based change data capture: the app writes only to the database, a tool such as Debezium reads the write-ahead log or binlog and publishes ordered change events (including deletes) to Kafka keyed by ID, and an idempotent indexer upserts each document using the log position as an external version, resuming from its offset after failures. For complex documents, the same can be done through a transactional outbox table.

sdsd:09.11.q: Document-partitioned vs term-partitioned index: which is more common and why?
sdsd:09.11.s: Document partitioning is far more common (Elasticsearch, Solr and web search engines use it). Each shard holds a full index of its own documents, so it can intersect postings and score locally and return only a small top-K list; a new document touches only one shard; load spreads evenly because every shard gets a similar slice of every term; and losing a shard only hides some documents. Term partitioning has to ship long postings lists between machines to answer multi-term queries, concentrates load on machines holding popular terms, and makes each new document update many machines. The price of document partitioning is that every query goes to every shard (so tail latency depends on the slowest one) and idf has to be kept global or approximated from local statistics.

sdsd:09.12.q: How does a crawler avoid hammering a single site?
sdsd:09.12.s: It never lets two fetches to the same host happen at once and spaces requests out per host. In the Mercator frontier, each back queue holds URLs for one host only (and each host has only one back queue), and a min-heap records the earliest time each host may be contacted again; a thread takes one URL from the queue whose time has come, fetches it, and the host must then wait a gap of roughly ten times that fetch's duration, so slow or struggling servers are automatically hit less often. Crawl-delay, 429 and 503 responses with Retry-After lengthen the wait, robots.txt is cached per host and checked just before fetching, and the crawl is partitioned by host so one machine enforces each host's limits, with about three times as many back queues as threads so many hosts are in rotation.

sdsd:09.13.q: Why combine BM25 with vector search instead of using only one?
sdsd:09.13.s: Because they fail in different places. BM25 is precise for exact tokens such as product codes, names, error messages and rare terms, but misses documents that express the same idea in different words. Vector search over embeddings catches synonyms, paraphrases and natural-language questions, but blurs exact identifiers and can rank near-misses highly. Running both in parallel and merging with reciprocal rank fusion, which only uses each document's rank in each list (summing 1/(60 + rank)), rewards documents both methods find and gets the strengths of each without having to make their incompatible scores comparable. Evaluations consistently show the hybrid beats either alone.

sdsd:09.14.q: Why cache the top 5 completions at each trie node?
sdsd:09.14.s: Without the cache, answering a prefix means traversing the whole subtree below its node and sorting every completion by frequency, which for a short prefix like "s" means visiting millions of nodes on every keystroke, far too slow for the few milliseconds available while a user types. Caching the top 5 completions at each node, computed when the trie is built, makes a lookup just a walk down the prefix plus one read, effectively constant time. The cost is extra memory (k entries per node, kept small by limiting the trie to popular queries) and that a count change affects every ancestor's list, so the trie is rebuilt periodically offline instead of updated per search.

sdsd:09.15.q: Why do you need both edit distance and word frequency to correct "speling"?
sdsd:09.15.s: Edit distance alone finds several known words one edit from "speling" (for example "spelling" and "spewing") and can't say which the user meant, while word frequency alone would pick very common words like "the" that look nothing like what was typed. In the model correction = argmax P(c) × P(w | c), edit distance acts as the error model, limiting candidates to plausible typos and preferring fewer edits, and frequency acts as the language model, picking the likeliest among the nearest candidates. So "spelling" wins because it is both one edit away and far more common than the alternatives.

sdsd:09.16.q: How would you mine "related searches" from query logs?
sdsd:09.16.s: Split the logs into sessions and count pairs where query B follows query A, giving extra weight to reformulations where A got no clicks and B did. Add pairs of queries that lead to clicks on the same documents, using the query-document click graph. Normalise by overall popularity (lift or PMI) so generic queries like "weather" don't dominate, require a minimum count and number of distinct users so rare or private queries never surface, drop near-duplicates, diversify across meanings, filter unsafe suggestions, and keep only queries that perform well. Store the top few per query in a key-value table rebuilt daily in a batch job, with content- or embedding-based fallbacks for rare queries.

sdsd:09.17.q: Store the last 10 searches per user. Where, with what eviction, and what about privacy?
sdsd:09.17.s: Use a Redis list per user (key recent:{user_id}), sharded by user across a Redis cluster; at under 1 KB per user, 10 million users need about 10 GB. On each search, asynchronously and in one MULTI/EXEC or Lua script, LREM any older copy of the query, LPUSH it to the head, LTRIM the list to indexes 0 to 9 and refresh an EXPIRE such as 90 days; read it with LRANGE 0 9. Eviction is by recency: the oldest entry falls off when an eleventh distinct search is pushed. Add a durable key-value copy only if history must sync across devices or persist, and use browser local storage for logged-out users. For privacy, let users delete single entries, clear all or turn history off, limit retention, delete it (and any durable copy) with the account or on a legal request, and never feed individual histories into suggestions shown to others.

sdsd:10.01.q: Why does one counter row in a DB fall over at 50k increments per second?
sdsd:10.01.s: Every increment must take an exclusive lock on the same row and hold it until its commit is flushed to the log, so all 50,000 writers queue on one lock and one sequence of commits. With around 1 ms per commit that caps the row at roughly a thousand to a few thousand updates per second; the waiting transactions exhaust the connection pool and the whole database stalls. Extra CPUs or replicas don't help, MVCC creates a dead row version per update, and a single row cannot be sharded. The fixes are to aggregate in memory (Redis INCR, or a stream consumer partitioned by key that sums counts and flushes one write per few seconds) and to split a hot counter into several sub-counters that are summed on read.

sdsd:10.02.q: Why did Reddit accept approximate view counts?
sdsd:10.02.s: Reddit wanted unique viewers counted in real time, which done exactly means keeping the set of every viewer ID per post and checking it on every view. For posts with over a million viewers that is 8 MB or more each plus a set lookup per view, multiplied across thousands of active posts, which was too heavy on memory and CPU, while a batch job would not be real time. A HyperLogLog gives a count within about 1% (0.81% standard error in Redis) using at most 12 KB, and far less for small posts thanks to the sparse encoding. Since a view count is only a popularity signal shown to users, not a billing figure, being within a few percent was explicitly good enough, so the product requirement allowed a much cheaper design.

sdsd:10.03.q: How do you avoid counting the same impression twice when events are retried?
sdsd:10.03.s: Attach a unique impression ID, signed with an HMAC so clients can't forge new ones, to every ad shown, and make it the idempotency key. The ingest service verifies the signature, checks the ID against a cache of recently seen IDs and drops repeats, appending the event to Kafka before marking the ID so a crash can cause a duplicate but never a loss. The stream processor keys events by impression ID to drop any duplicates that got through, uses checkpoints that save state and Kafka offsets together so replays after a crash don't double-count, and writes results as upserts keyed by ad and minute so retried writes are harmless. A daily batch job over raw events deduplicates by impression ID and corrects anything the real-time path missed.

sdsd:10.04.q: Why does the longest run of leading zeros in hashes estimate the number of unique items?
sdsd:10.04.s: With a uniform hash, each bit is an independent fair coin, so a hash starting with k zeros then a 1 has probability 1 in 2ᵏ⁺¹; a long run only becomes likely after many different hashes have been seen, so a maximum run of r suggests about 2ʳ items. The same item always produces the same hash, so duplicates can never raise the maximum, which is why it counts distinct items rather than events. One maximum is very noisy (a single lucky hash can overstate the count many times), so HLL uses the first bits of the hash to split items over many registers, keeps the maximum per register, and combines them with a harmonic mean, giving a standard error of 1.04/√m.

sdsd:10.05.q: Why can you merge HLL sketches from 100 servers but not merge their exact distinct counts?
sdsd:10.05.s: An exact distinct count is just a number; adding numbers from 100 servers counts every user seen on several servers multiple times, and nothing in the numbers says how big the overlap was, so it can't be removed.
