An HLL sketch keeps, for each register, the largest leading-zero value of the hashes routed there; a given user always produces the same hash, so they set the same register to the same value on every server. Taking the register-wise maximum across the 100 sketches therefore yields exactly the sketch you would have built from all the data in one place, counting each user once, and you can query it for the global estimate.

sdsd:10.06.q: Show the clicks in the last hour updated every minute. How many buckets do you keep?
sdsd:10.06.s: Keep 60 one-minute buckets of click counts, plus the one currently filling, in a ring buffer. Each click increments the bucket for the minute it happened in (event time). When a minute closes, after the watermark passes its end, add that bucket to a running total and subtract the bucket from 60 minutes ago, so each update is O(1) rather than re-counting the hour, and late events within the allowed lateness re-fire their bucket as an upsert. The bucket size sets the update granularity; for older data, roll minute buckets up into hour and day buckets, and for distinct counts or percentiles store a mergeable sketch per bucket and merge the 60 instead of subtracting.

sdsd:10.07.q: Why keep raw events if you already have aggregated tables?
sdsd:10.07.s: Aggregated tables throw information away and bake in today's grouping and logic: a per-minute count can't be split by a new dimension, have a newly discovered bot filtered out, or be checked against an advertiser's dispute. With raw events kept as the immutable source of truth (in Kafka for recent data and cheap columnar storage for history), you can fix a bug or filter and recompute the aggregates, build new metrics over past data, reconcile real-time results against a batch recomputation, and backfill new stores and models. Kappa-style, you replay the retained log through the corrected code into a new table and switch over once it catches up, instead of maintaining a second batch implementation.

sdsd:10.08.q: Count-min overestimates but never underestimates. Why?
sdsd:10.08.s: Each occurrence of an item increments one cell in every row, and no operation ever subtracts, so every cell the item maps to holds its true count plus the counts of whatever other items happened to collide there. Counts are never negative, so that collision noise is always zero or more, and every one of the item's cells is at least its true count. The minimum of numbers that are all at least the true count is also at least the true count, so the estimate can only be too high; taking the minimum simply picks the least-polluted cell, and with independent hash functions per row it is unlikely that all of them collided with heavy items.

sdsd:10.09.q: Find the top 10 hashtags over the last hour from 1M events/s. Sketch the pipeline.
sdsd:10.09.s: Send hashtag events to Kafka partitioned by hashtag (64 or more partitions) so each worker sees every occurrence of its hashtags and its counts are complete, salting any extremely hot tag. Each worker counts per hashtag in 1-minute buckets (exactly, or with count-min plus a heap or Misra-Gries if the key space is huge) and keeps a running hour per hashtag by adding the new minute and subtracting the expired one, with a min-heap tracking its local top 100. Every minute, workers send their local top lists to a merger; because the key sets are disjoint, the top 10 of the union is the global top 10, which the merger writes to Redis for the API to read. Using hourly rather than per-minute local lists avoids missing hashtags that are steady but never top in a single minute.

sdsd:10.10.q: Sample 1,000 items uniformly from a stream of unknown length. Explain the replacement probability.
sdsd:10.10.s: Fill the reservoir with the first 1,000 items. For the i-th item after that, draw a random integer from 1 to i; if it is at most 1,000, the item replaces that slot, so item i is kept with probability 1,000/i and evicts a uniformly random current member. By induction: an existing item is evicted at step i only if the new item is kept and picks its slot, probability (1,000/i) × (1/1,000) = 1/i, so if it was in the sample with probability 1,000/(i−1) it remains with probability 1,000/(i−1) × (i−1)/i = 1,000/i. The new item also has 1,000/i, so every item seen so far has the same probability 1,000/i of being in the sample at every point, using only 1,000 slots of memory.

sdsd:10.11.q: Why does t-digest keep more detail near the tails?
sdsd:10.11.s: Tail quantiles such as p99 and p99.9 are what people actually monitor, and they need accuracy relative to the edge: a quantile error of 0.001 is invisible at the median but turns p99.9 into p99.8, which can be a very different latency. Tail values are also spread far apart, so merging two slow requests into one centroid would report a latency neither had, while values in the dense middle are packed together and can be merged with little loss. t-digest's scale function therefore limits centroids to a tiny size, down to single values, near q = 0 and q = 1, and lets them grow to hundreds of thousands of values near the median, spending a fixed few kilobytes where the precision matters.

sdsd:10.12.q: Why can't you average p99s from 10 servers to get the global p99?
sdsd:10.12.s: A p99 is a single point of each server's distribution, not something that adds. Servers handle different amounts of traffic, and the global p99 is determined by where the slowest 1% of all requests fall, which may be almost entirely on one degraded server: with nine servers at 100 ms and one at 2 s handling a tenth of traffic, the average of p99s is 290 ms while the true global p99 is close to 2 s. No formula recovers the global value from ten percentiles, because the rest of each distribution has been thrown away. Instead, ship additive data such as histogram bucket counts or mergeable sketches like t-digest, sum or merge them across servers, and compute the global p99 once from the combined distribution.

sdsd:10.13.q: 1M viewers, 10k reactions/s. How do you aggregate and push without sending every reaction to everyone?
sdsd:10.13.s: Treat reactions as counts, not messages, because a heart from one user looks the same as a heart from any other. Clients POST reactions to stateless ingest servers that count per video and reaction type in memory and emit partial counts every 200 ms; an aggregator per video (Kafka partitioned by video, sharded for the hottest streams) sums the partials and publishes one update per tick, with the tick's counts and the running total, to that video's pub/sub channel. Realtime servers, which hold the video's viewers grouped by consistent hashing at the load balancer, receive the update once each and push it over SSE. Each viewer then gets about 5 small updates per second (about 5 million messages per second in total instead of 10 billion), whether there are 10,000 or a million reactions per second, and the client animates the counts and shows its own taps instantly.

sdsd:11.01.q: A user's WebSocket lands on server 7. How does a message from server 2 reach them?
sdsd:11.01.s: Server 7 registers interest when the user connects: it subscribes to a pub/sub topic for that user or for their channels (or, as with Slack's channel servers, each channel is owned by a server found through consistent hashing, and gateway 7 subscribes to the owners of the user's channels). When the message is sent, server 2 first writes it to the database, then publishes it to the recipient's topic or hands it to the channel's owner. The broker or owner forwards it to every server subscribed, including server 7, which pushes it down the open socket. If the user is offline or the push is lost, nothing breaks: on reconnect the client, possibly on a different server, fetches every message newer than its last seen ID from the database.

sdsd:11.02.q: Live sports scores: WebSocket or SSE? Why?
sdsd:11.02.s: SSE. Scores flow one way, from server to fans, and only a few times a minute, so a two-way channel is unnecessary, and anything a fan sends can be an ordinary POST. SSE runs over ordinary HTTP, so it passes through existing load balancers, proxies and CDNs, multiplexes over HTTP/2 (avoiding the 6-connection limit of HTTP/1.1) and uses normal cookie auth; EventSource reconnects automatically after a mobile network drop and sends Last-Event-ID so the server resumes exactly where the fan left off. WebSockets would add a protocol upgrade, stateful two-way connections and hand-written reconnect logic for no benefit; they suit cases where clients also send frequent real-time messages, such as chat or games.
sdsd:11.02.t: WebSockets vs SSE vs long polling

sdsd:11.03.q: Model follows so both "who I follow" and "who follows me" are fast.
sdsd:11.03.s: Use an edges table keyed by (follower_id, followee_id), which answers "who do I follow" as a range scan, "does A follow B" as a point lookup, and prevents duplicate follows, plus an index or second table keyed by (followee_id, created_at, follower_id) for "who follows me", newest first and pageable. When sharded, keep two copies of each edge, one in a following table partitioned by follower and one in a followers table partitioned by followee, written together through a transactional outbox or retrying queue with idempotent upserts, so each query touches a single shard instead of scattering to all of them. Store follower and following counts as counters rather than counting rows, batching increments for celebrities.

sdsd:11.04.q: Why did Twitter store each edge twice (forward and backward)?
sdsd:11.04.s: Because the graph was split across many shards by each row's first ID, a lookup is only cheap if all the rows it needs sit together on one shard. Storing the forward edge with the source and the backward edge with the destination makes both "whom does X follow" and "who follows X" single-shard, sorted, pageable reads. With a single copy, one of those two common queries, including the follower lookup needed to fan out every tweet, would have to scatter to every shard and wait for the slowest. The cost is double storage and two writes per change, which is cheap because follows are written far less often than they are read, and the copies are kept consistent with timestamped, idempotent writes that are retried until both succeed.

sdsd:11.05.q: Explain the hybrid model: who gets push and who gets pull?
sdsd:11.05.s: Accounts with ordinary follower counts get push: when they post, async workers prepend the new post's ID to every active follower's precomputed feed (skipping dormant users), so reads are a single lookup. Accounts above a tuned follower threshold, the celebrities, get pull: their posts are not fanned out at all, and when a user opens the feed, the service takes the precomputed feed and merges in the recent posts of the few celebrities that user follows, which are cheap to fetch because millions of readers hit the same cached timelines. This avoids tens of millions of writes per celebrity post, and the out-of-order delivery they cause, while keeping each feed read to one lookup plus a handful of cache fetches.

sdsd:11.06.q: Store last-read message ID per user per channel. How do you compute "has unread" cheaply?
sdsd:11.06.s: Keep the newest message ID on each channel and, per user per channel, the last read message ID, updated monotonically when the user catches up. Because message IDs increase over time, "has unread" is a single comparison, channel.last_message_id > last_read_id, with no messages scanned and no per-message read flags; dense per-channel sequence numbers turn an exact unread count into one subtraction too. Serve both values from RAM (a cache of read states partitioned by user and a cache of channel heads), batch-load them for all of a user's channels on connect, keep a separate mention counter, and persist read states lazily with coalesced writes, as Discord does with an LRU cache flushed to Cassandra 30 seconds after an update or on eviction.

sdsd:11.07.q: Tags in an array column vs a separate tag table: tradeoffs for "all posts with #x"?
sdsd:11.07.s: An array column with a GIN index keeps one row per post, is simple, and handles multi-tag queries with @> or &&, but GIN's posting lists are ordered by row, not time, so getting the newest 20 posts for a popular tag means fetching and sorting millions of matches; GIN writes are also relatively costly, and the index can't be sharded by tag because tags live with their posts. A separate tag table keyed by (tag, created_at, post_id) costs an extra row per tag per post, but "all posts with #x, newest first" becomes a 20-row range scan with keyset pagination at any depth, per-tag counts are easy to maintain, and the table can be partitioned by tag (plus a time bucket for very hot tags). Use the array for small datasets and multi-tag filters, and the tag table at scale.

sdsd:11.08.q: Store reactions per post. How do you show counts fast and still know if I reacted?
sdsd:11.08.s: Store each reaction as a row keyed by (post_id, user_id), which guarantees one reaction per user per post and makes changing or removing it an update of that row, and keep per-post counts per reaction type in a separate counter, cached and updated by events emitted only when a reaction row actually changes (batched or sharded for viral posts). To render a page, read counts for all posts with one multi-get from the cache and the viewer's own reactions with one batch query on a (user_id, post_id) index or user-keyed copy, optionally skipping lookups with a per-user Bloom filter. Show the user's own tap immediately on the client, and reconcile counters against the rows periodically to fix drift.

sdsd:11.09.q: Why store tag positions as fractions (0-1) of image size instead of pixels?
sdsd:11.09.s: The same photo is displayed at many sizes (thumbnails, phone, desktop, retina, the original, cropped previews), so a pixel position is only correct for the exact size it was captured at, and lands in the wrong place or off the image everywhere else; it is even ambiguous between CSS and device pixels. Fractions of width and height are independent of resolution: one stored value maps to any rendition by multiplying by its displayed width and height, including renditions and formats created later, and invalid values are easy to detect because they fall outside 0 to 1. Crops, rotation and letterboxing change the frame, so you map through the crop rectangle, normalise EXIF orientation on upload and use the image's actual rendered rectangle.

sdsd:11.10.q: How do you shard live commentary pub/sub by event to handle a World Cup final?
sdsd:11.10.s: Partition pub/sub by event: each event's comments go to a channel chosen by hash(eventId) mod N, and an L7 load balancer uses consistent hashing on the event ID so its viewers sit on the same few realtime servers, which subscribe only to that channel, so each comment crosses the server network as few times as possible. The World Cup final is a single hot key, so it is marked hot and its viewers are spread over a group of thousands of servers (hashing viewer within the event), all subscribed to the event's channel. Each comment is persisted once, filtered, sampled down to a readable rate that adapts to velocity (1 to 2% or less at a goal), batched every few hundred milliseconds and fanned out through a relay tier so no node sends to more than a bounded number of children; recent-comment history and, for the very largest audiences, snapshots of the stream are served from a cache or CDN, and the fleet is pre-scaled before kick-off.

sdsd:12.01.q: Why can't you index lat and lng separately and query both ranges efficiently?
sdsd:12.01.s: A B-tree sorts on one value, so a latitude index returns a band around the whole globe and a longitude index a band from pole to pole; even a composite (lat, lng) index only orders by the second column within equal first values, which almost never happen for real numbers. Either way the database reads tens or hundreds of thousands of entries to find the few hundred in the small area where the two ranges intersect, because a one-dimensional order cannot keep two-dimensional neighbours together. Spatial trees (quadtrees, R-trees, BKD trees) or cell encodings along a space-filling curve (geohash, S2, H3) keep nearby points together so only a small region is read, followed by an exact distance filter.

sdsd:12.02.q: Two nearby points can have very different geohashes. When, and how do you handle it?
sdsd:12.02.s: It happens whenever two points sit on opposite sides of a cell boundary: they can be a metre apart yet differ from an early character, because the boundary belongs to a coarse level of the halving (the north neighbours of dr5ru start dr72), and at the equator or prime meridian they may share no prefix at all because the very first bits differ. The antimeridian and poles cause the same effect. Handle it by choosing a precision whose cells are at least as large as the search radius, scanning the query point's cell plus its eight neighbouring cells (a 3 by 3 block that always covers the circle), and then filtering the candidates by exact haversine distance.

sdsd:12.03.q: Why do hexagons have more uniform neighbour distances than squares?
sdsd:12.03.s: A hexagon's six neighbours all share a full edge with it, and by symmetry all six centres are the same distance away; no neighbour touches only at a corner. A square has four edge neighbours at distance d and four corner neighbours at about 1.41d, so its neighbours sit at two different distances (triangles have three). With one distance, rings of hexagons approximate circles, smoothing can give every neighbour the same weight, movement always crosses into exactly one neighbour, and spatial maths needs a single set of coefficients; squares make diagonal directions behave differently from axis directions.

sdsd:12.04.q: Drivers update location every 4 s. Why keep that in Redis rather than Postgres?
sdsd:12.04.s: Location updates are hundreds of thousands of overwrites per second of data that is useless after about 30 seconds and refills itself within 4 seconds if lost. Postgres would pay for each update with a new MVCC row version, a spatial index insertion, WAL writes and fsync, replication to replicas and later vacuum, all to make worthless data durable. Redis keeps the positions in memory as 52-bit geohash scores in a sorted set, so GEOADD is an O(log N) in-memory update and GEOSEARCH answers radius queries with a few range scans in under a millisecond; durability is unnecessary because the next update rebuilds the state. Trips and sampled history go to a durable database on a separate, asynchronous path.

sdsd:12.05.q: You have 100k geofences. How do you avoid testing every polygon per location update?
sdsd:12.05.s: Use a two-stage filter and refine. Index the geofences' bounding boxes in a spatial index (an R-tree, which PostGIS uses automatically for ST_Contains) so each update finds only the handful of fences whose boxes contain the point in a few dozen comparisons, then run the exact point-in-polygon test on those few. For very high rates, precompute a covering of each fence with grid cells (H3, S2 or geohash) into a cell-to-fences map marking interior and boundary cells: a point in an interior or empty cell is answered by one hash lookup, and only boundary cells need an exact test against one or two polygons. Caching each vehicle's last cell and emitting only enter and exit events cuts the work further.

sdsd:12.06.q: Why does an odd number of crossings mean "inside"?
sdsd:12.06.s: A simple polygon's boundary divides the plane into an inside and an outside (the Jordan curve theorem), and the only way to move from one region to the other is to cross the boundary. The far end of the ray, beyond every edge, is certainly outside. Walking back along the ray from there to the point, each edge crossing flips you between outside and inside, so after an even number of crossings you are back outside and after an odd number you are inside, whatever the polygon's shape. Vertices lying on the ray are handled with a half-open rule so each true crossing is counted exactly once.

sdsd:12.07.q: A dating app must never show a profile twice. Bloom filter or exact set, and what happens on a false positive?
sdsd:12.07.s: A Bloom filter fits, because its errors go only one way: once a profile is added its bits are set and never cleared, so the filter never says "not seen" for a swiped profile and it is never shown again. A false positive means an unseen profile is judged "seen" and silently skipped, a small loss of one potential match at the designed rate (for example 1% with about 24 KB and 7 hashes for 20,000 swipes), not a violation of the rule, and nobody notices in a large pool. Size the filter for the expected number of swipes, keep the exact swipe log as the durable source of truth, grow or rebuild the filter before it overfills (its error rate climbs quickly past the design size), and use an exact set for users with very small candidate pools or for rules like blocks that must be exact.
sdsd:12.07.t: Seen filtering: Bloom vs exact sets

sdsd:12.08.q: Why split recommendations into candidate generation and ranking?
sdsd:12.08.s: The precise ranking model, with hundreds of user, item and context features, costs around a millisecond per item, so running it on millions of items per request would take hours of compute. Candidate generation uses cheap methods prepared offline, such as ANN search over two-tower embeddings, co-occurrence maps or follow graphs, to cut the catalogue to a few hundred items in milliseconds with high recall; the expensive ranker can then order that shortlist precisely within the latency budget using fresh request-time features. The split also lets each stage optimise its own goal (recall versus top-of-list precision), lets several retrieval sources feed one ranker, and leaves a re-ranking step for diversity and business rules.

sdsd:13.01.q: Why upload directly to object storage instead of through your app servers?
sdsd:13.01.s: Proxying makes every byte cross your servers twice, ties up connections, threads and buffers for the full length of slow uploads, runs into gateway request size and timeout limits, and forces you to scale API servers just to move data that object storage is built to absorb. With a presigned URL, the backend only authorises the upload and signs a short-lived URL for one server-chosen object key (optionally fixing size, type and checksum); the client sends the bytes straight to object storage, and an object-created event updates the pending database record, with reconciliation jobs and lifecycle rules cleaning up abandoned uploads.

sdsd:13.02.q: Resize on upload or resize on request? Tradeoffs?
sdsd:13.02.s: Resizing on upload makes every variant a ready static file with no request-time work and catches bad images early, but you must know the sizes up front, adding a size or format means reprocessing every image ever uploaded, and you store and compute variants that may never be viewed. Resizing on request generates any size or format the first time it is asked for and lets the CDN cache it for a year, so storage and compute follow actual demand and new layouts need no backfill; the costs are a one-time delay on the first view of each variant (and cold-cache storms after a redesign, softened by an origin shield or pre-warming) and the need for signed URLs, allowed sizes and decode limits to prevent abuse. Many systems pre-generate the common sizes and serve the rest on demand.

sdsd:13.03.q: How does Gravatar serve an avatar from just an email, and how would you cache it?
sdsd:13.03.s: The site trims and lower-cases the user's email, hashes it with SHA-256 and requests gravatar.com/avatar/<hash> with a size (1 to 2048, default 80) and a default-image option; Gravatar looks up the account by hash and returns its image resized, or, if there is none or its rating is too high, a 404, a silhouette or a deterministic generated image such as an identicon, so no lookup call is ever needed. To cache it, put a CDN in front with a small set of allowed sizes and normalised parameters; fixed URLs need a modest expiry (minutes to an hour) or purges, so it is better, in your own service, to use versioned image URLs cached for a year as immutable, changing the URL whenever the avatar changes, and to cache "no avatar" responses briefly too.

sdsd:13.04.q: A 5 GB upload fails at 80%. How does multipart upload let you resume?
sdsd:13.04.s: The file was started as a multipart upload with an upload ID, and each part acknowledged so far (about 400 of 500 with 10 MB parts) has a part number and ETag saved persistently by the client, the server or both. Initiated uploads do not expire, so after the failure the client resumes the same upload ID, optionally verifies received parts with ListParts, gets fresh presigned URLs and uploads only the parts that were not acknowledged (roughly the last 20%, possibly in parallel), then calls complete with all part numbers and ETags so the store assembles the object. Only the parts in flight at the failure are re-sent, not the whole 5 GB.
sdsd:13.04.t: Video upload: signed URLs and multipart

sdsd:13.05.q: Why split a video into chunks before transcoding?
sdsd:13.05.s: Encoding a whole film sequentially on one machine can take days, needs the entire huge source on local disk, and loses all progress if the machine fails late. Splitting it at keyframes into chunks lets many machines encode in parallel, so time stays roughly constant regardless of length (Netflix went from days to a few hours), a failed or reclaimed spot instance only costs one chunk's retry, each worker needs little storage, each chunk can be quality-checked as soon as it finishes, and the short tasks fit cheap elastic capacity. The price is reassembling chunks in the right order without dropped or duplicated frames and verifying the stitched stream, which Netflix does by comparing fingerprints with the source.

sdsd:13.06.q: Who decides the bitrate in ABR, the server or the player?
sdsd:13.06.s: The player. In HTTP adaptive streaming the server or CDN only serves the manifest and segment files and keeps no per-viewer state; the client measures its download throughput, buffer level and device capabilities and chooses which rendition to request for each next segment, starting low, stepping up when segments arrive fast and the buffer is healthy, and stepping down before the buffer empties. Keeping the logic in the client is what lets segments be cached on CDNs for millions of viewers. The service may separately steer which CDN or edge the player uses (through the URLs in the manifest, DNS or content steering), but the bitrate choice is client-side.
sdsd:13.06.t: Adaptive bitrate and the CDN decider

sdsd:13.07.q: Signed URLs stop link sharing. What do they not stop that DRM tries to?
sdsd:13.07.s: Signed URLs only control access to the files: who can download them and until when (and optionally from which IP), checked at the CDN edge. They do not stop an authorised user, while the URL or cookie is valid, from saving the downloaded segments, stitching them into a file and sharing or re-hosting it, because the content itself is unencrypted. DRM addresses that: the video is encrypted, and keys are issued through a licence server, after an entitlement check and with rules such as expiry, resolution limits and device counts, only to a protected decryption module (via EME in browsers) that decrypts for playback without exposing the key or, on hardware-backed devices, the decoded frames. Even DRM cannot stop filming the screen, which is why premium services add forensic watermarking.
sdsd:13.07.t: Signed URLs, DRM, and video security

sdsd:13.08.q: Why is HLS live latency 10+ seconds while WebRTC is sub-second?
sdsd:13.08.s: HLS works in whole files: the encoder must finish a multi-second segment before it can be published, the playlist must be updated and then discovered by the player's next poll, the CDN must fetch it, and players deliberately buffer about three segments to survive network hiccups, so 6-second segments alone add around 18 seconds and totals of 15 to 30 seconds are normal; that file-based, buffered, stateless design is what lets CDNs cache and serve millions cheaply. WebRTC streams individual frames as small RTP packets over UDP the moment they are encoded, does not block on retransmission (it conceals lost packets), keeps only a jitter buffer of tens to hundreds of milliseconds, adapts the encoder's bitrate in real time, and uses a direct or single-server path, so end-to-end delay is a few hundred milliseconds, at the cost of per-viewer media servers.

sdsd:13.09.q: A user edits 1 byte of a 1 GB file. How much should be uploaded?
sdsd:13.09.s: Roughly one block, not the file. Split the file into fixed blocks (Dropbox uses 4 MB) identified by SHA-256 hashes, so the file is a blocklist of 256 hashes. After the edit the client re-hashes and commits the new blocklist; only the block containing the changed byte has a new hash, so the server replies that it needs just that block, and the client uploads about 4 MB plus a blocklist of about 8 KB, around 0.4% of the file; other devices likewise download only that block. An rsync-style delta inside the block can cut it to a few kilobytes, and content-defined chunking keeps the cost small even when the edit inserts bytes and would otherwise shift every later fixed block boundary.

sdsd:13.10.q: What does content addressing give you for free? What's the problem with fixed-size blocks when bytes are inserted?
sdsd:13.10.s: Content addressing gives deduplication (identical content has the same hash and is stored once), integrity (data that does not hash to its key is corrupt or tampered with), cheap snapshots and versions (unchanged objects are reused by hash, and one root hash identifies a whole tree), cache-forever immutability (content at a hash never changes, so copies are never stale) and efficient sync by comparing hashes and sending only what the other side lacks. Fixed-size blocks are defined by position, so inserting or deleting even one byte shifts every later boundary and changes every later block's hash, making the rest of the file look new and defeating dedup. rsync's rolling checksum (matching blocks at any byte offset) or content-defined chunking (boundaries chosen by a rolling hash of the content, which resynchronise after the edit) solves it.

sdsd:13.11.q: A file version is a list of block hashes. How does that make version history cheap?
sdsd:13.11.s: Each version is just metadata, an immutable ordered list of block hashes, while the blocks themselves live once in a content-addressed store. A new version that changes a few blocks adds only those blocks plus one small row with a list of hashes; every unchanged block is shared with earlier versions by reference, so keeping hundreds of versions costs little more than the changes themselves (500 edits of a 200 MB file take about 4 GB, not 100 GB). Restoring an old version is a metadata write that points the file at an old list again, viewing one means fetching blocks the device mostly already has, and renames touch no data. The extra work is garbage-collecting blocks that no live version references, with grace periods so uncommitted uploads are not deleted.

sdsd:14.01.q: A checkout is slow. Which of logs, metrics and traces tells you which service is slow?
sdsd:14.01.s: Traces. Metrics show that checkout latency rose but are aggregated per service, and logs are per service and lack cross-service context. A trace follows one checkout request through every service as a tree of timed spans (connected by the propagated trace ID), so the waterfall shows directly which span, say the payment service's authorise call, takes most of the time. You then filter that service's logs by the trace ID to see why, and confirm the cause with a metric such as connection pool saturation.

sdsd:14.02.q: Your 99.9% SLO budget is half spent in week 1. What does the error budget policy say to do?
sdsd:14.02.s: Half the budget gone in week one means an average burn rate of 2: at that pace the budget runs out around the end of week two. You are not yet out, so the policy does not freeze everything, but reliability rises in priority now: do the incident's postmortem actions first, slow or postpone risky changes, and watch the slow-burn ticket alert. If the budget is exhausted, the policy freezes all changes except fixes and security patches and puts engineering time on reliability until the rolling window moves past the outage. Product, development and SRE agreed these actions in advance, so nobody has to argue about them now.

sdsd:14.03.q: Why separate the incident commander from the person fixing the problem?
sdsd:14.03.s: Fixing and coordinating need different kinds of attention. Fixing needs deep focus on one technical thread; coordinating needs a wide view of the whole incident: whether the current approach is still right, whether anyone is mitigating instead of diagnosing, who is working on what, and what stakeholders need to hear. One person cannot do both. In an unmanaged incident the on-call engineer gets absorbed in debugging, nobody coordinates helpers or communications, and someone freelances an untested change that makes things worse. A separate commander keeps the big picture, makes calls like "roll back now", shields the fixers from interruptions, and enforces that only the operations lead changes production.

sdsd:14.04.q: Why can a new version that writes a new data format make rollback unsafe?
sdsd:14.04.s: During a rolling or canary deployment, version N and N+1 run at the same time, and after a rollback version N must read whatever N+1 already wrote. If N+1 writes a format that N cannot read (compressed data, JSON instead of XML, a new required field), N hosts fail on that data mid-rollout, and rolling back leaves data the running code cannot read: the rollback does not undo the data. The fix is two phases: first deploy a version that reads both formats but still writes the old one, confirm it is on every host and let it bake, then deploy the version that writes the new format. Rolling back the second phase is safe because the first-phase version can read both.

sdsd:14.05.q: Why add a column as nullable first, backfill, then add NOT NULL?
sdsd:14.05.s: Adding a NOT NULL column directly can force the database to rewrite or scan the whole table under a heavy lock to fill or check the value, blocking traffic on a large table. It also breaks any old code still running during the deploy that inserts rows without the new column. Adding it as nullable is an instant metadata change that every version of the code tolerates. Code then starts writing the column, a batched backfill fills old rows without long locks or replication lag, and only when every row has a value do you add the constraint (in PostgreSQL as a NOT VALID check, then validated separately without blocking writes). Every step is small, safe while old and new code coexist, and reversible.

sdsd:14.06.q: How do you prove a new read path returns the same results before cutting over?
sdsd:14.06.s: Run both paths on live traffic with a tool like GitHub Scientist. The old path is the control and its result is always returned to the user. The new path runs as the candidate, its exceptions are caught and its result and timing are compared and published. First run control against control to learn the background noise, then start at a small percentage, investigate each mismatch and either fix it or add an explicit ignore or compare rule, and ramp up. Cut over only after a long period, covering rare jobs and big customers, with no unexplained mismatches. Keep dual writes so you can switch back, and never shadow code with side effects.

sdsd:14.07.q: Why is an untested backup not a backup?
sdsd:14.07.s: Because a backup's only purpose is the restore, and the restore path is exactly what silently breaks when it never runs: jobs that produce empty or partial files, lost encryption keys, missing tools or credentials, unreadable tapes, schemas that no longer match, or restores that take far longer than the outage you can afford. You only find out when you need it, which is the worst possible time. You only know you can recover if you actually do, so run restores continuously and automatically, verify the restored data and the time it took against your RTO, and alert when a restore test does not report success.

sdsd:14.08.q: Define RPO and RTO. Which DR strategy gives RTO of minutes?
sdsd:14.08.s: RPO (recovery point objective) is the most data the business can afford to lose, measured as time between the last copy that reached the recovery location and the disaster. RTO (recovery time objective) is the longest it can afford to be down, from the disaster (not from when someone notices) until service is restored. For an RTO of minutes, use warm standby: a scaled-down but fully working copy in another region with live data replication, which can serve traffic immediately after the database is promoted and traffic switched, and only needs scaling up. Active/active gets close to zero but costs much more and needs multi-region writes. Pilot light, which must start servers first, is typically tens of minutes, and backup and restore is hours.

sdsd:14.09.q: A user asks to be deleted. List every place their data might still exist.
sdsd:14.09.s: Primary databases across every service (the user row and everything that references it: posts, messages, orders); denormalised copies such as entries in other users' feeds, message threads and notifications; database replicas; caches and CDN copies; search indexes; object storage, including thumbnails and transcodes; event streams, queues and dead-letter queues; the data warehouse, data lake, ML training data and feature stores; application logs and traces; backups and archives; and third-party processors such as email, payments, analytics and support tools. Some data, such as invoices, may legally have to be kept, and backups are usually allowed to expire on a bounded schedule (or are made unreadable by destroying a per-user encryption key).

sdsd:14.10.q: Name 3 abuse vectors for a public signup endpoint and a defence for each.
sdsd:14.10.s: 1. Automated fake signups by bots (spam, free-tier abuse): rate limit per IP and per device, show a CAPTCHA only when traffic looks automated, and require email or phone verification before the account can act. 2. Account enumeration through "this email is already registered": return the same response with the same timing either way, and tell existing users by email instead. 3. SMS or email pumping through verification messages, which costs money per message: rate limit per phone number, number prefix and IP, block risky prefixes you do not serve, cap and alert on daily spend, and watch the sent-to-verified ratio. Also limit payload size and request time at the gateway against resource exhaustion.

sdsd:14.11.q: Rate limit by IP, user ID or API key? When each?
sdsd:14.11.s: Use **user ID** for authenticated traffic: it is fair per person and follows them across devices and IP addresses. Use **API key** for developer or B2B APIs, where limits match the customer's plan and billing and cover all of that customer's servers. Use **IP** for unauthenticated endpoints such as login, signup and public pages, and as a first line against floods, with higher limits because NAT puts many real users behind one IP (and by /64 prefix for IPv6). For login, also limit per target account so attacks spread across many IPs are caught. In practice combine them, with the most restrictive applicable rule winning.

sdsd:14.12.q: Why does a fixed window allow 2x the limit at a window boundary?
sdsd:14.12.s: A fixed window resets its counter at fixed calendar times, so it only limits requests inside each calendar window, not inside every rolling period of the same length. A client can use the whole limit at the very end of one window and the whole limit again at the start of the next, because the counter resets in between. For example, with 100 per minute, 100 requests at 12:00:59 and 100 at 12:01:00 are both allowed, giving 200 in about a second: twice the limit for any 60-second span that crosses the boundary. A sliding window counter fixes this by estimating 100 × 60/60 + 0 = 100 at 12:01:00 and rejecting the second burst.

sdsd:14.13.q: Shared tables with tenant_id vs a database per tenant: tradeoffs?
sdsd:14.13.s: Shared tables with a tenant_id are cheapest for many small tenants, make onboarding an insert, need one schema migration for everyone, and make cross-tenant analytics easy. But isolation depends on every query filtering correctly (row-level security and scoped credentials are the backstop), one tenant's heavy load can slow everyone, and per-tenant restore, data residency and per-tenant keys are hard. A database per tenant gives strong isolation even when code has bugs, no noisy neighbours, easy per-tenant backup, restore, residency and cost tracking, and suits regulated customers. But it wastes money on idle small tenants, onboarding means provisioning, and every migration runs thousands of times and can leave tenants on mixed versions. A common answer is to pool by default and silo large or regulated tenants.

sdsd:15.01.q: Base62 of an ID vs hash of the URL: which avoids collisions and why?
sdsd:15.01.s: Base62 of a unique ID avoids collisions. Each URL gets a distinct integer from a counter or ID generator, and Base62 is only a way of writing that number in 62 symbols, so two different IDs always give two different codes. Hashing the URL and keeping the first 7 characters throws most of the hash away, so different URLs can share the same 7 characters (by the birthday problem, after 1 billion links about 1 in 3,500 new links collides); you must check the database or a Bloom filter, rely on a unique index and rehash on a clash. The cost of Base62 IDs is that you need an ID generator, and codes are sequential and guessable unless you scramble the ID with a reversible permutation before encoding.

sdsd:15.02.q: How do 20 API servers share one rate limit per user?
sdsd:15.02.s: They share state. No server keeps its own counter; instead every request does an atomic check-and-decrement against the same per-user key in a central store like Redis: a token bucket (tokens and last refill time) updated by a Lua script that Redis runs as one step, so two servers cannot both spend the last token. Redis is sharded by the user key, so each user's bucket lives on exactly one shard, with a replica for failover, and a policy decides whether to fail open (with a coarse local fallback) if Redis is unreachable. However the load balancer spreads a user's requests, all 20 servers draw from the same bucket.

sdsd:15.03.q: Redirects are 100x writes. Where do you cache, and 301 or 302?
sdsd:15.03.s: Cache at every layer of the read path: a CDN or edge cache that answers popular links near users, an in-memory cache (Redis, plus a small in-process cache for hot keys) of code to long URL in front of the database, and indexed lookups on database replicas for the remaining misses. Links do not change, so the caches rarely need invalidating; just keep TTLs within any expiry and seed the cache on creation so new links work at once. With a 90% CDN hit rate and 99% Redis hit rate, a 600,000 per second peak leaves only about 600 per second for the database. Use 302 if you want click analytics, the ability to change, expire or block links, or to avoid browsers caching the redirect forever; the caching layers absorb the extra load, and clicks are logged asynchronously. Use 301 only if you never need to see or change repeat clicks.

sdsd:15.04.q: A product page is read 1M times per update. How do you keep price changes visible within seconds?
sdsd:15.04.s: Precompute a denormalised product view and serve it from layered caches (CDN, then Redis, then read replicas), since reads dwarf writes. For freshness, do not rely on TTLs: when a price changes, the write to the primary emits an event (via an outbox or change data capture), and a consumer overwrites the Redis entry with the new value and purges the CDN path, with a short TTL as a safety net. Serve price and stock as a small separate fragment with a very short cache time while the heavy page content stays cached for long. Overwrite rather than delete (or refill from the primary) so a lagging replica cannot re-cache the old price, use version numbers so out-of-order updates are ignored, coalesce requests to avoid a stampede, and have checkout always read the price from the source of truth.

sdsd:15.05.q: Two users type at the same position at once. How do OT and CRDTs each resolve it?
sdsd:15.05.s: Both users apply their own insert locally, then exchange operations. With OT, a central server puts the two inserts in a single order; the later one is transformed against the earlier, and because the positions are equal a fixed tie-break (for example, already-committed operation or lower user ID first) decides that it shifts one place right. Each client transforms the incoming operation against its own pending one using the same rule, so both end with the same text. With a CRDT, each insert refers to the unique ID of the character it follows, not to a position; both inserts follow the same character, so a deterministic rule on their own new IDs (counter, then site ID) decides which comes first. Every replica reaches the same order whatever order the operations arrive in, without needing a server.

sdsd:15.06.q: Draw an object store: API, metadata, data nodes, replication. Where is the bottleneck?
sdsd:15.06.s: API: PUT, GET (with ranges), DELETE and LIST by prefix on bucket/key over HTTP, plus multipart upload for large objects. A stateless front-end fleet authenticates and routes. A metadata service, partitioned by sorted key range, maps each key to the locations of its pieces and commits a key only after the data is durable, which gives read-after-write consistency. Storage nodes hold the data, either replicated (often 3 copies, 3× storage) or erasure coded (k data + m parity shards such as 10 + 4, any k rebuild it, 1.4× storage), spread across drives, racks and zones, with background repair and scrubbing. The main bottleneck is disk random I/O, about 120 IOPS per drive however large it gets, so hot data overloads disks unless every customer's data is spread thinly across very many drives; the second is hot key ranges in the metadata index, handled by splitting and moving ranges automatically.

sdsd:15.07.q: How does Kafka guarantee order, and over what scope?
sdsd:15.07.s: Kafka guarantees order only within a single partition: each partition is an append-only log, every message gets the next offset, the idempotent producer keeps retried batches in sequence, and consumers read a partition in offset order, with exactly one consumer per partition in a group. There is no order across partitions of a topic. Producers choose the partition by hashing the message key, so all messages with the same key (say the same order ID) go to the same partition and stay in order relative to each other. To keep related events ordered, give them the same key and do not change the partition count; keyless messages are spread across partitions and lose relative order.

sdsd:16.01.q: How do you avoid sending the same notification twice after a worker crash?
sdsd:16.01.s: Give every notification a unique ID (or a deterministic key such as order-123-shipped) and keep a notification log. Before calling the provider, a worker atomically claims the row (update status from queued to sending where status is still queued); after the provider accepts, it marks it sent and only then acknowledges the queue message. If the worker crashes and the job is redelivered, the next worker's claim fails because the row is already sent or being sent, so it skips. A crash between the provider accepting and the log update can still cause a rare duplicate: decide per message type whether a stale sending row is resent (rare duplicate) or dropped (rare loss), and pass the notification ID to providers that deduplicate, such as an APNs collapse ID, to close most of the window.

sdsd:16.02.q: How do you hold a seat for 10 minutes and release it if unpaid?
sdsd:16.02.s: Reserve with a claim that expires on its own. For example, Redis SET seat:A12 user42 NX EX 600 succeeds for only one buyer and Redis deletes the key after 10 minutes; or a reserved_until column where the claiming UPDATE treats a reservation whose reserved_until is in the past as available, so release is instant without depending on a cleanup job. When payment succeeds, an idempotent webhook marks the ticket sold in the database with a conditional write (only if not already sold), which stays the final guard even if Redis loses a hold. Extend the hold when payment starts so it does not expire mid-checkout. If the user never pays, the key or timestamp simply expires and the next buyer can claim the seat immediately.

sdsd:16.03.q: Your PSP call times out. Was the customer charged? How do you find out safely?
sdsd:16.03.s: You do not know: the request may have failed before reaching the PSP, failed midway, or the charge may have succeeded and only the response was lost. So mark the payment pending, not failed. Then retry with the same idempotency key and payload, so the PSP returns the stored original result if it charged and charges once if it did not; or query the PSP for the payment's status using your own reference or the key. PSP webhooks (handled idempotently) and a reconciliation job against the PSP's settlement reports settle anything left over. Never retry with a new key or ask the customer to pay again, which risks a double charge.

sdsd:16.04.q: How do new posts become searchable within seconds?
sdsd:16.04.s: Indexing is asynchronous and incremental. When a post is created, the posts service saves it and publishes an event to Kafka, then returns; ingestion workers consume the event, tokenise the text and append the new post's ID to each keyword's index lists, typically within tens of milliseconds to a few seconds, without slowing post creation. Consumer lag is monitored against the freshness target and workers scale out during bursts. In Elasticsearch, new documents sit in a buffer protected by the translog and become searchable at the next refresh, about every second, when a new immutable segment is written. Result caches use a TTL shorter than the freshness requirement so they never hide new posts for long.

sdsd:16.05.q: What's computed offline vs online in a recommender?
sdsd:16.05.s: Offline, in batch: training the embedding (for example two-tower) and ranking models, computing embeddings for every item, building ANN indexes and item-to-item similarity tables, and computing user and item features into a feature store (sometimes whole per-user lists for the most active users). Online, per request: building the context including the current session, running the user tower to embed the user, retrieving candidates via ANN and other generators such as similar-to-last-viewed and popular-in-region, filtering out seen or unavailable items, fetching features including real-time streaming ones, scoring the few hundred candidates with the ranking model, and re-ranking for diversity, freshness and business rules. The split exists because ranking every item per request would cost thousands of CPU-seconds.

sdsd:16.06.q: How does a message reach a user who is offline and later comes online on 2 devices?
sdsd:16.06.s: The sender's server first saves the message and creates an undelivered inbox entry for each of the recipient's registered devices, then acknowledges the sender. Because the recipient is offline, the live pub/sub publish reaches nobody, so a push notification goes out through APNs or FCM. When the first device comes online it connects to any chat server, fetches its pending inbox entries, receives the message and acknowledges it, which deletes only that device's entry. The second device does the same whenever it connects, because its own entry is still there. If an ack is lost the message is resent and the client deduplicates by ID. Alternatively, when history is kept forever, each device stores the last message ID it has seen and fetches everything newer on connect.

sdsd:16.07.q: Where does ranking happen in a feed, and what's precomputed?
sdsd:16.07.s: Ranking happens at read time: when the user opens the app, the feed service takes the precomputed candidates (post IDs fanned out to their feed list on write, plus recent posts from followed celebrities pulled at read time), fetches fresh features such as engagement in the last hour and whether the user has seen each post, scores the few hundred candidates with the ranking model, applies rules like author diversity, and hydrates the top page from the content, user and counter caches; the ranked order is cached for the session so paging stays stable. Precomputed ahead of time are the per-user lists of candidate post IDs, the social graph, slowly changing features such as user-author affinity and post embeddings, and the trained model itself.

sdsd:16.08.q: Search "pizza within 2 km". Combine text search and geo filter: which goes first?
sdsd:16.08.s: It depends on which filter is more selective, and the best answer is a single engine that does both, such as Elasticsearch with a text match plus a geo_distance filter, or PostGIS with full-text search, where the engine intersects the two sets and leads with the cheaper one. For "pizza", a common term, in a dense area, the 2 km geo filter shrinks the set most (thousands of nearby businesses against tens of thousands of pizza places worldwide), so filter by location first using geohash cells or a spatial index, then match "pizza". For a rare term such as an exact restaurant name or "ethiopian", matching text first gives a tiny set to distance-check. Either way, finish with exact distances because cells overshoot the circle, and rank by relevance, distance decay and rating.

sdsd:17.01.q: How do you stop two riders being matched to the same driver?
sdsd:17.01.s: Lock the driver before offering. The matcher runs an atomic SET lock:driver:ID ride NX EX 10 in Redis: only one matcher can create the key, so only one rider's offer goes to that driver, and any other matcher moves on to the next candidate. If the driver does not answer within 10 seconds, the key expires and the driver is free again without any cleanup job. When the driver accepts, the assignment is written to the database conditionally (only if the driver has no active ride and the ride is still in the matching state), so even if Redis loses a lock or a paused matcher acts on an expired one, the database stays the final guard against double assignment.

sdsd:17.02.q: Which videos go to the CDN and which are served from origin?
sdsd:17.02.s: Popular and trending videos, especially their first segments and the common renditions, are served from CDN edge caches near viewers, because a small share of videos gets most views and most of the bandwidth cost; predictable hits like premieres are pushed to edges in advance during off-peak hours. The long tail of rarely watched videos is served from origin object storage, usually through a regional shield cache that collapses repeated misses, because caching millions of rarely watched videos at every edge would evict popular content for almost no gain. In practice pull-through caching with LRU eviction sorts this out automatically.

sdsd:17.03.q: Two devices edit the same file offline. What happens on sync?
sdsd:17.03.s: When the devices reconnect, each tries to commit its edit stating the version it started from, and the server applies a compare-and-set on the file's version number. The first device's base version is still current, so its commit becomes the new version. The second device's base is now out of date, so its commit updates nothing and the server reports a conflict instead of overwriting. Because a sync service cannot merge arbitrary file formats, the client keeps both: the first edit stays as the file, the second is saved alongside as a "conflicted copy", the device downloads the winning version, and both files sync to every device for the user to reconcile. Last write wins would silently lose one edit, device clocks are not used to decide, and version history can still recover older versions.

sdsd:17.04.q: How do you store 10M metric series cheaply and still query the last hour fast?
sdsd:17.04.s: Compress each series Gorilla-style: delta-of-delta encoding for timestamps (regular intervals cost about 1 bit) and XOR of consecutive values for floats, about 1.4 bytes per point instead of 16. Keep the most recent hours as compressed in-memory chunks sharded by series and protected by a write-ahead log, so last-hour queries and alert rules hit RAM (about 5 GB for 10 million series at 10-second resolution). Flush older data as immutable, compacted blocks with a label index to disk and object storage, downsample them into 1-minute and 1-hour rollups keeping min, max, sum and count, and delete beyond retention. Keep label cardinality bounded, since every label combination is another series.

sdsd:17.05.q: Move a 2 TB table to a new database with zero downtime. List the phases.
sdsd:17.05.s: 1. Create the new table and put read and write targets behind feature flags. 2. Start capturing all changes to the new database, by dual writes or by change data capture from the old database's log. 3. Backfill existing rows in throttled, resumable batches by key range, using guarded upserts so a stale copy never overwrites newer data that arrived through step 2. 4. Verify with counts and checksums per key range and re-copy any range that differs. 5. Shadow-read both databases on live traffic and compare until mismatches are zero or explained. 6. Switch reads to the new database, keeping writes on both. 7. Switch writes, with a brief pause until CDC lag is zero or an atomic cut-over, optionally keeping reverse replication for rollback. 8. Keep the old table as a fallback for days or weeks, then remove it and the migration code.

sdsd:17.06.q: Walk through a photo upload from phone to followers' feeds.
sdsd:17.06.s: The app asks the posts service for a presigned URL and uploads the photo directly to object storage, so API servers never handle the bytes. An object-created event triggers media workers that validate the file and generate thumbnails and sized WebP or AVIF variants, stored under predictable keys and served via the CDN. The app finalises this post with a caption; the posts service stores it once with a time-sortable ID and publishes a post-created event. The fan-out service reads the poster's followers in batches, and workers push this post ID onto each follower's feed list in Redis (trimmed to a few hundred), unless the poster is a celebrity, whose posts are merged in at read time. When a follower opens the app, the feed service reads their list, merges celebrity posts, hydrates the posts and authors from caches, and returns CDN URLs that the phone loads from the nearest edge.

sdsd:18.01.q: Which boring choices let a team of 3 serve millions of users?
sdsd:18.01.s: They used well-understood, mostly managed technology so three engineers could run it: Amazon EC2 and load balancers instead of their own hardware; stateless Django app servers that scaled by adding machines; PostgreSQL with streaming replicas, later sharded into thousands of logical shards (schemas) on a few servers, with 64-bit time-sortable IDs (41 bits of time, 13 bits of shard, 10 bits of sequence) generated by a function inside PostgreSQL instead of a separate ID service; photos on S3 served via CloudFront so app servers never handled image bytes; Redis for feeds and sessions; memcached for caching; a task queue for slow work such as fan-out; and monitoring and paging from the start. Each piece did one job and had known failure modes.

sdsd:18.02.q: What does Stripe store per idempotency key, and for how long?
sdsd:18.02.s: Per key, scoped to the account by a unique index on account plus key, the server stores the original request's method, path and parameters (to reject a reuse with different parameters), a lock while a request is working on it (a concurrent duplicate gets 409 Conflict), the progress so far as a recovery point, and once finished the response status code and body, which are returned unchanged to every retry. Stripe saves the first result of a request that started executing whether it succeeded or failed, including 500s; requests rejected before executing save nothing. Keys are short-lived: Stripe prunes them after they are at least 24 hours old, after which the same value counts as a new key; a typical implementation lets a reaper delete them at about 72 hours so stranded requests can still be completed after a weekend.

sdsd:18.03.q: Why partition messages by (channel_id, time bucket)?
sdsd:18.03.s: Every query reads messages from one channel in time order, so channel_id in the partition key keeps a channel's messages together on one replica set and contiguous on disk, making "latest messages in this channel" a single sequential read, with message_id (a time-sortable Snowflake) as the clustering key giving newest-first order. But a busy channel's partition would grow without bound, and Cassandra partitions over about 100 MB hurt compaction and garbage collection and cannot be spread across nodes. Adding a time bucket (about 10 days, computed from the Snowflake timestamp, so no lookup is needed) caps each partition's size while keeping messages in order; older history is read bucket by bucket. The trade-off is that live reads for hot channels concentrate on the newest bucket.
sdsd:18.03.t: How Discord stores trillions of messages

sdsd:18.04.q: What is hinted handoff, and what availability problem does it solve?
sdsd:18.04.s: Hinted handoff is how Dynamo keeps a write's quorum when some of the key's home nodes are down or unreachable. With a strict quorum, a W = 2 write fails if two of the three preference-list nodes cannot be reached; with a sloppy quorum the coordinator instead sends the replica to the next healthy node on the ring, tagged with a hint naming the intended owner. That stand-in stores it in a separate local store, counts towards W, and periodically checks the owner; once the owner recovers it delivers the replica and deletes its own copy. It solves availability during temporary failures, partitions and even data-centre outages, so the shopping cart stays always writeable and the data keeps N copies. It does not guarantee reads see the write, and if the stand-in dies the hint is lost, which is why Merkle-tree anti-entropy repairs longer-lasting divergence.

sdsd:18.05.q: List the backup failures GitLab found. Which single practice would have caught them?
sdsd:18.05.s: The failures: pg_dump backups to S3 were empty because the job ran pg_dump 9.2 against PostgreSQL 9.6; the cron failure emails were silently rejected because DMARC was not configured, so nobody knew; Azure disk snapshots were enabled for the NFS servers but not the database servers; replication copied the problem and the secondary had been wiped during the rebuild anyway, with no WAL archive to fall back on; and LVM snapshots existed only for refreshing staging, so the best restore point was a 6-hour-old manual one on throttled disks that took about 18 hours to copy, losing about 5,000 projects, 5,000 comments and 700 accounts. The single practice that would have caught all of them is regularly restoring backups, automated and verified against production, with an alert that fires when no successful restore has been reported recently rather than only when a failure is reported.
